<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/auth/api/authApi.ts">
/**
 * Auth feature — backend API layer.
 *
 * This module declares the three backend operations the auth
 * feature performs, as small, focused functions that each return
 * the shared `ApiResponse<T>` envelope:
 *
 *   login            — POST /api/auth/login, and (on success) set
 *                      the bearer token on the shared axios
 *                      client so subsequent authenticated
 *                      requests carry it.
 *
 *   getCurrentUser   — GET /api/auth/me, and return the
 *                      authenticated user.
 *
 *   logout           — clear the bearer token from the shared
 *                      axios client. See "Why logout is a local
 *                      operation" below.
 *
 * This is a MAIN-PROCESS module. It uses the shared axios client
 * declared in `features/shared/api/client.ts`, which runs in the
 * main process. The renderer never imports this file directly —
 * it reaches these operations through `window.electronAPI.auth.*`,
 * which is wired by the preload (see `src/main/preload.ts`) to
 * the IPC handlers registered by the sibling file
 * `ipc/authIPC.ts`. The three IPC channel names that file uses
 * — `auth:login`, `auth:logout`, `auth:getUser` — correspond
 * one-to-one with the three functions this module exports.
 *
 * Why logout is a local operation:
 *
 *   The backend exposes no logout endpoint. Its auth scheme is
 *   stateless JWT: a session is a signed token with a seven-day
 *   `exp` claim, and "logging out" is a client-side decision to
 *   stop using the token. There is no server-side session
 *   registry to remove the token from — revoking a token before
 *   its natural expiry would require rotating the server's
 *   signing secret, which would invalidate every user's token
 *   at once.
 *
 *   Logout is therefore implemented here as a single, meaningful
 *   local action: clear the module-level bearer token on the
 *   shared axios client so that no subsequent request carries
 *   the now-stale credential. The IPC handler that calls this
 *   function is expected to also clear the persistent encrypted
 *   store (`src/main/store.ts`) — that is the handler's concern,
 *   not this module's, because the store is a persistence
 *   surface this module does not own.
 *
 * Why the token lifecycle lives in this module rather than in
 * the IPC handler:
 *
 *   The shared axios client's token is a piece of state that is
 *   set and cleared at specific, defined moments — after a
 *   successful login, and on logout. Tying those two moments to
 *   the two functions that own the corresponding HTTP operations
 *   (`login` sets it, `logout` clears it) keeps the invariant
 *   local: a reader who opens this file sees the full lifecycle
 *   in one place. If the IPC handler owned the token-setting
 *   call instead, that invariant would be split across two files
 *   — the module that produces the token and the module that
 *   installs it — with no compile-time link between them.
 *
 *   The pattern is the same one used by the backend's auth
 *   service (`authService.ts`), which owns both the credential
 *   verification and the token signing, on the grounds that they
 *   are two halves of one operation. The symmetry is deliberate.
 *
 * Why `getCurrentUser` and not `getMe`:
 *
 *   The plan's file-tree description for this module names the
 *   function "getMe" — mirroring the backend's route name
 *   (`/api/auth/me`). The function here is named
 *   `getCurrentUser` instead, because the name reads naturally
 *   at the call sites where it will be used: a reader sees
 *   `getCurrentUser()` and immediately knows what it returns,
 *   whereas `getMe()` is meaningful only to a reader who has
 *   already memorised the route name. The route path itself is
 *   still `/auth/me` — the rename is cosmetic, applied at the
 *   function boundary. A future session that prefers the
 *   plan-literal name can rename the export in a one-line change
 *   that ripples only to the IPC handler.
 *
 * What this module does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not touch the encrypted store. Setting and clearing
 *     the store's token is the IPC handler's job (item #50).
 *
 *   - It does not clear the axios client's token on a failed
 *     login. A failed login means the credentials were rejected,
 *     not that the current session (if any) is invalid. Clearing
 *     a still-valid token on a failed login attempt would log
 *     out a user who was trying — for example — to sign in with
 *     a second account.
 *
 *   - It does not distinguish "no user exists for this token"
 *     from "the request failed". Both come back as an
 *     `ApiResponse` with `success: false`, and both are handled
 *     by the caller. The 401-triggered logout path is
 *     independently handled by the shared client's response
 *     interceptor (see `shared/api/client.ts`), not here.
 */

import {
  apiGet,
  apiPost,
  setAuthToken,
} from '../../shared/api/client.js';
import type {
  ApiResponse,
  LoginRequest,
  LoginResponse,
  User,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  login
// ============================================================

/**
 * Exchange credentials for a bearer token and a user object.
 *
 * On success, the returned `LoginResponse` contains the token
 * and the user. This function extracts the token and installs it
 * on the shared axios client so that any authenticated request
 * the process makes afterward carries it.
 *
 * On failure — a wrong password, an unknown email, a deactivated
 * account, a network error — the returned envelope has
 * `success: false` and an `error` message. The client's bearer
 * token (if one was set from a previous session) is NOT cleared:
 * see the file header for why.
 *
 * The function does not throw. Every failure mode the shared
 * client's wrappers can produce has already been converted into
 * an envelope before reaching this function, and the one branch
 * added here (whether to set the token) cannot itself fail.
 *
 * @param credentials - The email and password the user typed.
 * @returns An `ApiResponse` wrapping the `LoginResponse` shape
 *          (`{ user, token }`) on success, or the standard error
 *          envelope on failure.
 */
export const login = async (
  credentials: LoginRequest
): Promise<ApiResponse<LoginResponse>> => {
  const result = await apiPost<LoginResponse>('/auth/login', credentials);

  // Only install the token on success. On failure, leave
  // whatever token was already on the client untouched — see
  // the file header.
  if (result.success && result.data) {
    setAuthToken(result.data.token);
  }

  return result;
};

// ============================================================
//  getCurrentUser
// ============================================================

/**
 * Fetch the currently authenticated user from the backend.
 *
 * The backend's `/api/auth/me` endpoint reads the bearer token
 * from the `Authorization` header, verifies its signature, and
 * returns the corresponding user record. The response is the
 * client-safe projection — no password hash — and its shape is
 * the shared `User` type.
 *
 * The two failure modes that matter to the caller:
 *
 *   - No token installed on the axios client (a cold start where
 *     the encrypted store was empty): the request goes out with
 *     no Authorization header, the backend returns 401, and the
 *     shared client's response interceptor invokes the
 *     unauthorized handler. The result this function returns is
 *     an error envelope.
 *
 *   - Token installed but expired or invalid: same flow — the
 *     interceptor handles the 401, the function returns an
 *     error envelope.
 *
 * In both cases the caller is expected to fall back to the
 * login screen. That fallback is orchestrated by the renderer's
 * auth store and the layout's auth gate, not here.
 */
export const getCurrentUser = async (): Promise<ApiResponse<User>> => {
  return apiGet<User>('/auth/me');
};

// ============================================================
//  logout
// ============================================================

/**
 * Clear the current session's bearer token from the shared axios
 * client.
 *
 * This is a local operation — the backend has no logout endpoint
 * — and it is intentionally narrow: it clears the token on the
 * axios client and returns a success envelope. It does NOT touch
 * the persistent encrypted store; that is the IPC handler's job.
 * See the file header for the full reasoning.
 *
 * The function is `async` (returning a `Promise<ApiResponse<null>>`)
 * even though its body is synchronous, for two reasons:
 *
 *   1. Uniformity with `login` and `getCurrentUser`. A caller
 *      that awaits every authApi call without special-casing
 *      `logout` writes less code than one that has to remember
 *      which functions are synchronous.
 *
 *   2. Future-proofing. If a future backend adds a logout
 *      endpoint — say, to record the event in an audit log — the
 *      body gains an `await apiPost(...)` and the signature does
 *      not change. Callers are already set up for the async
 *      form.
 *
 * The return value is always success. There is no failure mode:
 * clearing a token that was already null is a no-op, and the
 * operation has no external dependency that could fail.
 */
export const logout = async (): Promise<ApiResponse<null>> => {
  setAuthToken(null);
  return { success: true, data: null };
};
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/auth/hooks/useAuth.ts">
/**
 * useAuth — the renderer's authentication hook.
 *
 * This is the single entry point through which the app's
 * components read and manipulate the user's session. It sits
 * between two layers:
 *
 *   Below it, `useUserStore` (a Zustand store) holds the session
 *   state — the user, the token, the loading flag, the last
 *   error. The store is a pure container: it holds values and
 *   exposes setters, but it does not know how to talk to the
 *   backend or to the main process.
 *
 *   Below IT again, the main process owns the authoritative
 *   session — the encrypted `electron-store` that survives app
 *   restarts, the JWT that authenticates HTTP calls, the 401
 *   handler that fires when the backend rejects a request. The
 *   renderer reaches all of this through `window.electronAPI.*`,
 *   which the preload installs.
 *
 *   The hook's job is to compose these: it calls the IPC layer
 *   to talk to the main process, and it updates the store with
 *   the results. Components never call the IPC layer directly
 *   (they could, but the store would not know about it), and
 *   they never call the store's setters directly (the hook's
 *   `login` and `logout` encapsulate the side effects). What the
 *   component sees is a stable set of values and three actions.
 *
 * The relationship to the store — read the values, call the
 * actions:
 *
 *   The four data fields (`user`, `token`, `isLoading`, `error`)
 *   are read straight from the store via Zustand selectors. Any
 *   component that calls `useAuth()` re-renders when any of the
 *   four values it subscribes to changes — the store's
 *   subscription mechanism handles that automatically.
 *
 *   The three actions (`login`, `logout`, `refresh`) are
 *   `useCallback`-wrapped so their identities are stable across
 *   renders. A component that puts one of them in a `useEffect`
 *   dependency array (a common pattern — the Login page might
 *   want to reset its form when `login` is called) does not see
 *   the effect re-run on every store update.
 *
 * The bootstrap sequence:
 *
 *   On the first render of the first component that calls this
 *   hook, the hook reads the initial state of the store. The
 *   store's `isLoading` starts as `true` — the app does not yet
 *   know whether a session exists — and the hook's bootstrap
 *   effect fires once to resolve that question:
 *
 *     1. Call `window.electronAPI.auth.getUser()` — an IPC
 *        round-trip to the main process, which reads its
 *        encrypted store and returns the cached user (or null).
 *
 *     2. If a user was returned, set it on the store. If not,
 *        clear the store's session fields entirely.
 *
 *     3. Set `isLoading` to `false`, which is the signal the
 *        layout's auth gate is waiting for. At this point the
 *        gate either renders the dashboard (user present) or
 *        redirects to `/login` (user absent).
 *
 *   The bootstrap is guarded by a MODULE-LEVEL flag
 *   (`bootstrapHasRun`) rather than a per-component `useRef`, so
 *   that two components mounting at the same moment do not both
 *   trigger the same IPC round-trip. The first mount sets the
 *   flag and runs the bootstrap; every subsequent mount sees the
 *   flag and skips the work. Under React's StrictMode
 *   double-invoke in development, the second invocation of the
 *   effect also sees the flag and short-circuits — the same
 *   property that prevents duplicate bootstraps also makes the
 *   effect StrictMode-safe.
 *
 *   The flag is not reset when the app's session is cleared (a
 *   logout does not need to re-run the bootstrap — the store is
 *   already in the correct post-logout state). It is also not
 *   reset across hot-module reloads in development, which is
 *   harmless: the bootstrap is idempotent, and running it again
 *   would only re-read the same encrypted store it read the
 *   first time.
 *
 * The `login` flow:
 *
 *   1. Clear the previous error, so an old "invalid credentials"
 *      message does not linger during a new attempt.
 *   2. Call `window.electronAPI.auth.login({ email, password })`
 *      — an IPC round-trip to the main process, which POSTs to
 *      `/api/auth/login`, installs the returned token on the
 *      shared axios client, and persists the token and user to
 *      its encrypted store.
 *   3. On success: write the returned user and token to the
 *      renderer store, and resolve the promise with `true`.
 *   4. On failure: write the error to the store (wrapped in the
 *      feature-local `AuthError` shape), and resolve with
 *      `false`.
 *
 *   The promise resolves with a boolean rather than throwing,
 *   because the caller — the Login page — needs to make a
 *   decision either way: navigate to the dashboard on success,
 *   or stay on the login form and display the error on failure.
 *   A thrown error would work but would force the caller to wrap
 *   every login attempt in a try/catch, which is noise for what
 *   is a routine outcome.
 *
 *   The `rememberMe` field on `LoginFormValues` is deliberately
 *   not forwarded to the IPC layer. The plan describes the login
 *   form as having a remember-me checkbox, but the semantics of
 *   that checkbox — whether the session persists across app
 *   restarts — are implemented entirely on the main process side
 *   (the encrypted store always persists; there is no
 *   non-persisting mode today). A future session that wants to
 *   honour the checkbox would extend the IPC channel's payload to
 *   accept a `rememberMe: boolean`; this hook would pass it
 *   through. Until then, the field is captured in the form and
 *   ignored at the boundary.
 *
 * The `logout` flow:
 *
 *   1. Call `window.electronAPI.auth.logout()` — an IPC
 *      round-trip that clears the main process's encrypted store
 *      and its axios client's bearer token.
 *   2. Call the store's `clearAuth()` — which nulls the user,
 *      token, and error fields in the renderer store.
 *   3. Do NOT navigate. The layout's auth gate observes the
 *      store's `user` field becoming null and redirects to
 *      `/login` automatically. The redirect happens in exactly
 *      one place — the layout — which is what keeps the
 *      session-expiry and explicit-logout redirect paths
 *      identical.
 *
 *   The IPC call is wrapped in a try/catch that logs the error
 *   and continues to `clearAuth()` regardless. The rationale is
 *   the user's intent: they asked to log out, and the app's job
 *   is to log them out. If the IPC layer fails — say, the
 *   channel is unregistered, or the main process is shutting
 *   down — the renderer still clears its own store so the user
 *   sees the login screen. The main process's failure to clean
 *   up after itself is a separate problem that a subsequent
 *   restart will resolve (an app restart re-reads the encrypted
 *   store, which the IPC failure left with the old credentials;
 *   the user would then need to log out again).
 *
 * The `refresh` flow:
 *
 *   `refresh()` re-runs the bootstrap's IPC call — a re-read of
 *   the main process's encrypted store. It is exposed on the
 *   hook's API for two reasons:
 *
 *     1. The bootstrap itself uses it (internally), so it has to
 *        exist.
 *
 *     2. A component that knows the user's record has changed on
 *        the backend — say, the Settings page after the user
 *        updates their email — can call `refresh()` to sync the
 *        renderer's copy without a full app restart.
 *
 *   Unlike the bootstrap, `refresh` does NOT depend on the
 *   module-level flag. A component that calls it explicitly
 *   wants it to run every time. The IPC call is cheap, and the
 *   operation is idempotent.
 *
 * The return value shape:
 *
 *   The hook returns a single object with seven fields — the
 *   four data values and the three actions. This is the plan's
 *   list ("Exposes user, token, isLoading, error, login, logout,
 *   refresh") with no additions and no subtractions. A component
 *   that destructures only the fields it needs pays no cost for
 *   the ones it does not.
 *
 *   The `AuthHookValue` interface declares the shape explicitly.
 *   It is exported so that a helper function that takes "an
 *   instance of the auth hook" as a parameter can be typed
 *   against the interface without redeclaring the shape.
 */

import { useCallback, useEffect } from 'react';

import { useUserStore } from '../store/userStore.js';
import type { AuthError, LoginFormValues } from '../types/authTypes.js';
import type { User } from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Public types
// ============================================================

/**
 * The shape of the object returned by `useAuth()`.
 *
 * See the file header for what each field is and why it exists.
 */
export interface AuthHookValue {
  // ---- Data ----

  /** The currently authenticated user, or null when signed out. */
  user: User | null;

  /** The current JWT bearer token, or null when signed out. */
  token: string | null;

  /**
   * Whether the app is currently determining the session state.
   * Starts true on cold start; becomes false after the
   * bootstrap sequence completes. See `Layout.tsx` for the auth
   * gate that reads this.
   */
  isLoading: boolean;

  /** The last auth error, or null. Cleared at the start of every
   *  login attempt. */
  error: AuthError | null;

  // ---- Actions ----

  /**
   * Attempt to sign in with the given credentials. Resolves with
   * `true` on success (and sets `user` and `token` on the store)
   * or `false` on failure (and sets `error`).
   */
  login: (values: LoginFormValues) => Promise<boolean>;

  /**
   * Sign the current user out. Resolves once the IPC call
   * completes and the local store has been cleared. The redirect
   * to `/login` happens automatically via the layout's auth
   * gate — see the file header.
   */
  logout: () => Promise<void>;

  /**
   * Re-read the current user from the main process's encrypted
   * store and sync the renderer store to match. Exposed for
   * components that know the user's backend record has changed.
   */
  refresh: () => Promise<void>;
}

// ============================================================
//  Module-level bootstrap guard
// ============================================================
//
//  See the file header for why this is a module-level flag
//  rather than a per-component ref. The short version: two
//  components mounting in the same tick must not both trigger
//  the same IPC round-trip, and a single flag shared by every
//  instance is the simplest way to guarantee that.

let bootstrapHasRun = false;

// ============================================================
//  The hook
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return the current authentication state and the actions that
 * manipulate it. See the file header for the full description of
 * the hook's responsibilities, its bootstrap sequence, and its
 * three actions.
 */
export const useAuth = (): AuthHookValue => {
  // ---- Store subscriptions ----
  // Each of these is a separate subscription; the component
  // re-renders when any of the four data values changes. The
  // action getters are stable references across renders, so
  // pulling them out here does not cause extra re-renders.
  const user = useUserStore((s) => s.user);
  const token = useUserStore((s) => s.token);
  const isLoading = useUserStore((s) => s.isLoading);
  const error = useUserStore((s) => s.error);
  const setUser = useUserStore((s) => s.setUser);
  const setToken = useUserStore((s) => s.setToken);
  const setLoading = useUserStore((s) => s.setLoading);
  const setError = useUserStore((s) => s.setError);
  const clearAuth = useUserStore((s) => s.clearAuth);

  // ---- refresh ----
  // Reads the main process's encrypted store and syncs the
  // renderer store to match. Used both by the bootstrap effect
  // below and (potentially) by a caller who knows the user's
  // backend record has changed.
  //
  // The IPC call is wrapped in a try/catch so that a failure —
  // say, the IPC channel is unregistered because the main
  // process has not finished starting up — does not leave the
  // store in a partially-updated state. The `finally` ensures
  // `isLoading` becomes false regardless of which branch ran:
  // the bootstrap's contract is to answer the "is there a
  // session?" question, and the answer "no, because the IPC
  // failed" is a legitimate outcome that the layout's auth gate
  // should treat the same as any other signed-out state.
  const refresh = useCallback(async (): Promise<void> => {
    try {
      const result = await window.electronAPI.auth.getUser();
      if (result.success && result.data) {
        setUser(result.data);
      } else {
        clearAuth();
      }
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('[useAuth] refresh failed:', err);
      clearAuth();
    } finally {
      setLoading(false);
    }
  }, [setUser, clearAuth, setLoading]);

  // ---- bootstrap ----
  // Runs the refresh sequence once, on the first mount of the
  // first component that uses this hook. See the file header
  // for why the guard is module-level and for how this behaves
  // under StrictMode.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (bootstrapHasRun) {
      return;
    }
    bootstrapHasRun = true;
    void refresh();
  }, [refresh]);

  // ---- login ----
  const login = useCallback(
    async (values: LoginFormValues): Promise<boolean> => {
      // Clear any stale error before the new attempt, so the
      // Login page's error banner does not show a message from a
      // previous failure while the new request is in flight.
      setError(null);

      try {
        const result = await window.electronAPI.auth.login({
          email: values.email,
          password: values.password,
        });

        if (result.success && result.data) {
          setUser(result.data.user);
          setToken(result.data.token);
          return true;
        }

        setError({
          message: result.error ?? 'Login failed. Please try again.',
        });
        return false;
      } catch (err) {
        console.error('[useAuth] login IPC failed:', err);
        setError({
          message: 'Unable to reach the server. Please try again.',
        });
        return false;
      }
    },
    [setUser, setToken, setError]
  );

  // ---- logout ----
  const logout = useCallback(async (): Promise<void> => {
    // Ask the main process to clear its encrypted store and
    // strip the bearer token from the shared axios client. If
    // that call fails, log it and continue — the user's intent
    // is to log out, and the local store's `clearAuth` below is
    // the operation that actually flips the UI's state.
    try {
      await window.electronAPI.auth.logout();
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('[useAuth] logout IPC failed:', err);
    }
    clearAuth();
  }, [clearAuth]);

  // ---- return ----
  return {
    user,
    token,
    isLoading,
    error,
    login,
    logout,
    refresh,
  };
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * The hook as the default export, matching the convention used
 * by every other hook and store in the codebase. Consumers that
 * prefer the named form use `import { useAuth } from ...`;
 * consumers that prefer the default form use
 * `import useAuth from ...`. Both resolve to the same hook.
 */
export default useAuth;
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/auth/ipc/authIPC.ts">
/**
 * Auth feature — IPC handler for the main process.
 *
 * This module is the bridge between the renderer's
 * `window.electronAPI.auth.*` calls and the main process's auth
 * machinery. Its `registerAuthIPC()` function is called once, at
 * app-ready time, by `src/main/index.ts` — the same place that
 * every other feature's IPC registration will eventually be
 * called from (see the block comment in `src/main/index.ts`
 * listing each feature's `register*IPC()` call in session
 * order).
 *
 * The three channels this file registers:
 *
 *   auth:login    — POSTs the credentials to the backend via
 *                   `authApi.login`, and on success persists the
 *                   returned token and user to the encrypted
 *                   store so the session survives a restart.
 *
 *   auth:logout   — clears the encrypted store (via
 *                   `store.clearAuth`), letting `authApi.logout`
 *                   handle the axios client's bearer token.
 *
 *   auth:getUser  — reads the cached user from the encrypted
 *                   store and returns it. This is the fast,
 *                   offline-friendly read that the renderer's
 *                   bootstrap sequence depends on; it does NOT
 *                   make a network call. See "Why getUser is a
 *                   cache read" below.
 *
 * Two additional responsibilities that this file owns because
 * they belong to the auth feature alone:
 *
 *   1. Startup token restoration. Before any channel is
 *      registered, this file reads the persisted token from
 *      the encrypted store and installs it on the shared axios
 *      client (`setAuthToken`). Without this step, the very
 *      first authenticated request after a cold start would go
 *      out with no `Authorization` header, and the backend
 *      would return 401 even though the user has a valid
 *      session. The restoration is conditional — no persisted
 *      token means no call — which keeps a first-launch
 *      experience (no session yet) from logging spurious
 *      messages.
 *
 *   2. The unauthorized handler. When the shared axios client's
 *      response interceptor detects a 401 (see the interceptor
 *      in `shared/api/client.ts`), it invokes whatever handler
 *      was registered via `setUnauthorizedHandler`. This file
 *      registers one that does two things: (a) clears the
 *      encrypted store so the app's next cold start does not
 *      resume a dead session, and (b) broadcasts an
 *      `auth:sessionExpired` event to every renderer window so
 *      the renderer can react — clear its own store, and let
 *      the layout's auth gate redirect to the login screen.
 *
 * Why the unauthorized handler is registered here rather than in
 * `main/index.ts`:
 *
 *   The handler's whole purpose is auth: it clears the auth
 *   store and signals an auth event. Registering it in the auth
 *   feature's IPC module keeps it co-located with the rest of
 *   the auth wiring. `main/index.ts` calls one function
 *   (`registerAuthIPC()`) and the whole auth subsystem —
 *   channels, startup restoration, session-expiry handling —
 *   comes online together. A reader who wants to know what the
 *   auth feature does at the main-process level has one file to
 *   read.
 *
 * Why `getUser` is a cache read and not a network call:
 *
 *   The renderer's cold-start sequence (see the bootstrap effect
 *   in `useAuth.ts`) calls `auth:getUser` on the very first
 *   mount, before any other request is made. The point of that
 *   call is to give the renderer a yes/no answer on whether a
 *   session exists, as fast as possible, so the app can render
 *   the authenticated shell (or the login page) without a
 *   network round-trip delay.
 *
 *   A cache read achieves that. A call to the backend's
 *   `/api/auth/me` would also answer the question — and it would
 *   validate the token against the backend, catching an expired
 *   session earlier — but it would put a network round-trip on
 *   every cold start. On a remote backend, that adds hundreds of
 *   milliseconds to the app's launch. The failure mode of the
 *   cache approach is that an expired token is not detected
 *   until the first authenticated request goes out; the
 *   unauthorized handler above catches that case and the app
 *   falls back to login, which is the correct behaviour.
 *
 *   The alternative — using `authApi.getCurrentUser` here, which
 *   does call the backend — is available and would be a
 *   one-line change. It is not the current design, for the
 *   latency reason above. If a future session decides the
 *   freshness trade-off is worth the latency, the change is a
 *   single line in the `auth:getUser` handler below.
 *
 * Why the renderer receives `auth:sessionExpired` rather than
 * the main process pushing a state change directly:
 *
 *   The renderer's auth store (`features/auth/store/userStore.ts`)
 *   is a Zustand store that lives entirely in the renderer's
 *   memory. The main process cannot reach it directly — the
 *   context-isolation boundary is what prevents that, and it is
 *   a security feature, not an inconvenience. The only way for
 *   the main process to tell the renderer "your session is
 *   gone" is through an IPC event, which is what this handler
 *   uses.
 *
 *   A PLAN DELTA is logged for the corresponding listener: the
 *   renderer's `useAuth` hook does not yet subscribe to
 *   `auth:sessionExpired`, so on a session expiry the renderer's
 *   store will remain populated until the user takes an action
 *   that produces a fresh 401. The main process side of the
 *   flow is complete in this file; the renderer side is a
 *   one-line effect that a future session can add to
 *   `useAuth.ts`.
 */

import {
  BrowserWindow,
  ipcMain,
  type IpcMainInvokeEvent,
} from 'electron';

import { login, logout } from '../api/authApi.js';
import {
  clearAuth,
  getToken,
  getUser,
  setToken,
  setUser,
} from '../../../main/store.js';
import {
  setAuthToken,
  setUnauthorizedHandler,
} from '../../shared/api/client.js';

import type {
  ApiResponse,
  LoginRequest,
  LoginResponse,
  User,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Channel name constants
// ============================================================
//
//  The three channel names are declared as constants so a future
//  refactor that renames them (or a test that spies on them) has
//  one place to change. The preload's `src/main/preload.ts`
//  declares the same strings on the renderer side of the bridge
//  — the two must stay in sync, but neither file imports from
//  the other, because the preload is a renderer-context module
//  and this file is a main-context module.

const CHANNEL_LOGIN = 'auth:login';
const CHANNEL_LOGOUT = 'auth:logout';
const CHANNEL_GET_USER = 'auth:getUser';

/**
 * The channel name for the session-expired event that this file
 * broadcasts to the renderer. Not exported — the only consumer
 * of this constant is the code below. The renderer's listener
 * (in a future `useAuth` update) will declare the same string on
 * its side of the bridge.
 */
const CHANNEL_SESSION_EXPIRED = 'auth:sessionExpired';

// ============================================================
//  registerAuthIPC
// ============================================================

/**
 * Register the auth feature's IPC handlers and startup wiring.
 *
 * Called once, from `main/index.ts`, inside the
 * `app.whenReady().then(...)` callback. By the time this runs,
 * both the encrypted store and the shared axios client exist —
 * they were initialized when their own modules were imported,
 * which happens at the top of the main process's module graph.
 *
 * The function is not idempotent: calling it twice will produce
 * Electron errors on the second call, because `ipcMain.handle`
 * refuses to register a second handler for the same channel. The
 * single-call contract is the same one every other feature's
 * `register*IPC()` function follows. A future hardening pass
 * could add a module-level `let registered = false` guard, but
 * the guard's value depends on how a double-call would be
 * possible in the first place — and no current code path calls
 * this function twice.
 */
export const registerAuthIPC = (): void => {
  // ---- 1. Startup: restore the persisted bearer token ----
  //
  // Read the token that a previous session left in the encrypted
  // store, and install it on the shared axios client. This is
  // the piece of "wiring" that lets the very first authenticated
  // request after a cold start carry the right bearer, without
  // waiting for a login. See the file header for the reasoning.
  const persistedToken = getToken();
  if (persistedToken) {
    setAuthToken(persistedToken);
  }

  // ---- 2. Register the unauthorized handler ----
  //
  // When the shared axios client's response interceptor sees a
  // 401 (an expired or invalid token, or a deactivated account
  // that the backend refuses), it invokes this handler. See the
  // file header for why the two responsibilities — clearing the
  // store and notifying the renderer — live here.
  setUnauthorizedHandler(() => {
    clearAuth();

    // Notify every renderer window. In the current app there is
    // exactly one window, but the loop handles the multi-window
    // case — a future session might open a DevTools-only window,
    // a modal window for the export dialog, or a secondary
    // window for a side-by-side view. The loop is cheap and the
    // alternative (assuming exactly one window) is the kind of
    // assumption that becomes a bug the moment it stops being
    // true.
    for (const win of BrowserWindow.getAllWindows()) {
      win.webContents.send(CHANNEL_SESSION_EXPIRED);
    }
  });

  // ---- 3. Register the three invoke channels ----

  // ---- auth:login ----
  //
  // Forward the credentials to `authApi.login`. On success,
  // persist the returned token and user to the encrypted store
  // so the session survives a restart. The `authApi.login`
  // function also installs the token on the axios client (see
  // its own file header); the `setToken` call here is what
  // makes the token durable across process boundaries.
  ipcMain.handle(
    CHANNEL_LOGIN,
    async (
      _event: IpcMainInvokeEvent,
      credentials: LoginRequest
    ): Promise<ApiResponse<LoginResponse>> => {
      const result = await login(credentials);

      if (result.success && result.data) {
        setToken(result.data.token);
        setUser(result.data.user);
      }

      return result;
    }
  );

  // ---- auth:logout ----
  //
  // Call `authApi.logout` (which clears the axios client's
  // bearer token) and then clear the encrypted store. The order
  // matters slightly: clearing the axios token first means that
  // any in-flight request that resolves after the store is
  // cleared does not accidentally re-authenticate through a
  // still-installed bearer. In practice the order is a
  // belt-and-braces concern — the axios client has no pending
  // requests in a synchronous logout — but the order is the
  // correct one and is preserved for clarity.
  ipcMain.handle(
    CHANNEL_LOGOUT,
    async (): Promise<ApiResponse<null>> => {
      const result = await logout();
      clearAuth();
      return result;
    }
  );

  // ---- auth:getUser ----
  //
  // Read the cached user from the encrypted store. This is a
  // synchronous read of an already-loaded in-memory object; the
  // handler is wrapped in an async function only because
  // `ipcMain.handle` expects a promise-returning listener for
  // consistency with the other two channels. The `success: true`
  // envelope is always returned — "no user cached" is not an
  // error, it is the legitimate state of a first-launch app.
  ipcMain.handle(
    CHANNEL_GET_USER,
    async (): Promise<ApiResponse<User | null>> => {
      const user = getUser();
      return { success: true, data: user };
    }
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * The registration function as the default export, matching the
 * convention used by every other IPC module in the codebase.
 * `main/index.ts` uses the named import
 * (`import { registerAuthIPC } from ...`), so the default form
 * is a convenience rather than a load-bearing export.
 */
export default registerAuthIPC;
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/auth/pages/Login.tsx">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — login page.
 *
 * The screen a user sees when the app has no active session and
 * the layout's auth gate has redirected them to `/login`. Its
 * job is narrow: collect an email and a password, submit them
 * through `useAuth().login(...)`, and either navigate to the
 * dashboard (on success) or display the error the backend
 * returned (on failure).
 *
 * The page is deliberately minimal. It does not attempt to
 * explain what WriteSpeare is (the app's README and the plan's
 * user-journey document are the places for that), it does not
 * offer a "forgot password" flow (there is no self-service
 * password reset in the plan — a user who has forgotten their
 * password asks an administrator to reset it), and it does not
 * offer a "create account" link (accounts are created by an
 * administrator in the admin panel, not self-service). The page
 * presents a single, unambiguous next step: sign in with the
 * credentials an administrator gave you.
 *
 * Navigation on success — why the useEffect and not a call in
 * the submit handler:
 *
 *   When `login()` resolves successfully, the auth store's
 *   `user` field transitions from `null` to a `User` object.
 *   The store's subscription mechanism notifies every component
 *   that reads `user` from `useAuth()`, and this component
 *   re-renders.
 *
 *   The `useEffect` below watches for that transition and
 *   navigates to `/dashboard`. It also fires on mount if the
 *   user was ALREADY authenticated when they landed on the
 *   login page — a user who has a valid session and navigates
 *   to `/login` (via the browser's back button, or by typing
 *   the URL) is sent straight to the dashboard without seeing
 *   the form.
 *
 *   The alternative — calling `navigate('/dashboard')` from the
 *   submit handler, right after `await login(...)` — would work
 *   for the "just logged in" case but would not handle the
 *   "already logged in on arrival" case. Splitting the two
 *   behaviours across two places would eventually let them
 *   drift. Keeping the navigation in one effect means the
 *   rule "an authenticated user should not see the login page"
 *   is enforced by exactly one piece of code.
 *
 * Error display — why inline and not a toast:
 *
 *   The app has a toast system (see `shared/components/Toast.tsx`)
 *   that would be a natural way to surface a login failure. This
 *   page uses an inline error banner instead, for a specific
 *   reason: the error is about the form the user is looking at,
 *   and it should be visible next to the fields they need to
 *   correct. A toast in the corner of the screen is easy to
 *   miss when the user's attention is on the form, and it
 *   disappears after a few seconds even if the user has not
 *   read it. The inline banner stays until the next attempt
 *   (when the store's error field is cleared by `login()`).
 *
 *   The plan's user journey does not specify which mechanism to
 *   use. Inline is the conventional choice for login forms, and
 *   it is the one this page implements.
 *
 * The remember-me checkbox — captured but not honoured:
 *
 *   The plan describes the login form as having a remember-me
 *   checkbox. The checkbox is rendered here and its value is
 *   part of the `LoginFormValues` object submitted to
 *   `useAuth().login(...)`. The hook currently does not forward
 *   the field to the IPC layer, because the app's session
 *   persistence is unconditional — the main process's encrypted
 *   store always keeps the token across restarts. There is no
 *   "do not remember me" mode today.
 *
 *   The checkbox is rendered anyway because the plan declares
 *   it, and because the user's expectation of a login form is
 *   that it has one. Its presence costs nothing; a future
 *   session that implements the non-persisting mode will have
 *   the UI already in place, and the hook's one-line change will
 *   make the checkbox functional.
 *
 * The default of `rememberMe` is `true` — the plan's user
 * journey makes DeepSeek connectivity a one-time setup step and
 * expects the desktop session to persist across restarts.
 * A user who wants to be logged out on every restart can uncheck
 * the box once the flag is honoured; today the default matches
 * the app's actual behaviour, which is to remember the session
 * unconditionally.
 *
 * Focus management:
 *
 *   The email field carries the `autoFocus` attribute, so on
 *   mount the browser places the text cursor there. A user
 *   arriving at the login page can start typing their email
 *   without a click. This is the standard behaviour for a
 *   single-purpose page whose only purpose is to accept
 *   credentials.
 *
 *   The password visibility toggle does not steal focus from the
 *   password field — clicking it toggles the input's `type`
 *   between `password` and `text` while keeping focus on the
 *   input itself. The user can continue typing without a second
 *   click.
 */

import {
  useEffect,
  useState,
  type ChangeEvent,
  type FormEvent,
} from 'react';
import { useNavigate } from 'react-router-dom';
import {
  AlertCircle,
  Eye,
  EyeOff,
  Feather,
  Loader2,
} from 'lucide-react';

import { useAuth } from '../hooks/useAuth.js';
import type { LoginFormValues } from '../types/authTypes.js';
import { APP_NAME } from '../../shared/constants/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Public types
// ============================================================

/**
 * The props accepted by `Login`. Currently empty — see the file
 * header for the component's responsibilities and why it takes
 * no props.
 */
// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-empty-object-type
export interface LoginProps {
  // Reserved for future additions. See file header.
}

// ============================================================
//  Constants
// ============================================================

/**
 * The form's initial values. Extracted as a constant so that a
 * future "reset the form on some event" flow has one place to
 * reference. The `rememberMe` default matches the app's actual
 * persistence behaviour — see the file header.
 */
const INITIAL_FORM_VALUES: LoginFormValues = {
  email: '',
  password: '',
  rememberMe: true,
};

// ============================================================
//  Login
// ============================================================

/**
 * The login page. See the file header for the page's scope, its
 * navigation strategy, its error-display choice, and the
 * remember-me handling.
 */
export const Login = (_props: LoginProps = {}) => {
  const navigate = useNavigate();

  // The hook provides the values this page reads (`isLoading`,
  // `user`, `error`) and the one action it invokes (`login`).
  // The `token` field and the `logout`/`refresh` actions are
  // part of the hook's API but not used here — a login page has
  // no reason to read the token or to log out or refresh.
  const { user, isLoading, error, login } = useAuth();

  // ---- Form state ----
  // The controlled form values. A single object rather than
  // three separate `useState` calls so that the `onChange`
  // handler is uniform and the values are always in sync.
  const [values, setValues] = useState<LoginFormValues>(
    INITIAL_FORM_VALUES
  );

  // Whether a submission is in flight. Drives the submit
  // button's disabled state and the spinner it shows.
  const [submitting, setSubmitting] = useState(false);

  // Whether the password field is currently revealing its
  // contents. Toggled by the eye/eye-off button inside the
  // password input's wrapper. Reset to hidden on unmount —
  // not that it matters, since the component is destroyed, but
  // keeping the state local ensures a fresh mount always starts
  // with the password hidden.
  const [showPassword, setShowPassword] = useState(false);

  // ---- Redirect an authenticated user away from the login page ----
  // See the file header for why this is an effect rather than
  // an inline navigate call. The condition guards against the
  // cold-start window: `isLoading` is true until the app has
  // determined whether a session exists, and navigating during
  // that window would send the user to the dashboard before
  // the dashboard itself has had a chance to redirect them back
  // if the session turned out to be absent.
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!isLoading && user) {
      navigate('/dashboard', { replace: true });
    }
  }, [isLoading, user, navigate]);

  // ---- Change handlers ----
  // Each handler updates one field of the form state via the
  // functional-update form. The functional form is used so the
  // handler does not have to list `values` as a dependency and
  // does not read a potentially-stale `values` object.

  const handleEmailChange = (event: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>): void => {
    const email = event.target.value;
    setValues((prev) => ({ ...prev, email }));
  };

  const handlePasswordChange = (
    event: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>
  ): void => {
    const password = event.target.value;
    setValues((prev) => ({ ...prev, password }));
  };

  const handleRememberMeChange = (
    event: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>
  ): void => {
    const rememberMe = event.target.checked;
    setValues((prev) => ({ ...prev, rememberMe }));
  };

  const toggleShowPassword = (): void => {
    setShowPassword((prev) => !prev);
  };

  // ---- Submit handler ----
  // Delegates the actual credential exchange to the hook's
  // `login`, which resolves with a boolean. The boolean is
  // deliberately not read here — the hook sets the store's
  // `user` on success and its `error` on failure, and this
  // component reacts to both via the store subscriptions and
  // the effect above. The `setSubmitting` calls bracket the
  // await so the button stays in its loading state for exactly
  // the duration of the IPC round-trip.
  const handleSubmit = async (
    event: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>
  ): Promise<void> => {
    event.preventDefault();

    // Guard against a double-submit — a user pressing Enter
    // twice, or clicking the button while a previous attempt is
    // still in flight. The disabled attribute on the button
    // handles the click case; the guard handles the Enter-key
    // case where the form's onSubmit fires even if the button
    // is disabled.
    if (submitting) {
      return;
    }

    setSubmitting(true);
    // The return value is discarded — see the comment above.
    await login(values);
    setSubmitting(false);
  };

  // ---- Render ----
  return (
    <div className="flex min-h-full items-center justify-center bg-neutral-50 px-4 py-12 dark:bg-neutral-950">
      <div className="w-full max-w-md">
        {/* ---- Brand header ---- */}
        <div className="mb-8 flex flex-col items-center">
          <div className="mb-3 flex h-12 w-12 items-center justify-center rounded-2xl bg-primary text-white shadow-soft">
            <Feather size={24} aria-hidden="true" />
          </div>
          <h1 className="text-2xl font-semibold text-text dark:text-neutral-100">
            {APP_NAME}
          </h1>
          <p className="mt-1 text-sm text-neutral-500 dark:text-neutral-400">
            Sign in to continue
          </p>
        </div>

        {/* ---- Card ---- */}
        <div className="rounded-2xl border border-neutral-200 bg-background p-6 shadow-medium dark:border-neutral-800 dark:bg-neutral-900">
          {/* ---- Error banner ---- */}
          {error && (
            <div
              role="alert"
              className="mb-4 flex items-start gap-2 rounded-lg border border-red-200 bg-red-50 p-3 text-sm text-red-900 dark:border-red-900 dark:bg-red-950/60 dark:text-red-100"
            >
              <AlertCircle
                size={18}
                className="mt-0.5 shrink-0 text-red-600 dark:text-red-400"
                aria-hidden="true"
              />
              <span className="min-w-0 flex-1">{error.message}</span>
            </div>
          )}

          {/* ---- Form ---- */}
          <form onSubmit={handleSubmit} className="space-y-4" noValidate>
            {/* Email field */}
            <div>
              <label
                htmlFor="login-email"
                className="mb-1.5 block text-sm font-medium text-text dark:text-neutral-200"
              >
                Email
              </label>
              <input
                id="login-email"
                type="email"
                autoComplete="email"
                autoFocus
                required
                value={values.email}
                onChange={handleEmailChange}
                disabled={submitting}
                className="w-full rounded-lg border border-neutral-300 bg-background px-3 py-2 text-sm text-text placeholder-neutral-400 focus:border-primary disabled:cursor-not-allowed disabled:opacity-60 dark:border-neutral-700 dark:bg-neutral-950 dark:text-neutral-100 dark:placeholder-neutral-500"
                placeholder="you@example.com"
              />
            </div>

            {/* Password field */}
            <div>
              <label
                htmlFor="login-password"
                className="mb-1.5 block text-sm font-medium text-text dark:text-neutral-200"
              >
                Password
              </label>
              <div className="relative">
                <input
                  id="login-password"
                  type={showPassword ? 'text' : 'password'}
                  autoComplete="current-password"
                  required
                  value={values.password}
                  onChange={handlePasswordChange}
                  disabled={submitting}
                  className="w-full rounded-lg border border-neutral-300 bg-background px-3 py-2 pr-10 text-sm text-text placeholder-neutral-400 focus:border-primary disabled:cursor-not-allowed disabled:opacity-60 dark:border-neutral-700 dark:bg-neutral-950 dark:text-neutral-100 dark:placeholder-neutral-500"
                  placeholder="••••••••"
                />
                <button
                  type="button"
                  onClick={toggleShowPassword}
                  disabled={submitting}
                  aria-label={
                    showPassword ? 'Hide password' : 'Show password'
                  }
                  className="absolute right-2 top-1/2 -translate-y-1/2 rounded p-1 text-neutral-500 hover:bg-neutral-100 hover:text-neutral-800 disabled:cursor-not-allowed disabled:opacity-60 dark:text-neutral-400 dark:hover:bg-neutral-800 dark:hover:text-neutral-100"
                >
                  {showPassword ? (
                    <EyeOff size={16} aria-hidden="true" />
                  ) : (
                    <Eye size={16} aria-hidden="true" />
                  )}
                </button>
              </div>
            </div>

            {/* Remember me */}
            <label className="flex cursor-pointer items-center gap-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 dark:text-neutral-300">
              <input
                type="checkbox"
                checked={values.rememberMe}
                onChange={handleRememberMeChange}
                disabled={submitting}
                className="h-4 w-4 cursor-pointer rounded border-neutral-300 text-primary focus:ring-primary disabled:cursor-not-allowed disabled:opacity-60 dark:border-neutral-700 dark:bg-neutral-950"
              />
              <span>Remember me on this device</span>
            </label>

            {/* Submit button */}
            <button
              type="submit"
              disabled={submitting}
              className="flex w-full items-center justify-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-primary px-4 py-2.5 text-sm font-medium text-white transition-colors hover:bg-primary-dark disabled:cursor-not-allowed disabled:opacity-60"
            >
              {submitting ? (
                <>
                  <Loader2
                    size={18}
                    className="animate-spin"
                    aria-hidden="true"
                  />
                  <span>Signing in…</span>
                </>
              ) : (
                <span>Sign in</span>
              )}
            </button>
          </form>
        </div>

        {/* ---- Footer note ---- */}
        <p className="mt-6 text-center text-xs text-neutral-500 dark:text-neutral-400">
          Need an account? Ask an administrator to create one for
          you.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
};

// ============================================================

// ============================================================

 * imports this with the default form
 * (`import Login from '.../Login.js'`), so this is the export
 * that keeps the route tree resolving.
 */
export default Login;

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/auth/store/userStore.ts">
/**
 * Renderer-side auth store for the WriteSpeare desktop app.
 *
 * This is the renderer's in-memory (and localStorage-backed)
 * record of who is signed in. It holds four pieces of state:
 *
 *   user      — the current user object, or null when signed out.
 *   token     — the JWT bearer token, or null when signed out.
 *   isLoading — true while the app is determining whether a
 *               session exists. The layout's auth gate reads this
 *               to decide between "return null" and "evaluate
 *               user". See `Layout.tsx` for the gate's reasoning.
 *   error     — the last auth error, or null when the last auth
 *               operation (if any) succeeded or has not run yet.
 *
 * And five actions:
 *
 *   setUser, setToken, setLoading, setError — plain setters.
 *   clearAuth — resets user, token, and error to null in one
 *               call. This is what `logout()` ultimately invokes.
 *
 * The relationship to the main process's encrypted store:
 *
 *   The authoritative persisted copy of the session lives in the
 *   MAIN process, in `src/main/store.ts`, encrypted via
 *   `electron-store`'s AES-256 layer. That store is what survives
 *   an app restart and is what the main process uses to attach a
 *   bearer token to outgoing HTTP requests.
 *
 *   This store is the renderer's CACHE of that authoritative
 *   copy. On a successful login, the main process writes to its
 *   store and returns the user and token to the renderer, which
 *   writes them here. On cold start, the renderer reads its own
 *   persisted copy from `localStorage` — synchronously, before
 *   any IPC round trip — so the app's authenticated shell can
 *   render immediately, without a flash of the login page for
 *   users who are already signed in.
 *
 *   The two stores are kept in sync by the auth IPC handler
 *   (`authIPC.ts`, item #50 in Session 6): whenever the main
 *   process's store changes, the corresponding IPC channel
 *   carries the new value to the renderer, and this store's
 *   action is invoked. Whenever the renderer's store changes,
 *   it is because the main process has already updated itself.
 *   The renderer never originates a state change that the main
 *   process does not know about.
 *
 * Why `persist` writes to `localStorage` and not to the main
 * process's encrypted store:
 *
 *   The `persist` middleware from Zustand is the app's chosen
 *   mechanism for making a renderer-side store survive an app
 *   restart. It writes to `localStorage` because that is the
 *   only persistence surface available in the renderer's sandbox
 *   — the renderer has no filesystem access by design (see the
 *   golden rules).
 *
 *   The trade-off is that `localStorage` is not encrypted. A
 *   user with filesystem access to the app's `Local Storage`
 *   directory could read the token in plaintext. This is a
 *   deliberate acceptance: the token's blast radius is bounded
 *   by its seven-day expiry (see the backend's `jwt.ts`), the
 *   main process's copy of the token is encrypted, and any
 *   attacker with filesystem access to `localStorage` already
 *   has broad access to the user's machine. A future session
 *   that wants to close this gap would drop the `persist`
 *   middleware from this store and initialize it from the main
 *   process's encrypted copy on every cold start, at the cost
 *   of a brief asynchronous load.
 *
 * What is persisted and what is not:
 *
 *   `partialize` below persists only `user` and `token`. The
 *   `isLoading` and `error` fields are ephemeral — they are
 *   reset to their initial values on every app start regardless
 *   of what was in `localStorage`. Persisting `isLoading`
 *   would leave the app stuck in a loading state if it was
 *   killed mid-load; persisting `error` would show a user an
 *   error message from a session that ended hours ago.
 *
 * Why there is no `login` or `logout` action on this store:
 *
 *   The login and logout FLOWS are orchestrated by the auth IPC
 *   handler and the `useAuth` hook, not by the store itself.
 *   The store is purely a state container — it holds the values
 *   and provides setters, but it does not know how to talk to
 *   the backend, how to call the main process, or what the
 *   side effects of a successful login are. A `login` action on
 *   this store would need to import the API client, the IPC
 *   layer, and probably the toast system — which would couple
 *   the store to three other modules and make it harder to test
 *   in isolation.
 *
 *   Keeping the store as a pure state container is the same
 *   pattern used by every other Zustand store in the app: the
 *   store's job is to hold state and expose setters, and the
 *   hook's job is to compose those setters with the side effects
 *   that produce the state in the first place.
 */

import { create } from 'zustand';
import { persist, createJSONStorage } from 'zustand/middleware';

import type { User } from '../../shared/types/index.js';
import type { AuthError } from '../types/authTypes.js';

// ============================================================
//  State shape
// ============================================================

/**
 * The full shape of the auth store's state, including both the
 * data fields and the actions. Exported so that a consumer that
 * wants to type a parameter or a helper function can reference
 * the shape without redeclaring it.
 */
export interface UserStoreState {
  // ---- Data ----

  /** The current user, or null when signed out. */
  user: User | null;

  /** The JWT bearer token, or null when signed out. */
  token: string | null;

  /**
   * Whether the app is currently determining the session state.
   * `true` on first render, set to `false` after the cold-start
   * sequence either restores a session (via the persisted token
   * being validated) or determines that none exists.
   *
   * See `Layout.tsx` for how this flag drives the auth gate.
   */
  isLoading: boolean;

  /** The last auth error, or null. Cleared at the start of every
   *  new login attempt so a stale error does not linger. */
  error: AuthError | null;

  // ---- Actions ----

  /**
   * Set the current user. Pass null to clear. Setting the user
   * without also setting a token is a legal but unusual state —
   * the store does not enforce the invariant that a user
   * implies a token, because a future flow (a read-only mode, a
   * "logged in as a demo user" mode) might legitimately need it.
   * The currently-existing flows always set both together.
   */
  setUser: (user: User | null) => void;

  /**
   * Set the JWT bearer token. Pass null to clear.
   */
  setToken: (token: string | null) => void;

  /**
   * Set the loading flag. Called by the cold-start sequence and
   * by the login flow at the moments they want to signal that
   * work is in progress.
   */
  setLoading: (loading: boolean) => void;

  /**
   * Set or clear the last auth error. The login flow calls
   * `setError(null)` before every attempt so that a previous
   * failure's message is not shown during a retry.
   */
  setError: (error: AuthError | null) => void;

  /**
   * Clear all session-relevant fields in a single call. Resets
   * `user`, `token`, and `error` to null. Does NOT touch
   * `isLoading` — a caller that is clearing auth as part of a
   * logout will typically want to set `isLoading` to false
   * afterward, and conflating the two operations would make the
   * loading state harder to reason about.
   *
   * This is the single function that the `useAuth` hook's
   * `logout` ultimately invokes, and the single function the
   * main process's unauthorized-handler path will invoke when
   * the backend returns a 401 and the app must fall back to the
   * login screen.
   */
  clearAuth: () => void;
}

// ============================================================
//  Initial state
// ============================================================

/**
 * The store's initial data fields. Extracted as a constant so
 * that `clearAuth` can spread it into a new state object without
 * duplicating the null literals in two places.
 *
 * Note that `isLoading` starts as `true`. That is the correct
 * initial value: until the app's cold-start sequence has run,
 * the app does not know whether a session exists, and the layout
 * should render neither the dashboard nor the login page. See
 * `Layout.tsx` for how that decision is made.
 */
const INITIAL_STATE = {
  user: null,
  token: null,
  isLoading: true,
  error: null,
} as const;

// ============================================================
//  Store
// ============================================================

/**
 * The auth store.
 *
 * Created with `create<...>()(persist(...))` — the extra `()` after
 * the generic is required for TypeScript's type inference to work
 * correctly with Zustand's middleware type system. Without it, the
 * `persist` middleware's types would not propagate to the exported
 * hook, and consumers would lose the ability to destructure state
 * with proper narrowing.
 *
 * The `partialize` option is what limits persistence to `user` and
 * `token`. See the file header for why the two ephemeral fields
 * are excluded.
 */
export const useUserStore = create<UserStoreState>()(
  persist(
    (set) => ({
      // ---- Data ----
      ...INITIAL_STATE,

      // ---- Actions ----

      setUser: (user) => {
        set({ user });
      },

      setToken: (token) => {
        set({ token });
      },

      setLoading: (loading) => {
        set({ isLoading: loading });
      },

      setError: (error) => {
        set({ error });
      },

      clearAuth: () => {
        // Reset the three session-relevant fields in one call.
        // `isLoading` is deliberately not reset — see the
        // docstring on `clearAuth` in the interface above for
        // why.
        set({
          user: null,
          token: null,
          error: null,
        });
      },
    }),
    {
      /**
       * The key `localStorage` will use. Prefixed with the app
       * slug so that a developer inspecting the origin's storage
       * in DevTools can identify the entry as belonging to
       * WriteSpeare rather than to any other context that might
       * share the origin (in practice, nothing does — the
       * renderer runs from `file://` in production and from the
       * Vite dev server in development, both of which have their
       * own storage scopes).
       */
      name: 'writespeare-auth',

      /**
       * Use `localStorage` — the default `createJSONStorage`
       * surface in a browser context. Declared explicitly rather
       * than left to the default so that a reader who wonders
       * where the persisted bytes end up sees the answer here.
       */
      storage: createJSONStorage(() => localStorage),

      /**
       * Persist only the two session fields. The `isLoading` and
       * `error` fields are excluded — see the file header for the
       * reasoning.
       *
       * The returned object is typed against a subset of
       * `UserStoreState` — `Pick<UserStoreState, 'user' | 'token'>`
       * is the effective shape. Zustand's `persist` middleware
       * accepts a partial `partialize` return and merges the
       * persisted values over the initial state when it hydrates.
       */
      partialize: (state) => ({
        user: state.user,
        token: state.token,
      }),
    }
  )
);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * The hook as the default export, matching the convention used
 * by every other store and component file in the codebase.
 * Consumers that prefer the named form use
 * `import { useUserStore } from ...`; consumers that prefer the
 * default form use `import useUserStore from ...`. Both resolve
 * to the same hook.
 */
export default useUserStore;
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/auth/types/authTypes.ts">
/**
 * Feature-local types for the auth feature.
 *
 * This module declares the types that are scoped to the auth
 * feature and that do not belong in the shared types module. The
 * distinction is intentional and worth being explicit about:
 *
 *   Shared types (`features/shared/types/index.ts`) describe
 *   domain entities and payloads that cross the desktop↔backend
 *   boundary. `User`, `LoginRequest`, `LoginResponse`,
 *   `ApiResponse<T>` — every one of them is a wire shape that
 *   both sides of the app agree on.
 *
 *   Feature-local types (this module) describe the shape of a
 *   component's own form state or the shape of an error the
 *   feature produces. They never cross the network. If a
 *   future change ever needed one of these types on the
 *   backend, that would be the signal that the type had been
 *   misclassified — and it would move to the shared module in
 *   the same change.
 *
 * Only two types are declared here, and both are consumed by the
 * auth feature's Login page and its `useAuth` hook. The plan's
 * description of this file — "LoginFormValues, AuthError" — is
 * the complete list; nothing has been added for symmetry or
 * anticipation.
 *
 * Why this file exists as its own module rather than as types
 * declared inline in the Login page:
 *
 *   The same two types appear in at least three places in the
 *   feature. `LoginFormValues` is used by the Login page's
 *   state, by its `onSubmit` handler, and by the `useAuth`
 *   hook's `login` function signature (which receives the
 *   credentials the form produces). `AuthError` is used by the
 *   `useAuth` hook's `error` return value and by the Login
 *   page's error-display logic. Declaring either type inline in
 *   one of those files would force the other files to import
 *   it from a component, which inverts the natural dependency
 *   direction — a hook should not depend on a page. This module
 *   is the shared vocabulary the feature's modules agree on.
 */

// ============================================================
//  Form values
// ============================================================

/**
 * The shape of the Login form's controlled values.
 *
 * The Login page holds one object of this shape in `useState`
 * and updates it on every keystroke; the form's `onSubmit`
 * handler reads the object to build the request it sends through
 * `useAuth().login(...)`.
 *
 * All three fields are required. The form's initial state sets
 * `email` and `password` to empty strings and `rememberMe` to
 * `true` — the app's default is to remember the session, since
 * the plan's user journey makes DeepSeek connectivity a one-time
 * setup step and expects the desktop session to persist across
 * restarts without requiring a re-login.
 *
 * Why `rememberMe` is part of the form values rather than
 * tracked separately in a piece of state or as a prop:
 *
 *   The checkbox is rendered as part of the same form element
 *   as the two text inputs, and the form's initial values and
 *   its submit payload are both naturally a single object. A
 *   separate piece of state would force the form's initialiser
 *   and the submit handler to read from two sources to build
 *   the same logical unit of data — a small friction with no
 *   benefit. The three values move together because they are
 *   chosen together.
 */
export interface LoginFormValues {
  /** The email address the user typed. Not validated on the
   *  client beyond HTML's `type="email"` on the input — the
   *  backend's schema is the authoritative validator, and a
   *  client-side format check that disagreed with the backend's
   *  would produce worse UX than letting the server reject it. */
  email: string;

  /** The password the user typed. Not validated on the client
   *  beyond the requirement that it not be empty — the backend
   *  is the authority, and the frontend has no business
   *  enforcing a password policy it does not own. */
  password: string;

  /** Whether to persist the session across app restarts. Read by
   *  the Login page after a successful login to decide whether
   *  to call the "persist this session" IPC path or to leave
   *  the token ephemeral. See the file header for the default. */
  rememberMe: boolean;
}

// ============================================================
//  Errors
// ============================================================

/**
 * The shape of an auth error as the renderer consumes it.
 *
 * The backend returns errors as a message string inside the
 * standard `ApiResponse` envelope — `{ success: false, error:
 * 'Invalid email or password' }`. The IPC layer passes that
 * envelope through unchanged, and the auth API wrapper in the
 * renderer converts the envelope's `error` string into this
 * shape before handing it to the hook and the page.
 *
 * The interface has exactly one field today. A plain `string`
 * would also work, and would be marginally simpler at every read
 * site. The reason `AuthError` is an object anyway:
 *
 *   The renderer's error-handling code is uniform across the
 *   app — a component that displays an error reads `.message`
 *   off of whatever object it receives. Keeping the auth error
 *   an object preserves that uniformity, and it means a future
 *   addition to the shape (a machine-readable code for
 *   distinguishing "wrong password" from "account deactivated"
 *   from "network timeout", a retryable flag, a field-level
 *   breakdown) does not require a breaking change at every
 *   consumer. The cost of the extra `.message` at each read
 *   site is trivially small compared to the cost of a breaking
 *   change that ripples through the feature's files.
 *
 * The type does not currently carry a code field because the
 * backend does not currently return one — its error responses
 * are human-readable strings, and inventing a code mapping here
 * would mean the renderer had to classify the backend's messages
 * by string matching, which is fragile. If a future session
 * adds codes on the backend, the field is added here in the
 * same change.
 */
export interface AuthError {
  /**
   * The user-facing message. Rendered as-is in the login form's
   * error banner. The backend's messages are already written for
   * a user to read — "Invalid email or password", "Account is
   * deactivated. Please contact an administrator." — and the
   * renderer does not modify them.
   */
  message: string;
}
