<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/shared/components/Toast.tsx">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — toast notification system.
 *
 * This module provides the app's toast notifications: brief,
 * non-blocking messages that appear in a corner of the window in
 * response to an action. A toast is what a component uses to say
 * "the topic was created", "the export failed", "the DeepSeek
 * session expired" — a message the user should see but that does
 * not warrant a modal dialog blocking their work.
 *
 * Two pieces compose the module:
 *
 *   `ToastProvider` — the context provider. Mounted once, at the
 *     root of the renderer's component tree (see `App.tsx`). It
 *     owns the toast state, renders the viewport, and exposes
 *     the imperative API to its descendants through a React
 *     context.
 *
 *   `useToast()` — the hook. A component calls it to obtain the
 *     API object, then calls `toast.success(...)`,
 *     `toast.error(...)`, or one of the other two variant
 *     methods to fire a toast. The hook is defined here and
 *     re-exported from `hooks/useToast.ts` so that a future
 *     refactor can move the implementation without touching the
 *     import site.
 *
 * Four variants — what each is for:
 *
 *   success — an action completed successfully. "Topic created",
 *             "Article exported to Documents", "Settings saved".
 *             Rendered with a green check icon. Never interrupts
 *             the user — the operation succeeded and the toast
 *             is confirmation, not alarm.
 *
 *   error   — an action failed. "Unable to reach the server",
 *             "Invalid credentials", "Export failed: permission
 *             denied". Rendered with a red X icon. Uses
 *             `role="alert"` and `aria-live="assertive"` so
 *             screen readers announce it immediately rather than
 *             at the next polite pause.
 *
 *   warning — an action succeeded but produced a caveat. "Saved
 *             — but the backend did not acknowledge the change".
 *             Rendered with an amber triangle icon.
 *
 *   info    — neutral information. "DeepSeek is now connected",
 *             "Source extraction started". Rendered with a blue
 *             circle-i icon.
 *
 * Auto-dismiss:
 *
 *   Every toast dismisses itself after a default duration of five
 *   seconds. The duration is overridable per toast — a caller
 *   that knows its message is more important than usual can pass
 *   `{ duration: 10000 }`. Passing `{ duration: 0 }` produces a
 *   toast that never auto-dismisses; the user must close it
 *   manually. That escape hatch exists for messages that demand
 *   acknowledgement, though the plan does not currently call for
 *   any.
 *
 *   Five seconds is long enough for a user reading at a normal
 *   pace to finish a short message, and short enough that the
 *   viewport does not accumulate a wall of toasts during a burst
 *   of activity. When more than five toasts are fired in rapid
 *   succession, the oldest is dropped to keep the viewport
 *   readable.
 *
 * Why the API is imperative and not declarative:
 *
 *   The alternative design — a `<Toast variant="success">`
 *   component a caller renders conditionally — would require the
 *   caller to manage the toast's lifecycle: mount it, keep it
 *   mounted until the duration elapses, then unmount it. Every
 *   caller would re-implement the timer, the animation, and the
 *   cleanup. The imperative API centralizes all of that in the
 *   provider: the caller writes one line, and the provider owns
 *   the toast from birth to dismissal.
 *
 *   The imperative form also matches how the caller usually
 *   wants to fire a toast — from the `.then()` or `.catch()` of
 *   an async operation, or from an event handler, where a
 *   declarative component would require extra state to track
 *   whether the toast is currently visible.
 *
 * Why the file uses `framer-motion` for animations and not CSS
 * transitions alone:
 *
 *   The `AnimatePresence` wrapper from framer-motion solves a
 *   problem that CSS transitions cannot: keeping a component
 *   mounted after it has been removed from the parent's state,
 *   so that its exit animation can play before the DOM node is
 *   destroyed. Without `AnimatePresence`, a CSS-only solution
 *   would require the provider to track a "dismissing" flag on
 *   every toast and remove it from state only after a
 *   `transitionend` listener fired. `AnimatePresence` is the
 *   standard solution to that problem, and it is already a
 *   dependency of the app (declared in `package.json`).
 *
 * Accessibility:
 *
 *   The viewport is a `region` with `aria-label` describing its
 *   purpose. Each toast carries a `role` and an `aria-live`
 *   value appropriate to its variant (see the variant table
 *   above). The close button has an `aria-label`. The toast
 *   content — title and message — is plain text, so a screen
 *   reader announces it without any additional markup.
 */

import {
  createContext,
  useCallback,
  useContext,
  useEffect,
  useMemo,
  useRef,
  useState,
  type ReactNode,
} from 'react';
import { AnimatePresence, motion } from 'framer-motion';
import {
  AlertTriangle,
  CheckCircle,
  Info,
  X,
  XCircle,
  type LucideIcon,
} from 'lucide-react';

// ============================================================
//  Public types
// ============================================================

/**
 * The four variants a toast can take. See the file header for
 * the semantic meaning of each.
 */
export type ToastVariant = 'success' | 'error' | 'warning' | 'info';

/**
 * Optional per-toast configuration. Every field is optional; a
 * caller that passes no options object gets the defaults
 * documented on the fields below.
 */
export interface ToastOptions {
  /**
   * An optional short title rendered in bold above the message.
   * Useful for a two-line toast — "Export failed" as the title,
   * "Permission denied for this folder" as the message. A caller
   * that omits it gets a single-line toast.
   */
  title?: string;

  /**
   * How long the toast stays visible, in milliseconds. Defaults
   * to `DEFAULT_DURATION` (5000 ms). Passing `0` produces a
   * toast that never auto-dismisses — the user must close it
   * manually.
   */
  duration?: number;
}

/**
 * The imperative API returned by `useToast()`. A caller obtains
 * an instance of this object once at the top of its component
 * and calls the variant methods whenever a toast needs to fire.
 *
 * The four variant methods all share the same signature —
 * `(message, options?)` — and all return the id of the toast
 * they created. The id can be passed to `dismiss` to close the
 * toast before its auto-dismiss timer fires; the typical reason
 * is that the operation the toast was reporting has been
 * resolved in the meantime (say, the user reconnected and the
 * "offline" toast is now misleading).
 */
export interface ToastAPI {
  success: (message: string, options?: ToastOptions) => string;
  error: (message: string, options?: ToastOptions) => string;
  warning: (message: string, options?: ToastOptions) => string;
  info: (message: string, options?: ToastOptions) => string;

  /**
   * Dismiss a single toast by its id. A no-op if the id is not
   * currently visible — the toast may have already auto-dismissed,
   * which is not an error.
   */
  dismiss: (id: string) => void;

  /**
   * Dismiss every visible toast. Used on logout (to clear any
   * session-scoped messages) and by the Settings page's "test
   * notifications" button.
   */
  clear: () => void;
}

// ============================================================
//  Internal types
// ============================================================

/**
 * The shape of a toast as the provider stores it. This is the
 * public shape plus an id and a resolved variant. The `title`
 * field appears here only when the caller supplied one; the
 * object is built with a conditional spread so that
 * `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is satisfied without assigning
 * `undefined`.
 */
interface ToastRecord {
  id: string;
  variant: ToastVariant;
  message: string;
  title?: string;
}

// ============================================================
//  Constants
// ============================================================

/**
 * The default duration of a toast, in milliseconds. See the file
 * header for why five seconds was chosen.
 */
const DEFAULT_DURATION = 5000;

/**
 * The maximum number of toasts visible at once. When a new toast
 * arrives and this many are already on screen, the oldest is
 * dismissed first. See the file header for the reasoning.
 */
const MAX_TOASTS = 5;

// ============================================================
//  Variant styles
// ============================================================
//
//  One entry per variant, holding the lucide icon used in the
//  toast and the two Tailwind class strings that give the
//  container and the icon their color treatment. Declaring this
//  as a `Record<ToastVariant, ...>` forces the compiler to
//  enforce exhaustiveness: adding a fifth variant to the
//  `ToastVariant` union without adding an entry here is a
//  compile error, which is exactly the desired failure mode.
//
//  The colors are the standard Tailwind semantic palettes
//  (emerald, red, amber, sky) rather than the app's brand
//  palette. Status colors are a semantic axis — the app's brand
//  palette is an identity axis — and mixing the two would make
//  the toasts look like they belong to a different design
//  system than the rest of the app. The brand palette is
//  reserved for the app's primary actions and surfaces; status
//  feedback uses the color the user already associates with the
//  status.

interface VariantStyle {
  icon: LucideIcon;
  containerClass: string;
  iconClass: string;
}

const VARIANT_STYLES: Record<ToastVariant, VariantStyle> = {
  success: {
    icon: CheckCircle,
    containerClass:
      'bg-emerald-50 border-emerald-200 text-emerald-900 ' +
      'dark:bg-emerald-950/60 dark:border-emerald-900 ' +
      'dark:text-emerald-100',
    iconClass: 'text-emerald-600 dark:text-emerald-400',
  },
  error: {
    icon: XCircle,
    containerClass:
      'bg-red-50 border-red-200 text-red-900 ' +
      'dark:bg-red-950/60 dark:border-red-900 ' +
      'dark:text-red-100',
    iconClass: 'text-red-600 dark:text-red-400',
  },
  warning: {
    icon: AlertTriangle,
    containerClass:
      'bg-amber-50 border-amber-200 text-amber-900 ' +
      'dark:bg-amber-950/60 dark:border-amber-900 ' +
      'dark:text-amber-100',
    iconClass: 'text-amber-600 dark:text-amber-400',
  },
  info: {
    icon: Info,
    containerClass:
      'bg-sky-50 border-sky-200 text-sky-900 ' +
      'dark:bg-sky-950/60 dark:border-sky-900 ' +
      'dark:text-sky-100',
    iconClass: 'text-sky-600 dark:text-sky-400',
  },
};

// ============================================================
//  Context
// ============================================================

/**
 * The React context that carries the toast API down the tree.
 *
 * The context's value is `ToastAPI | null` rather than
 * `ToastAPI` so that `useToast()` can distinguish "the hook was
 * called inside a `ToastProvider`" from "the hook was called
 * outside one" — a distinction that produces a clear error
 * message when the second case happens, rather than a null
 * dereference at the first method call.
 */
const ToastContext = createContext<ToastAPI | null>(null);

// ============================================================
//  useToast hook
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return the toast API from the enclosing `ToastProvider`.
 *
 * Throws when called outside a provider. The throw is
 * deliberate — a component that expects to fire toasts but is
 * somehow rendered outside the provider has a programming error
 * that would otherwise manifest as a silent "my toasts never
 * appear" bug. The error message names the hook and the
 * provider so the fix is obvious.
 *
 * Every consumer of this hook is a component that lives inside
 * the app's provider tree (which is the entire app, since
 * `ToastProvider` mounts at the root). The throw is therefore
 * unreachable in normal use; it exists to catch a refactor
 * mistake at the moment it happens, not to handle a runtime
 * condition.
 */
export const useToast = (): ToastAPI => {
  const ctx = useContext(ToastContext);
  if (!ctx) {
    throw new Error(
      'useToast() was called outside a <ToastProvider>. ' +
        'Make sure the component is rendered inside the app root.'
    );
  }
  return ctx;
};

// ============================================================
//  Toast item
// ============================================================

/**
 * Props for the internal `ToastItem` component. Not exported —
 * no consumer outside this module ever renders a toast item
 * directly; the provider renders them.
 */
interface ToastItemProps {
  toast: ToastRecord;
  onDismiss: (id: string) => void;
}

/**
 * Render a single toast. The container is a `motion.div` so
 * that `AnimatePresence` can play its enter and exit animations;
 * the `layout` prop tells framer-motion to animate the sibling
 * toasts' positions when this one is added or removed, which is
 * what produces the smooth "push down / pull up" effect when a
 * stack of toasts grows or shrinks.
 *
 * The toast's `role` and `aria-live` are chosen by variant:
 * errors interrupt (`role="alert"`, `aria-live="assertive"`);
 * the other three use the polite channel (`role="status"`,
 * `aria-live="polite"`). This is the same convention assistive
 * technology uses for form validation — a fatal error deserves
 * the user's immediate attention, a confirmation does not.
 */
const ToastItem = ({ toast, onDismiss }: ToastItemProps) => {
  const { icon: Icon, containerClass, iconClass } =
    VARIANT_STYLES[toast.variant];

  const isError = toast.variant === 'error';

  return (
    <motion.div
      layout
      initial={{ opacity: 0, x: 48 }}
      animate={{ opacity: 1, x: 0 }}
      exit={{ opacity: 0, x: 48 }}
      transition={{ duration: 0.2, ease: 'easeOut' }}
      role={isError ? 'alert' : 'status'}
      aria-live={isError ? 'assertive' : 'polite'}
      className={
        'pointer-events-auto flex items-start gap-3 rounded-xl ' +
        'border p-4 shadow-medium ' +
        containerClass
      }
    >
      <Icon size={20} className={`mt-0.5 shrink-0 ${iconClass}`} />

      <div className="min-w-0 flex-1">
        {toast.title !== undefined && (
          <p className="text-sm font-semibold leading-snug">
            {toast.title}
          </p>
        )}
        <p className="text-sm leading-snug break-words">
          {toast.message}
        </p>
      </div>

      <button
        type="button"
        onClick={() => onDismiss(toast.id)}
        aria-label="Dismiss notification"
        className={
          'shrink-0 opacity-60 transition-opacity hover:opacity-100 ' +
          'focus-visible:opacity-100'
        }
      >
        <X size={16} />
      </button>
    </motion.div>
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  Toast viewport
// ============================================================

/**
 * Props for the internal `ToastViewport` component.
 */
interface ToastViewportProps {
  toasts: readonly ToastRecord[];
  onDismiss: (id: string) => void;
}

/**
 * Render the stack of visible toasts in the fixed top-right
 * corner of the window.
 *
 * The container is `fixed` and uses `pointer-events-none` so
 * that the empty area around the toasts does not intercept
 * clicks on the underlying application UI. Each individual
 * toast re-enables pointer events on itself so its close button
 * and any interactive content is clickable.
 *
 * The `z-50` class places the viewport above every other element
 * in the app. Tailwind's default scale runs from `z-0` to
 * `z-50`; the app does not currently declare any stacking
 * context higher than this, so `z-50` is the topmost value the
 * viewport needs.
 *
 * `AnimatePresence` tracks its direct children by their `key`
 * prop. Each toast has a unique id as its key, so when the
 * provider removes a toast from the `toasts` array,
 * `AnimatePresence` keeps the corresponding `ToastItem`
 * mounted until its exit animation completes and then
 * unmounts it. The `initial={false}` option suppresses the
 * enter animation on the very first render — it does not
 * matter here since the toasts array is empty on mount, but
 * the option is set to make the intent explicit.
 */
const ToastViewport = ({ toasts, onDismiss }: ToastViewportProps) => {
  return (
    <div
      role="region"
      aria-label="Notifications"
      className={
        'pointer-events-none fixed right-4 top-4 z-50 ' +
        'flex w-full max-w-sm flex-col gap-2'
      }
    >
      <AnimatePresence initial={false}>
        {toasts.map((toast) => (
          <ToastItem key={toast.id} toast={toast} onDismiss={onDismiss} />
        ))}
      </AnimatePresence>
    </div>
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  Provider
// ============================================================

/**
 * The context provider that owns the app's toast state and
 * renders the viewport.
 *
 * Mounted once, at the root of the renderer's component tree
 * (see `App.tsx`). Everything below it can call `useToast()` to
 * fire toasts.
 *
 * State:
 *
 *   `toasts` — the visible toasts, in display order (oldest
 *     first). New toasts are appended and appear at the bottom
 *     of the viewport; the oldest sits at the top and is the
 *     first to be dropped when the stack overflows.
 *
 *   `timersRef` — a Map from toast id to the `setTimeout`
 *     handle that will auto-dismiss it. The Map is what allows
 *     `dismiss` to cancel a pending timer when the user closes
 *     a toast manually — without it, the timer would fire
 *     later, find the toast already gone, and produce a
 *     harmless but noisy state update. The ref (rather than a
 *     state variable) is correct here because the Map's
 *     contents are not part of any render — mutating it does
 *     not and should not trigger a re-render.
 *
 * Cleanup:
 *
 *   The `useEffect` with an empty dependency array installs a
 *   cleanup function that clears every pending timer when the
 *   provider unmounts. Without it, a timer that was still
 *   pending at unmount time would fire after the component
 *   tree was gone and produce a React warning about a state
 *   update on an unmounted component. The provider normally
 *   lives for the app's entire lifetime and never unmounts,
 *   but StrictMode's double-invocation in development — and
 *   any future test that mounts and unmounts the provider —
 *   makes the cleanup non-optional.
 *
 * The `api` object is memoized with `useMemo` so that its
 * identity is stable across renders. Consumers of `useToast()`
 * receive the same object reference on every render unless
 * one of the underlying callbacks changes. This matters because
 * a consumer that lists the `toast` object in a `useEffect`
 * dependency array (a common pattern for firing a toast when a
 * piece of state changes) would otherwise re-run its effect on
 * every render.
 */
export const ToastProvider = ({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) => {
  const [toasts, setToasts] = useState<ToastRecord[]>([]);
  const timersRef = useRef<
    Map<string, ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>>
  >(new Map());

  /**
   * Dismiss a toast by id — remove it from state and cancel its
   * pending auto-dismiss timer, if any.
   */
  const dismiss = useCallback((id: string) => {
    const timer = timersRef.current.get(id);
    if (timer !== undefined) {
      clearTimeout(timer);
      timersRef.current.delete(id);
    }
    setToasts((prev) => prev.filter((t) => t.id !== id));
  }, []);

  /**
   * The internal "add a toast" function. The four public variant
   * methods on the API all delegate to this one, passing their
   * variant as an argument. Centralizing the logic here means
   * the id-generation, the overflow-trimming, and the timer
   * installation happen in exactly one place.
   *
   * The id is generated from the current time plus a random
   * suffix. The time component is included for human readability
   * during debugging — two toasts fired in the same millisecond
   * would still be distinguished by the random suffix, so
   * collisions are effectively impossible in practice.
   */
  const add = useCallback(
    (
      variant: ToastVariant,
      message: string,
      options?: ToastOptions
    ): string => {
      const id = `${Date.now()}-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 9)}`;
      const duration = options?.duration ?? DEFAULT_DURATION;

      const record: ToastRecord = {
        id,
        variant,
        message,
        ...(options?.title !== undefined ? { title: options.title } : {}),
      };

      setToasts((prev) => {
        const next = [...prev, record];
        if (next.length <= MAX_TOASTS) {
          return next;
        }
        // Drop the oldest toasts and cancel their pending timers
        // — otherwise those timers would fire later against ids
        // that are no longer in the state, which is harmless but
        // produces noise in the console.
        const dropped = next.slice(0, next.length - MAX_TOASTS);
        for (const toast of dropped) {
          const timer = timersRef.current.get(toast.id);
          if (timer !== undefined) {
            clearTimeout(timer);
            timersRef.current.delete(toast.id);
          }
        }
        return next.slice(next.length - MAX_TOASTS);
      });

      if (duration > 0) {
        const timer = setTimeout(() => {
          setToasts((prev) => prev.filter((t) => t.id !== id));
          timersRef.current.delete(id);
        }, duration);
        timersRef.current.set(id, timer);
      }

      return id;
    },
    []
  );

  /**
   * Clear every visible toast and cancel every pending timer.
   * The public API exposes this as `toast.clear()`.
   */
  const clear = useCallback(() => {
    for (const timer of timersRef.current.values()) {
      clearTimeout(timer);
    }
    timersRef.current.clear();
    setToasts([]);
  }, []);

  /**
   * Clear all pending timers on unmount. See the component's
   * docstring for why this is required.
   */
  useEffect(() => {
    const timers = timersRef.current;
    return () => {
      for (const timer of timers.values()) {
        clearTimeout(timer);
      }
      timers.clear();
    };
  }, []);

  /**
   * The stable, memoized API object exposed to consumers. The
   * four variant methods are thin curried wrappers around the
   * `add` callback — they fix the variant and forward the
   * remaining arguments. The `dismiss` and `clear` methods are
   * exposed directly.
   */
  const api = useMemo<ToastAPI>(
    () => ({
      success: (message, options) => add('success', message, options),
      error: (message, options) => add('error', message, options),
      warning: (message, options) => add('warning', message, options),
      info: (message, options) => add('info', message, options),
      dismiss,
      clear,
    }),
    [add, dismiss, clear]
  );

  return (
    <ToastContext.Provider value={api}>
      {children}
      <ToastViewport toasts={toasts} onDismiss={dismiss} />
    </ToastContext.Provider>
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * Same component as the named export, provided for consumers
 * that prefer the default-import form. `App.tsx` uses the named
 * form (`import { ToastProvider } from ...`), so this default
 * is a convenience rather than a load-bearing export.
 */
export default ToastProvider;
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/shared/hooks/useToast.ts">
/**
 * Re-export shim for the `useToast` hook.
 *
 * The hook's implementation lives in `../components/Toast.tsx`,
 * alongside the `ToastProvider` React context it consumes. The
 * provider and the hook are two halves of one contract — the
 * provider creates the context, the hook reads it — and keeping
 * them in the same file makes that contract easy to see. The
 * alternative (splitting the context, the provider, and the hook
 * across three files) is a common React pattern, but it forces a
 * reader who wants to understand the toast system to open three
 * files and hold the pieces in their head simultaneously.
 *
 * Why this file exists at all:
 *
 *   The codebase has a convention: hooks live in a `hooks/`
 *   directory. Components live in a `components/` directory.
 *   A consumer that wants a hook imports it from `hooks/`; a
 *   consumer that wants a component imports it from
 *   `components/`. The convention gives every file in the
 *   shared feature a predictable location, and it means an
 *   import line tells a reader what kind of thing they are
 *   bringing in.
 *
 *   The `useToast` hook technically lives in `components/`
 *   because that is where its provider lives. That would be a
 *   small exception to the convention, and this shim exists to
 *   close the gap: consumers who want `useToast` import it
 *   from `hooks/useToast.js`, and the shim forwards to the
 *   implementation. The convention holds, and the implementation
 *   location stays where it makes sense.
 *
 * What this file is NOT:
 *
 *   It is not a wrapper. It does not add behaviour, does not
 *   memoize anything, does not rename the hook. It re-exports
 *   the same function object that `../components/Toast.js`
 *   exports. A caller that imports `useToast` from this file
 *   and a caller that imports it directly from
 *   `../components/Toast.js` receive the *same reference* — so
 *   there is no risk of context mismatch or duplicated state
 *   from the two paths.
 *
 *   It is not a place to add a "convenience" wrapper in the
 *   future. If a session ever needs a variant of the hook that
 *   behaves differently (say, one that fires a toast with a
 *   default duration, or one that only fires errors), that
 *   variant belongs in `components/Toast.tsx` next to the hook
 *   itself, and this shim adds it to the re-export list. The
 *   shim's job is to be a forwarding address, not a wrapper.
 *
 * Re-exporting the associated types:
 *
 *   The four types — `ToastAPI`, `ToastVariant`, `ToastOptions`,
 *   and the hook's return type — are declared alongside the hook
 *   in `components/Toast.tsx`. They are re-exported here for the
 *   same reason the hook itself is: a consumer that imports from
 *   `hooks/` should not have to make a second import from
 *   `components/` to get the types that describe what the hook
 *   returns. The `type` modifier on the three interface/union
 *   re-exports tells TypeScript to erase them at emit time, so
 *   the compiled shim contains no runtime reference to the
 *   component module beyond the function re-export.
 */

export { useToast } from '../components/Toast.js';
export type {
  ToastAPI,
  ToastVariant,
  ToastOptions,
} from '../components/Toast.js';
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/topics/hooks/useTopics.ts">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — topics hook.
 *
 * This is the renderer's single entry point for reading and
 * mutating the user's topics from a component. It is a thin
 * wrapper over `useTopicStore` (the Zustand store created in the
 * previous step), mirroring the shape and the role of `useAuth`
 * in the auth feature:
 *
 *   - The store owns the state. The hook does not add any.
 *
 *   - The store owns the async actions that reach the backend.
 *     The hook does not reimplement them or wrap them.
 *
 *   - The hook's only job is to give a component a single,
 *     stable object with everything the topics feature exposes —
 *     the four data fields and the seven actions. A component
 *     that wants the whole surface calls `useTopics()`; a
 *     component that wants one slice calls
 *     `useTopicStore((s) => s.topics)` directly, if it prefers.
 *
 * Why there is a hook at all, if the store's hook already
 * exposes everything:
 *
 *   Three reasons:
 *
 *     1. Interface stability. Components import from a single
 *        symbol (`useTopics`) whose surface is documented and
 *        typed as `TopicHookValue`. If the store's internal
 *        shape changes — a field is renamed, an action is
 *        composed differently — the hook's shape is what the
 *        consumers depend on, and the store can be refactored
 *        behind it.
 *
 *     2. Composition. The hook is the natural place for a
 *        future composition the store cannot provide — a
 *        derived value (the count of topics grouped by status),
 *        a memoized selector, a chain that calls two actions in
 *        sequence for a specific workflow. Today the hook is a
 *        straight re-export; tomorrow it may not be.
 *
 *     3. Naming symmetry. `useAuth` is the auth feature's
 *        hook. `useTopics` is the topics feature's hook.
 *        `useDocuments` will be the documents feature's hook.
 *        The convention is that every feature exposes a
 *        `use<Feature>` hook over its store, so a reader who
 *        has seen one feature can predict the shape of every
 *        other.
 *
 * Why the actions are selected directly from the store rather
 * than wrapped in `useCallback`:
 *
 *   Zustand's `create` runs its state creator exactly once per
 *   store instance, and the functions returned by that creator
 *   are the same references for the entire life of the store.
 *   That means the action references obtained from
 *   `useTopicStore((s) => s.loadTopics)` are already stable
 *   across renders — a `useCallback` wrapper around them would
 *   be redundant.
 *
 *   The auth hook (`useAuth.ts`) DID use `useCallback`, but for
 *   a different reason: its `login` and `logout` actions are
 *   composed functions defined inside the hook body, not
 *   references pulled straight from the store. Composed
 *   functions need `useCallback` to be stable. A straight
 *   reference does not.
 *
 *   If a future change makes one of these actions a composed
 *   function rather than a store reference, the correct fix at
 *   that point is to add `useCallback` (with the appropriate
 *   dependencies) around the composed version. Until then, the
 *   direct selection is both simpler and correct.
 *
 * Why the hook subscribes to each data field separately:
 *
 *   Zustand re-renders a component when any of the values it
 *   has selected from the store change. By subscribing to each
 *   of the four data fields through its own selector, the hook
 *   gets the finest-grained re-render behaviour that Zustand
 *   supports for a multi-field read: a change to `topics` does
 *   not re-render a component whose only visible effect was
 *   `status`, because that component's `status` selection did
 *   not change.
 *
 *   The alternative — a single `useTopicStore((s) => s)` call —
 *   would re-render on every store change and would require a
 *   shallow-equality check to avoid wasted renders. The
 *   per-field form is the recommended Zustand pattern and the
 *   one this hook follows.
 *
 * What this hook does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not call `loadTopics` on mount. The hook is a
 *     passive reader; the component that mounts it decides when
 *     to fetch. The Topics page calls `loadTopics()` in its own
 *     `useEffect`; the Topic Detail page calls `loadTopic(id)`
 *     in its own `useEffect`. Centralizing the fetch in the
 *     hook would fire it from every component that ever calls
 *     `useTopics()`, including ones that only want to read the
 *     error state or invoke `duplicateTopic`.
 *
 *   - It does not guard against the "no session" case. The
 *     topics feature is authenticated-only; its pages render
 *     inside the layout's auth gate, which does not mount its
 *     children until a session exists. The hook trusts that
 *     invariant — the same way the store does.
 *
 *   - It does not expose the raw `set` from Zustand. Components
 *     that need to mutate state go through the store's named
 *     actions, which are the ones that carry the correct
 *     semantics (clear the error, flip status, update the list).
 */

import {
  useTopicStore,
  type TopicStoreStatus,
} from '../store/topicStore.js';
import type {
  Topic,
  TopicCreatePayload,
  TopicStatus,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Public types
// ============================================================

/**
 * The shape of the object returned by `useTopics()`.
 *
 * The interface is exported so that a helper function that takes
 * "an instance of the topics hook" as a parameter can be typed
 * against the interface without redeclaring the shape. A
 * component that destructures the return value does not need to
 * reference the interface at all.
 *
 * The interface mirrors `TopicStoreState`'s members one-to-one
 * with two differences: it omits nothing, and it adds no members.
 * The hook is a straight exposure of the store's public surface.
 * The only reason it is a distinct type is so that a consumer
 * can name the shape — `TopicStoreState` is the store's
 * interface, and a component should be able to refer to what it
 * receives from the hook by a type that matches the hook's own
 * name.
 */
export interface TopicHookValue {
  // ---- Data ----

  /** The list of topics for the current user, sorted newest
   *  first by the backend. */
  topics: Topic[];

  /** The topic currently being viewed on the detail page, or
   *  null if no detail page is open. */
  activeTopic: Topic | null;

  /** The store's async lifecycle state. See `topicStore.ts` for
   *  the meaning of the three values. */
  status: TopicStoreStatus;

  /** The last error message from an async action, or null. */
  error: string | null;

  // ---- Actions ----

  /** Load the topics list, optionally filtered by pipeline
   *  status. Resolves when the load completes (success or
   *  failure). The store's `status` and `error` fields reflect
   *  the outcome. */
  loadTopics: (statusFilter?: TopicStatus) => Promise<void>;

  /** Load a single topic into `activeTopic`. Resolves when the
   *  load completes. */
  loadTopic: (topicId: string) => Promise<void>;

  /** Create a new topic. Resolves with the created topic, or
   *  null on failure. */
  createTopic: (payload: TopicCreatePayload) => Promise<Topic | null>;

  /** Delete a topic. Resolves with `true` on success, `false` on
   *  failure. */
  deleteTopic: (topicId: string) => Promise<boolean>;

  /** Create a copy of the given topic. Resolves with the created
   *  topic, or null on failure. */
  duplicateTopic: (topic: Topic) => Promise<Topic | null>;

  /** Set the active topic directly, without a network call. */
  setActiveTopic: (topic: Topic | null) => void;

  /** Reset the store to its initial state. */
  clear: () => void;
}

// ============================================================
//  The hook
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return the topics feature's state and its actions. See the
 * file header for the hook's role, its relationship to the
 * store, and the reasoning behind the design choices.
 */
export const useTopics = (): TopicHookValue => {
  // ---- Data subscriptions ----
  // One selector per data field. See the file header for why the
  // fields are read individually rather than as one object.
  const topics = useTopicStore((s) => s.topics);
  const activeTopic = useTopicStore((s) => s.activeTopic);
  const status = useTopicStore((s) => s.status);
  const error = useTopicStore((s) => s.error);

  // ---- Action subscriptions ----
  // Zustand actions are stable references for the life of the
  // store, so selecting them here does not cause re-renders and
  // does not require `useCallback` around them. See the file
  // header for the reasoning.
  const loadTopics = useTopicStore((s) => s.loadTopics);
  const loadTopic = useTopicStore((s) => s.loadTopic);
  const createTopic = useTopicStore((s) => s.createTopic);
  const deleteTopic = useTopicStore((s) => s.deleteTopic);
  const duplicateTopic = useTopicStore((s) => s.duplicateTopic);
  const setActiveTopic = useTopicStore((s) => s.setActiveTopic);
  const clear = useTopicStore((s) => s.clear);

  // ---- Return ----
  // A single object literal with all eleven members. The order
  // matches the interface above, so a reader comparing the two
  // does not have to hunt for a member's position.
  return {
    topics,
    activeTopic,
    status,
    error,
    loadTopics,
    loadTopic,
    createTopic,
    deleteTopic,
    duplicateTopic,
    setActiveTopic,
    clear,
  };
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * The hook as the default export, matching the convention used
 * by every other hook and store in the codebase. Consumers that
 * prefer the named form use `import { useTopics } from ...`;
 * consumers that prefer the default form use
 * `import useTopics from ...`. Both resolve to the same hook.
 */
export default useTopics;
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/topics/ipc/topicsIPC.ts">
/**
 * Topics feature — IPC handler for the main process.
 *
 * This module is the bridge between the renderer's
 * `window.electronAPI.topics.*` calls and the main process's
 * topics API layer (`topicsApi.ts`, the previous file in this
 * session). Its `registerTopicsIPC()` function is called once,
 * at app-ready time, by `src/main/index.ts` — the same place
 * that calls `registerAuthIPC()` (see `auth/authIPC.ts`) and
 * that will eventually call each feature's `register*IPC()` in
 * session order.
 *
 * The five channels this file registers:
 *
 *   topics:list    — reads the user's topics, optionally
 *                    filtered by pipeline status. Forwards to
 *                    `listTopics` from the API layer.
 *
 *   topics:create  — creates a new topic from a
 *                    `TopicCreatePayload`. Forwards to
 *                    `createTopic`.
 *
 *   topics:get     — reads a single topic by id. Forwards to
 *                    `getTopic`.
 *
 *   topics:update  — applies a partial update to a topic.
 *                    Forwards to `updateTopic`.
 *
 *   topics:delete  — deletes a topic. Forwards to
 *                    `deleteTopic`.
 *
 * The channels correspond one-to-one with the five functions
 * exported by the API layer, and with the five methods on the
 * renderer side's `window.electronAPI.topics.*` object. There is
 * no channel here that does not correspond to a real backend
 * operation, and no backend operation that does not have a
 * channel — the three levels (renderer API, IPC channels,
 * main-process API) share the same shape by construction.
 *
 * Why this file has almost no logic:
 *
 *   Each handler is a one-line forward of its arguments to the
 *   corresponding function in the API layer, and a one-line
 *   return of the result. The API layer already converts any
 *   failure — an axios error, a network timeout, a malformed
 *   response — into the standard `ApiResponse<T>` envelope, so
 *   the handler does not need a try/catch of its own. The
 *   handler's job is only to translate the IPC call boundary
 *   into a function call, and back.
 *
 *   This is the same shape as `authIPC.ts`'s three handlers,
 *   and it is deliberate. A feature's IPC handler is a
 *   pass-through by design: the interesting work belongs to the
 *   service layer (which does the HTTP), and the handler should
 *   not duplicate or second-guess it. If a future session finds
 *   itself adding logic here — validation, transformation,
 *   caching — the correct move is almost always to push that
 *   logic down into the service, where it is testable without
 *   an IPC harness.
 *
 * What this file does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not touch the encrypted store. The auth store
 *     (see `main/store.ts`) is owned by the auth feature.
 *     Topics have no persistent main-process state.
 *
 *   - It does not set the bearer token on the shared axios
 *     client. That lifecycle belongs to the auth feature's
 *     `authIPC.ts` and is performed once at startup. Every
 *     other feature's IPC handler inherits the token from the
 *     shared client without touching it.
 *
 *   - It does not validate the arguments. The IPC channel is
 *     only reachable from the renderer, the renderer's calls
 *     are typed against the shared types, and the backend's own
 *     schema validation is the authoritative check. Adding
 *     a validation layer at the IPC boundary would duplicate
 *     what the backend already does and would need to be kept
 *     in sync with it — a maintenance cost with no benefit for
 *     the current single-client architecture.
 *
 *   - It does not log. Logging belongs one level down, in the
 *     service layer, where a request's outcome and its timing
 *     are both available without adding noise to every IPC
 *     call. The topics API layer does not log today, but if a
 *     future session adds request logging it belongs there,
 *     not here.
 */

import { ipcMain, type IpcMainInvokeEvent } from 'electron';

import {
  listTopics,
  createTopic,
  getTopic,
  updateTopic,
  deleteTopic,
} from '../services/topicsApi.js';

import type {
  ApiResponse,
  Topic,
  TopicCreatePayload,
  TopicUpdatePayload,
  TopicStatus,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Channel name constants
// ============================================================
//
//  The five channel names are declared as constants so a future
//  refactor that renames them (or a test that spies on them) has
//  one place to change. The preload's `src/main/preload.ts`
//  declares the same strings on the renderer side of the bridge
//  — the two must stay in sync, but neither file imports from
//  the other, because the preload is a renderer-context module
//  and this file is a main-context module.

const CHANNEL_LIST = 'topics:list';
const CHANNEL_CREATE = 'topics:create';
const CHANNEL_GET = 'topics:get';
const CHANNEL_UPDATE = 'topics:update';
const CHANNEL_DELETE = 'topics:delete';

// ============================================================
//  registerTopicsIPC
// ============================================================

/**
 * Register the topics feature's IPC handlers.
 *
 * Called once, from `main/index.ts`, inside the
 * `app.whenReady().then(...)` callback. By the time this runs,
 * the shared axios client exists — it was initialized when its
 * own module was imported at the top of the main process's
 * module graph — and the auth feature's `registerAuthIPC()` has
 * already run (or will run in the same sequence), so the shared
 * client has a bearer token restored from the encrypted store.
 *
 * The function is not idempotent: calling it twice will produce
 * Electron errors on the second call, because `ipcMain.handle`
 * refuses to register a second handler for the same channel.
 * The single-call contract is the same one every other
 * feature's `register*IPC()` function follows.
 */
export const registerTopicsIPC = (): void => {
  // ---- topics:list ----
  //
  // Read the user's topics, optionally filtered by status. The
  // optional filter is a `TopicStatus | undefined`; passing
  // `undefined` produces the unfiltered list.
  ipcMain.handle(
    CHANNEL_LIST,
    async (
      _event: IpcMainInvokeEvent,
      status?: TopicStatus
    ): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic[]>> => {
      return listTopics(status);
    }
  );

  // ---- topics:create ----
  //
  // Create a new topic. The payload is the user's chosen values
  // from the New Topic modal; the backend's service derives the
  // owner from the authenticated session.
  ipcMain.handle(
    CHANNEL_CREATE,
    async (
      _event: IpcMainInvokeEvent,
      payload: TopicCreatePayload
    ): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>> => {
      return createTopic(payload);
    }
  );

  // ---- topics:get ----
  //
  // Read a single topic by id. A topic that does not exist or
  // that belongs to a different user is treated identically by
  // the backend (both return 404), so a client cannot distinguish
  // "no such topic" from "not your topic".
  ipcMain.handle(
    CHANNEL_GET,
    async (
      _event: IpcMainInvokeEvent,
      topicId: string
    ): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>> => {
      return getTopic(topicId);
    }
  );

  // ---- topics:update ----
  //
  // Apply a partial update. Every field on `TopicUpdatePayload`
  // is optional; the backend's service merges the patch onto the
  // existing document.
  ipcMain.handle(
    CHANNEL_UPDATE,
    async (
      _event: IpcMainInvokeEvent,
      topicId: string,
      patch: TopicUpdatePayload
    ): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>> => {
      return updateTopic(topicId, patch);
    }
  );

  // ---- topics:delete ----
  //
  // Delete a topic. The backend returns the deleted document so
  // the renderer can render an undo affordance.
  ipcMain.handle(
    CHANNEL_DELETE,
    async (
      _event: IpcMainInvokeEvent,
      topicId: string
    ): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>> => {
      return deleteTopic(topicId);
    }
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * The registration function as the default export, matching the
 * convention used by every other IPC module in the codebase.
 * `main/index.ts` uses the named import
 * (`import { registerTopicsIPC } from ...`), so the default form
 * is a convenience rather than a load-bearing export.
 */
export default registerTopicsIPC;
</file>
