</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/topics/pages/Topics.tsx">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — topics home page.
 *
 * This is the app's default authenticated view — the screen a
 * signed-in user lands on immediately after logging in, and the
 * one they see every time they open the app with an active
 * session. It has one job: show the user's topics, and give them
 * a way to create a new one.
 *
 * The page has four visual states, driven by the store's `status`
 * and `error` fields and by whether the `topics` array is empty:
 *
 *   1. Loading      — `status === 'loading'` and no topics are
 *                     currently shown. A centered spinner.
 *
 *   2. Error        — `status === 'error'`. A banner with the
 *                     error message and a "Try again" button that
 *                     re-runs `loadTopics()`.
 *
 *   3. Empty        — `status === 'idle'` and `topics.length === 0`.
 *                     A friendly empty state with a call to
 *                     action that opens the New Topic modal.
 *
 *   4. Populated    — `status === 'idle'` and `topics.length > 0`.
 *                     A responsive grid of `<TopicCard />`.
 *
 * The distinction between (1) and (3) matters: a list that is
 * empty while a fetch is in progress is not the same as a list
 * that is empty because the user has no topics. The former should
 * show a spinner; the latter should invite the user to create
 * their first topic. This page keys off `status === 'loading'`
 * for the spinner, not off `topics.length === 0`.
 *
 * What the page does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not open the topic's detail view. That is the
 *     `<TopicCard />`'s job — the card renders a link (or a
 *     button that navigates) to `/dashboard/topics/:id`. The
 *     page composes the cards into a grid and stops there.
 *
 *   - It does not delete or duplicate topics. Those operations
 *     are invoked from the card's own menu — the card has the
 *     topic object in hand and the actions are colocated with
 *     it. The page's role is to render the list, not to mediate
 *     every operation a topic can undergo.
 *
 *   - It does not paginate. The plan's topics endpoint returns
 *     the user's full list, and the plan does not describe a
 *     paginated view. A user with hundreds of topics would see
 *     all of them; if a future session wants pagination, the
 *     correct change is a new endpoint parameter and a pager
 *     component, not a change to this page's layout.
 *
 *   - It does not filter. The topics API accepts an optional
 *     `?status=` filter, and the store's `loadTopics` forwards
 *     it, but the plan does not describe a filter UI on the
 *     home page. If a future session adds one, the state for
 *     the current filter lives here and the fetch call grows
 *     the argument.
 *
 * The empty-state copy:
 *
 *   The empty state invites the user to create their first
 *   topic with a short prompt — "Create your first topic" —
 *   and a button that opens the same New Topic modal the
 *   header button opens. The design uses the same primary
 *   color and the same iconography as the rest of the app, so
 *   the empty state reads as part of the product rather than as
 *   a placeholder screen.
 *
 * Modal ownership:
 *
 *   The `NewTopicModal` is a controlled child of this page —
 *   the page owns the boolean that determines whether it is
 *   open, and the modal reports back through `onClose` when
 *   the user dismisses it or completes the create flow. This
 *   mirrors the pattern of `Sidebar` in `Layout` (the parent
 *   owns the state, the child is presentational), and it means
 *   the page can open the modal from two places (the header
 *   button and the empty-state button) without threading an
 *   imperative API through a ref.
 *
 *   If a future session wants to open the modal from a
 *   component outside this page, the correct change is to
 *   promote the modal to an imperative API (via the modal
 *   context that `shared/components/Modal.tsx` already
 *   provides) — but the two-call-sites-in-one-page case does
 *   not justify that yet.
 *
 * Forward references:
 *
 *   This file imports `TopicCard` and `NewTopicModal` from the
 *   siblings `../components/TopicCard.js` and
 *   `../components/NewTopicModal.js`. Both are scheduled for
 *   later steps in this session (#58 and #59 respectively) and
 *   do not exist yet. Their absence produces two `TS2307`
 *   errors on the import lines until they are created. This is
 *   the same forward-reference pattern that appeared in
 *   Session 5 (Sidebar and Layout waiting on `useAuth`) and in
 *   Session 4 (App.tsx waiting on every feature page).
 */

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import {
  AlertCircle,
  FileText,
  Loader2,
  Plus,
} from 'lucide-react';

import { useTopics } from '../hooks/useTopics.js';
import TopicCard from '../components/TopicCard.js';
import NewTopicModal from '../components/NewTopicModal.js';

// ============================================================
//  Public types
// ============================================================

/**
 * The props accepted by `Topics`. Currently empty — the page
 * takes no props and derives everything from the store and the
 * router context.
 */
// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-empty-object-type
export interface TopicsProps {
  // Reserved for future additions. See file header.
}

// ============================================================
//  Topics
// ============================================================

/**
 * The topics home page. See the file header for the page's four
 * visual states, its scope, and the reasoning behind the modal
 * ownership and the empty-state design.
 */
export const Topics = (_props: TopicsProps = {}) => {
  const { topics, status, error, loadTopics } = useTopics();

  // Whether the New Topic modal is currently open. Owned here
  // and passed to the modal as a controlled prop — see the file
  // header for the reasoning.
  const [isNewTopicModalOpen, setIsNewTopicModalOpen] = useState(false);

  // ---- Initial fetch ----
  // Load the user's topics on mount. The empty dependency array
  // means this runs once per mount of the Topics page. Navigating
  // between topics and their detail views unmounts and remounts
  // this page each time, so a subsequent visit re-fetches — a
  // deliberate choice for the current design. The store is not
  // persisted and the backend is the source of truth for the
  // list, so a fresh fetch on every mount keeps the view in sync
  // with whatever changes might have happened elsewhere.
  //
  // The `void` on the call discards the promise; the store's
  // `status` field is what the render reacts to, and the caller
  // has no further work to do when the promise resolves.
  useEffect(() => {
    void loadTopics();
  }, [loadTopics]);

  // ---- Modal handlers ----

  const openNewTopicModal = (): void => {
    setIsNewTopicModalOpen(true);
  };

  const closeNewTopicModal = (): void => {
    setIsNewTopicModalOpen(false);
  };

  // ---- Render ----
  return (
    <div className="mx-auto flex h-full w-full max-w-6xl flex-col px-6 py-8">
      {/* ---- Header ---- */}
      <header className="mb-8 flex flex-wrap items-center justify-between gap-4">
        <div>
          <h1 className="text-2xl font-semibold text-text dark:text-neutral-100">
            Topics
          </h1>
          <p className="mt-1 text-sm text-neutral-500 dark:text-neutral-400">
            Research, write, and validate your articles.
          </p>
        </div>

        <button
          type="button"
          onClick={openNewTopicModal}
          className="inline-flex items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-primary px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium text-white transition-colors hover:bg-primary-dark focus-visible:outline-none"
        >
          <Plus size={18} aria-hidden="true" />
          <span>New Topic</span>
        </button>
      </header>

      {/* ---- Body ---- */}
      <div className="flex-1">
        <TopicsBody
          topics={topics}
          status={status}
          error={error}
          onRetry={() => void loadTopics()}
          onNewTopic={openNewTopicModal}
        />
      </div>

      {/* ---- New Topic modal ---- */}
      <NewTopicModal
        open={isNewTopicModalOpen}
        onClose={closeNewTopicModal}
      />
    </div>
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  TopicsBody — internal view
// ============================================================
//
//  The four visual states (loading, error, empty, populated) are
//  expressed as a small internal component rather than as a
//  sequence of ternaries in the page's JSX. The split keeps the
//  page's return value to two sections (header, body) and lets
//  the body's rendering be read as a flat sequence of
//  `if`-style early returns.

interface TopicsBodyProps {
  topics: ReturnType<typeof useTopics>['topics'];
  status: ReturnType<typeof useTopics>['status'];
  error: ReturnType<typeof useTopics>['error'];
  onRetry: () => void;
  onNewTopic: () => void;
}

const TopicsBody = ({
  topics,
  status,
  error,
  onRetry,
  onNewTopic,
}: TopicsBodyProps) => {
  // ---- 1. Loading ----
  // Shown when a fetch is in flight and there are no topics to
  // display. If topics are already loaded (a re-fetch is in
  // progress), the existing list is shown instead — see the
  // populated branch below.
  if (status === 'loading' && topics.length === 0) {
    return (
      <div className="flex h-64 items-center justify-center">
        <Loader2
          size={28}
          className="animate-spin text-primary"
          aria-hidden="true"
        />
        <span className="sr-only">Loading topics…</span>
      </div>
    );
  }

  // ---- 2. Error ----
  // Shown when the last fetch failed. The banner carries the
  // error message the store captured; the button re-runs the
  // fetch.
  if (status === 'error' && error) {
    return (
      <div
        role="alert"
        className="mx-auto flex max-w-lg flex-col items-center gap-3 rounded-xl border border-red-200 bg-red-50 p-6 text-center dark:border-red-900 dark:bg-red-950/60"
      >
        <AlertCircle
          size={24}
          className="text-red-600 dark:text-red-400"
          aria-hidden="true"
        />
        <p className="text-sm text-red-900 dark:text-red-100">{error}</p>
        <button
          type="button"
          onClick={onRetry}
          className="rounded-lg bg-red-600 px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium text-white transition-colors hover:bg-red-700 focus-visible:outline-none"
        >
          Try again
        </button>
      </div>
    );
  }

  // ---- 3. Empty ----
  // Shown when the fetch succeeded but the user has no topics.
  // The call to action opens the same modal the header button
  // opens.
  if (topics.length === 0) {
    return (
      <div className="mx-auto flex max-w-md flex-col items-center gap-4 py-16 text-center">
        <div className="flex h-14 w-14 items-center justify-center rounded-2xl bg-neutral-100 text-neutral-500 dark:bg-neutral-800 dark:text-neutral-400">
          <FileText size={28} aria-hidden="true" />
        </div>
        <div>
          <h2 className="text-lg font-semibold text-text dark:text-neutral-100">
            No topics yet
          </h2>
          <p className="mt-1 text-sm text-neutral-500 dark:text-neutral-400">
            Create your first topic to start the research and
            writing pipeline.
          </p>
        </div>
        <button
          type="button"
          onClick={onNewTopic}
          className="inline-flex items-center gap-2 rounded-lg bg-primary px-4 py-2 text-sm font-medium text-white transition-colors hover:bg-primary-dark focus-visible:outline-none"
        >
          <Plus size={18} aria-hidden="true" />
          <span>New Topic</span>
        </button>
      </div>
    );
  }

  // ---- 4. Populated ----
  // A responsive grid of topic cards. The grid collapses to one
  // column on narrow windows and expands to two or three columns
  // on wider ones — the app runs at a minimum of 1024 px per the
  // window's minWidth setting, which comfortably fits two
  // columns, and can expand to three on a large monitor.
  return (
    <div className="grid grid-cols-1 gap-4 sm:grid-cols-2 xl:grid-cols-3">
      {topics.map((topic) => (
        <TopicCard key={topic._id} topic={topic} />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * The `Topics` component as the default export. `renderer/App.tsx`
 * imports this with the default form
 * (`import Topics from '.../Topics.js'`), so this is the export
 * that keeps the route tree resolving.
 */
export default Topics;
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/topics/services/topicsApi.ts">
/**
 * Topics feature — backend API layer.
 *
 * This module declares the five backend operations the topics
 * feature performs, as small, focused functions that each return
 * the shared `ApiResponse<T>` envelope. It is the direct
 * counterpart to the backend's `topicController.ts` (File 20) —
 * every function here maps one-to-one to one of that controller's
 * five handlers, and to one of the five `topics:*` IPC channels
 * that will be registered by the sibling file `ipc/topicsIPC.ts`
 * (item #55 in Session 7).
 *
 * The five operations:
 *
 *   listTopics     — GET    /api/topics, with an optional
 *                    `?status=` filter. Returns `Topic[]`.
 *
 *   createTopic    — POST   /api/topics, with a
 *                    `TopicCreatePayload` body. Returns the
 *                    persisted `Topic`.
 *
 *   getTopic       — GET    /api/topics/:id. Returns one `Topic`
 *                    or a 404-shaped error envelope.
 *
 *   updateTopic    — PATCH  /api/topics/:id, with a
 *                    `TopicUpdatePayload` body. Returns the
 *                    updated `Topic`.
 *
 *   deleteTopic    — DELETE /api/topics/:id. Returns the deleted
 *                    `Topic`.
 *
 * This is a MAIN-PROCESS module. Like `authApi.ts`, it uses the
 * shared axios client that runs in the main process. The
 * renderer never imports this file directly — it reaches these
 * operations through `window.electronAPI.topics.*`, which is
 * wired by the preload to the IPC handlers registered by
 * `ipc/topicsIPC.ts`. The channel names the sibling file will
 * use (`topics:list`, `topics:create`, `topics:get`,
 * `topics:update`, `topics:delete`) correspond one-to-one with
 * the five functions here.
 *
 * No token handling:
 *
 *   Unlike `authApi.ts`, this module does not call
 *   `setAuthToken`. The bearer token is installed once at
 *   startup (restored from the encrypted store by
 *   `registerAuthIPC()` in `authIPC.ts`) and updated only on
 *   login and logout. Every other main-process API module —
 *   topics, documents, articles, reports, settings, admin —
 *   inherits the token from the shared axios client without
 *   touching it. Adding a token-set call here would be
 *   redundant and, more importantly, would imply that this
 *   module owns part of the token's lifecycle. It does not.
 *   The token belongs to the auth feature; the axios client
 *   holds it; every other module uses it implicitly through
 *   the client's request interceptor.
 *
 * The status filter and URL construction:
 *
 *   The backend's `GET /api/topics` endpoint accepts an optional
 *   `?status=` query parameter whose value is one of the eight
 *   `TopicStatus` literals. When `listTopics` is called with a
 *   status, this module appends the query string to the URL;
 *   when called without, it uses the bare path.
 *
 *   The status value is encoded with `encodeURIComponent` even
 *   though every legal value is already URL-safe. The encoding
 *   is defensive: if a future change ever added a status value
 *   with a character that needed escaping, the encoding here
 *   would handle it without a second look. The cost is a few
 *   hundred nanoseconds per call, which is nothing compared to
 *   the network round-trip.
 *
 * What this module does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not validate the `TopicStatus` value passed to
 *     `listTopics`. Every legal value comes from the shared
 *     types module's `TopicStatus` union, and TypeScript
 *     prevents a caller from passing an out-of-union string. If
 *     a caller in a future session casts past that safety, the
 *     backend's own validation would catch the bad value and
 *     return a 400, which the shared client converts to an
 *     error envelope. The validation is the backend's job, and
 *     this module trusts the type system on the client side.
 *
 *   - It does not touch the renderer's topic store. The store is
 *     updated by the renderer-side code — the topic IPC handler
 *     sends the API result back through the preload, and the
 *     renderer's `topicsApi.ts` consumer (or the hook that
 *     wraps it) writes the result to the store. This module is
 *     a pure data-fetching layer.
 *
 *   - It does not log or audit any operation. Logging belongs in
 *     the IPC handler layer, where a request's origin and the
 *     user's identity are both known. This module sees only the
 *     arguments it receives.
 */

import {
  apiGet,
  apiPost,
  apiPatch,
  apiDelete,
} from '../../shared/api/client.js';

import type {
  ApiResponse,
  Topic,
  TopicCreatePayload,
  TopicUpdatePayload,
  TopicStatus,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  URL prefix
// ============================================================

/**
 * The base path for every topics endpoint. Declared as a constant
 * so a future rename of the route prefix (unlikely, but possible
 * if the backend ever reorganized its paths) is a one-line change
 * with no risk of a partial edit leaving one function pointing at
 * the old prefix. The shared axios client's `baseURL` already
 * includes `/api`, so this constant only names the resource
 * segment.
 */
const TOPICS_PATH = '/topics';

// ============================================================
//  listTopics
// ============================================================

/**
 * List the authenticated user's topics, sorted by the backend
 * (newest first — the backend's controller passes the sort to the
 * service, which uses the `{ userId, createdAt: -1 }` compound
 * index).
 *
 * The optional `status` filter narrows the result to a single
 * pipeline state. When omitted, every topic owned by the user is
 * returned. The filter is expressed as the `?status=` query
 * parameter, matching the backend's controller, which validates
 * the value against the closed `TopicStatus` set.
 *
 * @param status - Optional pipeline-state filter.
 * @returns An `ApiResponse` wrapping the array of topics on
 *          success, or the standard error envelope on failure.
 */
export const listTopics = async (
  status?: TopicStatus
): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic[]>> => {
  // Build the URL with the optional query string. The two
  // branches are collapsed into a single template so the call
  // site does not have to pick between two apiGet overloads.
  const url =
    status !== undefined
      ? `${TOPICS_PATH}?status=${encodeURIComponent(status)}`
      : TOPICS_PATH;

  return apiGet<Topic[]>(url);
};

// ============================================================
//  createTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Create a new topic owned by the authenticated user.
 *
 * The `TopicCreatePayload` carries the user's chosen values from
 * the New Topic modal — the title (required), and optionally the
 * keywords, preset, profile, prompt file, word count, and source
 * count. The backend's service applies defaults for any omitted
 * field, so a minimal payload with just a title is valid.
 *
 * The authenticated user's identity is attached to the request
 * by the shared axios client's bearer token; the payload
 * deliberately does not include a `userId` field. The backend's
 * service derives the owner from the authenticated session, and
 * the type's shape (`TopicCreatePayload`) does not include the
 * field — so a caller cannot accidentally pass one.
 *
 * @param payload - The topic's creation values.
 * @returns An `ApiResponse` wrapping the persisted topic on
 *          success, or the standard error envelope on failure.
 */
export const createTopic = async (
  payload: TopicCreatePayload
): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>> => {
  return apiPost<Topic>(TOPICS_PATH, payload);
};

// ============================================================
//  getTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Fetch a single topic by its id.
 *
 * A topic that does not exist or that belongs to a different user
 * returns a 404 from the backend, which the shared axios client
 * converts to an `{ success: false, error: 'Topic not found.' }`
 * envelope. The two cases are merged on the backend for
 * enumeration-safety reasons — a caller cannot distinguish "no
 * such topic" from "topic belongs to someone else". See the
 * backend's `topicService.ts` for the full rationale.
 *
 * @param topicId - The topic's id (a hexadecimal string).
 * @returns An `ApiResponse` wrapping the topic on success, or the
 *          standard error envelope on failure.
 */
export const getTopic = async (
  topicId: string
): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>> => {
  return apiGet<Topic>(`${TOPICS_PATH}/${encodeURIComponent(topicId)}`);
};

// ============================================================
//  updateTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Apply a partial update to a topic.
 *
 * The `TopicUpdatePayload` accepts any subset of the topic's
 * mutable fields — title, keywords, preset, profile, prompt file,
 * word count, source count, status, error. Fields omitted from
 * the patch are left unchanged on the backend's document. Fields
 * present but invalid are rejected with a 400 by the backend's
 * schema validators, which the shared client converts to an error
 * envelope.
 *
 * The backend's service handles one cross-field rule the schema
 * does not: when `status` is changed to anything other than
 * `'failed'`, the `error` field is unset. That logic is entirely
 * server-side; this module does not need to know about it.
 *
 * @param topicId - The topic's id.
 * @param patch   - The fields to update.
 * @returns An `ApiResponse` wrapping the updated topic on
 *          success, or the standard error envelope on failure.
 */
export const updateTopic = async (
  topicId: string,
  patch: TopicUpdatePayload
): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>> => {
  return apiPatch<Topic>(
    `${TOPICS_PATH}/${encodeURIComponent(topicId)}`,
    patch
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  deleteTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete a topic.
 *
 * The backend returns the deleted document so the client has a
 * last-chance look at what was removed; the renderer's UI uses
 * that to render an undo affordance without a second round trip.
 *
 * The backend does NOT cascade the delete to the topic's child
 * records (documents, articles, reports). Cascade rules belong to
 * each owning feature and are not implemented in the current
 * plan — a topic delete leaves orphaned child records in the
 * database, which a future cleanup migration could address. This
 * module's job is to reflect the backend's behaviour, not to
 * invent a cascade.
 *
 * @param topicId - The topic's id.
 * @returns An `ApiResponse` wrapping the deleted topic on
 *          success, or the standard error envelope on failure.
 */
export const deleteTopic = async (
  topicId: string
): Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>> => {
  return apiDelete<Topic>(`${TOPICS_PATH}/${encodeURIComponent(topicId)}`);
};
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/topics/store/topicStore.ts">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — topics store.
 *
 * This is the renderer's in-memory record of the user's topics —
 * the list shown on the Topics home page, the active topic shown
 * on the Topic Detail page, and the transient loading/error state
 * that both pages render around their content.
 *
 * The store is populated by the two async load actions
 * (`loadTopics`, `loadTopic`) that the `useTopics` hook calls on
 * mount, and mutated by three further async actions
 * (`createTopic`, `deleteTopic`, `duplicateTopic`) that the topics
 * feature's UI invokes directly through the hook. Every async
 * action ultimately reaches the backend through
 * `window.electronAPI.topics.*`, which the preload installs and
 * which resolves to the main process's IPC handlers (see
 * `ipc/topicsIPC.ts`, item #55 of Session 7).
 *
 * Why the store's actions do IPC rather than the hook:
 *
 *   The plan's file-tree description of this module names three
 *   actions — `createTopic`, `deleteTopic`, `duplicateTopic` — as
 *   members of the store. That naming is read here literally: the
 *   store exposes these operations as callable actions, and a
 *   caller who invokes `useTopicStore.getState().createTopic(…)`
 *   gets the full operation — the IPC round-trip, the state
 *   update, and the error capture.
 *
 *   The alternative — putting the IPC calls in the `useTopics`
 *   hook and limiting the store to pure state mutations — would
 *   contradict the plan's explicit "Actions:" list. It would also
 *   split each topic mutation across two files: the hook would
 *   own the IPC call, the store would own the state update, and
 *   the two would have to agree on a narrow interface between
 *   them. Keeping the operation co-located with the state it
 *   mutates means there is one place to look for "what happens
 *   when a topic is created".
 *
 * Why the store is not persisted:
 *
 *   The topics list is server-authoritative. It is owned by the
 *   backend's `Topic` collection, and its contents change whenever
 *   another device the user owns (a second workstation, a mobile
 *   client that a future session might add) creates or deletes a
 *   topic. Caching the list across app restarts would let the
 *   renderer show stale data — a topic that was deleted from
 *   another device would still appear until the next refresh, and
 *   a topic that was added from another device would be absent
 *   until the next refresh.
 *
 *   The auth store (see `auth/store/userStore.ts`) IS persisted,
 *   because the user's identity and token are stable across
 *   restarts and the renderer needs them to render the
 *   authenticated shell before the first network round-trip.
 *   Topics are different — the user's expectation when they open
 *   the app is to see the current state of their topics, not a
 *   cached snapshot. The store therefore does not use Zustand's
 *   `persist` middleware.
 *
 * The `status` field — why the store has one:
 *
 *   The plan names `status` as a data field of this store,
 *   alongside `topics` and `activeTopic`. Its role is to reflect
 *   whether the store is currently performing an async operation,
 *   so that a page can render a spinner (during `loading`), a
 *   message (during `error`), or the content (during `idle`)
 *   without having to track its own per-operation loading flag.
 *
 *   The three states are:
 *
 *     'idle'    — no operation is in progress, and the last one
 *                 (if any) succeeded. The default state.
 *
 *     'loading' — an async operation is in flight. Set by every
 *                 async action at its start; the corresponding
 *                 success or failure path sets it back to
 *                 'idle' or 'error'.
 *
 *     'error'   — the last async operation failed. The `error`
 *                 field carries a user-facing message. The next
 *                 async action to start resets both fields.
 *
 *   The field is deliberately NOT called `isLoading`. A single
 *   boolean would not distinguish "the store is idle" from "the
 *   store is in an error state that has not yet been cleared" —
 *   both would read as `false` and the page would have to consult
 *   the `error` field separately to tell them apart. The
 *   three-valued status collapses the two checks into one.
 *
 *   Note that `status` here is the STORE's status, not a Topic's
 *   pipeline status. The two share a name but not a domain — the
 *   `Topic` type itself has a `status: TopicStatus` field whose
 *   value is one of the eight pipeline states. The store's
 *   `status` is a page-lifecycle signal. The two live on
 *   different objects and never collide.
 *
 * Why `duplicateTopic` takes a full `Topic` rather than an id:
 *
 *   The caller of `duplicateTopic` is always a component that is
 *   rendering a specific topic — a card in the list, a header on
 *   the detail page. The topic object is already in the caller's
 *   hands. Accepting the full object avoids a second lookup (the
 *   store would have to find it in `topics[]`) and avoids a
 *   network call in the case where the topic is not in the list
 *   (for example, if the detail page loaded it directly via
 *   `loadTopic` without the list being populated).
 *
 *   The alternative signature — `duplicateTopic(topicId: string)`
 *   — would look cleaner in isolation but would force the store to
 *   either assume the topic is in the list (fragile) or fetch it
 *   from the backend (slow, and duplicates information the caller
 *   already has). The full-object signature is the honest one for
 *   the actual call site.
 *
 * The title suffix:
 *
 *   `duplicateTopic` appends `" (copy)"` to the original topic's
 *   title. The plan does not specify a suffix — it says only that
 *   duplicate makes "a copy and start a new variant from the same
 *   research." The suffix is a small, conventional choice: it
 *   makes the duplicate visually distinguishable from its source
 *   in the topics list, and it signals to the user that the two
 *   topics are related. A user who wants a different title edits
 *   the duplicate after creating it — the same flow they would use
 *   for any other topic.
 *
 * What this store does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not run the research, extraction, or writer steps.
 *     Those are separate operations driven by the pipeline's
 *     later stages and by separate stores (`researchStore`,
 *     `writerStore`, `validationStore`). The topics store is
 *     concerned only with the topic's metadata, not with its
 *     pipeline state machine.
 *
 *   - It does not cascade deletes to the topic's child records
 *     (documents, articles, reports). The backend does not cascade
 *     either, and the renderer's job is to reflect the backend's
 *     behaviour, not to invent a cascade. A future cleanup
 *     migration — or a future explicit cascade endpoint on the
 *     backend — would be the correct place for that logic.
 *
 *   - It does not implement an `updateTopic` action. The plan
 *     names three actions for this store, and update is not among
 *     them. The renderer's topic-editing flows (if any) are
 *     covered by the backend's PATCH endpoint and by the API
 *     layer's `updateTopic` function (File 27), but the store
 *     does not expose it as an action. A future session that
 *     needs topic editing in the UI adds the action here.
 */

import { create } from 'zustand';

import type {
  Topic,
  TopicCreatePayload,
  TopicStatus,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Public types
// ============================================================

/**
 * The three-value lifecycle of the store's async activity. See
 * the file header for what each value means.
 */
export type TopicStoreStatus = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'error';

/**
 * The full shape of the topics store's state, including both the
 * data fields and the actions. Exported so that a consumer that
 * wants to type a parameter or a helper function can reference
 * the shape without redeclaring it.
 */
export interface TopicStoreState {
  // ---- Data ----

  /** The topics visible on the home page, in the order the
   *  backend returned them (newest first). */
  topics: Topic[];

  /** The topic currently being viewed on the detail page, or
   *  null if no detail page is open. */
  activeTopic: Topic | null;

  /** The store's async lifecycle state. See the file header. */
  status: TopicStoreStatus;

  /** The last error message from an async action, or null. */
  error: string | null;

  // ---- Async actions ----

  /**
   * Load the topics list. Called by `useTopics` on the Topics
   * page's mount, and by any component that wants to refresh the
   * list after an external change.
   *
   * @param statusFilter - Optional pipeline-state filter,
   *                        matching the backend's `?status=`
   *                        query parameter.
   */
  loadTopics: (statusFilter?: TopicStatus) => Promise<void>;

  /**
   * Load a single topic into `activeTopic`. Called by
   * `useTopics` on the Topic Detail page's mount.
   *
   * @param topicId - The topic's id.
   */
  loadTopic: (topicId: string) => Promise<void>;

  /**
   * Create a new topic. On success, the new topic is prepended
   * to the `topics` list (matching the backend's newest-first
   * sort) and set as the `activeTopic`, so the caller can
   * immediately navigate to the detail page.
   *
   * @returns The created topic on success, or null on failure.
   *          The caller can use the return value to decide
   *          whether to navigate.
   */
  createTopic: (payload: TopicCreatePayload) => Promise<Topic | null>;

  /**
   * Delete a topic. On success, the topic is removed from the
   * `topics` list, and `activeTopic` is cleared if it was the
   * topic being deleted.
   *
   * @returns `true` on success, `false` on failure.
   */
  deleteTopic: (topicId: string) => Promise<boolean>;

  /**
   * Create a copy of the given topic, with " (copy)" appended to
   * the title and every other configuration field preserved. On
   * success, the new topic is prepended to the `topics` list and
   * set as the `activeTopic`.
   *
   * @returns The created topic on success, or null on failure.
   */
  duplicateTopic: (topic: Topic) => Promise<Topic | null>;

  // ---- Sync setters ----

  /**
   * Set the active topic directly, without a network call. Used
   * by the Topics page when it wants to hand off a topic it
   * already has in memory to the detail page — avoids a
   * redundant `loadTopic` round-trip on navigation.
   */
  setActiveTopic: (topic: Topic | null) => void;

  /**
   * Reset the store to its initial state. Called by the root
   * store's `reset` action during logout.
   */
  clear: () => void;
}

// ============================================================
//  Initial state
// ============================================================

/**
 * The store's initial data fields. Extracted as a constant so
 * that the `clear` action can reference the same values without
 * duplicating them.
 */
const INITIAL_STATE = {
  topics: [] as Topic[],
  activeTopic: null as Topic | null,
  status: 'idle' as TopicStoreStatus,
  error: null as string | null,
};

// ============================================================
//  Store
// ============================================================

/**
 * The topics store.
 *
 * Created without any middleware — see the file header for why
 * the store is not persisted. The state creator receives only
 * `set` and `get`: `set` for the synchronous updates, `get` for
 * the one action (`duplicateTopic`) that needs to call another
 * action (`createTopic`) on the same store.
 */
export const useTopicStore = create<TopicStoreState>((set, get) => ({
  // ---- Initial data ----
  ...INITIAL_STATE,

  // ============================================================
  //  Async actions
  // ============================================================

  loadTopics: async (statusFilter) => {
    // Flip the status to loading and clear any previous error.
    // The error clear is deliberate — a page that was showing an
    // error from the previous load attempt should not still show
    // it while a new attempt is in flight.
    set({ status: 'loading', error: null });

    try {
      const result = await window.electronAPI.topics.list(statusFilter);

      if (result.success && result.data) {
        set({ topics: result.data, status: 'idle' });
      } else {
        set({
          status: 'error',
          error: result.error ?? 'Failed to load topics.',
        });
      }
    } catch (err) {
      // The `window.electronAPI.topics.list` call itself can
      // reject if the IPC channel is unregistered — for example,
      // during the window between the app's startup and the
      // `registerTopicsIPC()` call in the main process. The
      // catch converts that rejection into the same error state
      // the response-envelope failure path produces, so the
      // page's render logic does not need two cases.
      console.error('[topicStore] loadTopics failed:', err);
      set({ status: 'error', error: 'Unable to load topics.' });
    }
  },

  loadTopic: async (topicId) => {
    set({ status: 'loading', error: null });

    try {
      const result = await window.electronAPI.topics.get(topicId);

      if (result.success && result.data) {
        set({ activeTopic: result.data, status: 'idle' });
      } else {
        set({
          status: 'error',
          error: result.error ?? 'Topic not found.',
        });
      }
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('[topicStore] loadTopic failed:', err);
      set({ status: 'error', error: 'Unable to load topic.' });
    }
  },

  createTopic: async (payload) => {
    set({ status: 'loading', error: null });

    try {
      const result = await window.electronAPI.topics.create(payload);

      if (result.success && result.data) {
        const created = result.data;
        // Prepend to the list — the backend sorts newest first,
        // so a newly-created topic belongs at the top. Setting
        // `activeTopic` here means a caller that navigates to
        // the detail page right after creation finds the topic
        // already loaded.
        set((state) => ({
          topics: [created, ...state.topics],
          activeTopic: created,
          status: 'idle',
        }));
        return created;
      }

      set({
        status: 'error',
        error: result.error ?? 'Failed to create topic.',
      });
      return null;
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('[topicStore] createTopic failed:', err);
      set({ status: 'error', error: 'Unable to create topic.' });
      return null;
    }
  },

  deleteTopic: async (topicId) => {
    // Unlike the load and create actions, `deleteTopic` does not
    // flip `status` to `loading`. The reason is that a delete is
    // usually initiated from a row in the topics list, and the
    // list should stay visible during the operation — a full
    // page-level loading state would replace the list with a
    // spinner, which is more disruptive than the operation
    // warrants. The caller is responsible for showing a
    // row-level spinner or disabled state.
    try {
      const result = await window.electronAPI.topics.remove(topicId);

      if (result.success) {
        set((state) => ({
          topics: state.topics.filter((t) => t._id !== topicId),
          // Clear the active topic if it was the one being
          // deleted — otherwise the detail page would keep
          // showing a topic that no longer exists on the
          // backend.
          activeTopic:
            state.activeTopic !== null &&
            state.activeTopic._id === topicId
              ? null
              : state.activeTopic,
        }));
        return true;
      }

      set({ error: result.error ?? 'Failed to delete topic.' });
      return false;
    } catch (err) {
      console.error('[topicStore] deleteTopic failed:', err);
      set({ error: 'Unable to delete topic.' });
      return false;
    }
  },

  duplicateTopic: async (topic) => {
    // Build the create payload from the original's configuration
    // fields. The id, userId, timestamps, status, and error are
    // deliberately omitted — the backend assigns a new id, the
    // authenticated session provides the userId, Mongoose
    // supplies the timestamps, and the new topic starts its
    // lifecycle at the schema's default status. The keywords
    // array is copied (spread) rather than shared by reference so
    // that mutating the duplicate's keywords cannot accidentally
    // affect the original.
    const payload: TopicCreatePayload = {
      title: `${topic.title} (copy)`,
      keywords: [...topic.keywords],
      preset: topic.preset,
      profile: topic.profile,
      promptFile: topic.promptFile,
      wordCount: topic.wordCount,
      sourceCount: topic.sourceCount,
    };

    // Delegate to `createTopic` rather than reimplementing the
    // IPC call and the state update. The two actions share the
    // entire create-topic behavior — the only difference is how
    // the payload is built.
    return get().createTopic(payload);
  },

  // ============================================================
  //  Sync setters
  // ============================================================

  setActiveTopic: (topic) => {
    set({ activeTopic: topic });
  },

  clear: () => {
    set({
      topics: [],
      activeTopic: null,
      status: 'idle',
      error: null,
    });
  },
}));

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * The hook as the default export, matching the convention used
 * by every other store in the codebase. Consumers that prefer
 * the named form use `import { useTopicStore } from ...`;
 * consumers that prefer the default form use
 * `import useTopicStore from ...`. Both resolve to the same
 * hook.
 */
export default useTopicStore;
</file>

<file path="apps/server/handler/index.ts">
/**
 * Vercel serverless entry point for the WriteSpeare backend.
 *
 * Exports one async function that Vercel invokes for every HTTP
 * request routed to this deployment. The function's job is
 * narrow:
 *
 *   1. Ensure the MongoDB connection is live. On a cold start
 *      this means awaiting `connectDB()`; on a warm start it
 *      reuses the connection the previous request opened.
 *
 *   2. Hand the request to the shared Express app from
 *      `src/app.ts`, which owns all routing, middleware, and
 *      error handling. Nothing in this file needs to know what
 *      routes exist.
 *
 * The file deliberately does not duplicate any middleware or
 * route logic. Everything below the connection check is a single
 * `return app(req, res)` call — the Express app does the work, and
 * the two entry points (`src/index.ts` for local development and
 * this file for Vercel) stay in lockstep by sharing the same app
 * instance.
 *
 * Why the connection is cached in a module-level promise:
 *
 *   Vercel keeps a warm serverless process alive across requests.
 *   Reconnecting to MongoDB on every invocation would exhaust the
 *   connection pool, add 50–200 ms of latency to each request
 *   during the handshake, and — on MongoDB Atlas's free tier —
 *   burn through the monthly connection limit in a few hours.
 *   Caching the *promise* (rather than the resulting connection
 *   object) means two concurrent cold-start requests both await
 *   the same in-flight connection attempt rather than racing to
 *   open two.
 *
 *   If a connection attempt fails, the cache is cleared so the
 *   next request retries from a clean slate. Without that reset,
 *   a single transient failure would leave the process holding a
 *   rejected promise and every subsequent request would fail with
 *   the same stale error for the life of the process.
 *
 * Why a diagnostic endpoint exists:
 *
 *   A 500 from a Vercel deployment with no log access is one of
 *   the hardest failure modes to debug — the platform's own logs
 *   often lag by minutes, and the deployed environment differs
 *   from local in ways that are invisible without introspection.
 *   The `/api/diagnostic` branch short-circuits the Express app
 *   and answers with the resolved environment and connection
 *   state. It is read-only: it reports booleans and masked
 *   strings, never the secret values themselves, and never
 *   mutates anything.
 *
 *   The endpoint is deliberately narrow. It runs BEFORE Express
 *   so a failure in the app's middleware chain cannot prevent the
 *   diagnostic from answering. And it is scoped to the exact
 *   `/api/diagnostic` prefix, so no legitimate route can collide
 *   with it.
 *
 * Type-only imports:
 *
 *   `VercelRequest` and `VercelResponse` are imported with the
 *   `import type` form. They are erased by the compiler, so no
 *   runtime require of `@vercel/node` is emitted — the package is
 *   a devDependency, and the compiled output must not depend on
 *   its presence at deploy time.
 */

import type { VercelRequest, VercelResponse } from '@vercel/node';
import mongoose from 'mongoose';

import app from '../src/app.js';
import { connectDB } from '../src/features/shared/config/db.js';

// ============================================================
//  Connection cache
// ============================================================

/**
 * A single in-flight or resolved connection promise, shared
 * across every invocation within a warm process.
 *
 *   `null`  — no connection has been attempted in this process
 *             yet, OR the last attempt failed and the cache was
 *             reset.
 *   Promise — either an in-flight connection or a resolved one.
 *             Awaiting the same promise from multiple concurrent
 *             requests is safe: the first one performs the
 *             handshake, the rest receive the same resolution.
 *
 * Mutated only by `ensureDB` below. Never exported.
 */
let dbReady: Promise<void> | null = null;

/**
 * Return a promise that resolves once the database is connected.
 *
 * On the first call after a cold start (or after a failed
 * attempt), starts a new `connectDB()` and caches the promise. On
 * every subsequent call, returns the cached promise unchanged.
 *
 * If the underlying `connectDB()` rejects, the cache is cleared
 * before the rejection propagates. That is what lets the NEXT
 * request retry rather than being permanently wedded to a dead
 * promise for the life of the process.
 *
 * The re-throw is deliberate — the caller must see the failure
 * so it can return a 500 with an explanation. The reset is
 * equally deliberate — the failure must not be sticky.
 */
const ensureDB = (): Promise<void> => {
  if (!dbReady) {
    dbReady = connectDB().catch((err: unknown) => {
      console.error('MongoDB connection failed:', err);
      dbReady = null;
      throw err;
    });
  }
  return dbReady;
};

// ============================================================
//  Diagnostics helpers
// ============================================================

/**
 * Mask the credentials portion of a MongoDB connection URI so it
 * can be safely included in a diagnostic response.
 *
 * A URI of the shape `mongodb+srv://user:pass@host/db` becomes
 * `mongodb+srv://user:***@host/db`. The username is left in place
 * — it is not a secret on its own, and seeing it confirms which
 * cluster the process is talking to. The password is the only
 * credential that would allow an attacker to open the database,
 * so it is the only field the mask replaces.
 *
 * Returns `'NOT SET'` when the input is null or empty so a caller
 * does not have to distinguish "no URI configured" from "URI
 * configured but unparseable". A URI that does not match the
 * user:pass pattern is returned unchanged with a trailing
 * `'(unrecognized format — inspect manually)'` note so the
 * diagnostic is honest rather than silently misleading.
 */
const maskMongoUri = (uri: string | undefined): string => {
  if (typeof uri !== 'string' || uri.length === 0) {
    return 'NOT SET (falls back to mongodb://localhost:27017/writespeare)';
  }
  const masked = uri.replace(/:\/\/([^:]+):([^@]+)@/, '://$1:***@');
  if (masked === uri && uri.includes('://')) {
    // The pattern did not match but the string looks like a URI.
    // Most likely an unauthenticated URI (no credentials to mask)
    // or an unusual scheme. Return it with a note rather than
    // pretend masking happened.
    return `${uri} (no credentials present — nothing to mask)`;
  }
  return masked;
};

// ============================================================
//  Handler
// ============================================================

/**
 * The Vercel serverless handler.
 *
 * Flow, in order:
 *
 *   1. If the incoming URL begins with `/api/diagnostic`, answer
 *      the diagnostic probe and return. This branch runs BEFORE
 *      the database check so a diagnostic works even when the
 *      database is unreachable — which is exactly the scenario
 *      the diagnostic exists to help debug.
 *
 *   2. Otherwise, await `ensureDB()`. If the connection cannot be
 *      established, respond with a 500 and a short, non-leaking
 *      error message. The full error is logged for the operator;
 *      the client sees a bounded explanation.
 *
 *   3. Hand the request to the shared Express app and return its
 *      response. From this point on, this file has no
 *      responsibility — routing, middleware, and error handling
 *      all live in the app.
 *
 * The return type is `Promise<unknown>` rather than
 * `Promise<void>` because the Express app's `app(req, res)` call
 * has a return value (the `Server` instance in some overloads)
 * that this function deliberately passes through rather than
 * discards. Neither Vercel nor Express cares about the return
 * value in a serverless context, but returning it keeps the
 * function transparent — a caller inspecting the result sees
 * exactly what Express returned.
 */
export default async function handler(
  req: VercelRequest,
  res: VercelResponse
): Promise<unknown> {
  // ============================================================
  //  Diagnostic branch
  // ============================================================
  //
  // Runs before the database check so it answers even when the
  // database is down. Reports booleans and a masked URI, never
  // the secret values themselves.

  if (typeof req.url === 'string' && req.url.startsWith('/api/diagnostic')) {
    const info: Record<string, unknown> = {
      mongoUriPresent: Boolean(process.env['MONGODB_URI']),
      mongoUriMasked: maskMongoUri(process.env['MONGODB_URI']),
      jwtSecretPresent: Boolean(process.env['JWT_SECRET']),
      nodeEnv: process.env['NODE_ENV'] ?? '(unset)',
      readyStateBefore: mongoose.connection.readyState,
    };

    try {
      await ensureDB();
      info['connectResult'] = 'resolved';
    } catch (err: unknown) {
      info['connectResult'] = 'threw';
      info['connectError'] =
        err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err);
    }

    info['readyStateAfter'] = mongoose.connection.readyState;

    // The `?.` on `connection.db` is required: mongoose types the
    // field as `Db | undefined` and a diagnostic must not assume
    // a live handle just because `readyState` looks healthy.
    try {
      await mongoose.connection.db?.admin().command({ ping: 1 });
      info['pingResult'] = 'ok';
    } catch (err: unknown) {
      info['pingResult'] = 'failed';
      info['pingError'] =
        err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err);
    }

    res.status(200).json(info);
    return undefined;
  }

  // ============================================================
  //  Normal request path
  // ============================================================

  try {
    await ensureDB();
  } catch (err: unknown) {
    const message = err instanceof Error ? err.message : 'Unknown error';
    // The full error is logged for the operator. The client sees
    // only the first line of the message, prefixed with a stable
    // label, so a misconfigured MONGODB_URI does not leak the URI
    // itself back to an unauthenticated caller. The URI is
    // routinely echoed in driver-level error messages.
    console.error('Handler: database unavailable:', err);
    const safeMessage = message.split('\n')[0] ?? 'Unknown error';
    res.status(500).json({
      success: false,
      error: `Database connection failed: ${safeMessage}`,
    });
    return undefined;
  }

  return app(req, res);
}

// ============================================================
//  Named re-export
// ============================================================
//
// A caller that prefers `import { handler } from './handler/index.js'`
// over the default import gets the same function. Vercel itself
// accepts either form; the named export exists so a future test
// harness can import the handler without pulling the whole module
// through the default-export convention.

export { handler };
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/admin/middleware/adminGuard.ts">

</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/auth/controllers/authController.ts">
/**
 * Authentication controller.
 *
 * Thin HTTP layer over the auth service. Each handler:
 *
 *   1. Validates the shape of the request body or query — enough
 *      to catch a malformed client before it reaches the service.
 *
 *   2. Calls the service.
 *
 *   3. Formats the success response using the shared `ApiResponse`
 *      envelope.
 *
 * Any error the service throws (an `AppError` for known cases, a
 * raw error for unexpected cases) propagates up to the terminal
 * error middleware. Neither handler contains a try/catch — the
 * `asyncHandler` wrapper installed at the route registration site
 * forwards rejections, and the middleware classifies and formats
 * them. This keeps the controller free of any error-handling
 * logic that would duplicate what the middleware already does.
 *
 * Request validation here is intentionally minimal. The service
 * already performs the authoritative checks (email format is
 * enforced by the schema, password requirements by the login
 * flow). The controller's checks only exist to reject a request
 * that is so malformed the service would produce a confusing
 * error — a missing email, a non-string password. Anything
 * subtler is the service's concern.
 */

import type { Response } from 'express';
import {
  loginUser,
  getUserById,
  type PublicUser,
} from '../services/authService.js';
import type { AuthRequest } from '../middleware/authGuard.js';
import type {
  LoginRequest,
  LoginResponse,
  ApiResponse,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  POST /api/auth/login
// ============================================================

/**
 * Authenticate a user and return a token.
 *
 * The request body is typed as `LoginRequest` (email and password
 * as strings). TypeScript types are erased at runtime, so a
 * non-conforming request — a missing field, a numeric password,
 * a null body — is possible. The guards below check for the two
 * cases that would produce a confusing service error: an absent
 * body and non-string field values.
 *
 * On success, the response carries the `LoginResponse` shape:
 * `{ user, token }` inside the standard envelope.
 *
 * On failure, the service throws an `AppError` with a deliberate
 * status code (401 for invalid credentials, 403 for a deactivated
 * account), and the terminal middleware formats the response.
 */
export const login = async (
  req: AuthRequest<Record<string, string>, unknown, LoginRequest>,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<LoginResponse>>
): Promise<void> => {
  const body = req.body;

  // ---- Guard: body must be an object ----
  if (!body || typeof body !== 'object' || Array.isArray(body)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Request body must be a JSON object.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- Guard: email and password must be strings ----
  if (typeof body.email !== 'string' || typeof body.password !== 'string') {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Email and password are required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- Delegate to the service ----
  //
  // The service throws on any credential failure. That throw
  // propagates out of this handler, is caught by the asyncHandler
  // wrapper at the route registration site, and is forwarded to
  // the terminal middleware, which honours the AppError status
  // code. No try/catch here — the middleware is the single place
  // that knows how to format errors.
  const { token, user } = await loginUser(body.email, body.password);

  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: { user, token },
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/auth/me
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return the currently authenticated user's profile.
 *
 * This handler is always reached through the `authenticate`
 * middleware, which has already verified the token and populated
 * `req.user` with the decoded payload. The `req.user` field is
 * optional on `AuthRequest` because the type is shared with
 * unauthenticated handlers, so this handler narrows it with a
 * defensive check — if the middleware chain were ever misconfigured
 * and this handler reached without a user attached, the correct
 * response is a 401, not a crash on a null dereference.
 *
 * Two distinct failure cases, each with its own status code:
 *
 *   - No `req.user` on the request → 401. The authentication
 *     middleware did not run, or ran and rejected. Either way,
 *     the caller has no session.
 *
 *   - `req.user.userId` does not resolve to a user → 404. The
 *     token is valid and was signed for a user ID, but that user
 *     no longer exists in the database. This happens when an
 *     admin deletes an account while the client still holds a
 *     token. The correct response is 404 (the resource — the
 *     user — is gone), not 401 (the token is still valid).
 */
export const getMe = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<PublicUser>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- Guard: authentication middleware must have run ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- Delegate to the service ----
  const user = await getUserById(userId);
  if (!user) {
    res.status(404).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'User not found.',
    });
    return;
  }

  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: user,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  login,
  getMe,
};
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/auth/middleware/authGuard.ts">
/**
 * Authentication and authorization middleware for the WriteSpeare
 * backend.
 *
 * Three middleware functions live here, each serving a distinct
 * gate:
 *
 *   authenticate          — the strict gate. Requires a valid,
 *                           unexpired token belonging to a user
 *                           who still exists and is active.
 *                           Anything less produces a 401 (or 403
 *                           for the deactivated-user case). Used
 *                           by every route except login and the
 *                           public version endpoint.
 *
 *   optionalAuthenticate  — the lenient gate. Attaches a user to
 *                           the request when a valid token is
 *                           present and swallow-fails in every
 *                           other case, always calling `next()`.
 *                           Used by routes that behave differently
 *                           for logged-in and anonymous callers
 *                           but do not require a session.
 *
 *   requireAdmin          — the role gate. Must be layered AFTER
 *                           `authenticate` (or after any other
 *                           middleware that populates `req.user`).
 *                           Returns 403 when the attached user is
 *                           not an admin. Never verifies a token
 *                           itself.
 *
 * Token extraction, verification, and user lookup are the three
 * steps that would otherwise be duplicated across every protected
 * route. Centralising them here means the authentication contract
 * lives in exactly one file, and a change to that contract (say,
 * adding a token-version check) has exactly one place to go.
 *
 * Request typing:
 *
 *   `AuthRequest` extends Express's `Request` with an optional
 *   `user` field. Every controller that needs to read `req.user`
 *   types its handler parameter as `AuthRequest`, which gives the
 *   compiler the shape of `user` without a cast. The `user` field
 *   is optional because unauthenticated requests reaching a
 *   handler typed as `AuthRequest` still have `req.user === undefined`.
 *   Handlers that require a user check for it explicitly, or are
 *   protected by `authenticate` and can rely on it being present.
 */

import type { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import { verifyToken, type TokenPayload } from '../utils/jwt.js';
import { UserModel } from '../models/User.js';
import { UserRole, type ApiResponse } from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Request shape
// ============================================================

/**
 * Express `Request` extended with the decoded JWT payload.
 *
 * The `user` field is populated by `authenticate` (or
 * `optionalAuthenticate`, when a valid token is present) and read
 * by every downstream middleware and controller that needs to
 * know who is making the request.
 *
 * The field is optional because a handler typed as `AuthRequest`
 * can be reached by an unauthenticated request if the route is
 * not wrapped in `authenticate`. Handlers that require a user
 * either check for the field's presence or rely on `authenticate`
 * having run — the choice is theirs, not the middleware's.
 *
 * `TokenPayload` is deliberately used as-is rather than narrowed
 * to a richer shape. The middleware has verified the signature by
 * the time `user` is populated, so the payload's fields are
 * trustworthy; the fact that `role` is a plain string rather than
 * the `UserRole` enum is deliberate — the token payload is client-
 * visible, and keeping its type surface minimal discourages
 * callers from leaning on it for anything beyond the ID.
 */
export interface AuthRequest extends Request {
  user?: TokenPayload;
}

// ============================================================
//  Token extraction
// ============================================================

/**
 * Extract the bearer token from an incoming request's
 * `Authorization` header, or return `null` when the header is
 * missing, malformed, or empty.
 *
 * The accepted form is `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The
 * scheme match is case-insensitive because the HTTP specification
 * declares the scheme token to be case-insensitive, and some
 * clients send `bearer` in lowercase.
 *
 * The returned token is trimmed of surrounding whitespace, so a
 * stray `\r` from a CRLF-terminated header (rare but observed on
 * some HTTP clients) does not produce a verification failure that
 * looks like a signature problem.
 *
 * Exported as a standalone helper so a future audit-log
 * middleware can read the token for diagnostics without pulling
 * in the whole `authenticate` flow.
 */
export const extractToken = (req: Request): string | null => {
  const authHeader = req.headers.authorization;
  if (typeof authHeader !== 'string') {
    return null;
  }

  // Case-insensitive scheme match, then take everything after the
  // first space. Using `indexOf` rather than `split` avoids
  // copying the token when the string is large.
  const schemeEnd = authHeader.indexOf(' ');
  if (schemeEnd < 0) {
    return null;
  }

  const scheme = authHeader.slice(0, schemeEnd).toLowerCase();
  if (scheme !== 'bearer') {
    return null;
  }

  const token = authHeader.slice(schemeEnd + 1).trim();
  return token.length > 0 ? token : null;
};

// ============================================================
//  authenticate — the strict gate
// ============================================================

/**
 * Verify the request's bearer token and attach the decoded
 * payload to `req.user`. Reject the request with a structured
 * error response in every failure case.
 *
 * Failure cases, in the order they are checked:
 *
 *   1. Missing or malformed Authorization header → 401.
 *   2. Token fails signature or format verification → 401,
 *      with a message that distinguishes the expired case
 *      ("Session expired") from the invalid case ("Invalid
 *      authentication token").
 *   3. Signature is valid but the user ID in the token does not
 *      resolve to an existing user → 401. This is what happens
 *      when an admin deletes a user while that user's token is
 *      still live.
 *   4. User exists but `active` is `false` → 403. A deactivated
 *      account is a distinct case from a non-existent one; the
 *      client-side UI uses the status code to show a different
 *      message ("Account deactivated" rather than "Please log in
 *      again").
 *   5. User lookup fails for any other reason (database error,
 *      malformed ObjectId in a compromised token) → 500. The
 *      underlying error is logged server-side; the client sees
 *      a generic authentication failure so nothing about the
 *      server's internals leaks.
 *
 * On success, `next()` is called and the request proceeds down
 * the middleware chain with `req.user` populated.
 *
 * The function is `async` because it awaits the user lookup. The
 * explicit `next()` calls in each terminal branch are what keep
 * the middleware chain linear and predictable — a silent return
 * after sending a response would leave Express waiting for a
 * `next` that never comes, and the request would hang.
 */
export const authenticate = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<null>>,
  next: NextFunction
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- Step 1: extract the token ----
  const token = extractToken(req);
  if (!token) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required. Please provide a valid token.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- Step 2: verify the token ----
  //
  // `verifyToken` throws on any verification failure — expired,
  // malformed, wrong signature. The thrown error's message wraps
  // the underlying reason, so we inspect the message text to
  // distinguish the expired case, which the client should handle
  // differently from a generic invalid-token error.
  //
  // The message inspection is deliberate and documented as
  // fragile in the honesty notes for this file. The alternative —
  // exposing the raw jsonwebtoken error classes from the util
  // layer — would couple every consumer of the util to the
  // library's internal error taxonomy, which is not worth it for
  // one string comparison.
  let decoded: TokenPayload;
  try {
    decoded = verifyToken(token);
  } catch (error) {
    const raw = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error);
    const message = raw.toLowerCase().includes('expired')
      ? 'Session expired. Please log in again.'
      : 'Invalid authentication token.';
    res.status(401).json({ success: false, error: message });
    return;
  }

  // ---- Steps 3, 4, 5: user lookup, activity check, error handling ----
  try {
    // Project only the fields needed for the checks below. The
    // password hash is `select: false` on the schema, so it is
    // excluded by default; the explicit projection narrows the
    // network payload further.
    const user = await UserModel.findById(decoded.userId).select('_id active');

    if (!user) {
      res.status(401).json({
        success: false,
        error: 'User no longer exists.',
      });
      return;
    }

    if (!user.active) {
      res.status(403).json({
        success: false,
        error: 'Account is deactivated. Please contact an administrator.',
      });
      return;
    }

    // Populate the request. From this point on, every downstream
    // middleware and controller can read `req.user.userId`,
    // `req.user.email`, and `req.user.role`.
    req.user = decoded;
    next();
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('authGuard: user lookup failed:', error);
    res.status(500).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication failed due to a server error.',
    });
  }
};

// ============================================================
//  optionalAuthenticate — the lenient gate
// ============================================================

/**
 * Attempt to authenticate the request. Attach a user to the
 * request when the token is valid and belongs to an active user;
 * otherwise, do nothing. Always calls `next()`.
 *
 * This middleware NEVER sends a response. Its contract is
 * "populate `req.user` if you can, then move on regardless". The
 * downstream handler is responsible for deciding whether the
 * absence of a user is acceptable (a public profile view, for
 * example) or not (a protected action, in which case the handler
 * checks `req.user` explicitly).
 *
 * The internal token-verification block is wrapped in its own
 * try/catch so that an invalid token on an optional-auth route
 * does not produce the same 401 that `authenticate` would emit —
 * the whole point of this middleware is that a bad token is
 * treated identically to a missing one.
 *
 * The user-existence check is also wrapped, and its failure is
 * swallowed for the same reason: a stale user ID in a client's
 * stored token should not break an anonymous-accessible route.
 */
export const optionalAuthenticate = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  _res: Response,
  next: NextFunction
): Promise<void> => {
  try {
    const token = extractToken(req);
    if (!token) {
      next();
      return;
    }

    let decoded: TokenPayload;
    try {
      decoded = verifyToken(token);
    } catch {
      next();
      return;
    }

    try {
      const user = await UserModel.findById(decoded.userId).select('_id active');
      if (user && user.active) {
        req.user = decoded;
      }
    } catch {
      // swallow — this path is best-effort by contract
    }

    next();
  } catch {
    // Defensive outer catch: any unexpected throw still results in
    // a request that proceeds without an authenticated user.
    next();
  }
};

// ============================================================
//  requireAdmin — the role gate
// ============================================================

/**
 * Reject the request unless the attached user has the admin role.
 *
 * Must be layered AFTER a middleware that populates `req.user` —
 * typically `authenticate`, but `optionalAuthenticate` also
 * qualifies for routes where admin access is optional (a rare
 * case but one the layering supports without modification).
 *
 * Two failure modes:
 *
 *   - No `req.user` on the request → 401. The admin gate cannot
 *     be the first middleware on a route; if it is reached
 *     without an attached user, the route configuration is
 *     wrong, and the correct response is to reject the request
 *     rather than assume an identity.
 *
 *   - `req.user.role !== 'admin'` → 403. The user is
 *     authenticated, but lacks the required privilege. 403 (not
 *     401) is the correct status for an authenticated request
 *     that the server refuses to authorize.
 *
 * The role comparison uses the `UserRole.ADMIN` enum value
 * rather than the string literal `'admin'` so a future rename of
 * the enum value propagates here automatically. The comparison
 * itself is a plain string equality at runtime — enum values in
 * TypeScript are string literals when the enum is a string enum.
 */
export const requireAdmin = (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<null>>,
  next: NextFunction
): void => {
  if (!req.user) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  if (req.user.role !== UserRole.ADMIN) {
    res.status(403).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Admin privileges required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  next();
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  authenticate,
  optionalAuthenticate,
  requireAdmin,
  extractToken,
};
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/auth/models/User.ts">
/**
 * Mongoose model for the WriteSpeare User entity.
 *
 * Responsibilities:
 *
 *   1. Enforce the schema-level invariants of a user record — a
 *      unique, well-formed email; a non-empty password hash; a
 *      role drawn from the closed `UserRole` enum; and an `active`
 *      flag with a safe default of `true`.
 *
 *   2. Own the one operation on a user that must never be
 *      reimplemented by a caller: verifying a candidate password
 *      against the stored hash. Exposing this as an instance
 *      method (`comparePassword`) keeps `bcrypt` out of the
 *      service layer entirely, so a future refactor of the hashing
 *      strategy has exactly one file to change.
 *
 *   3. Defend the hash from accidental serialisation. The
 *      `passwordHash` path is marked `select: false`, which
 *      excludes it from every query by default; the `toJSON`
 *      transform strips it again from any document that was
 *      fetched with an explicit `.select('+passwordHash')`. Two
 *      independent guards, because a leaked hash is not the kind
 *      of mistake that announces itself until it is too late.
 *
 * The pre-save hook performs a defensive hash. It hashes the
 * `passwordHash` field ONLY when the incoming value does not
 * already look like a bcrypt hash. This is what allows the model
 * to be correct regardless of which convention the calling service
 * adopts: a service that hashes before assigning works, and a
 * service that assigns plaintext works, and neither path produces
 * a double-hashed value.
 */

import mongoose, { Schema, Document } from 'mongoose';
import { User, UserRole } from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Document interface
// ============================================================

/**
 * The runtime shape of a User document as returned by Mongoose.
 *
 * Extends `Omit<User, '_id'>` (the shared domain interface minus
 * its loosely-typed `_id`) and then re-declares `_id` with the
 * concrete ObjectId type Mongoose actually produces. This is the
 * standard pattern for a document interface: the shared domain
 * type stays transport-agnostic (its `_id` is `string | ObjectId`
 * so it can cross JSON boundaries), while the document interface
 * pins `_id` to what the ODM actually gives you in-process.
 *
 * `comparePassword` is declared here rather than on the schema's
 * `methods` object because declaring it on the interface is what
 * gives every consumer of `UserDocument` compile-time knowledge
 * that the method exists. The runtime attachment happens below via
 * `UserSchema.methods`.
 */
export interface UserDocument extends Omit<User, '_id'>, Document {
  _id: mongoose.Types.ObjectId;
  comparePassword(candidatePassword: string): Promise<boolean>;
}

// ============================================================
//  Helpers
// ============================================================

/**
 * The structural prefix shared by every bcrypt hash produced by
 * any major bcrypt implementation. The `$2a$`, `$2b$`, and `$2y$`
 * variants are all in active use; the cost factor follows as two
 * decimal digits.
 *
 * Used by the pre-save hook to detect an already-hashed value.
 * A plaintext password cannot accidentally match this pattern —
 * a user would have to type something like `$2a$10$...` verbatim,
 * which the email/password validation layer rejects upstream.
 */
const BCRYPT_HASH_PATTERN = /^\$2[aby]\$\d{2}\$/;

// ============================================================
//  Schema
// ============================================================

const UserSchema = new Schema<UserDocument>(
  {
    email: {
      type: String,
      required: [true, 'Email is required'],
      unique: true,
      trim: true,
      lowercase: true,
      match: [/^\S+@\S+\.\S+$/, 'Please provide a valid email address'],
    },
    passwordHash: {
      type: String,
      required: [true, 'Password is required'],
      select: false,
    },
    role: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: Object.values(UserRole),
        message: 'Role must be either "admin" or "user".',
      },
      default: UserRole.USER,
      required: true,
    },
    active: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: true,
      required: true,
    },
  },
  {
    timestamps: true,
    toJSON: {
      transform: (_doc, ret) => {
        delete ret['passwordHash'];
