<file path="apps/server/src/features/shared/utils/seedAdmin.ts">
/**
 * Admin seeder for the WriteSpeare backend.
 *
 * Reads ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASSWORD from the environment,
 * connects to MongoDB, and creates the super-admin user if one
 * with that email does not already exist. Run once after the
 * database is provisioned and the .env file is populated:
 *
 *     npm run seed
 *
 * The npm script (`"seed": "tsx src/features/shared/utils/seedAdmin.ts"`)
 * invokes this file directly. When `tsx` runs it, the IIFE at the
 * bottom of the file drives the whole lifecycle — seed, disconnect,
 * exit — with a status code the shell can inspect:
 *
 *     0  success (including the "already existed" no-op case)
 *     1  any failure (missing env var, weak password, database
 *        error, email collision with a non-admin user)
 *
 * Idempotency
 * -----------
 * Running the seed more than once is safe. The second run finds
 * the admin created on the first run (matched by email) and exits
 * successfully without modifying anything. The email is the
 * identity anchor: same email + existing admin = no-op.
 *
 * Safety rails
 * ------------
 *   - ADMIN_EMAIL is trimmed and lowercased to match the
 *     normalization the User schema applies on store. Without
 *     this, seeding with "Admin@Example.com" would create a user
 *     that a subsequent login with "admin@example.com" could not
 *     find — the schema lowercases on save, but only after the
 *     first write, so the in-memory value the seeder thought it
 *     created would not match what the login path looks for.
 *
 *   - ADMIN_PASSWORD must be at least eight characters. The seed
 *     is the one place a human types an admin password directly,
 *     so it is also the one place a weak password can reach the
 *     database without passing through any form validation.
 *     Refusing to seed a short password is the correct default:
 *     an admin account with a three-character password is a
 *     production incident waiting to happen.
 *
 *   - If a user with the target email already exists but is NOT
 *     an admin, the seed throws rather than silently promoting
 *     them or silently returning a success. The operator either
 *     chose the wrong email, or they intend to promote that user
 *     through the admin panel — both are decisions the seed script
 *     does not have the context to make on its own.
 *
 *   - The password is passed as plaintext to the User model's
 *     `passwordHash` field. The model's pre-save hook detects
 *     that the value does not match the bcrypt hash pattern and
 *     hashes it before persisting. This mirrors how `loginUser`
 *     handles a new user's password, and it means the seeder
 *     never needs to import the bcrypt helpers directly.
 *
 * Module-scope side effect
 * ------------------------
 * The IIFE at the bottom of the file runs whenever this module is
 * evaluated, including when it is imported by another module. That
 * is deliberate and matches the pattern established in ROOKIE's
 * seedAdmin. It has two consequences a future reader should be
 * aware of:
 *
 *   - Running `tsx src/features/shared/utils/seedAdmin.ts` (which
 *     `npm run seed` does) triggers the whole lifecycle and exits
 *     the process — exactly what a CLI script should do.
 *
 *   - Importing `{ seedAdmin }` from a test or a script would also
 *     trigger the IIFE and exit the process, which is not what a
 *     test would want. If a programmatic caller is ever needed,
 *     the correct fix is to extract the logic into a sibling
 *     `seedAdminCore.ts` and leave this file as a thin wrapper
 *     around it. That refactor is not required today.
 */

import 'dotenv/config';

import { UserModel, type UserDocument } from '../../auth/models/User.js';
import { UserRole } from '../types/index.js';
import { connectDB, disconnectDB } from '../config/db.js';

// ============================================================
//  Constants
// ============================================================

/**
 * Minimum length accepted for the ADMIN_PASSWORD environment
 * variable.
 *
 * Eight characters is the shortest conventional baseline. A
 * shorter value is nearly always a placeholder that was forgotten
 * about — the example in `.env.example` uses a much longer string
 * for exactly that reason — and catching it at seed time is
 * cheaper than discovering it in production.
 */
const MIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH = 8;

// ============================================================
//  Public API
// ============================================================

/**
 * Create the super-admin user if one with the configured email
 * does not already exist.
 *
 * Returns the admin document in both the "created" and "already
 * existed" cases so a caller can log the resulting account. Throws
 * on any configuration or database failure — the caller (the IIFE
 * below, or a future test harness) decides whether to exit or
 * retry.
 *
 * The function connects to MongoDB itself rather than requiring
 * the caller to do so. That keeps the script self-contained when
 * run directly via `tsx`, and it means a test that has already
 * opened a connection reuses it — `connectDB` is idempotent.
 */
export const seedAdmin = async (): Promise<UserDocument> => {
  // ---- 1. Read and validate environment ----
  const rawEmail = process.env['ADMIN_EMAIL'];
  const rawPassword = process.env['ADMIN_PASSWORD'];

  if (typeof rawEmail !== 'string' || rawEmail.trim().length === 0) {
    throw new Error(
      'ADMIN_EMAIL environment variable is not set. ' +
        'Set it in apps/server/.env before running the seed.'
    );
  }

  if (
    typeof rawPassword !== 'string' ||
    rawPassword.length < MIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH
  ) {
    throw new Error(
      `ADMIN_PASSWORD environment variable must be at least ` +
        `${MIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD_LENGTH} characters. ` +
        `Set it in apps/server/.env before running the seed.`
    );
  }

  const adminEmail = rawEmail.trim().toLowerCase();

  // ---- 2. Connect to the database ----
  // `connectDB` is idempotent — a caller that already opened a
  // connection reuses it rather than opening a second one. The
  // matching `disconnectDB` runs in the IIFE below, on both the
  // success and failure paths.
  await connectDB();

  // ---- 3. Look for an existing user with this email ----
  const existing = await UserModel.findOne({ email: adminEmail });

  if (existing) {
    if (existing.role === UserRole.ADMIN) {
      console.log(`Admin user already exists: ${adminEmail}`);
      return existing;
    }

    // A non-admin user with this email already exists. Refuse to
    // modify their role silently — the operator either mistyped
    // the email, or they intend to promote this user, and neither
    // is a decision this script has the context to make.
    throw new Error(
      `A user with email "${adminEmail}" already exists but is ` +
        `not an admin. Choose a different ADMIN_EMAIL, or promote ` +
        `the user through the admin panel.`
    );
  }

  // ---- 4. Create the admin ----
  // The plaintext password is passed to `passwordHash`. The User
  // model's pre-save hook detects that the value does not match
  // the bcrypt hash pattern and hashes it before persisting.
  const newAdmin = new UserModel({
    email: adminEmail,
    passwordHash: rawPassword,
    role: UserRole.ADMIN,
    active: true,
  });

  await newAdmin.save();
  console.log(`Admin user created successfully: ${adminEmail}`);
  return newAdmin;
};

// ============================================================
//  Standalone execution
// ============================================================
//
// The IIFE below runs whenever this module is evaluated — that
// includes both "run directly via tsx" and "imported by another
// module". See the file header for the consequences and for the
// refactor that would remove the import-time side effect if a
// programmatic caller ever needs it.

(async () => {
  try {
    await seedAdmin();
    await disconnectDB();
    console.log('Admin seeding completed.');
    process.exit(0);
  } catch (error) {
    const message = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error);
    console.error(`Admin seeding failed: ${message}`);

    // Best-effort cleanup. The process is about to exit regardless
    // of whether the disconnect succeeds, and a failure here must
    // not mask the original error — which is the one the operator
    // actually needs to see.
    try {
      await disconnectDB();
    } catch {
      // swallow — see comment above
    }

    process.exit(1);
  }
})();

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  seedAdmin,
};
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/topics/models/Topic.ts">
/**
 * Mongoose model for the WriteSpeare Topic entity.
 *
 * A Topic is the atomic unit of work in WriteSpeare: one title
 * in, one article out. Every Document, Article, and Report
 * references its owning Topic by `_id`. The Topic document is
 * where the user's per-topic choices live — which preset they
 * picked, which profile, which prompt template, how many sources
 * and how many words they asked for — plus the runtime status
 * that tracks where the pipeline currently is.
 *
 * Responsibilities:
 *
 *   1. Enforce the schema-level invariants of a topic record:
 *      a non-empty title, legal values for the three closed
 *      unions (status / preset / profile), numeric ranges on the
 *      two count fields, and a bounded error string.
 *
 *   2. Own the indexes that make the two access patterns the
 *      Topics page exercises efficient:
 *
 *        - "list every topic belonging to the current user,
 *           newest first" — served by { userId, createdAt }.
 *        - "filter the current user's topics by status" —
 *           served by { userId, status }.
 *
 *      Both indexes are compound with `userId` as the prefix
 *      because every query on this collection is scoped to a
 *      single user. A bare `{ status }` index would never be
 *      used: no code path queries topics across all users, and
 *      adding a wide cross-user index would slow writes for no
 *      read benefit.
 *
 *   3. Provide a single `toJSON` transform that strips Mongoose's
 *      `__v` version field, so a Topic serialised to the client
 *      matches the `Topic` interface from `shared/types` exactly.
 *      Without this, every response would carry an extra
 *      `__v: 0` field that the TypeScript type on the renderer
 *      side does not declare — the kind of small drift that
 *      eventually causes a runtime bug in code that iterates
 *      `Object.keys(topic)`.
 *
 * What this model does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not run business logic. The pipeline state
 *     transitions (draft → researching → extracting → …) are
 *     enforced by the topic service, which has the context to
 *     validate them against the caller's identity and the
 *     operation they are performing. The schema only knows the
 *     closed set of legal status values; it does not know which
 *     transitions are legal from which state.
 *
 *   - It does not enforce per-user uniqueness on `title`. A user
 *     may legitimately create two topics with the same title —
 *     for example, a rewrite under a different preset, or a
 *     duplicate they intend to edit before running. The plan's
 *     UI explicitly supports a "Duplicate" action that relies
 *     on this being allowed.
 *
 * Type unions vs. runtime enums:
 *
 *   The `TopicStatus`, `PresetName`, and `ProfileName` types in
 *   `shared/types` are string-literal union types, not runtime
 *   enums. A union type does not exist at runtime — it is erased
 *   by the compiler. To give Mongoose a runtime `enum` option
 *   for each field, this file declares an explicit array of the
 *   legal values. The three arrays are the ONLY runtime source
 *   of truth for what values are legal; if the union types in
 *   `shared/types` ever change, these arrays must be updated in
 *   the same commit or the schema and the types will drift. The
 *   pattern is intentionally verbose in exchange for being easy
 *   to grep and easy to audit against the shared types.
 */

import mongoose, { Schema, Document } from 'mongoose';
import {
  Topic,
  TopicStatus,
  PresetName,
  ProfileName,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Document interface
// ============================================================

/**
 * The runtime shape of a Topic document as returned by Mongoose.
 *
 * Extends `Omit<Topic, '_id'>` (the shared domain interface minus
 * its loosely-typed `_id`) and then re-declares `_id` with the
 * concrete ObjectId type Mongoose actually produces in-process.
 * This is the same pattern as `UserDocument` in
 * `features/auth/models/User.ts`: the shared domain type stays
 * transport-agnostic (its `_id` is `string | ObjectId` so it can
 * cross JSON boundaries), while the document interface pins
 * `_id` to what the ODM gives you.
 *
 * No instance methods are declared on this interface. Unlike the
 * User model — which needs a `comparePassword` method to keep
 * the bcrypt library out of the service layer — a Topic has no
 * per-document behaviour beyond what Mongoose provides out of the
 * box (save, validate, toJSON). Business logic lives in the
 * service.
 */
export interface TopicDocument extends Omit<Topic, '_id'>, Document {
  _id: mongoose.Types.ObjectId;
}

// ============================================================
//  Legal values (runtime counterparts of the union types)
// ============================================================
//
// Each array is annotated with its union type, which gives us a
// compile-time guarantee that every string in the array is a
// member of the union. A typo such as 'complete' instead of
// 'completed' would be flagged by tsc — the one class of drift
// this pattern is designed to catch. What it does NOT catch is a
// value MISSING from the array (a new union member added without
// a corresponding array update); that has to be caught by a
// reviewer or by an integration test that tries to save every
// legal status.

const TOPIC_STATUS_VALUES: TopicStatus[] = [
  'draft',
  'researching',
  'extracting',
  'extracted',
  'writing',
  'validating',
  'completed',
  'failed',
];

const PRESET_NAME_VALUES: PresetName[] = [
  'quick',
  'balanced',
  'deep',
  'custom',
];

const PROFILE_NAME_VALUES: ProfileName[] = [
  'blog-post',
  'news-article',
  'product-review',
  'academic',
];

// ============================================================
//  Schema
// ============================================================

const TopicSchema = new Schema<TopicDocument>(
  {
    // ---- Ownership ----
    // Every topic belongs to exactly one user. This field is the
    // anchor for every query and every authorization check: a
    // request may only read or mutate a topic where
    // `topic.userId === req.user.userId`. Indexed below as part
    // of both compound indexes.
    userId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      required: [true, 'userId is required'],
    },

    // ---- User-supplied fields ----
    title: {
      type: String,
      required: [true, 'Title is required'],
      trim: true,
      minlength: [3, 'Title must be at least 3 characters.'],
      maxlength: [300, 'Title must be at most 300 characters.'],
    },

    // Keywords arrive as an array of strings. Mongoose will
    // attempt to cast each element to a string on write; a value
    // that cannot be cast throws a CastError, which the terminal
    // error middleware maps to a 400. The service layer is
    // expected to have already trimmed and filtered empty strings
    // before calling save — the schema accepts what it is given
    // rather than silently mutating the array, so a bug in the
    // service's sanitization is visible rather than masked.
    keywords: {
      type: [String],
      default: [],
    },

    // ---- Pipeline configuration ----
    preset: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: PRESET_NAME_VALUES,
        message: 'Preset must be one of: quick, balanced, deep, custom.',
      },
      default: 'balanced',
      required: true,
    },
    profile: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: PROFILE_NAME_VALUES,
        message:
          'Profile must be one of: blog-post, news-article, product-review, academic.',
      },
      default: 'blog-post',
      required: true,
    },
    promptFile: {
      type: String,
      default: 'default.md',
      trim: true,
      maxlength: [200, 'promptFile must be at most 200 characters.'],
    },
    wordCount: {
      type: Number,
      default: 1200,
      min: [100, 'wordCount must be at least 100.'],
      max: [10000, 'wordCount must be at most 10000.'],
      validate: {
        // The built-in Number type in Mongoose is a double. Word
        // counts are conceptually integers — a target of "1200.5
        // words" is meaningless and would only appear if a caller
        // passed a float by mistake. This validator catches that
        // at the schema boundary so no downstream consumer has to
        // think about rounding.
        validator: (value: number) => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'wordCount must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    sourceCount: {
      type: Number,
      default: 10,
      min: [1, 'sourceCount must be at least 1.'],
      max: [50, 'sourceCount must be at most 50.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number) => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'sourceCount must be an integer.',
      },
    },

    // ---- Runtime status ----
    // The closed set of pipeline states. The schema validates
    // that the value is one of them; it does not enforce which
    // transitions between them are legal. That is the service's
    // job — see the file header.
    status: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: TOPIC_STATUS_VALUES,
        message:
          'Status must be one of: draft, researching, extracting, ' +
          'extracted, writing, validating, completed, failed.',
      },
      default: 'draft',
      required: true,
    },

    // ---- Failure detail ----
    // Populated only when `status === 'failed'`. The schema does
    // not enforce that invariant — the service sets and clears
    // this field in step with the status transition. Bounded at
    // 2000 characters to match the truncation the pipeline
    // already applies to error messages before they reach this
    // field.
    error: {
      type: String,
      trim: true,
      maxlength: [2000, 'error must be at most 2000 characters.'],
    },
  },
  {
    timestamps: true,
    toJSON: {
      transform: (_doc, ret) => {
        delete ret['__v'];
        return ret;
      },
    },
  }
);

// ============================================================
//  Indexes
// ============================================================
//
//  Two compound indexes cover every read path the Topics page
//  exercises. Both are prefixed by `userId` because every query
//  on this collection is scoped to a single authenticated user;
//  a query across all users is not a supported operation, so an
//  index without the userId prefix would never be selected by
//  the query planner.
//
//    { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 }
//      Serves the default "list my topics, newest first" view.
//      The `-1` on createdAt means the sort is ascending-index /
//      descending-scan — the sort clause in the query does not
//      need a separate in-memory sort step.
//
//    { userId: 1, status: 1 }
//      Serves the "filter my topics by status" view, and by
//      extension the two-index intersection the planner picks
//      for "filter by status, sorted by createdAt": MongoDB 4.4+
//      can combine the two indexes rather than falling back to a
//      collection scan.
//
//  A third index on `{ userId: 1, title: 1 }` was considered for
//  the "search my topics by title substring" workflow and
//  deliberately not added: a leading-substring search is not an
//  indexed operation regardless of the index shape, and a full-
//  text index would force a different query structure on the
//  renderer side. If title search becomes a requirement, the
//  correct index is a text index on { title } with a compound
//  variant, and that is a decision for a future session.

TopicSchema.index({ userId: 1, createdAt: -1 });
TopicSchema.index({ userId: 1, status: 1 });

// ============================================================
//  Model
// ============================================================

export const TopicModel = mongoose.model<TopicDocument>('Topic', TopicSchema);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default TopicModel;
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/topics/services/topicService.ts">
/**
 * Business logic for the WriteSpeare Topic entity.
 *
 * Five CRUD operations, each ownership-scoped. See the file
 * header in the source repository for the design rationale.
 */

import { TopicModel, type TopicDocument } from '../models/Topic.js';
import type {
  MongoId,
  TopicStatus,
  TopicCreatePayload,
  TopicUpdatePayload,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';
import { AppError } from '../../shared/middleware/errorHandler.js';

// ============================================================
//  createTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Create a new topic owned by the given user.
 *
 * The `userId` is supplied by the caller (the controller extracts
 * it from `req.user.userId`), never by the request payload. That
 * is what makes it impossible for a client to create a topic on
 * behalf of another user: the ownership field is set from the
 * authenticated session, not from anything the client controls.
 *
 * Defaults for optional fields (preset, profile, promptFile,
 * wordCount, sourceCount, status) are applied by the schema, not
 * here. Passing an explicit `undefined` would violate
 * `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, so the function conditionally
 * spreads only the fields the caller actually provided.
 *
 * Throws `AppError(400)` for an empty title (the schema's
 * `minlength: 3` also catches this, but doing it here produces a
 * clearer message than the Mongoose ValidationError's first-error
 * extraction). Any other validation failure — a bad preset, a
 * non-integer wordCount — propagates from the schema as a
 * Mongoose ValidationError, which the terminal middleware maps
 * to a 400.
 */
export const createTopic = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  payload: TopicCreatePayload
): Promise<TopicDocument> => {
  const trimmedTitle = payload.title.trim();
  if (trimmedTitle.length < 3) {
    throw new AppError(
      'Title must be at least 3 characters.',
      400
    );
  }

  const doc = new TopicModel({
    userId,
    title: trimmedTitle,
    ...(payload.keywords !== undefined
      ? { keywords: payload.keywords }
      : {}),
    ...(payload.preset !== undefined ? { preset: payload.preset } : {}),
    ...(payload.profile !== undefined ? { profile: payload.profile } : {}),
    ...(payload.promptFile !== undefined
      ? { promptFile: payload.promptFile.trim() }
      : {}),
    ...(payload.wordCount !== undefined
      ? { wordCount: payload.wordCount }
      : {}),
    ...(payload.sourceCount !== undefined
      ? { sourceCount: payload.sourceCount }
      : {}),
  });

  return await doc.save();
};

// ============================================================
//  listTopics
// ============================================================

/**
 * List every topic owned by the given user, sorted newest first.
 *
 * The optional `statusFilter` narrows the result to a single
 * pipeline state. It is a separate argument rather than a field on
 * a filter object because the service currently supports exactly
 * one filter dimension; a future addition (e.g. preset filter)
 * would arrive as a second argument, at which point the signature
 * changes to accept a filter object. Until then, the flat form is
 * the honest one.
 *
 * The sort is `createdAt: -1` — newest first, matching the
 * default view the Topics page renders. The index
 * `{ userId: 1, createdAt: -1 }` on the schema serves this query
 * without an in-memory sort stage.
 */
export const listTopics = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  statusFilter?: TopicStatus
): Promise<TopicDocument[]> => {
  const filter: { userId: MongoId; status?: TopicStatus } = { userId };
  if (statusFilter !== undefined) {
    filter.status = statusFilter;
  }

  return await TopicModel.find(filter).sort({ createdAt: -1 });
};

// ============================================================
//  getTopicById
// ============================================================

/**
 * Read a single topic by ID, scoped to the requesting user.
 *
 * Returns `null` when no topic with that ID exists OR when the
 * topic exists but belongs to a different user. The two cases are
 * deliberately indistinguishable from this function's return
 * value. A caller (the controller) converts the null into a 404,
 * never a 403, so an authenticated user cannot enumerate other
 * users' topic IDs by probing the endpoint and watching for the
 * status code to change.
 *
 * A malformed `topicId` string (not a valid ObjectId) causes
 * Mongoose's `findOne` to throw a CastError, which the terminal
 * middleware maps to a 400. That is the correct distinction:
 * "the ID is not a valid identifier" is a client error, not a
 * "topic not found" case.
 */
export const getTopicById = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  topicId: string
): Promise<TopicDocument | null> => {
  return await TopicModel.findOne({ _id: topicId, userId });
};

// ============================================================
//  updateTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Apply a partial update to a topic, scoped to the requesting
 * user.
 *
 * Only the fields present in the patch are modified. Fields
 * omitted from the patch are left unchanged on the document.
 * Fields passed as `null` are not currently supported — the
 * schema does not use `null` as a sentinel for any field, and
 * clearing a field is achieved by omitting it or by passing an
 * empty value of the field's type (an empty string for string
 * fields, an empty array for the keywords list).
 *
 * One business rule lives here rather than in the schema: when
 * `status` is being changed to anything other than `'failed'`,
 * the `error` field is unset. A topic whose status is
 * `'researching'` must not carry a stale failure message from a
 * previous attempt — the two together would be misleading in the
 * Topics list, and the pipeline only sets the error field
 * immediately before setting `status: 'failed'`.
 *
 * The reverse is not automated: if `patch.status === 'failed'`
 * and `patch.error` is not provided, the error field is left as
 * it was. The schema permits a failed topic with no error string,
 * and the pipeline may set the error in a follow-up write.
 *
 * Throws `AppError(404)` when the topic does not exist or is not
 * owned by the requesting user. The two cases are merged for the
 * same reason as in `getTopicById`.
 */
export const updateTopic = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  topicId: string,
  patch: TopicUpdatePayload
): Promise<TopicDocument> => {
  // Build the $set and $unset operations separately. Fields that
  // are being set go into $set; the `error` field being cleared
  // goes into $unset. Mixing the two into a single $set with an
  // empty-string value would leave a non-undefined `error` in the
  // document, which is not the same as the field being absent and
  // which would surface as `error: ''` in any code that checks
  // `'error' in topic`.
  const setFields: Record<string, unknown> = {};
  const unsetFields: Record<string, 1> = {};

  if (patch.title !== undefined) {
    const trimmedTitle = patch.title.trim();
    if (trimmedTitle.length < 3) {
      throw new AppError('Title must be at least 3 characters.', 400);
    }
    setFields['title'] = trimmedTitle;
  }

  if (patch.keywords !== undefined) {
    setFields['keywords'] = patch.keywords;
  }

  if (patch.preset !== undefined) {
    setFields['preset'] = patch.preset;
  }

  if (patch.profile !== undefined) {
    setFields['profile'] = patch.profile;
  }

  if (patch.promptFile !== undefined) {
    setFields['promptFile'] = patch.promptFile.trim();
  }

  if (patch.wordCount !== undefined) {
    setFields['wordCount'] = patch.wordCount;
  }

  if (patch.sourceCount !== undefined) {
    setFields['sourceCount'] = patch.sourceCount;
  }

  if (patch.status !== undefined) {
    setFields['status'] = patch.status;

    // Status moved away from 'failed' — clear any stale error.
    // Status moved TO 'failed' — only overwrite the error if the
    // caller supplied one; otherwise leave the existing message
    // in place (the schema permits a failed topic with no error
    // string, and a caller that sets 'failed' without an error
    // may set it in a follow-up write).
    if (patch.status !== 'failed') {
      unsetFields['error'] = 1;
    } else if (patch.error !== undefined) {
      setFields['error'] = patch.error;
    }
  } else if (patch.error !== undefined) {
    // Status is not being changed, but the caller is supplying an
    // error. This is a legitimate write — a caller that wants to
    // annotate an existing failed topic with a better message.
    setFields['error'] = patch.error;
  }

  // If the patch contains no actionable fields, return the
  // current document unchanged. This is more honest than issuing
  // an empty $set and returning whatever Mongoose decides.
  if (
    Object.keys(setFields).length === 0 &&
    Object.keys(unsetFields).length === 0
  ) {
    const existing = await TopicModel.findOne({ _id: topicId, userId });
    if (!existing) {
      throw new AppError('Topic not found.', 404);
    }
    return existing;
  }

  const updateOps: Record<string, Record<string, unknown>> = {};
  if (Object.keys(setFields).length > 0) {
    updateOps['$set'] = setFields;
  }
  if (Object.keys(unsetFields).length > 0) {
    updateOps['$unset'] = unsetFields;
  }

  const updated = await TopicModel.findOneAndUpdate(
    { _id: topicId, userId },
    updateOps,
    { new: true, runValidators: true }
  );

  if (!updated) {
    throw new AppError('Topic not found.', 404);
  }

  return updated;
};

// ============================================================
//  deleteTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete a topic, scoped to the requesting user.
 *
 * Returns the deleted document so the caller can cascade the
 * deletion (removing the topic's Documents, Articles, and Reports
 * if the pipeline stages that own them decide to do so). The
 * service does NOT cascade the delete itself — that is a decision
 * for each owning feature, and keeping it out of this function
 * means a future change to the cascade rules does not require
 * touching the topic service.
 *
 * Throws `AppError(404)` when the topic does not exist or is not
 * owned by the requesting user. Same merge as the other
 * ownership-scoped operations.
 */
export const deleteTopic = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  topicId: string
): Promise<TopicDocument> => {
  const deleted = await TopicModel.findOneAndDelete({
    _id: topicId,
    userId,
  });

  if (!deleted) {
    throw new AppError('Topic not found.', 404);
  }

  return deleted;
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  createTopic,
  listTopics,
  getTopicById,
  updateTopic,
  deleteTopic,
};
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/index.ts">
/**
 * Local development and long-running-server entry point for the
 * WriteSpeare backend.
 *
 * Responsibilities, in the order they execute:
 *
 *   1. Load environment variables via the `dotenv/config` side
 *      effect. This runs first because everything below reads from
 *      `process.env`.
 *
 *   2. Connect to MongoDB. If the connection cannot be
 *      established, the process exits with a non-zero code rather
 *      than serving requests against an unavailable database. A
 *      listener that accepts traffic but fails every query is
 *      worse than no listener at all — it turns a clear startup
 *      failure into a confusing runtime one.
 *
 *   3. Start the HTTP listener on the resolved port. The Express
 *      app itself is imported from `./app.js`, where all
 *      middleware and routes are configured. This file does not
 *      know what routes exist — its only job is to give them a
 *      socket to listen on.
 *
 *   4. Register the process-level signal handlers (SIGINT,
 *      SIGTERM) and the fatal-error handlers (uncaughtException,
 *      unhandledRejection). Both categories route through the
 *      same shutdown routine so the database connection is closed
 *      cleanly in every exit path.
 *
 * Why this file is not used on Vercel:
 *
 *   Vercel invokes a single exported handler function per
 *   request; it never starts a long-running HTTP listener. The
 *   serverless entry point lives in `handler/index.ts`, which
 *   imports the same Express app and hands it each incoming
 *   request. Both entry points share the app instance via the
 *   module cache, so the middleware configuration and route table
 *   are identical regardless of which one is serving.
 *
 * Why the `PORT` resolution is a function and not a constant:
 *
 *   The environment variable arrives as a string, may be absent,
 *   may be an empty string, or may contain garbage. The
 *   `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` compiler flag means
 *   `process.env['PORT']` is typed as `string | undefined`, so the
 *   resolution has to be explicit at every read. Wrapping it in a
 *   function that returns a validated `number` (or the default)
 *   keeps the rest of the file free of ad-hoc parsing.
 *
 * Why there is no top-level `await`:
 *
 *   The `startServer` function is exported and the call to it at
 *   the bottom of the file is deliberately un-awaited. Awaiting it
 *   at module scope would require the file to be an async module,
 *   which changes how the module cache behaves under some Node
 *   versions and interacts badly with the singleton pattern used
 *   by `app.ts`. The un-awaited call is fine: `startServer` handles
 *   every failure internally and only throws if `process.exit`
 *   itself fails, which is not a recoverable condition.
 */

import 'dotenv/config';

import type { Server } from 'node:http';

import app from './app.js';
import { connectDB, disconnectDB } from './features/shared/config/db.js';

// ============================================================
//  Configuration
// ============================================================

/**
 * Port the listener falls back to when the environment does not
 * provide a valid one. Five thousand is a widely used default for
 * local Node development, and it does not collide with the ports
 * the desktop app's embedded Chrome instances occupy (those start
 * at 9222 and climb from there).
 */
const DEFAULT_PORT = 5000;

/**
 * The environment name, defaulting to `'development'`.
 *
 * Read once here and referenced from every log line and branch
 * below. Using a single constant means the environment cannot be
 * logged differently from the way it is checked — a class of bug
 * that would only show up when someone wonders why production logs
 * say "development" or vice versa.
 */
const NODE_ENV = process.env['NODE_ENV'] ?? 'development';

/**
 * Resolve the listener port from the environment.
 *
 * Order of preference:
 *
 *   1. `process.env['PORT']` if it parses to a valid TCP port.
 *   2. `DEFAULT_PORT` if the variable is absent, empty, whitespace-
 *      only, non-numeric, negative, zero, or above 65535.
 *
 * The validation is deliberately strict rather than permissive. A
 * typo in `.env` that produced `PORT=50O0` (letter O) would parse
 * as `50` under a lenient `parseInt` call, silently binding the
 * server to a port nobody expects. Failing over to the default is
 * louder than that: the startup log line will show the port the
 * server actually bound to, and the discrepancy between that and
 * what the developer typed is visible at a glance.
 *
 * Only the `PORT` variable is read here. The database URI and the
 * JWT secret are validated by their own modules (`db.ts` and
 * `jwt.ts` respectively) — each module owns the validation for the
 * variables it consumes, so a missing secret fails at the JWT
 * module's load time with a message that names the variable.
 */
const resolvePort = (): number => {
  const raw = process.env['PORT'];
  if (typeof raw !== 'string') return DEFAULT_PORT;

  const trimmed = raw.trim();
  if (trimmed.length === 0) return DEFAULT_PORT;

  const parsed = Number.parseInt(trimmed, 10);
  if (!Number.isFinite(parsed)) return DEFAULT_PORT;
  if (parsed <= 0 || parsed > 65535) return DEFAULT_PORT;

  return parsed;
};

// ============================================================
//  Graceful shutdown
// ============================================================

/**
 * Close the database connection and exit the process.
 *
 * Called from every terminal signal handler below. Swallows the
 * disconnect error on the way out — at this point the process is
 * terminating regardless, and there is no useful recovery from a
 * failed close. Logging the error and exiting with a non-zero
 * code would be a stronger signal, but that would also cause a
 * monitoring platform to distinguish "clean shutdown" from
 * "shutdown after a close error" for what is, from the outside,
 * the same event: the process is going down.
 *
 * The `signal` argument is included in the log so an operator
 * reading the console can tell whether the shutdown was user-
 * initiated (SIGINT from Ctrl+C), service-manager-initiated
 * (SIGTERM from a supervisor), or a crash (uncaughtException /
 * unhandledRejection).
 */
const gracefulShutdown = async (signal: string): Promise<void> => {
  console.log(`Received ${signal}. Shutting down...`);
  try {
    await disconnectDB();
    console.log('Database connection closed.');
    process.exit(0);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error during shutdown:', error);
    process.exit(1);
  }
};

// ============================================================
//  Server bootstrap
// ============================================================

/**
 * Connect the database, start the listener, and install the
 * process-level handlers.
 *
 * Ordering rationale:
 *
 *   The database connection is awaited before the listener starts.
 *   A listener that accepts traffic before the database is ready
 *   would return 500s for the brief window between `app.listen()`
 *   returning and the first successful query — and a health check
 *   that happens to hit during that window would restart the
 *   process on a platform that treats a failing health check as a
 *   signal to recycle. Serializing the two eliminates the window.
 *
 *   The signal handlers are registered after the listener starts.
 *   Before that point there is no connection to close gracefully
 *   and no reason to intercept signals — the default behaviour of
 *   terminating the process is already the correct response to a
 *   SIGINT that arrives during startup.
 *
 * Returns the `http.Server` instance the caller can use to close
 * the listener from a test or from a future admin endpoint. The
 * return type is `Promise<Server>` rather than `Promise<void>`
 * because the caller may legitimately want to await shutdown, and
 * exposing the server handle costs nothing while making that
 * possible.
 *
 * Throws only if `connectDB` throws. That throw is not caught here
 * — it propagates to the caller at the bottom of the file, where
 * it is logged and converted into a `process.exit(1)`. Every other
 * failure inside the function is handled locally so the caller
 * only has to reason about one throw path.
 */
export const startServer = async (): Promise<Server> => {
  // ---- 1. Connect to the database ----
  // The `connectDB` function is idempotent, so a test that boots
  // the app more than once in the same process reuses the
  // existing connection rather than opening a second one.
  await connectDB();
  console.log('Database connected.');

  // ---- 2. Start the HTTP listener ----
  // `app.listen` returns the `http.Server` instance. The callback
  // runs once the listener is bound; the log lines inside it are
  // the first indication that the server is ready to accept
  // traffic.
  const server = app.listen(resolvePort(), () => {
    console.log(
      `Server listening on http://localhost:${resolvePort()}`
    );
    console.log(`API base:    http://localhost:${resolvePort()}/api`);
    console.log(`Health:      http://localhost:${resolvePort()}/health`);
    console.log(`Environment: ${NODE_ENV}`);
    console.log('Press Ctrl+C to stop.');
  });

  // ---- 3. Register the shutdown handlers ----
  // SIGINT: the user pressed Ctrl+C in the terminal. SIGTERM: a
  // service manager or process supervisor asked the process to
  // stop. Both route through `gracefulShutdown` so the database
  // connection is closed cleanly regardless of who initiated the
  // shutdown.
  process.on('SIGINT', () => {
    void gracefulShutdown('SIGINT');
  });

  process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
    void gracefulShutdown('SIGTERM');
  });

  // ---- 4. Register the fatal-error handlers ----
  // An uncaught exception or an unhandled promise rejection means
  // the process is in an undefined state. Node's default behaviour
  // is to print the error and exit with a non-zero code; the only
  // thing this handler adds is a clean database disconnect before
  // that exit, so a monitoring platform does not see a dangling
  // TCP socket that it has to reap.
  process.on('uncaughtException', (error: Error) => {
    console.error('Uncaught exception:', error);
    void gracefulShutdown('uncaughtException');
  });

  process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason: unknown) => {
    console.error('Unhandled rejection:', reason);
    void gracefulShutdown('unhandledRejection');
  });

  return server;
};

// ============================================================
//  Bootstrap
// ============================================================

/**
 * Boot the server immediately when this module is imported.
 *
 * The call is un-awaited because `startServer` handles every
 * internal failure except `process.exit` itself. The `.catch` is
 * a defensive net against an unexpected synchronous throw from
 * `resolvePort` (which is total, so it cannot throw) or from
 * `app.listen` (which only throws if the port is invalid, but
 * `resolvePort` guarantees a valid port). If the catch ever runs,
 * the input is a bug worth surfacing, not a state worth
 * recovering from.
 *
 * The log line inside the catch names the file so the failure is
 * traceable without a stack dive.
 */
void startServer().catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error('Failed to start server:', error);
  process.exit(1);
});

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  startServer,
};
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/shared/api/client.ts">
/**
 * Axios client for talking to the WriteSpeare backend.
 *
 * This module owns the one HTTP connection the desktop app makes
 * to the backend. It is used by the main process's feature
 * services — for example `topics/services/topicsApi.ts` — which
 * call `apiGet`, `apiPost`, and the other wrappers below. The
 * IPC handlers that feature modules register then pass the
 * resulting envelope straight through to the preload, which
 * resolves the renderer's `window.electronAPI.*` call with the
 * same envelope. See the file header of `src/main/preload.ts`
 * for the full chain.
 *
 * The renderer does not import this module. The golden rules
 * forbid the renderer from making backend calls directly —
 * everything goes through `window.electronAPI.*`. The compiled
 * renderer bundle therefore does not contain any of the code
 * below; the module is compiled only into the main-process
 * output (via tsc) because only the main process reaches it.
 *
 * The three concerns this module owns:
 *
 *   1. Base URL. The axios instance's `baseURL` is set to the
 *      `API_BASE_URL` constant declared in
 *      `shared/constants/index.ts`. That constant is the app's
 *      default; a future session that adds a runtime override
 *      (the settings page can, in principle, point the app at a
 *      self-hosted backend) will call `setBaseURL(url)` — the
 *      setter is not defined yet because no caller needs it, and
 *      adding it speculatively would give future code a place
 *      to write state that nothing currently reads.
 *
 *   2. Auth header. A module-level `authToken` holds the bearer
 *      token, and the request interceptor attaches it to every
 *      outgoing request as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The
 *      token is injected by the main process via `setAuthToken`,
 *      which `main/index.ts` and the auth IPC handler call on
 *      every login and logout. Storing the token in a module
 *      variable rather than in the electron-store is deliberate:
 *      the store is the source of truth, and the variable here
 *      is a fast-access cache of it. When the store changes, the
 *      variable is updated. When the process restarts, the
 *      variable is reinitialized from the store during startup.
 *
 *   3. 401 handling. The response interceptor inspects every
 *      error response for a 401 status. On a 401, it clears the
 *      module-level token and invokes the handler registered via
 *      `setUnauthorizedHandler`. That handler is expected to
 *      clear the persistent store and notify the renderer (via
 *      IPC) to redirect to the login page. The interceptor
 *      itself does neither — it has no access to the store or
 *      the window — which is why the handler indirection exists.
 *
 * The uniform return contract:
 *
 *   The four wrapper functions (`apiGet`, `apiPost`, `apiPatch`,
 *   `apiDelete`) all return `Promise<ApiResponse<T>>` and never
 *   reject. Any failure — a 4xx/5xx from the server, a network
 *   error, a DNS failure, a JSON parse failure, a timeout — is
 *   converted into an envelope with `success: false` and a
 *   human-readable `error` string. This mirrors the backend's
 *   own response contract and the IPC contract, so the same
 *   envelope flows from the HTTP boundary all the way to the
 *   renderer's caller without any conversion layer in between.
 *
 *   The alternative — throwing on failure — would force every
 *   caller (each feature's service, each IPC handler, each
 *   renderer hook) to wrap its call in a try/catch. That
 *   duplication is exactly what the envelope pattern exists to
 *   avoid.
 *
 * Why the module-level state and not a factory:
 *
 *   The plan's file-tree description for this module says
 *   "Axios instance" — singular. There is one backend, one
 *   token, and one 401 handler per process; a factory that
 *   produced multiple instances would have no caller. A
 *   module-level singleton with setters for the two pieces of
 *   mutable state (the token, the handler) is the simplest
 *   shape that fits the description and the usage.
 */

import axios, { type AxiosError, type AxiosInstance } from 'axios';

import { API_BASE_URL } from '../constants/index.js';
import type { ApiResponse } from '../types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Module state
// ============================================================

/**
 * The bearer token the request interceptor attaches to every
 * outgoing request. `null` means "no active session" — the
 * interceptor skips the Authorization header in that case, which
 * is what the login endpoint needs and what the app wants before
 * any session exists.
 *
 * Mutated only by `setAuthToken` below. The interceptor reads it
 * on every request; there is no caching to invalidate.
 */
let authToken: string | null = null;

/**
 * The callback the response interceptor invokes when the backend
 * returns a 401. Registered by `main/index.ts` (or by the auth
 * IPC handler) at startup. `null` means "no handler registered"
 * — the interceptor still clears the local token but cannot
 * trigger a UI redirect, which is the correct fallback when the
 * app is shutting down or the handler has not yet been wired.
 */
let unauthorizedHandler: (() => void) | null = null;

/**
 * Set or clear the bearer token the client attaches to
 * subsequent requests.
 *
 * Called at three points in the app's lifetime:
 *
 *   - On startup, from `main/index.ts`, with the token read from
 *     the encrypted store — this restores the session before any
 *     request is made.
 *   - On login success, from the auth IPC handler, with the
 *     token returned by the backend.
 *   - On logout (or 401-triggered session expiry), with `null`.
 *
 * Passing `null` is equivalent to clearing — there is no separate
 * `clearAuthToken` function because the two operations are the
 * same and a distinct name for the same behavior would be
 * redundant surface.
 */
export const setAuthToken = (token: string | null): void => {
  authToken = token;
};

/**
 * Register the callback the response interceptor invokes on a
 * 401 response. Passing `null` unregisters the current handler
 * * and leaves the interceptor's token-clearing behavior intact.
 *
 * The handler is expected to (a) clear the encrypted store's
 * token and cached user, (b) call `setAuthToken(null)` — though
 * the interceptor already does this — and (c) notify the
 * renderer via IPC so the UI can redirect to `/login`. The
 * interceptor does not attempt any of these itself; it only
 * signals that the session is gone.
 */
export const setUnauthorizedHandler = (
  handler: (() => void) | null
): void => {
  unauthorizedHandler = handler;
};

// ============================================================
//  Axios instance
// ============================================================

/**
 * The single axios instance shared by every feature service in
 * the main process. Constructed once at module load, with the
 * default base URL and a thirty-second timeout.
 *
 * The timeout is generous because the backend's endpoints are
 * all fast CRUD operations — the desktop-side operations that
 * take seconds (research, extraction, writing) run as Python
 * child processes in the main process and do not go through the
 * backend's HTTP API. A thirty-second ceiling catches a
 * genuinely hung connection without cutting off a legitimate
 * request during a moment of unusual load.
 *
 * `Content-Type` is set as a default for the same reason axios
 * would set it anyway on a request with a body. Making it
 * explicit here means a future code path that forgets to pass
 * a body still sends the header, and the backend's JSON parser
 * treats the (empty) body as an empty object rather than as a
 * form-encoded payload.
 */
const client: AxiosInstance = axios.create({
  baseURL: API_BASE_URL,
  timeout: 30_000,
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
});

// ============================================================
//  Request interceptor
// ============================================================

/**
 * Attach the bearer token to every outgoing request, when one
 * exists.
 *
 * The check is `if (authToken)` rather than `if (authToken !==
 * null)` — an empty string token and a null token both skip the
 * header, which is the correct behavior because the backend
 * would reject an empty-string token with the same 401 it would
 * return for a missing one.
 *
 * The header is set via `headers.set(...)` — the type-safe form
 * for axios v1's `AxiosHeaders` class — rather than by direct
 * property assignment. Both work at runtime; the `.set()` form
 * is the one axios v1 documents and type-checks cleanly under
 * the project's strict TypeScript settings.
 */
client.interceptors.request.use((config) => {
  if (authToken) {
    config.headers.set('Authorization', `Bearer ${authToken}`);
  }
  return config;
});

// ============================================================
//  Response interceptor
// ============================================================

/**
 * Detect 401 responses and dispatch to the unauthorized handler.
 *
 * The interceptor does three things on a 401:
 *
 *   1. Clears the module-level token so no subsequent request
 *      carries the stale credential. Without this, every
 *      request after the first 401 would fire another 401 —
 *      each one triggering the handler — until the app finally
 *      cleared the token through some other path.
 *
 *   2. Invokes the registered handler, if any. The handler
 *      performs the store cleanup and the IPC notification
 *      described in its own docstring.
 *
 *   3. Re-rejects the error so the wrapper function that
 *      initiated the request can convert it into a
 *      `{ success: false, error }` envelope. Rejecting rather
 *      than silently swallowing is what lets the caller see the
 *      failure; without the re-throw, the promise would resolve
 *      to `undefined` and every caller would need a null check.
 *
 * The handler invocation is wrapped in a `try`/`catch` so a
 * bug in the handler does not mask the original 401 from the
 * caller. The handler's own error is logged; the caller still
 * sees the 401 as the reason the request failed.
 *
 * The interceptor does NOT convert the 401 into a success
 * envelope — that is the wrapper functions' job, performed on
 * the way back up the chain. Keeping the interceptor's
 * responsibility narrow (detect and signal) and the wrappers'
 * responsibility broad (fully normalize any failure into the
 * envelope) means there is exactly one place where the envelope
 * is constructed.
 */
client.interceptors.response.use(
  (response) => response,
  (error: AxiosError) => {
    if (error.response?.status === 401) {
      authToken = null;
      if (unauthorizedHandler) {
        try {
          unauthorizedHandler();
        } catch (handlerError) {
          // The handler is expected to be well-behaved; a throw
          // from it is a bug in the handler. Log it and continue
          // — the caller still sees the 401 rejection.
          console.error(
            '[api/client] unauthorized handler threw:',
            handlerError
          );
        }
      }
    }
    return Promise.reject(error);
  }
);

// ============================================================
//  Error conversion
// ============================================================

/**
 * Convert any thrown value — an axios error, a network failure,
 * a parsing error, a programming error in a caller — into a
 * standard `ApiResponse<T>` with `success: false`.
 *
 * Three cases, handled in order of specificity:
 *
 *   1. An axios error whose `response.data` already looks like
 *      our envelope. This is the common case — the backend
 *      returns `{ success: false, error: '...' }` for 4xx and
 *      5xx responses — and the correct behavior is to pass the
 *      envelope through unchanged. The check for
 *      `typeof body.success === 'boolean'` is what distinguishes
 *      a real envelope from an arbitrary JSON object the server
 *      might have returned (a raw 404 body, a proxy's HTML
 *      error page that got parsed as JSON, and so on).
 *
 *   2. An axios error with a response but no recognizable
 *      envelope. This happens when a proxy or an intermediary
 *      returns a non-JSON error body, or when the backend
 *      itself returns a shape the desktop does not recognize.
 *      The response's status code is used to build a generic
 *      message — enough for the caller to log or display
 *      something actionable, without leaking the raw body.
 *
 *   3. An axios error with no response at all — a network
 *      timeout, a DNS failure, a connection refused. The
 *      axios error's `message` carries the reason; it is used
 *      directly.
 *
 * Any non-axios error falls through to the last branch, which
 * wraps its message (or a generic string for non-`Error` values)
 * into the envelope. This branch should never fire in production
 * — every path in this module produces an axios error — but
 * treating it as an explicit case avoids an `any`-typed fallback.
 */
const toApiResponse = <T>(error: unknown): ApiResponse<T> => {
  if (axios.isAxiosError(error)) {
    const data: unknown = error.response?.data;

    if (
      typeof data === 'object' &&
      data !== null &&
      typeof (data as { success?: unknown }).success === 'boolean'
    ) {
      return data as ApiResponse<T>;
    }

    if (error.response) {
      return {
        success: false,
        error: `Request failed with status ${error.response.status}.`,
      };
    }

    return {
      success: false,
      error: error.message || 'Unable to reach the server.',
    };
  }

  return {
    success: false,
    error:
      error instanceof Error
        ? error.message
        : 'An unexpected error occurred.',
  };
};

// ============================================================
//  Typed wrappers
// ============================================================

/**
 * Send a GET request and return the response body as an
 * `ApiResponse<T>`. Never rejects. See the file header for why
 * the uniform "always returns an envelope" contract is the
 * right one for this layer.
 */
export const apiGet = async <T>(url: string): Promise<ApiResponse<T>> => {
  try {
    const response = await client.get<ApiResponse<T>>(url);
    return response.data;
  } catch (error) {
    return toApiResponse<T>(error);
  }
};

/**
 * Send a POST request with an optional JSON body. Never rejects.
 */
export const apiPost = async <T>(
  url: string,
  body?: unknown
): Promise<ApiResponse<T>> => {
  try {
    const response = await client.post<ApiResponse<T>>(url, body);
    return response.data;
  } catch (error) {
    return toApiResponse<T>(error);
  }
};

/**
 * Send a PATCH request with an optional JSON body. Never rejects.
 */
export const apiPatch = async <T>(
  url: string,
  body?: unknown
): Promise<ApiResponse<T>> => {
  try {
    const response = await client.patch<ApiResponse<T>>(url, body);
    return response.data;
  } catch (error) {
    return toApiResponse<T>(error);
  }
};

/**
 * Send a DELETE request with an optional JSON body. Never rejects.
 *
 * The body parameter is optional because the backend's delete
 * endpoints do not currently accept one, but the signature
 * accepts it so that a future endpoint that needs to carry a
 * reason or a confirmation token can do so without a signature
 * change here.
 */
export const apiDelete = async <T>(
  url: string,
  body?: unknown
): Promise<ApiResponse<T>> => {
  try {
    const response = await client.delete<ApiResponse<T>>(url, {
      data: body,
    });
    return response.data;
  } catch (error) {
    return toApiResponse<T>(error);
  }
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * The raw axios instance, exported for consumers that need to
 * configure something the typed wrappers do not expose — a
 * request with a custom response type, a streaming response, a
 * request that overrides the default timeout for one call.
 *
 * The feature services should use the wrappers. The default
 * export exists as an escape hatch, not as the recommended
 * interface. If a caller reaches for the raw instance, the
 * caller takes on responsibility for handling the axios error
 * shape — the wrappers do not.
 */
export default client;
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/shared/constants/index.ts">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — shared constants.
 *
 * The app's shared constants — the values that more than one
 * feature needs and that must not drift between the places that
 * reference them. Everything in this file is either a primitive
 * (a string, a number) or a closed set of primitives represented
 * as a readonly tuple with a matching literal-type alias.
 *
 * Why this module is a leaf:
 *
 *   This file imports nothing. Every symbol it exports is either
 *   a literal value or a type derived from a literal value using
 *   TypeScript's own `as const` / `typeof` machinery. That
 *   property matters because it is the first file of Session 5 —
 *   the "shared UI" session — and every other shared module
 *   (the types file, the API client, the UI components) either
 *   imports from this one or from nothing. A leaf that requires
 *   no other file to exist before it can compile is what makes
 *   it safe to create first.
 *
 * Why the preset and profile names are exported as both a
 * runtime array and a derived type:
 *
 *   The two closed sets — the set of preset names and the set of
 *   profile names — are consumed in two different ways by the
 *   rest of the codebase:
 *
 *     - At runtime, as iterable lists. The preset selector and
 *       the profile picker in the New Topic modal both need to
 *       render one option per name; both need an array to `.map`
 *       over. The arrays exported here are that array.
 *
 *     - At compile time, as literal-union types. Every service,
 *       store, and IPC handler that carries a preset name or a
 *       profile name needs the type to be the specific union, not
 *       `string`. The two type aliases derived below — via
 *       `(typeof ARRAY)[number]` — give exactly that literal
 *       union without redeclaring the list of names in two forms.
 *
 *   The alternative — declaring the union type by hand and the
 *   array separately — has the classic drift risk: someone adds
 *   a preset to the array but forgets to add it to the union (or
 *   vice versa), and the compiler either complains in a confusing
 *   place or, worse, accepts a mismatch that surfaces as a
 *   runtime bug. Deriving the type from the array makes the array
 *   the single source of truth; the compiler automatically
 *   narrows any consumer of `PresetName` to exactly the strings
 *   the array contains.
 *
 * Relationship to the backend's mirror declarations:
 *
 *   The backend's `apps/server/src/features/shared/types/index.ts`
 *   declares the same two unions — `PresetName` and
 *   `ProfileName` — because the desktop app and the backend are
 *   independent compilation units and neither can import from
 *   the other. The two declarations are kept in sync by hand.
 *   When a new preset or profile is added on one side, the
 *   corresponding array on the other side must be updated in the
 *   same change, or a request that the desktop considers legal
 *   will be rejected by the backend's schema (or vice versa).
 *   This is the accepted cost of the two-app architecture; the
 *   alternative — a shared package — was considered and rejected
 *   in the plan because it would force the backend and the
 *   desktop to be built and deployed together.
 */

// ============================================================
//  Identity
// ============================================================

/**
 * The product's display name. Used in window titles, toast
 * messages, log lines, and any user-facing string that needs to
 * name the app.
 *
 * Declared here rather than read from `package.json` at runtime
 * because the renderer bundle does not have filesystem access —
 * and because a template-literal import from package.json would
 * force the bundler to inline the entire manifest, which carries
 * far more than the one field anyone needs.
 */
export const APP_NAME = 'WriteSpeare';

// ============================================================
//  API
// ============================================================

/**
 * The default base URL for the backend API.
 *
 * In development, the backend runs on `http://localhost:5000` —
 * the port is the `DEFAULT_PORT` constant declared in the
 * backend's `src/index.ts`. The `/api` suffix is the mount prefix
 * every backend route lives under.
 *
 * At runtime, the renderer does not read this constant directly.
 * The main process owns the actual URL, which can be overridden
 * from the settings page (the app supports pointing at a
 * self-hosted backend), and exposes the current value to the
 * renderer via the `config:getApiBaseUrl` IPC channel. This
 * constant is the fallback the main process uses when no override
 * has been configured, and the default the settings page shows
 * in its "API base URL" field.
 *
 * The URL has no trailing slash — the axios client concatenates
 * paths with a leading slash (`/topics`, `/auth/login`), and a
 * trailing slash on the base would produce `//topics`, which
 * some proxies reject. The rule "no trailing slash on the base"
 * is enforced by convention, not by a runtime check; a wrong
 * value here would be caught the first time the app made a
 * request.
 */
export const API_BASE_URL = 'http://localhost:5000/api';

/**
 * The closed set of preset identifiers.
 *
 * The four values are the three system presets shipped with the
 * app plus the sentinel `'custom'`, which marks a topic that has
 * been configured with settings not matching any named preset.
 * The `'custom'` value is not a selectable preset in the picker;
 * it exists so that a topic's `preset` field has a well-typed
 * value in the case where the user has overridden the preset's
 * defaults through the Advanced Settings panel.
 *
 * The array is `readonly` and declared with `as const` so that
 * TypeScript infers it as a tuple of literal string types rather
 * than as `string[]`. That inference is what makes the
 * `PresetName` type below resolve to the literal union rather
 * than to `string`.
 */
export const PRESET_NAMES = [
  'quick',
  'balanced',
  'deep',
  'custom',
] as const;

/**
 * The literal-union type of preset identifiers, derived from the
 * `PRESET_NAMES` tuple above. Consumers that want the type should
 * import this, not redeclare it — a redeclaration would drift the
 * moment the tuple changed.
 */
export type PresetName = (typeof PRESET_NAMES)[number];

/**
 * Human-readable labels for each preset, keyed by identifier.

 * object so that the compiler enforces exhaustiveness: if a new
 * preset identifier is added to `PRESET_NAMES` and the label is

 * is selectable but renders as `undefined` in the picker.

  quick: 'Quick',
  balanced: 'Balanced',
  deep: 'Deep',
  custom: 'Custom',

/**

 * selectable option. The text reflects what the value means when
 * it appears as a topic's state.
 */
export const PRESET_DESCRIPTIONS: Record<PresetName, string> = {
  quick: '5 sources, 800 words. Fast — good for a first draft.',
  balanced: '10 sources, 1200 words. The recommended default.',
  deep: '20 sources, 2000+ words. For in-depth, pillar content.',
  custom: 'Configured with custom settings.',
};

<file path="apps/desktop/src/features/shared/types/index.ts">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — shared domain types for the desktop app.
 *
 * This module is the desktop's mirror of the backend's
 * `apps/server/src/features/shared/types/index.ts`. It declares
 * every domain entity, every request payload, and every status
 * union that crosses the HTTP boundary between the two apps.
 * Both sides of the desktop app — the main process (which makes
 * the HTTP requests and parses the responses) and the renderer
 * (which renders the parsed data) — import from here.
 *
 * The two apps are independent compilation units:
 *
 *   The desktop app and the backend app share no TypeScript
 *   source. The plan's golden rules make this explicit — the
 *   boundary between them is HTTP and JSON, not an import. Both
 *   sides declare their own copy of each shared shape, and the
 *   two declarations are kept in sync by hand. When a field is
 *   added to a backend entity, the corresponding field must be
 *   added here in the same change, or the desktop will silently
 *   omit it from the objects it constructs or fails to render
 *   it when it arrives. This is the accepted cost of the
 *   two-app architecture; a shared package was considered and
 *   rejected because it would force the two apps to be built
 *   and deployed together.
 *
 * Wire format vs. backend's in-process shape:
 *
 *   Where the backend's types describe an in-process Mongoose
 *   document, this module describes what the same data looks
 *   like after the JSON round trip. Three differences are
 *   systematic:
 *
 *     1. IDs. The backend declares `_id` and every foreign key
 *        as `string | ObjectId` — the Mongoose `MongoId` type.
 *        A JSON response serializes an ObjectId to its hex
 *        string form, so on the desktop every ID is a `string`.
 *        This module uses `string` for every ID field without
 *        exception.
 *
 *     2. Timestamps. The backend declares `createdAt`,
 *        `updatedAt`, and every other date field as `Date`. A
 *        JSON response serializes a Date to its ISO-8601 string
 *        form, and axios does not parse strings into Dates. So
 *        on the desktop every timestamp is a `string`, and any
 *        component that needs a `Date` object constructs one at
 *        the display site (`new Date(createdAt)`).
 *
 *     3. The password hash. The backend's `User` interface
 *        includes `passwordHash` because the field is part of
 *        the entity. The backend strips it before serializing,
 *        so the desktop's `User` does NOT include the field at
 *        all. A consumer that tried to read `user.passwordHash`
 *        would be a compile error, which is the correct
 *        behaviour — the field never reaches the desktop, so
 *        the desktop should not be able to reference it.
 *
 *   Two types declared on the backend — `MongoId` and
 *   `PaginatedResponse<T>` — are not declared here. `MongoId`
 *   exists only to describe the union of serialized and
 *   in-process forms, and there is no in-process form on the
 *   desktop. `PaginatedResponse<T>` is not used by any
 *   endpoint the desktop consumes; the topics list, the
 *   documents list, and the reports list all return plain
 *   arrays.
 *
 * Re-export of PresetName and ProfileName:
 *
 *   The two literal-union types `PresetName` and `ProfileName`
 *   are declared in `../constants/index.ts` — where their
 *   runtime arrays live — and re-exported here so that a
 *   consumer that wants to import "everything domain-shaped"
 *   from this module can do so without a second import from
 *   the constants module. The constants module remains the
 *   single source of truth for both the arrays and the derived
 *   unions; this module's re-export is a convenience, not a
 *   second declaration.
 *
 * UserRole is a union type, not an enum:
 *
 *   The backend declares `UserRole` as a string enum
 *   (`UserRole.ADMIN = 'admin'`, `UserRole.USER = 'user'`).
 *   The enum has a runtime representation, which the backend
 *   uses in `requireAdmin` middleware to compare a caller's
 *   role against the admin value. The desktop never performs
 *   that comparison — the backend rejects a non-admin request
 *   with a 403, and the renderer's `Layout` component only
 *   reads the role to decide whether to show the "Admin" nav
 *   link. A union type (`'admin' | 'user'`) is enough for both
 *   uses and has no runtime cost. The full literal set is
 *   declared here rather than imported because the desktop's
 *   union and the backend's enum are independent declarations
 *   of the same two values.
 */

import type {
  PresetName,
  ProfileName,
} from '../constants/index.js';

// Re-export the two constants-declared unions so that a
// consumer can import "everything domain-shaped" from one
// module. See the file header for why the constants module is
// the source of truth and this re-export is a convenience.
export type { PresetName, ProfileName } from '../constants/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  API response envelope
// ============================================================

/**
 * The shape of every response that crosses the backend's HTTP
 * boundary — success or failure.
 *
 * The `success` flag is the discriminator. On `true`, `data`
 * carries the payload; on `false`, `error` carries a
 * human-readable message. `message` is reserved for optional
 * non-fatal context that a caller may surface as a toast.
 *
 * The generic parameter `T` is unconstrained; consumers
 * instantiate it with the payload type of the specific endpoint
 * they are calling. A default of `null` is used for endpoints
 * that return no payload (`logout`, `clearToken`) so that a
 * caller does not have to write `ApiResponse<null>` in every
 * case.
 */
export interface ApiResponse<T = null> {
  success: boolean;
  data?: T;
  message?: string;
  error?: string;
}

// ============================================================
//  User & Authentication
// ============================================================

/**
 * The two roles a user account can hold.
 *
 * See the file header for why this is a union type rather than
 * an enum.
 */
export type UserRole = 'admin' | 'user';

/**
 * The public shape of a user account as the desktop receives it
 * from the backend.
 *
 * The `passwordHash` field that the backend's `User` interface
 * declares is deliberately absent — the backend strips it before
 * serializing, so the field never reaches the desktop. See the
 * file header for the systematic ID and timestamp conversions
 * that apply to every entity in this module.
 */
export interface User {
  _id: string;
  email: string;
  role: UserRole;
  active: boolean;
  createdAt: string;
  updatedAt: string;
}

/**
 * The payload the admin feature sends when creating a new user
 * through the `POST /api/users` endpoint.
 */
export interface UserCreatePayload {
  email: string;
  password: string;
  role?: UserRole;
  active?: boolean;
}

/**
 * The payload for a partial update to a user. Every field is
 * optional; the backend merges the patch onto the existing
 * document.
 */
export interface UserUpdatePayload {
  email?: string;
  password?: string;
  role?: UserRole;
  active?: boolean;
}

/**
 * The body of a login request. Sent to `POST /api/auth/login`.
 */
export interface LoginRequest {
  email: string;
  password: string;
}

/**
 * The body of a successful login response.
 *
 * The `user` object is the desktop's `User` type — which is
 * already the client-safe shape, with the password hash
 * stripped. The `token` is a bearer JWT the desktop stores in
 * the encrypted `electron-store` and attaches to every
 * subsequent request through the axios client's request
 * interceptor.
 */
export interface LoginResponse {
  user: User;
  token: string;
}

/**
 * The lifecycle state of a topic. Matches the backend's
 * `TopicStatus` union exactly — the string values are what
 * crosses the wire, and the backend's schema validates the
 * value against the same set.
 */
export type TopicStatus =
  | 'draft'
  | 'researching'
  | 'extracting'
  | 'extracted'
  | 'writing'
  | 'validating'
  | 'completed'
  | 'failed';

/**
 * A topic — the atomic unit of work in WriteSpeare. One topic
 * owns one pipeline: search → extraction → writing → validation
 * → export. Every document, article, and report references its
 * owning topic by `_id`.
 */
export interface Topic {
  _id: string;
  userId: string;
  title: string;
  keywords: string[];
  preset: PresetName;
  profile: ProfileName;
  promptFile: string;
  wordCount: number;
  sourceCount: number;
  status: TopicStatus;
  /** Populated only when `status === 'failed'`. */
  error?: string;
  createdAt: string;
  updatedAt: string;
}

/**
 * The payload for creating a topic.
 *
 * `userId` is derived from the authenticated session on the
 * backend and is not part of the payload. The remaining fields
 * are the values the user chose in the New Topic modal, all
 * optional except the title.
 */
export interface TopicCreatePayload {
  title: string;
  keywords?: string[];
  preset?: PresetName;
  profile?: ProfileName;
  promptFile?: string;
  wordCount?: number;
  sourceCount?: number;
}

/**
 * The payload for a partial update to a topic. Every field is
 * optional; the backend merges the patch onto the existing
 * document.
 */
export interface TopicUpdatePayload {
  title?: string;
  keywords?: string[];
  preset?: PresetName;
  profile?: ProfileName;
  promptFile?: string;
  wordCount?: number;
  sourceCount?: number;
  status?: TopicStatus;
  error?: string;
}

/**
 * The narrowing criteria the topics list supports.
 *
 * The backend's `GET /api/topics` endpoint accepts an optional
 * `?status=` query parameter; this type models that filter. It
 * is the closest equivalent on the desktop to the ROOKIE plan's

 * passed through to a list endpoint. If a future session adds
 * another filter dimension (a preset filter, a date range), it

export interface TopicFilters {
  status?: TopicStatus;
}
