/**
 * The pass/warn/fail classification of a validation section.
 * Matches the backend's `ReportStatus` union.
 */
export type ReportStatus = 'good' | 'warning' | 'fail';

/**
 * The readability section of a validation report. Values are
 * produced by `textstat` on the article body with Markdown
 * markup stripped.
 */
export interface ReadabilityReport {
  /** 0–100, higher is easier to read. Plain-English band: 60–70. */
  fleschReadingEase: number;
  /** Approximate US school grade level. Target band: 7–9. */
  fleschKincaidGrade: number;
  /** Gunning Fog index. Target: under 12. */
  gunningFog: number;
  /** SMOG index. Target: under 12. */
  smogIndex: number;
  /** Average words per sentence across the article. */
  avgSentenceLength: number;
  /** Estimated reading time for an average adult reader, in seconds. */
  readingTimeSeconds: number;
  status: ReportStatus;
}

/**
 * The structural SEO section of a report. Measures shape, not
 * content quality — heading counts, paragraph sizes, and the
 * ratio of passive to active voice.
 */
export interface SeoReport {
  wordCount: number;
  h2Count: number;
  h3Count: number;
  /** Average words per paragraph, split on blank-line boundaries. */
  avgParagraphWords: number;
  /** 0–1; fraction of sentences flagged as passive by the parser. */
  passiveVoicePercent: number;
  /** 0–1; fraction of sentences containing a transition word. */
  transitionWordsPercent: number;
  status: ReportStatus;
}

/**
 * Per-keyword placement and density. One entry per keyword the
 * user supplied on the topic, plus any keyword extracted from
 * the source corpus and accepted by the user.
 */
export interface KeywordReportEntry {
  keyword: string;
  priority: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'supporting';
  /** Total occurrences in the article body. */
  count: number;
  /** `count / wordCount`, expressed as a fraction (0–1). */
  density: number;
  /** Whether the keyword appears in the H1 title. */
  inTitle: boolean;
  /** Whether the keyword appears in the first 100 words. */
  inIntro: boolean;
  /** Number of H2 sections whose heading contains the keyword. */
  inH2Count: number;
  status: ReportStatus;
}

/**
 * The keywords section of a report. Wraps the per-entry array
 * with an aggregate status so the section matches the shape of
 * every other section.
 */
export interface KeywordReport {
  keywords: KeywordReportEntry[];
  status: ReportStatus;
}

/**
 * One sentence from the generated article that scored above the
 * configured similarity threshold against one or more source
 * documents.
 */
export interface FlaggedSentence {
  text: string;
  /** 0–1; the highest similarity this sentence scored against any source. */
  similarity: number;
  /** Human-readable label of the source document it matched. */
  sourceTitle: string;
}

/**
 * The originality section of a report. Two independent
 * similarity signals are reported side by side: TF-IDF catches
 * lexical overlap, semantic similarity catches paraphrase.
 */
export interface OriginalityReport {
  /** Highest TF-IDF cosine similarity against any source doc. */
  maxTfidfSimilarity: number;
  /** Highest embedding cosine similarity against any source doc. */
  maxSemanticSimilarity: number;
  flaggedSentences: FlaggedSentence[];
  status: ReportStatus;
}

/**
 * One overused AI-tell phrase and how many times it appeared.
 */
export interface AiMarkerEntry {
  phrase: string;
  count: number;
}

/**
 * The AI-marker section of a report. Counts occurrences of
 * phrases that are statistically over-represented in LLM output.
 */
export interface AiMarkersReport {
  markerCount: number;
  markers: AiMarkerEntry[];
  status: ReportStatus;
}

/**
 * One grammatical or stylistic issue raised by LanguageTool.
 * `offset` and `length` are character positions in the article
 * body, used by the UI to highlight the offending span.
 */
export interface GrammarIssue {
  ruleId: string;
  message: string;
  offset: number;
  length: number;
  replacements: string[];
}

/**
 * The grammar section of a report.
 */
export interface GrammarReport {
  issueCount: number;
  issues: GrammarIssue[];
  status: ReportStatus;
}

/**
 * The complete validation report for one article. Every section
 * is required — a report is only written when all six validators
 * have completed, so a partially-populated report would indicate
 * a bug in the runner.
 */
export interface Report {
  _id: string;
  articleId: string;
  topicId: string;
  userId: string;
  readability: ReadabilityReport;
  seo: SeoReport;
  keywords: KeywordReport;
  originality: OriginalityReport;
  aiMarkers: AiMarkersReport;
  grammar: GrammarReport;
  /** The weakest status across all six sections. */
  overallStatus: ReportStatus;
  createdAt: string;
}

<file path="apps/desktop/src/main/index.ts">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — Electron main process entry point.
 *
 * This is the file `package.json` points at via its `main` field
 * (`dist/main/index.js`). When Electron starts the app, it runs
 * this script in the Node.js context of the main process — the
 * one process that can create windows, spawn child processes,
 * read and write the user's filesystem, and reach the OS's native
 * APIs. Every other script in the app runs either in the
 * preload's isolated context or in the sandboxed renderer, both
 * of which are strictly more limited.
 *
 * Responsibilities, in execution order:
 *
 *   1. Declare the custom `writespeare-asset://` scheme to
 *      Chromium via `registerProtocolSchemes()`. This must run
 *      BEFORE the `ready` event — Electron enforces the ordering
 *      by throwing if the call happens later. See
 *      `./protocols.ts` for the full rationale.
 *
 *   2. Inside `app.whenReady()` — after Chromium has finished
 *      initialising but before any window is created — install
 *      the request handler for the scheme via
 *      `registerProtocolHandlers()`.
 *
 *   3. Create the app's main `BrowserWindow` and load the
 *      renderer into it. In development, the window loads the
 *      Vite dev server URL; in production, it loads the bundled
 *      `dist/renderer/index.html`.
 *
 *   4. Install the three lifecycle hooks every Electron app
 *      needs:
 *
 *        - `window-all-closed` — quit the app on Windows and
 *          Linux when the last window closes. On macOS, stay
 *          running (the platform's convention is that the app
 *          survives with no windows and reopens on a dock click).
 *
 *        - `activate` — on macOS, reopen the main window when the
 *          user clicks the dock icon with no windows open.
 *
 *        - `before-quit` — the shutdown hook. This is where the
 *          app will kill any running Python child processes and
 *          dispose any schedulers before the process exits. The
 *          hook exists today with no work to do; it will grow as
 *          the research, extraction, and writer features are
 *          built in later sessions.
 *
 * What this file does NOT do yet — IPC handler registration:
 *
 *   The plan says this file is responsible for "IPC handler
 *   registration" — importing each feature's IPC module and
 *   calling its registration function. None of those modules
 *   exists on disk yet: they are declared in Sessions 6–19 of
 *   the plan (auth, topics, research, documents, writer,
 *   validation, export, settings, admin, automation).
 *
 *   This file therefore does not import them. Importing a module
 *   that does not exist would be a compile error, and stubbing
 *   one would violate the execution protocol. Instead, the file
 *   is written so that IPC registration happens in a single,
 *   clearly marked place inside the `whenReady` callback. As each
 *   feature's IPC module is created in its session, one import
 *   line is added at the top of this file and one registration
 *   call is added in that block — the exact incremental pattern
 *   the backend's `app.ts` uses for its route mounts.
 *
 *   The consequence today is that `window.electronAPI` exists in
 *   the renderer (its shape is defined by the preload), but every
 *   method it exposes will reject with "no handler registered for
 *   'channel:name'" until the corresponding IPC module is wired
 *   in. That is expected: the shell is what Session 4 produces;
 *   the IPC handlers are what Sessions 6–19 produce.
 *
 * Window creation — the settings that matter and why:
 *
 *   contextIsolation: true — the security boundary that keeps
 *     the preload's JavaScript context separate from the
 *     renderer's. Without it, the renderer could reach into the
 *     preload's scope and modify the exposed API. This is
 *     Electron's default and must never be turned off.
 *
 *   nodeIntegration: false — the renderer runs in the browser
 *     sandbox and has no access to Node's `require`, `process`,
 *     or `fs`. All access flows through the preload's
 *     `contextBridge`. Also Electron's default.
 *
 *   sandbox: false — this one is a deliberate deviation from
 *     Electron's default. The app's `package.json` declares
 *     `"type": "module"`, which makes the compiled preload an
 *     ESM file (`.js` interpreted as ESM). Electron's sandboxed
 *     preload context only supports CommonJS; to run an ESM
 *     preload, sandbox must be disabled. The trade-off is
 *     acceptable because `contextIsolation` and
 *     `nodeIntegration` are the two boundaries that actually
 *     protect the renderer from the OS; `sandbox` protects
 *     against a compromised Node context being able to install
 *     itself into a compromised renderer, which is a narrower
 *     concern. A future session that wants to re-enable the
 *     sandbox would need to compile the preload as CommonJS —
 *     a build-pipeline change that is out of scope for this
 *     file.
 *
 *   preload — the path to the compiled preload script. In the
 *     built app, this file lives at `dist/main/index.js`, and
 *     the preload lives alongside it at `dist/main/preload.js`,
 *     so the path is `path.join(__dirname, 'preload.js')`. The
 *     `__dirname` equivalent for an ESM module is derived from
 *     `import.meta.url` below.
 *
 *   show: false + ready-to-show — the window is created hidden
 *     and only shown once its content has painted. Without this,
 *     the user would see a blank white rectangle for the first
 *     few hundred milliseconds while the renderer loads. The
 *     `ready-to-show` event fires when the first frame has been
 *     rendered, and `win.show()` at that point produces a window
 *     that opens with content already in place.
 *
 * Renderer loading — dev vs. production:
 *
 *   `app.isPackaged` is the standard Electron flag for "am I a
 *   packaged app or a development process". In development, it
 *   is `false`, and the window loads the Vite dev server URL so
 *   the renderer gets hot-module-replacement. In production, it
 *   is `true`, and the window loads the bundled HTML from the
 *   app's own resources.
 *
 *   The dev URL is hard-coded to `http://localhost:5173` because
 *   `vite.config.ts` pins the dev server to that port with
 *   `strictPort: true`. If the port is ever changed in the Vite
 *   config, the constant below must change with it.
 */

import { app, BrowserWindow } from 'electron';
import path from 'node:path';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';

import {
  registerProtocolSchemes,
  registerProtocolHandlers,
} from './protocols.js';

// ============================================================
//  Constants
// ============================================================

/**
 * The Vite dev server URL the renderer is loaded from while
 * `app.isPackaged` is `false`. Must match the `server.port`
 * value declared in `vite.config.ts` — see the file header for
 * why the two are coupled.
 */
const DEV_SERVER_URL = 'http://localhost:5173';

/**
 * Default window dimensions. The width and height are the size
 * the window opens at; the minimums are the smallest size the
 * user is allowed to shrink it to. 1024×720 is the smallest
 * size at which the app's sidebar + main content layout still
 * fits without horizontal scrolling; the default of 1440×900 is
 * a comfortable size on a modern high-DPI display.
 */
const WINDOW_DEFAULT_WIDTH = 1440;
const WINDOW_DEFAULT_HEIGHT = 900;
const WINDOW_MIN_WIDTH = 1024;
const WINDOW_MIN_HEIGHT = 720;

/**
 * The background color the window paints before its content
 * loads. Matches the light-mode `background` token declared in
 * `tailwind.config.js`, so the brief moment between window
 * creation and first paint is not a flash of a different color.
 *
 * If the user has the app configured for dark mode, this color
 * is wrong for them — but the window only shows this color for
 * the few hundred milliseconds before React mounts and the theme
 * applies. Using a fixed value here is simpler than reading the
 * user's theme preference before the renderer has loaded it, and
 * the flash is small enough that the complexity is not worth it.
 */
const WINDOW_BACKGROUND = '#ffffff';

// ============================================================
//  ESM directory resolution
// ============================================================

/**
 * The directory this file lives in, as an absolute path. In the
 * built app, that is `dist/main/`.
 *
 * ESM does not provide `__dirname` as a global the way CommonJS
 * does, so it is reconstructed here from `import.meta.url` — the
 * file's own `file://` URL — via `fileURLToPath` and
 * `path.dirname`. This is the canonical replacement and is used
 * by every ESM module in the codebase that needs its own
 * directory.
 */
const currentDir = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));

// ============================================================
//  Module-scope state
// ============================================================

/**
 * The app's main window, held in a module-scope binding so that
 * the `activate` handler (macOS) and the `before-quit` handler
 * can reach it. The binding is set when the window is created
 * and cleared when it is closed — a window's `closed` event
 * fires after the window has been destroyed, so leaving the
 * reference in place would risk a use-after-destroy from any
 * later code that touched it.
 */
let mainWindow: BrowserWindow | null = null;

/**
 * `true` when running from source (development), `false` when
 * running from a packaged build. Read once at module load and
 * cached so the numerous dev/prod branches throughout this file
 * do not each re-read the property.
 */
const isDev = !app.isPackaged;

// ============================================================
//  Phase 1 — protocol scheme registration
// ============================================================
//
//  MUST run before app.whenReady() resolves. Electron throws if
//  a scheme is registered after ready, and the throw happens
//  inside the ready callback rather than at startup, which
//  produces a confusing delayed failure. Doing it here, at
//  module load, is the correct timing.

registerProtocolSchemes();

// ============================================================
//  Window factory
// ============================================================

/**
 * Build the app's main window and load the renderer into it.
 *
 * Called from inside the `whenReady` handler (for the first
 * window) and again from the macOS `activate` handler when the
 * user clicks the dock icon with no windows open. Because the
 * function has no state beyond its arguments and the module-
 * scope `mainWindow` binding, calling it twice produces two
 * independent windows rather than a shared one — which is what
 * the macOS convention expects.
 *
 * The return value is the newly-created window; the caller is
 * responsible for storing it in `mainWindow` if it wants to
 * track it.
 */
const createWindow = (): BrowserWindow => {
  const win = new BrowserWindow({
    width: WINDOW_DEFAULT_WIDTH,
    height: WINDOW_DEFAULT_HEIGHT,
    minWidth: WINDOW_MIN_WIDTH,
    minHeight: WINDOW_MIN_HEIGHT,

    // Do not show the window until its content has rendered.
    // The `ready-to-show` listener below calls `.show()` at the
    // right moment. See the file header for the rationale.
    show: false,

    // Hide the menu bar on Windows and Linux. The app does not
    // declare a custom menu, and the default Electron menu
    // (File / Edit / View / Window / Help) is not part of the
    // app's design. On macOS the menu bar is OS-level and not
    // affected by this setting.
    autoHideMenuBar: true,

    // The color the window paints before its content loads. See
    // the constant's docstring for why it is a fixed value.
    backgroundColor: WINDOW_BACKGROUND,

    // The web preferences that govern the renderer's security
    // posture. See the file header for the reasoning behind each.
    webPreferences: {
      preload: path.join(currentDir, 'preload.js'),
      contextIsolation: true,
      nodeIntegration: false,
      sandbox: false,
      // `webSecurity` is left at its default (`true`), which
      // enforces the same-origin policy in the renderer. It is
      // spelled out here as a comment rather than a value so a
      // future reader does not mistake its absence for an
      // oversight.
    },
  });

  // Reveal the window once Chromium has rendered the first frame.
  win.once('ready-to-show', () => {
    win.show();
  });

  // Load the renderer. In development, from the Vite dev server;
  // in production, from the bundled HTML file that Vite wrote to
  // `dist/renderer/`.
  if (isDev) {
    void win.loadURL(DEV_SERVER_URL);

    // Open the Chromium DevTools in a separate window so the
    // developer can inspect the renderer. Detached mode is
    // deliberate — docking the DevTools inside the app's window
    // would shrink the renderer to a size the design was not
    // laid out for, which produces misleading visual bugs.
    win.webContents.openDevTools({ mode: 'detach' });
  } else {
    void win.loadFile(path.join(currentDir, '../renderer/index.html'));
  }

  // Clear the module-scope reference when this window is
  // destroyed. See the docstring on `mainWindow` for why.
  win.on('closed', () => {
    if (mainWindow === win) {
      mainWindow = null;
    }
  });

  return win;
};

// ============================================================
//  Lifecycle — ready
// ============================================================

/**
 * The app's startup sequence. Runs once, when Electron has
 * finished loading Chromium and the Node runtime is fully
 * available.
 *
 * The three steps are ordered deliberately:
 *
 *   1. `registerProtocolHandlers()` before any window is
 *      created. The window's first paint will request images
 *      through the custom scheme; if the handler is not yet
 *      installed, those requests fail with a network error and
 *      the window's content shows broken-image placeholders.
 *      Installing the handler first guarantees the scheme is
 *      ready before the renderer asks for anything.
 *
 *   2. IPC handler registration. See the block comment below.
 *
 *   3. Window creation. The window is the last step so that
 *      everything it will need at first paint — the scheme
 *      handler and the IPC handlers — is already in place.
 *
 * The `activate` listener is installed inside this callback
 * rather than at module scope because the listener references
 * `BrowserWindow.getAllWindows()`, which is only meaningful once
 * the app is ready. Installing it earlier would work but would
 * tie the listener to an app in a pre-ready state, which is a
 * corner case worth avoiding.
 */
void app.whenReady().then(() => {
  // ---- 1. Install the protocol handler ----
  // See `./protocols.ts` for the scheme's full specification.
  registerProtocolHandlers();

  // ---- 2. IPC handler registration ----
  //
  // Feature IPC modules are registered here, one per feature,
  // as each session of the plan creates them. Each module is
  // expected to export a `register*IPC()` function whose body
  // calls `ipcMain.handle(...)` for the channels that feature
  // serves.
  //
  // The lines below are ordered by session number so that a
  // future reader scanning this block sees the same sequence
  // the plan's coding order uses. They are commented out until
  // their target modules exist.
  //
  //   import { registerAuthIPC } from '../features/auth/ipc/authIPC.js';              // Session 6
  //   import { registerTopicsIPC } from '../features/topics/ipc/topicsIPC.js';        // Session 7
  //   import { registerResearchIPC } from '../features/research/ipc/researchIPC.js';  // Session 10
  //   import { registerDocumentsIPC } from '../features/documents/ipc/documentsIPC.js'; // Session 12
  //   import { registerWriterIPC } from '../features/writer/ipc/writerIPC.js';        // Session 14
  //   import { registerValidationIPC } from '../features/validation/ipc/validationIPC.js'; // Session 16
  //   import { registerExportIPC } from '../features/export/ipc/exportIPC.js';        // Session 17
  //   import { registerSettingsIPC } from '../features/settings/ipc/settingsIPC.js';  // Session 18
  //   import { registerAdminIPC } from '../features/admin/ipc/adminIPC.js';           // Session 19
  //   import { registerAutomationIPC } from '../features/automation/ipc/automationIPC.js'; // Session 20
  //
  //   registerAuthIPC();
  //   registerTopicsIPC();
  //   registerResearchIPC();
  //   registerDocumentsIPC();
  //   registerWriterIPC();
  //   registerValidationIPC();
  //   registerExportIPC();
  //   registerSettingsIPC();
  //   registerAdminIPC();
  //   registerAutomationIPC();

  // ---- 3. Create the main window ----
  mainWindow = createWindow();

  // ---- macOS activate handler ----
  // On macOS, closing the last window does not quit the app.
  // When the user clicks the dock icon with no windows open,
  // macOS fires the `activate` event and the app is expected to
  // reopen its main window. On other platforms this event does
  // not fire — the app's lifecycle is simpler — so the handler
  // is effectively a no-op there.
  app.on('activate', () => {
    if (BrowserWindow.getAllWindows().length === 0) {
      mainWindow = createWindow();
    }
  });
});

// ============================================================
//  Lifecycle — window-all-closed
// ============================================================

/**
 * Quit the app when its last window closes, except on macOS.
 *
 * This is the standard Electron pattern. On Windows and Linux,
 * a desktop app that has no windows has no reason to keep
 * running — the process should exit and free its resources. On
 * macOS, the platform convention is the opposite: the app stays
 * alive with no windows, and the user reopens a window by
 * clicking the dock icon (which fires the `activate` event
 * handled above). Respecting the platform convention on each
 * OS is what makes an Electron app feel native rather than
 * ported.
 */
app.on('window-all-closed', () => {
  if (process.platform !== 'darwin') {
    app.quit();
  }
});

// ============================================================
//  Lifecycle — before-quit
// ============================================================

/**
 * The app's shutdown hook.
 *
 * This is where the app disposes of anything that would otherwise
 * become an orphaned process or a leaked resource when the app
 * exits. As of this session, there is nothing to dispose — the
 * research, extraction, and writer features that spawn Python
 * child processes are built in later sessions.
 *
 * The hook exists now so that the shape of the shutdown
 * sequence is in place from the start. When a feature begins
 * spawning child processes, the cleanup call is added here in
 * the same session that introduces the spawning. The alternative
 * — adding the hook when the first child process is created —
 * would mean a session that adds a feature but forgets to add
 * the cleanup, and that forgetfulness would produce zombies
 * that are hard to diagnose.
 *
 * The handler is `async` even though the current body is
 * synchronous, because every future addition to it (killing a
 * child process via `tree-kill`, awaiting a `childProcess.kill`
 * promise, waiting for a Chrome instance to disconnect) will be
 * asynchronous. The `void` in front of the callback invocation
 * suppresses the "floating promise" lint warning that would
 * otherwise fire on the ignored return value.
 */
app.on('before-quit', () => {
  void (async () => {
    // ---- Shutdown sequence ----
    //
    // When feature sessions add child processes, the cleanup
    // calls go here, in reverse order of their creation so that
    // a process that depends on another is killed first. The
    // ordering note is preserved even though the list is empty
    // today, so the first future addition does not have to
    // rediscover it.
    //
    // Example shape once populated (commented for reference):
    //
    //   await writerService.killAll();
    //   await extractionService.killAll();
    //   await searchService.killAll();
    //   await chromeLauncher.killAll();
  })();
});

<file path="apps/desktop/src/main/preload.ts">
/**
 * Electron preload script for the WriteSpeare desktop app.
 *
 * This file runs in a special context that Electron creates
 * between the main process and each renderer — it has access to
 * the full `ipcRenderer` API but is not visible to the page's own
 * JavaScript except through the objects the script explicitly
 * exposes on `window`. That isolation is the whole point of the
 * preload: it is the only sanctioned bridge between the sandboxed
 * renderer and the capabilities of the Node/Electron environment.
 *
 * The app's golden rule is that the renderer never touches Node
 * or Python directly — everything goes through
 * `window.electronAPI.*`. This file is where that API is defined.
 * Every method on every namespace ultimately calls
 * `ipcRenderer.invoke(channel, ...args)` and awaits the main
 * process's response. The main process registers a handler for
 * each channel via `ipcMain.handle(...)`; the channels are named
 * `namespace:action` and the namespaces here mirror the feature
 * folders under `src/features/` one-for-one.
 *
 * Why the API is typed as `Promise<ApiResponse<T>>`:
 *
 *   The backend's HTTP API and the main process's IPC handlers
 *   both follow the same envelope convention — `{ success,
 *   data?, error? }` — so a caller cannot accidentally treat a
 *   failed operation as a success by checking only for the
 *   presence of `data`. The preload preserves that envelope as
 *   the return type of every `invoke` method, so the renderer's
 *   service layer (`shared/api/client.ts` and the feature-level
 *   `services/*.ts` files) can unwrap it once and return plain
 *   data up the chain. Making the envelope visible at this layer
 *   is what keeps the error-handling contract consistent from
 *   the HTTP boundary all the way to the renderer's stores.
 *
 * The `on` / `off` / `once` registry — why the wrappers:
 *
 *   `ipcRenderer.on(channel, listener)` registers a listener that
 *   receives an `IpcRendererEvent` as its first argument. The
 *   renderer's own callbacks do not want the event object; they
 *   want only the payload the main process sent. The three
 *   wrappers below strip the event and pass the remaining
 *   arguments through, so the renderer sees a callback signature
 *   of `(...args: unknown[]) => void`.
 *
 *   `off` cannot simply call `ipcRenderer.removeListener(channel,
 *   callback)` because `callback` is the renderer's original
 *   function, not the wrapped function that was actually
 *   registered. Without the wrapper, `removeListener` would be
 *   passed a function that was never added to the emitter and the
 *   removal would silently fail — the listener would keep firing
 *   forever. The registry below remembers the wrapped function
 *   for each `(channel, callback)` pair, so `off` can look up the
 *   correct reference and remove it.
 *
 *   `once` uses Electron's own `once` — it removes itself after
 *   the first invocation, so no registry entry is needed.
 *
 * Forward references:
 *
 *   The `../features/shared/types/index.js` module does not yet
 *   exist on disk (it is created in Session 5 of the plan). All
 *   the type imports from it are `import type`, which TypeScript
 *   erases at emit time — the compiled JavaScript never contains
 *   a `require` for that module. As a consequence, the file will
 *   run correctly at runtime even before Session 5 completes;
 *   only the `npm run type-check` pass will complain until the
 *   types file is in place.
 */

import { contextBridge, ipcRenderer, type IpcRendererEvent } from 'electron';

import type {
  ApiResponse,
  AppVersion,
  Article,
  Document,
  LoginRequest,
  LoginResponse,
  Preset,
  PresetCreatePayload,
  PresetName,
  ProfileName,
  Report,
  Topic,
  TopicCreatePayload,
  TopicStatus,
  TopicUpdatePayload,
  User,
  UserRole,
  UserSetting,
  UserSettingsMap,
} from '../features/shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Type definitions
// ============================================================
//
//  The interface below is the single source of truth for the
//  shape of `window.electronAPI`. Every method's signature —
//  argument types and return type — is declared here rather than
//  inferred from the implementation, so the renderer's `Window`
//  augmentation (bottom of this file) can reference it without
//  duplicating any type information. If a method's runtime
//  implementation ever drifted from its signature, the compiler
//  would flag the mismatch at the point of assignment.

/**
 * A listener callback registered through `on`, `off`, or `once`.
 *
 * The parameter type is `unknown[]` rather than a typed payload
 * because the events flowing main→renderer carry different
 * payload shapes per channel (a string for a status update, a
 * number for progress, an object for a candidate list). The
 * renderer's listener is expected to narrow the arguments it
 * receives using a runtime check before using them, since the
 * event source is out of TypeScript's reach. The same trade-off
 * applies at the HTTP boundary, where responses are also
 * untyped until the client narrows them.
 */
type IpcListener = (...args: unknown[]) => void;

/**
 * The auth namespace — login, logout, and reading the cached
 * user profile.
 */
interface AuthNamespace {
  /**
   * Exchange credentials for a bearer token and a user object.
   * On success the main process also persists both to the
   * encrypted store, so a subsequent cold start can restore the
   * session before the network round trip completes.
   */
  login: (
    credentials: LoginRequest
  ) => Promise<ApiResponse<LoginResponse>>;

  /**
   * Clear the session on the main process side — delete the
   * stored token and the cached user from the encrypted store.
   * The backend has no logout endpoint; sessions are stateless
   * JWTs, and revoking one requires either waiting for its `exp`
   * or rotating the signing secret.
   */
  logout: () => Promise<ApiResponse<null>>;

  /**
   * Read the currently cached user, or null if no session exists.
   * Used by the renderer's cold-start sequence to populate the
   * auth store before any network request is made.
   */
  getUser: () => Promise<ApiResponse<User | null>>;
}

/**
 * The config namespace — read-only access to the desktop app's
 * own configuration: which backend URL it points at, which
 * version is running, and which platform it is on.
 *
 * Nothing in this namespace writes to the config; the settings
 * the user can change live under the `settings` namespace. The
 * config here is the app's own boot-time state, established
 * before any user is signed in and not editable from the UI.
 */
interface ConfigNamespace {
  /** The backend base URL the app is currently pointed at. */
  getApiBaseUrl: () => Promise<ApiResponse<string>>;

  /** The desktop app's own version, as declared in package.json. */
  getAppVersion: () => Promise<ApiResponse<string>>;

  /** The OS platform — 'win32', 'darwin', or 'linux'. */
  getPlatform: () => Promise<ApiResponse<string>>;
}

/**
 * The topics namespace — CRUD over the user's topics.
 *
 * Mirrors the backend's `/api/topics` surface one-for-one. The
 * main-process IPC handlers translate each call into an HTTP
 * request against the backend, so the renderer never needs to
 * know the backend's URL or authentication mechanism — that
 * lives entirely on the main-process side.
 */
interface TopicsNamespace {
  list: (
    status?: TopicStatus
  ) => Promise<ApiResponse<Topic[]>>;
  create: (
    payload: TopicCreatePayload
  ) => Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>>;
  get: (topicId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>>;
  update: (
    topicId: string,
    patch: TopicUpdatePayload
  ) => Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>>;
  remove: (topicId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<Topic>>;
}

/**
 * The research namespace — search and extraction, both of which
 * drive Python child processes on the main-process side. The
 * renderer sees only the async results; the process management,
 * the Chrome window, and the marker parsing live entirely in the
 * main process.
 */
interface ResearchNamespace {
  /**
   * Run the search step for a topic. Resolves once the search
   * has finished and returns the candidate URLs it found. Live
   * progress arrives through the `research:progress` event, not
   * through this promise.
   */
  search: (
    topicId: string,
    title: string,
    keywords?: string[]
  ) => Promise<ApiResponse<{ candidates: string[] }>>;

  /**
   * Fetch and extract the selected candidate URLs. Resolves
   * once every extraction has completed (or failed) and returns
   * the list of documents saved. Live progress arrives through
   * `research:progress`.
   */
  extract: (
    topicId: string,
    urls: string[]
  ) => Promise<ApiResponse<{ savedCount: number }>>;

  /**
   * Cancel any in-flight search or extraction for the topic.
   * Kills the associated Python child process (if one is
   * running) and removes the topic from the automation store's
   * active-task list.
   */
  cancel: (topicId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<null>>;
}

/**
 * The documents namespace — read the extracted documents
 * attached to a topic. The documents themselves are `.md` files
 * on disk; the main process reads them on the renderer's behalf.
 */
interface DocumentsNamespace {
  list: (topicId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<Document[]>>;
  read: (path: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<{ content: string }>>;
  remove: (path: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<null>>;
}

/**
 * The writer namespace — the DeepSeek automation step.
 */
interface WriterNamespace {
  /**
   * Kick off a generate-the-article run for the topic. Resolves
   * once the writer process has finished and the article has
   * been persisted. Live progress arrives through
   * `writer:progress`.
   */
  generate: (
    topicId: string
  ) => Promise<ApiResponse<Article>>;

  /** Cancel any in-flight writer run for the topic. */
  cancel: (topicId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<null>>;
}

/**
 * The validation namespace — run the six-validator suite against
 * an article and read the resulting report.
 */
interface ValidationNamespace {
  run: (articleId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<Report>>;
  report: (articleId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<Report>>;
}

/**
 * The export namespace — write the article to disk in one of the
 * supported formats.
 *
 * Each method opens a native Save-As dialog on the main-process
 * side and calls the corresponding Python export script. The
 * resolved value is the path the user chose, or `null` if they
 * cancelled the dialog.
 */
interface ExportNamespace {
  docx: (articleId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<string | null>>;
  md: (articleId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<string | null>>;
  txt: (articleId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<string | null>>;
}

/**
 * The settings namespace — the user's app-level preferences,
 * which are cached on the main process side and mirrored to the
 * backend's UserSetting document.
 */
interface SettingsNamespace {
  /**
   * Read the current settings. If none have ever been saved,
   * the main process returns the schema's defaults, so this
   * method never returns null in practice.
   */
  get: () => Promise<ApiResponse<UserSettingsMap>>;

  /**
   * Save a partial update to the settings. Fields omitted from
   * the patch are left unchanged on both the local cache and the
   * backend.
   */
  save: (
    patch: Partial<UserSettingsMap>
  ) => Promise<ApiResponse<UserSettingsMap>>;

  /**
   * Ask the update service to check whether a newer desktop
   * build exists. Returns the latest version, or null if the
   * app is up to date.
   */
  checkUpdates: () => Promise<ApiResponse<AppVersion | null>>;
}

/**
 * The admin namespace — user management, available only to
 * callers whose cached user has `role === 'admin'`.
 */
interface AdminNamespace {
  listUsers: () => Promise<ApiResponse<User[]>>;
  createUser: (payload: {
    email: string;
    password: string;
    role?: UserRole;
    active?: boolean;
  }) => Promise<ApiResponse<User>>;
  updateUser: (
    userId: string,
    patch: {
      email?: string;
      password?: string;
      role?: UserRole;
      active?: boolean;
    }
  ) => Promise<ApiResponse<User>>;
  deleteUser: (userId: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<User>>;
}

/**
 * The utils namespace — small capabilities that do not belong to
 * a feature but that the renderer needs occasionally. Every one
 * of them maps to an Electron API that is only reachable from
 * the main process.
 */
interface UtilsNamespace {
  /** Open a URL in the user's default browser. */
  openExternal: (url: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<null>>;
  /** Show the given path in the OS's file browser, highlighting the file. */
  showItemInFolder: (path: string) => Promise<ApiResponse<null>>;
}

/**
 * The window namespace — operations on the app's own window,
 * used by the automation layer when a task needs to draw the
 * user's attention.
 */
interface WindowNamespace {
  /** Flash the taskbar icon / bounce the dock icon to notify the user. */
  notify: () => Promise<ApiResponse<null>>;
}

/**
 * The full API surface exposed on `window.electronAPI`.
 *
 * Adding a namespace here without a corresponding runtime
 * implementation would be caught by the compiler at the point
 * where the runtime object is assigned to this interface — the
 * same guarantee that every other typed object in the codebase
 * benefits from.
 */
export interface ElectronAPI {
  auth: AuthNamespace;
  config: ConfigNamespace;
  topics: TopicsNamespace;
  research: ResearchNamespace;
  documents: DocumentsNamespace;
  writer: WriterNamespace;
  validation: ValidationNamespace;
  export: ExportNamespace;
  settings: SettingsNamespace;
  admin: AdminNamespace;
  utils: UtilsNamespace;
  window: WindowNamespace;

  /**
   * Register a persistent listener for a main→renderer event.
   *
   * The `off` counterpart must be called with the same
   * `(channel, callback)` pair when the listener is no longer
   * needed; the registry below uses the pair as a key to look
   * up the wrapped function that was actually registered.
   */
  on: (channel: string, callback: IpcListener) => void;

  /** Remove a listener that was previously registered via `on`. */
  off: (channel: string, callback: IpcListener) => void;

  /** Register a one-shot listener that fires at most once. */
  once: (channel: string, callback: IpcListener) => void;
}

// ============================================================
//  Event listener registry
// ============================================================
//
//  See the file header for why this exists. The map is keyed by
//  channel, then by the renderer's original callback, and its
//  values are the wrapped functions that were actually registered
//  with `ipcRenderer.on`. This lets `off` find and remove the
//  correct reference.

const listenerRegistry = new Map<
  string,
  Map<IpcListener, (event: IpcRendererEvent, ...args: unknown[]) => void>
>();

/**
 * Register a listener and remember the wrapped function so
 * `off` can remove it later. The wrapped function is what
 * `ipcRenderer` actually calls; it discards the `IpcRendererEvent`
 * first argument before invoking the renderer's callback.
 */
const on = (channel: string, callback: IpcListener): void => {
  const wrapped = (_event: IpcRendererEvent, ...args: unknown[]): void => {
    callback(...args);
  };

  let channelMap = listenerRegistry.get(channel);
  if (!channelMap) {
    channelMap = new Map();
    listenerRegistry.set(channel, channelMap);
  }

  // If the same callback is registered twice on the same channel
  // without an intervening `off`, the earlier registration is
  // discarded here. That matches `ipcRenderer`'s own behaviour
  // when the same listener reference is added twice.
  const existing = channelMap.get(callback);
  if (existing) {
    ipcRenderer.removeListener(channel, existing);
  }

  channelMap.set(callback, wrapped);
  ipcRenderer.on(channel, wrapped);
};

/**
 * Remove a listener that was previously registered via `on`.
 * A no-op if the pair was never registered — the removal is
 * best-effort and a caller who calls `off` with an unknown pair
 * has not caused a bug that would benefit from a throw.
 */
const off = (channel: string, callback: IpcListener): void => {
  const channelMap = listenerRegistry.get(channel);
  if (!channelMap) {
    return;
  }
  const wrapped = channelMap.get(callback);
  if (!wrapped) {
    return;
  }
  ipcRenderer.removeListener(channel, wrapped);
  channelMap.delete(callback);
  if (channelMap.size === 0) {
    listenerRegistry.delete(channel);
  }
};

/**
 * Register a one-shot listener. Electron's own `once` removes
 * the listener after the first invocation, so no registry entry
 * is needed — but the wrapper still strips the event argument.
 */
const once = (channel: string, callback: IpcListener): void => {
  ipcRenderer.once(
    channel,
    (_event: IpcRendererEvent, ...args: unknown[]): void => {
      callback(...args);
    }
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  Runtime API
// ============================================================
//
//  The object below is the concrete value that gets exposed on
//  `window.electronAPI`. Its type is asserted to `ElectronAPI`
//  by the assignment that follows — a type error at that line
//  would mean a method's signature drifted from the interface
//  declared above, which is exactly the failure mode the type
//  annotation exists to catch.
//
//  The generic `invoke<T>` helper erases the boilerplate of
//  `ipcRenderer.invoke(channel, ...args) as Promise<ApiResponse<T>>`.
//  Because `ipcRenderer.invoke` returns `Promise<any>` in
//  Electron's types, the assertion is required — but it is a
//  single, localized assertion with a clearly documented
//  contract, not a scatter of `any` casts throughout the file.
//  The contract is: every IPC handler registered by the main
//  process returns an `ApiResponse<T>` for the corresponding
//  channel; a handler that violated that contract would be a
//  bug in the main process, not in the renderer's consumption
//  of it.

const invoke = <T>(
  channel: string,
  ...args: unknown[]
): Promise<ApiResponse<T>> => {
  return ipcRenderer.invoke(channel, ...args) as Promise<ApiResponse<T>>;
};

const api: ElectronAPI = {
  // ---- Auth ----
  auth: {
    login: (credentials) => invoke<LoginResponse>('auth:login', credentials),
    logout: () => invoke<null>('auth:logout'),
    getUser: () => invoke<User | null>('auth:getUser'),
  },

  // ---- Config ----
  config: {
    getApiBaseUrl: () => invoke<string>('config:getApiBaseUrl'),

  // ---- Topics ----

    update: (topicId, patch) => invoke<Topic>('topics:update', topicId, patch),

  // ---- Documents ----
  documents: {
    list: (topicId) => invoke<Document[]>('documents:list', topicId),

    remove: (path) => invoke<null>('documents:delete', path),
  },

  // ---- Writer ----
  writer: {
    generate: (topicId) => invoke<Article>('writer:generate', topicId),

  },

  // ---- Validation ----
  validation: {

    report: (articleId) => invoke<Report>('validation:report', articleId),

  // ---- Export ----

    md: (articleId) => invoke<string | null>('export:md', articleId),

    checkUpdates: () => invoke<AppVersion | null>('settings:checkUpdates'),
  },

  // ---- Admin ----

    createUser: (payload) => invoke<User>('admin:createUser', payload),
    updateUser: (userId, patch) =>

    deleteUser: (userId) => invoke<User>('admin:deleteUser', userId),

  utils: {

    showItemInFolder: (path) => invoke<null>('utils:showItemInFolder', path),
  },

  // ---- Window ----

  // ---- Event registry ----

// ============================================================
//  Expose
// ============================================================

/**
 * Hand the API to the renderer through the contextBridge.
 *
 * `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld` installs the object at the
 * given name on the renderer's `window`, with the deep-cloning
 * and function-serialization machinery of the bridge handling the
 * context crossing. From the renderer's point of view,
 * `window.electronAPI` looks and behaves like an ordinary
 * JavaScript object with methods that return promises.
 *
 * The methods cannot leak anything from this file's own scope
 * into the renderer — the bridge copies the API surface across
 * the context boundary. That is what lets this file import
 * `ipcRenderer` and `contextBridge` at the top without exposing
 * either of them.
 */
contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('electronAPI', api);

// ============================================================
//  Global type augmentation
// ============================================================
//
//  Declare `window.electronAPI` as a known property of the DOM's
//  `Window` interface so that every renderer file can write
//  `window.electronAPI.auth.login(...)` with full type
//  information and no `any` cast. The `declare global` block
//  lives in the preload script because that is where the runtime
//  value actually gets installed on `window` — keeping the type
//  and the value side by side makes it obvious that they are two
//  halves of the same contract.
//
//  Because the desktop app is compiled as a single TypeScript
//  project (one tsconfig, `include: ['src/**/*']`), a global
//  augmentation declared in any file applies to every other file
//  in the same compilation. In particular, the renderer's `.tsx`
//  files see the `electronAPI` property without needing their own
//  declaration file.

declare global {
  interface Window {
    electronAPI: ElectronAPI;
  }
}
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/main/protocols.ts">
/**
 * Custom protocol registration for the WriteSpeare desktop app.
 *
 * A "custom protocol" is a scheme that the app itself defines and
 * that Electron's Chromium instance knows how to resolve. This
 * file registers one such scheme — `writespeare-asset://` — so
 * that the renderer can load the app's bundled images with
 * ordinary HTML URLs:
 *
 *   <img src="writespeare-asset://images/logo.svg" alt="WriteSpeare" />
 *
 * Without the custom scheme, the renderer would have to know the
 * absolute filesystem path of every asset, which differs between
 * development (source tree) and production (packaged app
 * resources). With the scheme, the URL is the same in both
 * environments: the scheme's handler resolves it against a base
 * directory it computes at request time from `app.isPackaged`.
 *
 * Two-phase registration — why this file exports two functions
 * instead of one:
 *
 *   Electron requires custom schemes to be declared to Chromium
 *   BEFORE the app's `ready` event fires, so that Chromium knows
 *   how to treat URLs of that scheme when the first renderer
 *   starts loading. After `ready`, the handler that actually
 *   serves responses can be installed.
 *
 *   These two phases use two different Electron APIs:
 *
 *     `protocol.registerSchemesAsPrivileged(...)` — must run
 *       before `ready`. Declares the scheme's properties
 *       (whether it's a standard scheme, whether it's considered
 *       secure, etc.). Calling it after `ready` throws.
 *
 *     `protocol.handle(scheme, handler)` — must run after
 *       `ready`. Installs the request handler that returns
 *       responses for URLs of this scheme.
 *
 *   Because the APIs have different timing requirements, they
 *   live in two functions. `main/index.ts` calls
 *   `registerProtocolSchemes()` at module load (before the
 *   `app.whenReady().then(...)` block) and calls
 *   `registerProtocolHandlers()` inside the `whenReady` block.
 *   Trying to combine the two into one function would force the
 *   caller to invoke a single function at one of the two
 *   timings, which would be wrong either way.
 *
 * The URL shape:
 *
 *   `writespeare-asset://images/logo.svg`
 *     host     = 'images'
 *     pathname = '/logo.svg'
 *
 *   The handler below treats the union of host and pathname as
 *   the path relative to the resource base. The triple-slash
 *   form `writespeare-asset:///images/logo.svg` also works — it
 *   puts `images/logo.svg` entirely in the pathname with an
 *   empty host — and produces the same resolved file. Both
 *   forms are accepted because the handler strips any leading
 *   slashes before joining.
 *
 * The resource base:
 *
 *   In production (`app.isPackaged === true`), the base is
 *   `process.resourcesPath`, which is where electron-builder
 *   copies the `extraResources` blocks declared in package.json.
 *   The four extraResources sources (`src/resources/images`,
 *   `.../config`, `.../python`, `.../scripts`) all land as
 *   direct subdirectories of that path, so
 *   `writespeare-asset://images/logo.svg` resolves to
 *   `<resourcesPath>/images/logo.svg`.
 *
 *   In development (`app.isPackaged === false`), the base is
 *   `apps/desktop/src/resources/`, computed relative to this
 *   module's own location. The compiled file lives at
 *   `dist/main/protocols.js`, so the relative path from there to
 *   the source resources is `../../src/resources`.
 *
 * Path traversal protection:
 *
 *   The handler resolves the requested path against the base
 *   directory, then verifies that the resolved path still lives
 *   inside the base. A request like
 *   `writespeare-asset://images/../../../etc/passwd` — if the
 *   URL parser did not already normalize the `..` segments —
 *   would resolve outside the base directory and be rejected
 *   with a 403.
 *
 *   The check compares the resolved path against the base
 *   followed by a path separator, which ensures that a sibling
 *   directory whose name shares a prefix with the base (say,
 *   `resources-secret` when the base is `resources`) does not
 *   pass the check.
 *
 *   The check does NOT guard against symlinks inside the base
 *   directory that point outside it. Symlinks are the app's own
 *   responsibility — nothing in the bundled resources tree is a
 *   symlink, and the plan does not call for one. If a future
 *   session adds a symlinked resource, the check would need to
 *   be strengthened with `fs.realpath` and a second prefix
 *   comparison against the resolved real path.
 *
 * Security posture:
 *
 *   The scheme is registered as `secure: true`, which means
 *   Chromium treats it as a secure context — no mixed-content
 *   warnings, and resources loaded through it are not flagged
 *   as insecure by any future browser-level policy.
 *
 *   The scheme is registered as `standard: true`, which makes
 *   Chromium parse URLs of this scheme as standard URLs (with
 *   host, port, and path components) rather than as opaque
 *   strings. Without this privilege, `<img src="writespeare-asset://...">`
 *   would not be treated as a URL by the resource loader and
 *   the tag would fail silently.
 *
 *   The scheme is registered as `supportFetchAPI: true` so that
 *   a future renderer component that wants to `fetch()` an SVG
 *   and inline it as text — a common technique for styling SVG
 *   fills with CSS — can do so. It costs nothing today: the
 *   flag only affects what APIs Chromium exposes for URLs of
 *   this scheme.
 *
 *   The scheme is NOT registered with `corsEnabled: true`.
 *   Without CORS enforcement, `<img>` tags work from any origin
 *   (the renderer in dev is at `http://localhost:5173`, in prod
 *   at `file://`) and cross-origin restrictions do not apply to
 *   display of the image. If a future feature needs the
 *   renderer to `fetch()` an asset and READ its body (as
 *   opposed to just displaying it), the correct change is to
 *   add `corsEnabled: true` here and add the appropriate
 *   `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header in the
 *   handler. Until then, the simpler posture is correct.
 */

import { app, protocol } from 'electron';
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
import path from 'node:path';

// ============================================================
//  Constants
// ============================================================

/**
 * The custom scheme this module registers.
 *
 * Exported so that main/index.ts (or a future preload helper)
 * can reference the scheme by its constant name rather than by a
 * string literal. The literal form `'writespeare-asset'` also
 * works — the string appears in exactly this one place, and any
 * consumer that needs it can import it from here.
 */
export const SCHEME = 'writespeare-asset';

/**
 * The prefix that every URL of this scheme starts with. Cached
 * at module load so the handler does not recompute it on every
 * request.
 */
const SCHEME_PREFIX = `${SCHEME}://`;

/**
 * MIME type lookup keyed by lowercased file extension.
 *
 * This map covers only image types — that is the class of asset
 * the plan describes the scheme as serving ("the logo and UI
 * assets"). A request for a file whose extension is not in this
 * map is served with `application/octet-stream`, which causes
 * the browser to treat the response as a binary download rather
 * than attempting to render it as an image or a document.
 *
 * Adding a new type to this map is a two-line change: add the
 * extension (with its leading dot) as a key, and the MIME type
 * string as the value. If a future session needs to serve fonts
 * or JSON through this scheme, that is where the change goes.
 */
const MIME_TYPES: Record<string, string> = {
  '.svg': 'image/svg+xml',
  '.png': 'image/png',
  '.jpg': 'image/jpeg',
  '.jpeg': 'image/jpeg',
  '.webp': 'image/webp',
  '.gif': 'image/gif',
  '.ico': 'image/x-icon',
};

// ============================================================
//  Helpers
// ============================================================

/**
 * Resolve the resource base directory — the parent of every file
 * the scheme is allowed to serve. See the file header for the
 * distinction between the two branches.
 *
 * The function is called on every request rather than computed
 * once at module load, because `app.isPackaged` is a property
 * whose value is stable across the app's lifetime but whose
 * correctness depends on the value being read AFTER Electron has
 * finished its own initialization. Reading it at module load
 * would work for a packaged app (where the value is set before
 * the main script loads) but is fragile if the module is ever
 * imported earlier than expected. Reading it per-request is
 * cheap — it is a property access and a `path.resolve` call —
 * and correct regardless of when the module is first loaded.
 */
const resolveResourceBase = (): string => {
  if (app.isPackaged) {
    return process.resourcesPath;
  }

  // In development, this module is at `dist/main/protocols.js`.
  // The source resources directory is at `src/resources/`, two
  // levels up from `dist/main/` and then into `src/resources`.
  const currentDir = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
  return path.resolve(currentDir, '../../src/resources');
};

/**
 * Return the MIME type for a resolved file path, based on its
 * extension. Falls back to `application/octet-stream` for any
 * extension not in the map — see the file header for the
 * consequences of that fallback.
 */
const getContentType = (filePath: string): string => {
  const ext = path.extname(filePath).toLowerCase();
  return MIME_TYPES[ext] ?? 'application/octet-stream';
};

// ============================================================
//  Phase 1 — register the scheme as privileged
// ============================================================

/**
 * Declare the `writespeare-asset` scheme and its privileges to
 * Chromium.
 *
 * MUST be called BEFORE `app.whenReady()` resolves — Electron
 * enforces this by throwing if the call happens after `ready`.
 * See the file header for the three privileges chosen and the
 * reasoning behind each.
 *
 * Synchronous, no return value. `main/index.ts` calls this once
 * at module scope, at the top of the file, before the
 * `app.whenReady().then(...)` block.
 */
export const registerProtocolSchemes = (): void => {
  protocol.registerSchemesAsPrivileged([
    {
      scheme: SCHEME,
      privileges: {
        standard: true,
        secure: true,
        supportFetchAPI: true,
      },
    },
  ]);
};

// ============================================================
//  Phase 2 — install the request handler
// ============================================================

/**
 * Install the handler that answers every request to the
 * `writespeare-asset` scheme.
 *
 * MUST be called AFTER `app.whenReady()` resolves — the
 * `protocol.handle` API is only available once Chromium is ready
 * to route requests. `main/index.ts` calls this inside the
 * `whenReady` block, before the first BrowserWindow is created.
 *
 * The handler is `async` because serving a file is I/O bound.
 * Electron's `protocol.handle` supports async handlers and awaits
 * the returned promise before using the response.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Extract the requested path by stripping the scheme prefix
 *      and any leading slashes. Both `writespeare-asset://images/x.svg`
 *      and `writespeare-asset:///images/x.svg` reduce to the same
 *      `images/x.svg` at this point.
 *
 *   2. Reject with 404 if the resulting path is empty — an empty
 *      request has nothing to serve and is not a valid asset
 *      reference.
 *
 *   3. Percent-decode the path so that a URL like
 *      `writespeare-asset://images/logo%2Esvg` resolves to the
 *      same file as `logo.svg`. A malformed percent sequence is
 *      rejected with 400 — a client that produces one has a bug,
 *      and the correct response is a clear error.
 *
 *   4. Resolve the decoded path against the resource base. The
 *      `path.resolve` call normalizes any `.` and `..` segments
 *      in the decoded path, which is what makes the traversal
 *      check below meaningful.
 *
 *   5. Reject with 403 if the resolved path is not inside the
 *      resource base. The check appends a trailing separator to
 *      the base before comparing, so that a sibling directory
 *      whose name shares a prefix with the base does not pass.
 *
 *   6. Read the file. Any error — ENOENT (file does not exist),
 *      EISDIR (path is a directory), EACCES (permission), or
 *      anything else — is logged and converted to a 404. The
 *      caller receives a uniform "not found" response rather
 *      than a response that reveals which failure mode occurred,
 *      which would leak filesystem state to a renderer that
 *      probed the scheme.
 *
 *   7. Return the file contents with the correct MIME type and a
 *      one-hour cache directive. The assets are static and
 *      versioned by filename in practice — if the logo changes,
 *      the filename changes — so a one-hour cache is safe and
 *      substantially reduces the number of file reads during a
 *      long session.
 */
export const registerProtocolHandlers = (): void => {
  protocol.handle(SCHEME, async (request) => {
    // ---- 1. Extract the requested path ----
    const rawPath = request.url
      .slice(SCHEME_PREFIX.length)
      .replace(/^\/+/, '');

    // ---- 2. Reject empty paths ----
    if (rawPath.length === 0) {
      return new Response('Not Found', { status: 404 });
    }

    // ---- 3. Percent-decode ----
    let decodedPath: string;
    try {
      decodedPath = decodeURIComponent(rawPath);
    } catch {
      // A malformed percent sequence (`%2` with no following hex
      // digit, for example) throws a URIError. Reject with 400
      // rather than trying to salvage the string — a client that
      // produced a malformed URL has a bug, and silent recovery
      // would hide it.
      return new Response('Bad Request', { status: 400 });
    }

    // ---- 4. Resolve against the resource base ----
    const base = resolveResourceBase();
    const resolved = path.resolve(base, decodedPath);

    // ---- 5. Path traversal guard ----
    // The base is normalized to end with a path separator, so the
    // comparison cannot be fooled by a sibling directory whose
    // name shares a prefix (e.g. `resources-secret` when the base
    // is `resources`).
    const baseWithSep = base.endsWith(path.sep) ? base : base + path.sep;
    if (!resolved.startsWith(baseWithSep)) {
      return new Response('Forbidden', { status: 403 });
    }

    // ---- 6. Read and return the file ----
    try {
      const data = await readFile(resolved);
      return new Response(new Uint8Array(data), {
        status: 200,
        headers: {
          'Content-Type': getContentType(resolved),
          'Cache-Control': 'public, max-age=3600',
        },
      });
    } catch (err) {
      // The error is logged for the operator; the client sees a
      // uniform 404 regardless of which failure mode occurred.
      console.error(
        '[protocols] failed to serve asset:',
        resolved,
        err
      );
      return new Response('Not Found', { status: 404 });
    }
  });
};
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/main/store.ts">
/**
 * Local persistent store for the WriteSpeare desktop app.
 *
 * This module wraps `electron-store` — the standard key-value
 * persistence layer for Electron apps — and exposes a small,
 * typed API for the three kinds of data the desktop client
 * needs to keep across restarts:
 *
 *   1. Authentication state — the JWT bearer token the backend
 *      issued at login, plus a cached copy of the user object.
 *      Both are cleared on logout.
 *
 *   2. Synced settings — a cached copy of the user's
 *      `UserSettingsMap`, mirrored from the backend's
 *      UserSetting document. The cache lets the app render the
 *      correct theme and defaults on the very first frame after
 *      a cold start, before the network round trip to fetch
 *      the settings completes.
 *
 *   3. Session state — the user's last-selected preset, kept
 *      across restarts so the "New Topic" modal pre-populates
 *      with what they used last time.
 *
 * This file runs in the MAIN process only. The renderer never
 * touches it directly — all access flows through IPC handlers
 * (`authIPC.ts`, `settingsIPC.ts`, etc.) which call the helpers
 * exported below. That boundary is what keeps the file path,
 * the encryption key, and the raw store object out of the
 * renderer's reach.
 *
 * Encryption — why and how:
 *
 *   electron-store's `encryptionKey` option applies AES-256 to
 *   the entire store file. Without a key, the file would be
 *   plain JSON on disk, readable by anything that can open the
 *   app's userData directory. That would be fine for the cached
 *   settings and the last-used preset — both are non-sensitive
 *   — but the JWT is a live credential. Anyone with read access
 *   to the file could use the token to make authenticated API
 *   requests until the token's `exp` claim expired. Encrypting
 *   the store closes that window.
 *
 *   The key is derived from the OS's per-installation userData
 *   path, which is stable for a given installation on a given
 *   machine but unique across machines. That gives two
 *   properties:
 *
 *     - Stability: the key is the same on every launch of the
 *       app on the same machine, so the store can be read back.
 *
 *     - Isolation: a store file copied to a different machine
 *       (or a different user's account on the same machine)
 *       cannot be decrypted with the key derived there, so a
 *       leaked store file is not portable.
 *
 *   The key is not user-password-protected and not stored in the
 *   OS keychain. That is deliberate — the file's confidentiality
 *   protects against casual inspection of the userData directory,
 *   not against a determined attacker with local code execution.
 *   A future session that wants stronger protection would replace
 *   this scheme with `safeStorage.encryptString` from Electron,
 *   which uses the OS's credential vault.
 *
 * Schema:
 *
 *   `token`           — the JWT bearer token from a successful
 *                       login, or `null` when logged out.
 *   `user`            — a cached copy of the current user
 *                       object, or `null`.
 *   `settings`        — the last-known `UserSettingsMap` fetched
 *                       from the backend, or `null` before the
 *                       first successful fetch.
 *   `lastUsedPreset`  — the preset name the user selected on the
 *                       most recent topic, or `null` before any
 *                       topic has been created.
 *
 *   Every field defaults to `null`. That means a
 *   freshly-installed app has a valid, fully-typed store from
 *   the moment the module loads, and every helper below can
 *   return a well-typed value without needing to distinguish
 *   "not set" from "null". The two are the same thing in this
 *   schema.
 *
 * Why the store is instantiated at module load:
 *
 *   The `store` instance is created once, when this module is
 *   first imported. Every subsequent import (from any other
 *   main-process module) receives the same instance, because
 *   Node's module cache guarantees that a module's top-level
 *   statements run exactly once. The alternative — lazily
 *   creating the store on first access — would add a race
 *   condition risk for concurrent IPC calls without providing
 *   any benefit; the store's construction is cheap and has no
 *   side effect on disk until the first write.
 */

import Store from 'electron-store';
import { app } from 'electron';
import type {
  User,
  UserSettingsMap,
  PresetName,
} from '../features/shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Schema
// ============================================================

/**
 * The shape of the persisted store. Every key is nullable
 * because every key represents "state that may not exist yet" —
 * a freshly-installed app has no token, no user, no cached
 * settings, and no last-used preset, and none of those is an
 * error condition.
 */
interface StoreSchema {
  token: string | null;
  user: User | null;
  settings: UserSettingsMap | null;
  lastUsedPreset: PresetName | null;
}

// ============================================================
//  Encryption key
// ============================================================

/**
 * The app slug used both as the store's filename and as the
 * static prefix of the derived encryption key.
 *
 * Using one constant for both purposes keeps the two in sync: a
 * future rename of the app would change this string, and the
 * change would propagate to both the filename and the key
 * without needing a second edit.
 */
const APP_SLUG = 'writespeare';

/**
 * Derive the store's encryption key from the OS's per-installation
 * userData path. See the file header for the design rationale.
 *
 * `app.getPath('userData')` is safe to call before `app.whenReady()`
 * — Electron resolves it from the app's name and the platform's
 * standard user-data directory, both of which are known by the
 * time the main script is loaded. The function that wraps this
 * call is invoked once, at module load, from the `new Store(...)`
 * line below.
 */
const buildEncryptionKey = (): string => {
  const userDataPath = app.getPath('userData');
  return `${APP_SLUG}-v1:${userDataPath}`;
};

// ============================================================
//  Store instance
// ============================================================

/**
 * The single store instance, shared by every consumer in the
 * main process. See the file header for why this is created at
 * module load rather than lazily.
 *
 * The `defaults` object satisfies the schema fully — every key
 * is present with its nullable default — so the store is
 * readable and writable from the moment the module loads, even
 * on a fresh install with no persisted state.
 */
const store = new Store<StoreSchema>({
  name: APP_SLUG,
  encryptionKey: buildEncryptionKey(),
  defaults: {
    token: null,
    user: null,
    settings: null,
    lastUsedPreset: null,
  },
});

// ============================================================
//  Auth helpers
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return the stored JWT bearer token, or `null` when there is
 * no active session.
 *
 * The IPC handler that reads this uses `null` as the signal for
 * "not logged in" and returns a `{ success: false }` envelope to
 * the renderer, which in turn redirects to the login screen. The
 * null is not an error state — it is the correct representation
 * of "no session yet".
 */
export const getToken = (): string | null => store.get('token');

/**
 * Persist a JWT issued by the backend at login.
 *
 * The token is written encrypted — see the file header for the
 * encryption scheme. A second login overwrites the previous
 * token; there is no history of tokens and no way to retrieve a
 * superseded one.
 */
export const setToken = (token: string): void => {
  store.set('token', token);
};

/**
 * Clear the stored token without touching anything else.
 *
 * The auth IPC handler uses this during a successful logout. It
 * is deliberately narrower than `clearAuth` — a logout that
 * wants to also clear the cached user object calls `clearAuth`
 * instead.
 */
export const clearToken = (): void => {
  store.set('token', null);
};

/**
 * Return the cached user object, or `null` when there is no
 * active session.
 *
 * The cached user is written once at login and refreshed on
 * every successful call to `GET /api/auth/me`. It is the source
 * of truth for the renderer's "who am I?" question between
 * network round trips; the auth store in the renderer is
 * populated from this cache on cold start before the `me`
 * request completes.
 */
export const getUser = (): User | null => store.get('user');

/**
 * Persist the current user object.
 *
 * Called at login (with the user returned by `POST /api/auth/login`)
 * and on every successful `GET /api/auth/me`. The value replaces
 * whatever was previously cached.
 */
export const setUser = (user: User): void => {
  store.set('user', user);
};

/**
 * Clear the cached user object without touching the token.
 *
 * Used when the cached user is known to be stale — for example,
 * after an admin deactivates the account and the next API call
 * returns a 403 — but before the token itself is invalidated.
 * The usual sequence is `clearToken` then `clearUser` via
 * `clearAuth`.
 */
export const clearUser = (): void => {
  store.set('user', null);
};

/**
 * Clear both the token and the cached user object — the standard
 * logout sequence.
 *
 * The cached settings and last-used preset are deliberately left
 * in place. They are per-user data, but if the same user logs
 * back in, keeping them avoids a network round trip before the
 * UI can render correctly. If a different user logs in, the
 * login handler overwrites the settings cache on the first
 * `getUserSettings` call. The last-used preset is left alone
 * across users on the same machine for the same reason — it
 * pre-populates a convenience field that the user can override
 * with one click.
 */
export const clearAuth = (): void => {
  store.set('token', null);
  store.set('user', null);
};

// ============================================================
//  Settings helpers
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return the cached `UserSettingsMap`, or `null` before the
 * first successful fetch from the backend.
 *
 * The renderer reads this on cold start to apply the user's
 * theme preference and defaults before the network request for
 * the live settings has completed. A `null` means "use the
 * app's built-in defaults" — the same defaults the backend
 * would apply on a first-ever call.
 */
export const getSettings = (): UserSettingsMap | null =>
  store.get('settings');

/**
 * Cache a `UserSettingsMap` that was fetched from the backend.
 *
 * Called after every successful `getUserSettings` or
 * `updateUserSettings` IPC call. The cached copy is not
 * authoritative — the backend is — but it lets the renderer
 * skip a network round trip on the next cold start.
 */
export const setSettings = (settings: UserSettingsMap): void => {
  store.set('settings', settings);
};

/**
 * Clear the cached settings.
 *
 * Exposed for a future "reset to defaults" flow. Not called
 * anywhere today.
 */
export const clearSettings = (): void => {
  store.set('settings', null);
};

// ============================================================
//  Preset helpers
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return the last-used preset name, or `null` before the user
 * has created any topic.
 *
 * "Last used" means the preset the user selected on the most
 * recent topic-creation modal. It is a per-machine convenience,
 * not a per-user preference — it does not sync to the backend
 * and it does not change when the user's `defaultPreset`
 * preference changes.
 */
export const getLastUsedPreset = (): PresetName | null =>
  store.get('lastUsedPreset');

/**
 * Record the preset the user selected on the most recent topic
 * creation.
 *
 * Called by the topic-creation IPC handler after a successful
 * `POST /api/topics`. Failures to write are silently ignored by
 * the caller — the last-used preset is a convenience, and its
 * absence does not break any flow.
 */
export const setLastUsedPreset = (preset: PresetName): void => {
  store.set('lastUsedPreset', preset);
};

// ============================================================
//  Bulk operations
// ============================================================

/**
 * Wipe every key from the store, returning it to its default
 * state.
 *
 * Used by a "reset app data" flow if one is ever added, and by
 * tests that need a clean slate between cases. It is
 * deliberately not called by `clearAuth` — logging out does
 * not erase the user's cached settings.
 */
export const clearAll = (): void => {
  store.clear();
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

/**
 * The raw `electron-store` instance, exported for consumers that
 * need direct access to a key not covered by the helper
 * functions above.
 *
 * The plan's IPC handlers use the named helpers wherever
 * possible — they are typed against `StoreSchema` and free of
 * string-literal key names. The raw store is exported as an
 * escape hatch, not as the recommended interface.
 */
export default store;
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/renderer/styles/tailwind.css">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — renderer stylesheet.
 *
 * This is the single CSS entry point for the entire renderer. It
 * does three things, in order:
 *
 *   1. Emits Tailwind's three directive layers via the `@tailwind`
 *      statements below. The Tailwind PostCSS plugin (registered
 *      in `postcss.config.js`) replaces each `@tailwind` line
 *      with the corresponding slice of generated CSS — the
 *      preflight reset (`base`), the small set of component
 *      classes Tailwind ships (`components`), and every utility
 *      class actually used in the codebase (`utilities`, driven
 *      by the `content` glob in `tailwind.config.js`).
 *
 *   2. Adds the app's own base styles inside a `@layer base`
 *      block. Everything in this block sits below every Tailwind
 *      utility in the cascade, so a component that needs a
 *      different value can override any of these rules with a
 *      utility class — no `!important`, no specificity war.
 *
 *   3. Styles the scrollbar via WebKit and Firefox pseudo-element
 *      and pseudo-property selectors. This is outside the
 *      `@layer base` block because scrollbar styling is not
 *      something a utility class should ever need to override —
 *      a component that wants a different scrollbar has to
 *      provide its own wrapper element, not fight these rules.
 *
 * The `theme()` function — used in several rules below — is a
 * Tailwind PostCSS feature, not native CSS. It resolves its
 * argument against the values declared in `tailwind.config.js`
 * at build time. `theme('colors.primary.DEFAULT')`, for example,
 * is replaced with `#03A791` before the CSS reaches the browser.
 * Using `theme()` instead of hard-coding the hex means a palette
 * change in the config propagates here automatically, and the
 * file has no hidden duplication of the design tokens.
 *
 * Dark mode — Tailwind is configured with `darkMode: 'class'` in
 * `tailwind.config.js`, which means a `dark` class on the root
 * `<html>` element enables every `dark:` variant in the codebase.
 * The base styles below cooperate with that scheme: the `body`
 * rule sets the light-mode colors, and an `html.dark body` rule
 * overrides them for dark mode. The override uses Tailwind's
 * built-in neutral palette rather than custom tokens because the
 * app's own palette (primary, secondary, accent) does not declare
 * dark-mode variants — it is a brand palette, not a light/dark
 * palette pair. If a future design iteration specifies exact
 * dark-mode brand values, they belong in `tailwind.config.js` and
 * this rule updates to reference them.
 */

/* ============================================================
 *  Tailwind directives
 * ============================================================
 *
 *  Order is required, not arbitrary. `base` (the preflight
 *  reset) must come first so that everything after it can build
 *  on a clean slate. `components` follows so the few component
 *  classes Tailwind ships are available to the app. `utilities`
 *  comes last so that utility classes have the highest priority
 *  in the cascade among the three layers, which is what makes
 *  the "utility overrides component overrides base" contract
 *  hold.
 *
 *  Reversing the order would produce a stylesheet where a
 *  utility class could be overridden by the preflight reset —
 *  the exact opposite of what the design system needs.
 */

@tailwind base;
@tailwind components;
@tailwind utilities;

/* ============================================================
 *  Base styles
 * ============================================================
 *
 *  App-level rules that every page inherits. Everything in this
 *  block can be overridden by a utility class in any component,
