 *  because `@layer base` places these rules below utilities in
 *  the cascade.
 */

@layer base {
  /*
   * The layout root — full viewport height.
   *
   * The Electron window is the viewport. Every ancestor of the
   * React tree is set to 100% height so that a page which wants
   * to fill the window (a sidebar + main content layout, for
   * example) does not need to know how tall the window is; it
   * just uses `h-full` or `flex-1` and inherits the chain of
   * 100% heights from here.
   *
   * Without this, `h-full` on a child element resolves against
   * the parent's computed height, which is `auto` for a `<div>`
   * with no explicit height — and `auto` means the child's own
   * content height, which is almost never what the layout
   * intends. Setting `html`, `body`, and `#root` to 100% breaks
   * that cycle at the top of the tree.
   */
  html,
  body,
  #root {
    @apply h-full;
  }

  /*
   * Body defaults — font, colors, smooth text rendering.
   *
   * The font stack is the one declared in `tailwind.config.js`
   * (`Inter, system-ui, sans-serif`). The colors come from the
   * same config's `text` and `background` tokens. `antialiased`
   * applies the grayscale smoothing that Tailwind ships as a
   * utility and that modern apps use by default for a cleaner
   * rendering of thin font weights.
   *
   * `overscroll-behavior: none` disables the rubber-band overscroll
   * that a browser tab produces when scrolled past its edges. In
   * an Electron window this behaviour looks like a rendering
   * glitch — the content bounces against the window frame — and
   * the correct behaviour for a native-feeling desktop app is to
   * stop scrolling at the content boundary. This is not a
   * Tailwind utility; it is set as plain CSS.
   */
  body {
    @apply bg-background text-text font-sans antialiased;
    overscroll-behavior: none;
  }

  /*
   * Dark-mode body colors.
   *
   * The `html.dark` selector matches when the root element has
   * the `dark` class, which the renderer applies based on the
   * user's stored `UserSettingsMap.theme` preference. The
   * specific values (`neutral-900` for background, `neutral-100`
   * for text) come from Tailwind's built-in neutral palette, not
   * the app's brand palette — see the file header for why.
   *
   * This rule overrides the light-mode `body` rule above because
   * it has higher specificity (`html.dark body` is two compound
   * selectors where `body` is one). The override is intentional
   * and does not require `!important` or a `@layer` escape hatch.
   */
  html.dark body {
    @apply bg-neutral-900 text-neutral-100;
  }

  /*
   * Text selection — brand-colored highlight.
   *
   * By default, the browser highlights selected text with the
   * OS's accent color (blue on Windows, blue on macOS, a lighter
   * blue on Linux). Using the app's primary-light token instead
   * keeps the highlight visually consistent with the rest of the
   * UI, and the dark text color ensures the selected text stays
   * legible against the light-green background.
   *
   * `::selection` applies to user-selected text in a normal
   * document flow. It does not apply to text inside form
   * controls (`<input>`, `<textarea>`) on all browsers, so those
   * elements will fall back to the OS default. That is acceptable
   * — the contrast between the app highlight and the OS highlight
   * is not jarring.
   */
  ::selection {
    background-color: theme('colors.primary.light');
    color: theme('colors.text');
  }

  /*
   * Focus ring — visible, on-brand, and only on keyboard focus.
   *
   * The `:focus-visible` pseudo-class matches when the browser
   * determines focus should be visible — currently, that means
   * keyboard navigation and programmatic focus, but NOT a mouse
   * click. This is the modern replacement for the older pattern
   * of styling `:focus` and then trying to suppress it for mouse
   * users with a `:focus:not(:focus-visible)` override.
   *
   * The outline uses the primary color (`#03A791`) at 2px with a
   * 2px offset. The offset is what keeps the outline visually
   * separate from the element it is applied to — a focused button
   * shows a green ring with a small gap between the button's
   * border and the ring, rather than a green border hugging the
   * button's own edges.
   *
   * Using `outline` (rather than `box-shadow` or a `ring` utility)
   * is deliberate: `outline` is drawn outside the element's layout
   * box and never affects the element's size or position, so
   * applying focus to an element does not cause the surrounding
   * layout to shift by a couple of pixels. A `ring` (which is a
   * box-shadow) sits inside the layout box on some configurations
   * and can trigger reflow in flex containers.
   */
  :focus-visible {
    outline: 2px solid theme('colors.primary.DEFAULT');
    outline-offset: 2px;
  }

  /*
   * Cursor affordances for interactive controls.
   *
   * Tailwind's preflight resets a lot of button styling but does
   * NOT set `cursor: pointer` on `<button>` elements — the
   * browser's default cursor for a `<button>` is the platform's
   * arrow cursor, not the hand cursor that web users expect.
   *
   * The two rules below restore the web-idiomatic behaviour:
   * enabled buttons show the pointer cursor, disabled buttons
   * show the "not allowed" cursor so the user can tell at a
   * glance that clicking will do nothing. The `[role="button"]`
   * selector covers custom button-shaped elements that use the
   * ARIA role instead of the native `<button>` tag — a pattern
   * the app's `Modal` and `Sidebar` components are expected to
   * use for clickable areas that are not semantically buttons.
   *
   * The `:not(:disabled)` and `:not([aria-disabled="true"])`
   * guards ensure the disabled rule wins where both apply — a
   * `<button disabled>` matches both `button` and `button:disabled`,
   * and the second rule's higher specificity wins, giving the
   * correct cursor for the disabled state.
   */
  button:not(:disabled),
  [role='button']:not([aria-disabled='true']) {
    cursor: pointer;
  }

  button:disabled,
  [role='button'][aria-disabled='true'] {
    cursor: not-allowed;
  }
}

/* ============================================================
 *  Scrollbar styling
 * ============================================================
 *
 *  Custom scrollbars for the two rendering engines that will
 *  ever render this stylesheet:
 *
 *    - Chromium (WebKit) — Electron's rendering engine. Uses the
 *      `::-webkit-scrollbar-*` pseudo-elements.
 *
 *    - Gecko (Firefox) — a secondary target that only matters if
 *      the same renderer is opened in a Firefox browser during
 *      development (Vite's dev server serves the same HTML that
 *      Electron loads). Uses the `scrollbar-*` CSS properties.
 *
 *  Both engines get the same visual treatment: a thin, rounded
 *  thumb that is subtle in both light and dark modes.
 *
 *  These rules are NOT inside `@layer base` because their
 *  selectors target pseudo-elements of the scrollbar machinery
 *  itself, not the app's own elements. A utility class can style
 *  an app element's `overflow` or `scrollbar-gutter`, but it
 *  cannot reach inside the browser's scrollbar rendering — so
 *  keeping these rules in a layer would not make them overridable
 *  and would only add a level of indirection.
 *
 *  WebKit (Chromium):
 *
 *    `::-webkit-scrollbar` sets the overall size of the scrollbar
 *    track. 10px is thin enough to be unobtrusive on a modern
 *    high-DPI display and thick enough to be a comfortable
 *    click target for dragging.
 *
 *    `::-webkit-scrollbar-track` is set to `transparent` rather
 *    than a specific color so the underlying content shows
 *    through behind the scrollbar. This is what gives the "floating
 *    scrollbar" appearance that modern apps use.
 *
 *    `::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb` is the draggable handle. It uses
 *    a neutral gray in light mode and a darker gray in dark mode,
 *    with `background-clip: content-box` and a transparent border
 *    creating a small visual inset from the scrollbar track edges
 *    — the same technique GitHub, VS Code, and most modern
 *    applications use to make the thumb look like a rounded pill
 *    floating inside the track.
 */

::-webkit-scrollbar {
  width: 10px;
  height: 10px;
}

::-webkit-scrollbar-track {
  background: transparent;
}

::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
  background-color: theme('colors.neutral.300');
  border-radius: 9999px;
  border: 2px solid transparent;
  background-clip: content-box;
}

::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover {
  background-color: theme('colors.neutral.400');
}

html.dark ::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
  background-color: theme('colors.neutral.700');
}

html.dark ::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb:hover {
  background-color: theme('colors.neutral.600');
}

/*
 * Firefox (Gecko) — the equivalent treatment via the two
 * standard properties that have shipped in Firefox since 64:
 *
 *   `scrollbar-width: thin` reduces the scrollbar to a narrow
 *   form. The engine does not offer a way to specify the exact
 *   width in pixels.
 *
 *   `scrollbar-color` takes two values — the thumb color first,
 *   the track color second. The track is `transparent` to match
 *   the WebKit treatment above.
 *
 * The `html.dark` override sits directly below so the light-mode
 * rule sets one pair and the dark-mode rule replaces it with the
 * other. Firefox resolves the two rules by cascade order (the
 * later rule wins on the same selector set), which is the same
 * mechanism the WebKit rules above use.
 */

html {
  scrollbar-width: thin;
  scrollbar-color: theme('colors.neutral.300') transparent;
}

html.dark {
  scrollbar-color: theme('colors.neutral.700') transparent;
}
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/renderer/App.tsx">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — renderer root component and route tree.
 *
 * This is the component that `src/renderer/index.tsx` mounts into
 * the `#root` element. It composes the app's top-level structure
 * in one place:
 *
 *   1. `<HashRouter>` — the router.
 *   2. `<ToastProvider>` — the toast notification context.
 *   3. `<ModalProvider>` — the modal context.
 *   4. `<Routes>` — the top-level route tree.
 *
 * Why HashRouter and not BrowserRouter:
 *
 *   The packaged Electron app loads the renderer from a `file://`
 *   URL, and there is no server behind that URL to which a
 *   SPA-fallback rule could be attached. BrowserRouter would put
 *   the route in the URL's pathname, and a user who refreshed on
 *   a route other than the root would get a "file not found"
 *   because no file exists at `file:///dashboard/topics` — the
 *   only file is `index.html`. HashRouter puts the route in the
 *   URL fragment (`#/dashboard/topics`), which never reaches the
 *   filesystem and never needs a fallback rule. In the dev server
 *   the difference is invisible, but in the packaged app it is
 *   the difference between working and broken.
 *
 * Provider order — why Router is outermost:
 *
 *   The two providers (`ToastProvider`, `ModalProvider`) do not
 *   use routing — they expose imperative APIs (`useToast()`,
 *   `useModal()`) that components call to open a toast or a modal.
 *   Because those APIs are consumed by components INSIDE the
 *   route tree, the providers must wrap the routes. They do not
 *   need the router's own hooks, so they could sit outside or
 *   inside the router with equal correctness. The order used here
 *   (Router > Toast > Modal > Routes) is the convention, and it
 *   means a provider that ever wanted to react to a navigation
 *   event would already have access to the router's hooks.
 *
 * The route tree:
 *
 *   `/login` — the login page. Rendered standalone, without
 *     `<Layout />` and therefore without the sidebar. An
 *     unauthenticated user has no data to put in the sidebar,
 *     and no navigation to offer except "log in".
 *
 *   `/dashboard` — the authenticated area. `<Layout />` is the
 *     element for this route; it renders the sidebar and an
 *     `<Outlet />` where the nested routes below appear. Layout
 *     also performs the auth check — an unauthenticated user
 *     hitting any `/dashboard/*` URL is redirected to `/login`
 *     by Layout's own logic, not by anything in this file.
 *
 *   Nested under `/dashboard`:
 *     index          → redirect to `topics`.
 *     `topics`       → the topics list (the app's home screen).
 *     `topics/:id`   → a single topic's detail view.
 *     `settings`     → the settings page.
 *     `admin`        → the admin panel. Visibility for a non-admin
 *                      is enforced by Layout (which reads the
 *                      user's role from the auth store), not by
 *                      the router. The route exists in the tree
 *                      regardless of who is logged in.
 *
 *   `*` — catch-all. Redirects to `/dashboard`, which in turn
 *     redirects to `/topics` (via the index redirect above). This
 *     handles both the root path `/` and any typo'd path. The
 *     `replace` on the Navigate is deliberate — it prevents the
 *     browser's back button from returning to the mistyped URL.
 *
 * Forward references — why this file imports files that do not
 * yet exist on disk:
 *
 *   App.tsx is the renderer's integration point. Its whole
 *   purpose is to compose the route tree, and the route tree
 *   references the feature pages and the shared layout. Those
 *   files are declared in later sessions of the plan's coding
 *   order — the shared components in Session 5, the feature
 *   pages in Sessions 6, 7, 18, and 19. This file is therefore
 *   the first in the session whose TypeScript compile depends on
 *   files that do not yet exist.
 *
 *   The consequence is that this file will be STATE B (expected
 *   errors) until those files are created. That is not a bug in
 *   this file — it is the natural shape of an integration point
 *   written ahead of its dependencies. The errors will resolve
 *   one by one as each dependency is created, and the file will
 *   become STATE A once the last dependency is in place.
 *
 *   An alternative — replacing each page with a placeholder
 *   component so the file compiles today — is forbidden by
 *   Section 6 of the execution protocol. A placeholder route
 *   would compile but would not be the file the plan declares,
 *   and it would have to be replaced later anyway. The forward
 *   references are the correct choice.
 *
 * Route path conventions:
 *
 *   The `path` values on the nested routes are relative — a
 *   `<Route path="topics" />` nested under
 *   `<Route path="/dashboard" />` matches `/dashboard/topics`.
 *   This is React Router v6+'s default behaviour, and it is what
 *   makes the route tree read as a hierarchy rather than a flat
 *   list of absolute paths.
 *
 * Why there is no ErrorBoundary or Suspense here:
 *
 *   The plan does not declare either at this level. Global error
 *   handling for errors that escape the tree entirely is
 *   installed in `index.tsx` via `window.addEventListener`. A
 *   React ErrorBoundary — which catches errors during rendering
 *   of its descendants — would belong in a component closer to
 *   where the error occurs (a feature page, a data view), not at
 *   the router level, because a boundary here would replace the
 *   entire app with a fallback rather than just the failing
 *   subtree. Suspense boundaries are similarly per-data-source
 *   and are not needed until a component actually suspends.
 */

import {
  HashRouter,
  Routes,
  Route,
  Navigate,
} from 'react-router-dom';

// Shared providers and layout — declared in Session 5.
import { ToastProvider } from '../features/shared/components/Toast.js';
import { ModalProvider } from '../features/shared/components/Modal.js';
import Layout from '../features/shared/components/Layout.js';

// Feature pages — declared in later sessions.
import Login from '../features/auth/pages/Login.js';
import Topics from '../features/topics/pages/Topics.js';
import TopicDetail from '../features/topics/pages/TopicDetail.js';
import Settings from '../features/settings/pages/Settings.js';
import Admin from '../features/admin/pages/Admin.js';

// ============================================================
//  App
// ============================================================

/**
 * The renderer's root component.
 *
 * No state, no effects, no logic beyond the route tree itself.
 * Every piece of app-wide behaviour that could live here lives
 * in a provider (the toasts, the modals) or in Layout (the auth
 * check, the sidebar). What remains for this component is
 * exactly the composition the file header describes.
 */
const App = () => {
  return (
    <HashRouter>
      <ToastProvider>
        <ModalProvider>
          <Routes>
            {/* ---- Public routes ---- */}
            <Route path="/login" element={<Login />} />

            {/* ---- Authenticated area ---- */}
            {/*
              * `<Layout />` renders the sidebar and an
              * `<Outlet />`. Its own logic decides whether the
              * user is authenticated; a user without a valid
              * session is redirected to `/login` from inside
              * Layout, so the routes below never render for an
              * anonymous visitor.
              */}
            <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Layout />}>
              {/*
                * The bare `/dashboard` path redirects to the
                * topics list, which is the app's default view
                * once a user is signed in.
                */}
              <Route
                index
                element={<Navigate to="topics" replace />}
              />

              <Route path="topics" element={<Topics />} />
              <Route path="topics/:id" element={<TopicDetail />} />

              <Route path="settings" element={<Settings />} />
              <Route path="admin" element={<Admin />} />
            </Route>

            {/* ---- Catch-all ---- */}
            {/*
              * Any path not matched above — including the root
              * path `/` — is sent to `/dashboard`. From there
              * the auth gate in Layout decides whether the user
              * sees the dashboard or the login page.
              */}
            <Route
              path="*"
              element={<Navigate to="/dashboard" replace />}
            />
          </Routes>
        </ModalProvider>
      </ToastProvider>
    </HashRouter>
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default App;
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/src/renderer/index.tsx">
/**
 * WriteSpeare — renderer entry point.
 *
 * This is the module that `apps/desktop/index.html` loads via its
 * `<script type="module" src="/src/renderer/index.tsx">` tag. In
 * development, Vite serves it from `http://localhost:5173`; in
 * production, Vite rewrites the tag to point at the bundled,
 * minified copy under `dist/renderer/assets/`.
 *
 * Responsibilities, in order:
 *
 *   1. Register global error handlers BEFORE the React tree
 *      mounts. Two listeners — one for uncaught synchronous
 *      errors and one for unhandled promise rejections — write a
 *      diagnostic line to the console. Installing them first is
 *      what makes them able to catch an error thrown during the
 *      initial render; installing them after the mount would
 *      miss exactly the class of failures they exist to catch.
 *
 *   2. Import the app's stylesheet. This import is what causes
 *      Vite to include `tailwind.css` in the bundle — the file
 *      has no other way to be discovered by the build. The
 *      import is side-effect-only; the imported binding is
 *      never used, and there is no default or named export to
 *      bind it to.
 *
 *   3. Mount the React tree into `<div id="root">`, wrapped in
 *      `<StrictMode>` so that React 19's development-only checks
 *      run in dev builds. StrictMode has no effect in production
 *      builds — it is erased at build time.
 *
 *   4. Guard against the case where the root element is missing.
 *      This should never happen — the `#root` div is declared in
 *      `index.html` and is a fixed part of the app shell — but
 *      if a future refactor renamed it, a silent null-dereference
 *      during startup would be much harder to diagnose than an
 *      explicit "root element not found" error.
 *
 * What this file deliberately does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not import React itself. React 19 with the
 *     `react-jsx` transform (enabled in tsconfig.json) does not
 *     require `import React from 'react'` at the top of a file
 *     that uses JSX. Only the two named imports this file
 *     actually uses — `StrictMode` and `createRoot` — are pulled
 *     in.
 *
 *   - It does not install an ErrorBoundary at this level. Error
 *     boundaries are a React concept and belong in the component
 *     tree (typically in `App.tsx`) where the boundary's layout
 *     context makes sense. The two window listeners below catch
 *     errors that escape the tree entirely — a category no
 *     boundary can address.
 *
 *   - It does not check for the React DevTools global or print a
 *     banner about it. Vite's dev-mode banner already announces
 *     the dev server, and React itself prints a warning if the
 *     extension is missing in dev.
 *
 * The import paths use the `.js` extension convention that the
 * rest of the codebase follows — `./App.js` resolves to
 * `./App.tsx` under the `NodeNext` module resolution configured
 * in tsconfig.json and the Vite resolver plugin in
 * `vite.config.ts`. The CSS import keeps its own extension
 * because Vite's asset pipeline keys on the extension to
 * determine how to process the file (CSS files go through the
 * PostCSS pipeline configured in `postcss.config.js`).
 */

import { StrictMode } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

import App from './App.js';
import './styles/tailwind.css';

// ============================================================
//  Global error handlers
// ============================================================
//
// Installed before the mount so that any error thrown during
// the initial render is captured. Both handlers log to the
// console and return — they do not prevent default browser
// behaviour and do not attempt to recover. Recovery is not
// possible from a global handler; the correct response to an
// uncaught error is a clear diagnostic and letting the process
// continue in whatever state it is in. A future error-boundary
// component inside the React tree can add user-visible recovery
// for errors that occur within the tree; these two listeners
// exist for the errors that escape it.

/**
 * Uncaught synchronous errors.
 *
 * The `error` event is triggered by any error that reaches the
 * top of the call stack without a `try/catch` — including
 * errors thrown during a React render phase, errors in event
 * handlers that are not caught by a boundary, and resource load
 * failures (images, stylesheets, scripts) that the browser
 * reports through this same channel.
 *
 * The `event.error` field carries the actual `Error` object
 * when the browser can supply one. `event.message` is the
 * fallback string for cases where the error object is not
 * available — cross-origin script errors, for example, are
 * sanitized by the browser to a generic string for security
 * reasons. Logging whichever is present ensures a diagnostic
 * line regardless of which form the event takes.
 */
window.addEventListener('error', (event) => {
  console.error(
    '[renderer] uncaught error:',
    event.error ?? event.message
  );
});

/**
 * Unhandled promise rejections.
 *
 * The `unhandledrejection` event is triggered when a rejected
 * promise has no `.catch()` handler and the rejection reaches
 * the event loop unclaimed. This is a common failure mode in
 * async code that uses `await` inside an event handler without
 * a `try/catch` — the promise rejects and nothing observes it,
 * which silently swallows an error that would otherwise surface.
 *
 * `event.reason` carries the rejection value — usually an
 * `Error` object, but sometimes a string or an arbitrary value
 * if the promise was rejected with something other than an
 * `Error`. Logging it directly preserves whatever the code threw.
 */
window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', (event) => {
  console.error(
    '[renderer] unhandled rejection:',
    event.reason
  );
});

// ============================================================
//  Mount
// ============================================================

/**
 * Locate the root element declared in `index.html`.
 *
 * A missing element is treated as a fatal configuration error
 * rather than a silent fallback. The alternative — creating a
 * detached `<div>` and mounting into it — would produce a
 * functioning React tree with no visible output, which is a
 * harder failure to diagnose than the explicit throw below.
 *
 * The non-null assertion that would typically follow this lookup
 * (`document.getElementById('root')!`) is deliberately not used.
 * The explicit null check produces a named error with a
 * descriptive message if the element ever disappears, and the
 * cost — one branch that never fires in a working app — is
 * negligible compared to the diagnostic value if it ever does.
 */
const container = document.getElementById('root');
if (!container) {
  throw new Error(
    'Renderer: root element #root not found. ' +
      'Check that index.html declares <div id="root"></div>.'
  );
}

/**
 * Create the React root and render the app.
 *
 * `createRoot` is React 18+'s concurrent root API — the modern
 * replacement for the legacy `ReactDOM.render`. It returns a
 * root handle whose `.render()` method starts the initial render
 * and then reconciles subsequent updates on the concurrent
 * scheduler.
 *
 * `<StrictMode>` wraps the app in development-only checks: it
 * double-invokes certain lifecycle methods, warns about unsafe
 * patterns, and surfaces deprecated APIs early. In production
 * builds, StrictMode is a no-op and adds no runtime cost — the
 * compiler and React both erase its behaviour.
 */
const root = createRoot(container);
root.render(
  <StrictMode>
    <App />
  </StrictMode>
);
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/index.html">
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />

    <!--
      Content-Security-Policy — baseline policy for the renderer.

      This meta tag is the renderer's first line of defense. It
      applies in both development (Vite serving the file over
      http://localhost:5173) and production (Electron loading the
      bundled HTML over file:// or a custom protocol). The policy
      is deliberately permissive on the two directives Vite
      requires to function in dev — 'unsafe-inline' and
      'unsafe-eval' on script-src, plus ws: on connect-src — and
      correspondingly strict everywhere else.

      The intent is:
        - default-src 'self'     — every resource type not
                                    overridden below is
                                    restricted to the app's own
                                    origin. External scripts,
                                    external images, external
                                    styles: all blocked by
                                    default.
        - script-src             — the app's own bundle plus the
                                    two unsafe-* keywords Vite's
                                    HMR injects in dev. In a
                                    production build the main
                                    process is expected to
                                    tighten this (drop the two
                                    unsafe keywords) via
                                    session.defaultSession.webRequest
                                    .onHeadersReceived, which
                                    overrides the meta tag's policy
                                    for the packaged app.
        - style-src              — the app's own CSS plus
                                    'unsafe-inline', which Tailwind
                                    and Vite's dev-mode style
                                    injection both require.
        - img-src                — the app's own images plus
                                    data: and blob: URLs, which
                                    the renderer uses for icons and
                                    in-memory previews.
        - font-src               — the app's own fonts plus
                                    data: URLs (some build
                                    pipelines inline small fonts).
        - connect-src            — the app's own origin, plus
                                    ws:/wss: for Vite's HMR
                                    websocket, plus http:/https:
                                    so the renderer can reach the
                                    backend API at whatever URL
                                    the app is configured with.

      The policy is intentionally not locked down to specific
      hostnames: the backend API URL is a runtime configuration
      (it lives in the app's settings store), and hard-coding a
      hostname here would either break the app for users who
      point it at a self-hosted server, or require rebuilding the
      renderer for each deployment. The main process is the
      correct place to enforce host-level restrictions if and
      when they are needed.
    -->
    <meta
      http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"
      content="
        default-src 'self';
        script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval';
        style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
        img-src 'self' data: blob:;
        font-src 'self' data:;
        connect-src 'self' ws: wss: http: https:;
        object-src 'none';
        base-uri 'self';
        form-action 'self';
      "
    />

    <title>WriteSpeare</title>
  </head>

  <body>
    <!--
      The single mount point the React renderer attaches to.

      Every component tree in the app lives under this element.
      The id is `root` by convention — every React quick-start
      and every `createRoot(document.getElementById('root'))`
      call in the codebase expects exactly this id. Changing it
      would require changing the renderer's bootstrap file to
      match, and there is no benefit to either.
    -->
    <div id="root"></div>

    <!--
      The renderer's entry module.

      Vite resolves this path relative to the Vite project root
      (which is `apps/desktop/`, the directory containing this
      HTML file). The leading slash makes the path root-relative,
      which is what Vite's dev server expects.

      In development, this script tag causes the browser to
      request the module from the Vite dev server. Vite compiles
      the TypeScript on the fly and serves it with HMR wired in.

      In production, Vite's build step rewrites this tag to point
      at the bundled, minified, content-hashed JavaScript asset
      under `dist/renderer/assets/`. The relative base (`base:
      './'` in vite.config.ts) ensures the rewritten URL resolves
      correctly when the packaged app loads the HTML over
      `file://`.

      `type="module"` is required — it tells the browser to load
      the script as an ES module, which is what enables top-level
      `import` statements and what Vite's transform pipeline
      emits. A classic (non-module) script tag would fail to
      parse the bundled output.
    -->
    <script type="module" src="/src/renderer/index.tsx"></script>
  </body>
</html>
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/postcss.config.js">
/**
 * PostCSS configuration for the WriteSpeare renderer.
 *
 * PostCSS is the CSS transformation pipeline that Vite runs every
 * stylesheet through during development and at build time. This
 * file tells PostCSS which plugins to apply, in what order. The
 * renderer's stylesheet — `src/renderer/styles/tailwind.css` — is
 * written using Tailwind's directive syntax (`@tailwind base;`,
 * `@tailwind components;`, `@tailwind utilities;`) plus a small
 * set of custom base styles. Those directives are not valid CSS;
 * they are placeholders that the Tailwind PostCSS plugin replaces
 * with the actual generated CSS. Without this config, Vite would
 * pass the stylesheet through unchanged, the directives would
 * remain in the output as unknown at-rules, and every Tailwind
 * utility class in the app's `.tsx` files would have no matching
 * CSS rule — the renderer would display unstyled HTML.
 *
 * The two plugins — what each one does and why it is here:
 *
 *   1. `tailwindcss` — reads the `content` glob from
 *      `tailwind.config.js`, scans every file the glob matches
 *      for class-name strings, generates the minimal set of
 *      utility rules that covers the class names it found, and
 *      substitutes the generated rules in place of the
 *      `@tailwind` directives. This is the plugin that makes
 *      every `bg-primary`, `text-accent`, `rounded-2xl`, and
 *      `shadow-soft` class in the app do something.
 *
 *   2. `autoprefixer` — parses the CSS that Tailwind produced
 *      (and the custom base styles in the same stylesheet),
 *      checks each rule against a browser-target list, and adds
 *      the vendor prefixes (`-webkit-`, `-moz-`, `-ms-`) that
 *      the target browsers need. Electron 44 bundles a modern
 *      Chromium, so most modern CSS is supported unprefixed;
 *      the prefixes Autoprefixer adds are for the few edge cases
 *      Chromium still requires (certain flexbox gap behaviours,
 *      `user-select`, `appearance` on form controls). Removing
 *      Autoprefixer would not visibly break the app today, but
 *      it would leave those edge cases as a latent bug — a
 *      property that renders correctly in a fresh install but
 *      breaks on an older Chromium on a user's machine.
 *
 * Plugin order matters and is not alphabetical:
 *
 *   Tailwind runs first, Autoprefixer runs second. The order is
 *   required, not a preference:
 *
 *     - Tailwind's job is to expand the `@tailwind` directives
 *       into generated utility rules. The generated rules are
 *       what Autoprefixer needs to see — if Autoprefixer ran
 *       first, it would see only the `@tailwind` directives and
 *       have nothing to prefix.
 *
 *     - Autoprefixer's job is to inspect every rule in the
 *       stylesheet (both the ones Tailwind generated and the
 *       custom base styles written by hand) and add any missing
 *       vendor prefixes. Running it after Tailwind is what
 *       ensures the generated utilities are also prefixed where
 *       needed.
 *
 *   PostCSS runs plugins in the order they appear in the
 *   `plugins` object. Object key order is insertion order in
 *   JavaScript — the language specification guarantees this for
 *   string keys — so `tailwindcss` appearing first is what
 *   enforces the order. There is no separate "order" field; the
 *   order is the file.
 *
 * File format:
 *
 *   The `.js` extension with `export default` matches
 *   `tailwind.config.js` and reflects the workspace's
 *   `"type": "module"` setting in package.json. PostCSS's own
 *   loader detects the module system from the file extension
 *   and the enclosing package.json, so the ESM form is the
 *   correct one here.
 *
 * String-literal plugin names:
 *
 *   The `plugins` object uses string keys (`tailwindcss` and
 *   `autoprefixer`) that PostCSS resolves against node_modules
 *   at load time. This is the standard PostCSS config format and
 *   is what Vite's PostCSS integration expects. An alternative
 *   form — `import tailwindcss from 'tailwindcss'` followed by
 *   `plugins: [tailwindcss(), autoprefixer()]` — is also legal
 *   and equivalent. The string-literal form is used here because
 *   it is the convention established by Tailwind's own docs and
 *   because it produces a shorter file with no import statements
 *   whose resolution could fail if a future refactor moved
 *   `node_modules/`.
 *
 * What this file deliberately does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not configure PostCSS plugins beyond the two
 *     above. `postcss-import`, `postcss-nesting`, `cssnano` —
 *     none are enabled. Vite handles CSS imports at the
 *     bundler level, so `postcss-import` would be redundant.
 *     Vite's production build minifies CSS on its own, so
 *     `cssnano` would be redundant. Nested CSS is not used
 *     anywhere in the renderer's stylesheet.
 *
 *   - It does not set a `from` or `to` path. Those options are
 *     for PostCSS's own CLI; Vite's integration supplies them
 *     automatically from the file being processed.
 *
 *   - It does not reference `tailwind.config.js` by path.
 *     Tailwind's PostCSS plugin discovers the config file by
 *     convention — a file named `tailwind.config.js` at the
 *     project root — and loads it automatically. Naming the
 *     path explicitly would be redundant as long as the config
 *     file remains where it is (and it will: the plan's file
 *     tree fixes its location).
 */

export default {
  plugins: {
    tailwindcss: {},
    autoprefixer: {},
  },
};
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/tailwind.config.js">
/**
 * Tailwind CSS configuration for the WriteSpeare renderer.
 *
 * This file is the single source of truth for the app's visual
 * design tokens. Every color, font, radius, and shadow that the
 * renderer uses is declared here, and every Tailwind utility class
 * (`bg-primary`, `text-accent`, `rounded-2xl`, `shadow-soft`) is
 * generated from the values below. Nothing in the codebase should
 * hard-code a hex color or a raw pixel value for a design token —
 * if a new color is needed, it belongs here, not in a `style`
 * attribute or a CSS file.
 *
 * File format:
 *
 *   The file uses the `.js` extension even though it is consumed
 *   by a Node build tool that could load `.mjs` or `.cjs` equally
 *   well, because the plan's file tree declares it as
 *   `tailwind.config.js` and because `package.json` in this
 *   workspace declares `"type": "module"` — which makes this file
 *   ESM by default. The `export default` at the bottom is the
 *   correct form for an ESM module. There is no CommonJS
 *   alternative to consider; the surrounding package is ESM.
 *
 * No runtime import of Tailwind's types:
 *
 *   The `/** @type {import('tailwindcss').Config} *\/` JSDoc
 *   comment at the top of the exported object is what gives the
 *   editor IntelliSense for the `theme`, `content`, and other
 *   keys. It is a documentation-only reference — the `import(...)`
 *   inside a JSDoc comment is resolved by the language server
 *   without generating a runtime `require` or a bundler-side
 *   import. The same pattern is used in `postcss.config.js`.
 *
 * Color tokens — what each one is for:
 *
 *   `primary`     — the app's hero color. Used for primary action
 *                   buttons, active navigation states, focused
 *                   inputs, and any element that should read as
 *                   "the user's main path forward". The three
 *                   variants (DEFAULT, light, dark) cover hover,
 *                   disabled, and pressed states.
 *
 *   `secondary`   — a softer supporting color. Used for badges,
 *                   tags, secondary buttons, and any element
 *                   that needs to read as "related to primary
 *                   but not the main action".
 *
 *   `accent`      — a warm attention color. Used for warnings,
 *                   AI-marker flags, and any UI element that
 *                   needs to draw the eye without being as
 *                   dominant as a full primary button.
 *
 *   `text` and `background` — the two neutral base tokens. Used
 *                   as the foreground and background of every
 *                   page. The values are pure black and pure
 *                   white, which is deliberate: contrast is a
 *                   design decision made per-element with the
 *                   tinted tokens above, not a global choice
 *                   baked into these two.
 *
 *   The full palette for each token is a nested object with
 *   `DEFAULT`, `light`, and `dark` keys. Tailwind flattens this
 *   so that `bg-primary` maps to `primary.DEFAULT`, `bg-primary-light`
 *   maps to `primary.light`, and `bg-primary-dark` maps to
 *   `primary.dark` — the same convention Tailwind's built-in
 *   color palettes (`blue-500`, `blue-600`) follow.
 *
 * Font family — why the app declares its own stack:
 *
 *   The default Tailwind sans stack is a generic system font
 *   list. WriteSpeare wants a specific look — Inter for prose,
 *   JetBrains Mono for code and prompt templates — with system
 *   fallbacks so the app still renders correctly if the primary
 *   font is not installed on the user's machine. Neither font
 *   is bundled with the app by the plan; they are expected to
 *   be present on the developer's machine during development
 *   and available from the OS's font stack during use. If a
 *   future session decides to bundle them, the change is to add
 *   the font files under `src/resources/` and reference them
 *   from the CSS — not to change this file.
 *
 * Border radius — why the app extends Tailwind's defaults:
 *
 *   Tailwind's default scale stops at `rounded-3xl` (1.5rem).
 *   The plan's mockups use `rounded-xl` and `rounded-2xl` heavily,
 *   and the app wants a softer, more modern feel than Tailwind's
 *   built-in `xl` (0.75rem) provides. The extension overrides
 *   the two default tokens at the sizes the app actually uses,
 *   so that `rounded-xl` renders at 1rem rather than 0.75rem.
 *   This is an override, not an addition — the defaults it
 *   replaces were not in use anywhere in the codebase.
 *
 * Box shadow — why the app declares two named shadows:
 *
 *   Named shadows (`shadow-soft`, `shadow-medium`) are easier to
 *   reason about than numeric Tailwind sizes and easier to
 *   change globally: bumping the opacity of every card shadow
 *   in the app is a one-line change here rather than a search-
 *   and-replace across fifty components. The two values are
 *   deliberately subtle — this is a productivity app, not a
 *   marketing site, and heavy drop shadows read as dated on a
 *   UI that a user spends hours inside.
 *
 * Dark mode — why `class`, not `media`:
 *
 *   Tailwind's two dark-mode strategies are `'media'` (follow
 *   the OS preference via `prefers-color-scheme`) and `'class'`
 *   (toggle by adding a `dark` class to an ancestor element).
 *   The app uses `'class'` because the theme preference is an
 *   explicit, per-user setting stored in `UserSettingsMap.theme`
 *   — a user who prefers light mode on a dark-mode OS, or vice
 *   versa, should get what they chose, not what the OS chose.
 *   The `dark` class is applied to the `<html>` element by the
 *   renderer's root component based on the stored setting.
 *
 * The `content` glob — why it lists both HTML and TSX:
 *
 *   Tailwind works by scanning source files for class-name
 *   strings, then emitting only the CSS utilities that were
 *   actually found. Files that are not in this list are not
 *   scanned, and any class name that appears only in an
 *   unscanned file is silently dropped from the output — the
 *   utility exists but its styles do not, which produces a
 *   visually broken element with no error message. The glob
 *   below covers the two places class names ever appear: the
 *   Vite entry HTML (which carries a small number of classes on
 *   the `<body>` and a loading splash), and every TS/TSX file
 *   under `src/` (where all component classes live).
 */

/** @type {import('tailwindcss').Config} */
export default {
  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  //  Content
  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  //  The two patterns below cover the only two file locations
  //  where Tailwind class names appear in this app. See the
  //  file header for why an unscanned file is a silent failure.
  content: [
    './index.html',
    './src/**/*.{js,ts,jsx,tsx}',
  ],

  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  //  Dark mode
  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  //  'class' rather than 'media' — the user's stored theme
  //  preference wins over the OS preference. See the file header.
  darkMode: 'class',

  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  //  Theme
  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  theme: {
    extend: {
      // ---- Brand colors ----
      //  The three brand tokens plus the two neutral base tokens.
      //  Every color used in the UI resolves to one of these, or
      //  to a Tailwind built-in for status colors (red-600 for
      //  errors, amber-500 for warnings) that the design does
      //  not need to override.
      colors: {
        text: '#000000',
        background: '#ffffff',
        primary: {
          DEFAULT: '#03A791',
          light: '#81E7AF',
          dark: '#028A78',
        },
        secondary: {
          DEFAULT: '#81E7AF',
          dark: '#5BC98A',
        },
        accent: {
          DEFAULT: '#F1BA88',
          dark: '#E0A06A',
        },
      },

      // ---- Font families ----
      //  Two stacks: `sans` for prose, `mono` for code and
      //  prompt templates. Both fall back to the system stack
      //  so the app renders correctly on a machine where Inter
      //  and JetBrains Mono are not installed.
      fontFamily: {
        sans: ['Inter', 'system-ui', 'sans-serif'],
        mono: ['JetBrains Mono', 'monospace'],
      },

      // ---- Border radius ----
      //  Overrides Tailwind's `xl` and `2xl` defaults at the
      //  sizes the app actually uses. See the file header for
      //  why these are overrides rather than additions.
      borderRadius: {
        xl: '1rem',
        '2xl': '1.5rem',
      },

      // ---- Box shadows ----
      //  Two named, deliberately subtle shadows. See the file
      //  header for why they are named and why they are soft.
      boxShadow: {
        soft: '0 2px 8px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.08)',
        medium: '0 4px 16px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.12)',
      },
    },
  },

  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  //  Plugins
  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  //  No plugins are enabled. Every utility the app uses is
  //  either a Tailwind core utility or one of the theme
  //  extensions declared above. If a future session needs a
  //  plugin (forms, typography, aspect-ratio), it is added to
  //  this array — the plan does not declare any.
  plugins: [],
};
</file>

<file path="apps/desktop/tsconfig.json">
{
  // ============================================================
  //  WriteSpeare — Desktop TypeScript Configuration
  // ============================================================
  //  A single config serves both compilation targets of the
  //  desktop app:
  //
  //    - The Electron main process, under `src/main/`, compiled
  //      by `tsc` (via the `build:main` script in package.json)
  //      to `dist/main/` and executed by Electron under Node's
  //      ESM loader.
  //
  //    - The React renderer, under `src/renderer/`, type-checked
  //      by the same `tsc` run but bundled into `dist/renderer/`
  //      by Vite. The compiled output of the renderer that `tsc`
  //      writes is unused — Vite produces the actual runtime
  //      bundle — but running the type check across it is
  //      valuable, because a type error in a `.tsx` file should
  //      fail `npm run type-check` the same way a type error in
  //      a `.ts` file does.
  //
  //  The two targets have different runtime environments (Node
  //  vs. browser) but share the same TypeScript language rules
  //  and the same import convention — the `.js`-suffixed
  //  specifier that points at a `.ts` source. That shared
  //  convention is what makes a single config possible: both
  //  targets resolve imports the same way, and the only
  //  environment-specific difference is the set of global types
  //  each target needs (Node globals for the main process, DOM
  //  globals for the renderer), which is expressed by listing
  //  both environments in the `lib` array.
  //
  //  The config is deliberately kept in lockstep with the
  //  server's tsconfig where the two overlap. Any change to the
  //  strictness flags here should be weighed against the same
  //  change on the server; the two configs are the same shape on
  //  purpose so that a reader who has internalised one has
  //  internalised both.
  // ============================================================

  "compilerOptions": {
    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  File Layout
    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  `rootDir` is `src/` so that compiled paths mirror source
    //  paths: `src/main/index.ts` → `dist/main/index.js`. The
    //  `main` field of package.json points at
    //  `dist/main/index.js`, so this mapping is what makes the
    //  Electron entry point resolvable.
    //
    //  `outDir` is `dist/`, the same directory the renderer
    //  build writes to. Vite writes to `dist/renderer/` (per
    //  `build.outDir` in vite.config.ts); `tsc` writes to
    //  whatever subdirectory each source file's path dictates.
    //  The two writers never collide, because Vite clears only
    //  its own subdirectory and `tsc` never writes to
    //  `dist/renderer/`.
    "rootDir": "./src",
    "outDir": "./dist",

    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  Environment Settings
    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  `module` and `moduleResolution` are `NodeNext`, matching
    //  the server config and the codebase-wide convention of
    //  `.js`-suffixed import specifiers that resolve to `.ts`
    //  sources. NodeNext is the only resolution mode that
    //  requires the runtime extension to be present in the
    //  source, which is exactly what the codebase does — so
    //  NodeNext is the only mode that will accept the imports
    //  as written.
    //
    //  `target` is ES2022. Electron 44 ships a modern V8 that
    //  supports all of ES2022 natively, and the renderer is
    //  bundled by Vite which does not care about the target. The
    //  choice between ES2020 and ES2022 is invisible to the
    //  running app; ES2022 is used here for consistency with the
    //  `lib` list below.
    //
    //  `lib` lists both DOM and ES2022. DOM is needed by the
    //  renderer (for `document`, `window`, `HTMLElement`, and
    //  every other browser global). ES2022 is needed by both
    //  targets. Listing both libraries in a single config means
    //  a main-process file could technically reference a DOM
    //  global without the compiler complaining — an acceptably
    //  small risk given the alternative would be two configs and
    //  a project-references setup that the plan does not
    //  declare.
    //
    //  `jsx` is `react-jsx`, the automatic JSX runtime introduced
    //  in React 17 and used exclusively by React 19. It means
    //  `.tsx` files do not need to `import React from 'react'`
    //  at the top — the compiler inserts the runtime import
    //  automatically.
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "target": "ES2022",
    "lib": ["ES2022", "DOM", "DOM.Iterable"],
    "jsx": "react-jsx",

    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  Outputs
    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  Sourcemaps are emitted for both targets. Vite produces
    //  its own renderer sourcemaps (see `build.sourcemap` in
    //  vite.config.ts); the sourcemaps produced here cover the
    //  main-process build, which is what a stack trace from the
    //  Electron main process will need in order to be readable.
    "sourceMap": true,

    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  Strict Typechecking
    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  Identical set to the server config. See the server's
    //  tsconfig.json for the reasoning behind each flag; the
    //  same reasoning applies here verbatim.
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,

    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  Style / Hygiene
    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "noImplicitOverride": true,
    "noUnusedLocals": true,
    "noUnusedParameters": true,
    "noFallthroughCasesInSwitch": true,
    "noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature": true,

    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  Recommended / Module Hygiene
    // ----------------------------------------------------------
    //  `isolatedModules` is required by Vite. Vite's transform
    //  pipeline handles one file at a time and cannot see the
    //  whole module graph, so it depends on the compiler having
    //  already enforced that every file is independently
    //  transpilable. This flag is what guarantees that.
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "noUncheckedSideEffectImports": true,
    "moduleDetection": "force",

    //  `skipLibCheck` is enabled — even more important for the
    //  desktop app than for the server, because Electron's
    //  bundled `.d.ts` files are large and occasionally reference
    //  types from other libraries that are not installed in a
    //  given configuration. Skipping the check means a `.d.ts`
    //  file authored by a third party cannot break the app's
    //  build by being slightly out of date with its own
    //  dependencies.
    "skipLibCheck": true,

    //  `esModuleInterop` and `allowSyntheticDefaultImports` are
    //  both enabled, matching the server config. They let code
    //  written against CommonJS modules (some Electron packages,
    //  some Node builtins) be imported with a default-import
    //  syntax that would otherwise be a type error.
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "allowSyntheticDefaultImports": true,

    //  `forceConsistentCasingInFileNames` is required on a
    //  project that builds on Windows and is likely to be
    //  checked out on a case-insensitive filesystem. It ensures
    //  that an import of `./Foo` does not accidentally resolve
    //  to `./foo` on the developer's machine and then fail on
    //  a case-sensitive CI runner.
    "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true,

    //  `resolveJsonModule` is enabled so that a source file can
    //  import a `.json` file (for example, `package.json` for a
    //  version string, or a config fixture) with a typed
    //  import. No file currently does, but the flag costs
    //  nothing and prevents a future surprise.
    "resolveJsonModule": true
  },

  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  //  Scope
  // ----------------------------------------------------------
  //  Every source file under `src/` is included. The main
  //  process, the renderer, the features, the shared utilities —
  //  all of it — is type-checked by a single `tsc` run.
  //
  //  `exclude` covers the three directories that never contain
  //  TypeScript source: `node_modules/` (dependencies),
  //  `dist/` (compiled output), and `release/` (electron-builder
  //  packaging output). None of them would contain a `.ts` or
  //  `.tsx` file, but listing them explicitly is the correct
  //  hygiene and prevents a stray generated file from being
  //  pulled into the compilation.
  "include": ["src/**/*"],
  "exclude": ["node_modules", "dist", "release"]
}
