<file path="apps/desktop/vite.config.ts">
/**
 * Vite configuration for the WriteSpeare renderer.
 *
 * The renderer is the React half of the Electron app — the code
 * that runs in the browser context of the desktop window and
 * talks to the main process through `window.electronAPI.*`. This
 * file configures the build and dev-server behaviour for that
 * half only. The main process is compiled separately by `tsc`
 * (see `build:main` in `package.json`) and is not touched by
 * Vite.
 *
 * What this config does, in order:
 *
 *   1. Sets `base: './'` — the single most important setting in
 *      this file. When the packaged Electron app loads the
 *      renderer from a `file://` URL, an asset path like
 *      `/assets/index-abc123.js` resolves to
 *      `file:///assets/index-abc123.js` (the filesystem root)
 *      instead of the app's own directory. The resulting page
 *      loads with a blank white screen and a stack of "failed to
 *      load resource" errors in the devtools console — one of
 *      the most common Electron packaging bugs and one of the
 *      hardest to diagnose without knowing to look for it. A
 *      relative base makes every asset URL resolve against the
 *      HTML file's own location, which works correctly in both
 *      the dev server and the packaged app.
 *
 *   2. Registers `@vitejs/plugin-react` — the official React
 *      plugin. It wires up the JSX/TSX transform (via esbuild)
 *      and Fast Refresh in dev. Every `.tsx` file in the
 *      renderer depends on it.
 *
 *   3. Registers a small custom plugin — `tsFromJsResolver` —
 *      that maps a relative import specifier ending in `.js` or
 *      `.jsx` to the matching `.ts` or `.tsx` file on disk. Every
 *      import in this codebase uses the `.js` extension even
 *      though the source files are `.ts`, because the main
 *      process is compiled under NodeNext resolution which
 *      requires the extension. Without this plugin, Vite would
 *      fail to resolve those imports in the renderer — the
 *      `.js` file does not exist on disk, only its `.ts` source.
 *      See the plugin's own docstring for the mechanics.
 *
 *   4. Pins the dev server to port 5173 with `strictPort: true`.
 *      The Electron main process hard-codes the same port when
 *      loading the renderer from the dev server, so a port
 *      collision must fail loudly rather than silently shifting
 *      to 5174 and leaving the main process pointed at a dead
 *      URL.
 *
 *   5. Disables Vite's clear-screen behaviour. When Electron and
 *      Vite are run together under a single terminal — the
 *      common dev loop — Vite's default clear-screen would wipe
 *      Electron's startup logs every time Vite restarts. That is
 *      the opposite of helpful when debugging.
 *
 * What this config deliberately does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not set `root`. Vite defaults `root` to the
 *     directory containing the config file, which is
 *     `apps/desktop/` — exactly where `index.html` lives. Setting
 *     it explicitly to the same value would be redundant.
 *
 *   - It does not set `resolve.alias` for `@` or any other
 *     shorthand. No source file in the plan's structure uses an
 *     alias — every import is a relative path — and adding an
 *     alias now would be a solution without a problem. If a
 *     future refactor introduces one, it belongs here.
 *
 *   - It does not configure the main-process build. That is
 *     `tsc`'s job, and the two builds are orchestrated by the
 *     `build` script in `package.json`.
 */

import { defineConfig, type Plugin } from 'vite';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { existsSync } from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';

// ============================================================
//  Module-local paths
// ============================================================
//
// This config file is ESM (the desktop package.json declares
// `"type": "module"`), so the CommonJS `__dirname` global is not
// available. It is reconstructed from `import.meta.url` below
// for any code that needs the config file's own directory. Vite
// itself defaults `root` to this directory, so `currentDir` is
// only used inside the resolver plugin, where it is not needed —
// the plugin resolves specifiers relative to the importer, not
// the config file.

const currentDir = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));

/**
 * Resolve a relative import specifier that ends in `.js` or
 * `.jsx` to the matching `.ts` or `.tsx` source file on disk.
 *
 * Why this is necessary:
 *
 *   Every import specifier across this codebase — in the backend,
 *   in the desktop main process, and in the renderer — ends in
 *   `.js`, even though the source files are `.ts`. This is the
 *   NodeNext ESM convention: TypeScript's `moduleResolution:
 *   "NodeNext"` requires the runtime extension to appear in the
 *   source, because Node.js resolves imports literally and does
 *   not try alternate extensions.
 *
 *   Vite, by contrast, resolves imports the way a bundler does —
 *   it tries a list of extensions when the specifier has no
 *   extension, but it does NOT try to substitute extensions when
 *   the specifier already HAS one. An import of `./foo.js` asks
 *   Vite for a file literally named `foo.js`; the fact that a
 *   sibling file is named `foo.ts` is invisible to Vite's default
 *   resolver.
 *
 *   This plugin closes that gap. It runs `enforce: 'pre'`, so it
 *   sees every import before Vite's default resolver does. When
 *   it matches the pattern it is looking for, it returns the
 *   absolute path to the correct `.ts`/`.tsx` file; when it does
 *   not match, it returns `null` and Vite's default resolver
 *   proceeds unchanged.
 *
 * What it does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not touch bare package specifiers (`react`,
 *     `axios`) or subpath imports of packages (`react/jsx-runtime`).
 *     Those are handled by Vite's node resolution against
 *     `node_modules`. The check `source.startsWith('.')` limits
 *     this plugin to relative specifiers only.
 *
 *   - It does not handle absolute paths. The codebase does not
 *     use any, and relative specifiers are the only shape this
 *     plugin needs to recognize.
 *
 *   - It does not handle imports from another file's `.js` output
 *     in `dist/`. The renderer only ever imports from `.ts`/`.tsx`
 *     sources; the compiled `.js` output of the main process is
 *     never loaded into the renderer's module graph.
 *
 * The plugin is defined inline (rather than as a separate module)
 * because it is used exactly once, here, and its entire purpose
 * is expressed by this single function. Splitting it into its own
 * file would add a layer of indirection without adding a decision.
 */
const tsFromJsResolver = (): Plugin => ({
  name: 'ts-from-js-resolver',
  enforce: 'pre',

  /**
   * Vite calls this hook for every import specifier in the
   * module graph. Returning a string short-circuits the default
   * resolution; returning `null` delegates to the next resolver.
   *
   * The signature matches Vite's `Plugin['resolveId']` — Vite's
   * own type definitions make `importer` possibly `undefined`
   * when the specifier is the entry point, so the guard checks
   * for its presence explicitly rather than assuming it is
   * always defined.
   */
  resolveId(source, importer) {
    // No importer means this is the entry point itself — the
    // index.html or the renderer entry file — which is always a
    // real file on disk. Nothing to resolve.
    if (!importer) {
      return null;
    }

    // Only relative specifiers. Bare package names and absolute
    // paths are handled by Vite's own resolution chain.
    if (!source.startsWith('.')) {
      return null;
    }

    // Only specifiers that already carry a `.js` or `.jsx`
    // extension. Specifiers without an extension are correctly
    // resolved by Vite's default extension list.
    const isJs = source.endsWith('.js');
    const isJsx = source.endsWith('.jsx');
    if (!isJs && !isJsx) {
      return null;
    }

    // Build the candidate `.ts` / `.tsx` paths by stripping the
    // `.js` / `.jsx` extension and appending the TypeScript
    // extensions. Both extensions are tried for `.js` — a file
    // named `foo.js` could originate from either `foo.ts` or
    // `foo.tsx`. For `.jsx` only `.tsx` is tried, because the
    // `.jsx` extension in this codebase is only used to refer to
    // `.tsx` sources.
    const candidates = isJsx
      ? [source.slice(0, -4) + '.tsx']
      : [source.slice(0, -3) + '.ts', source.slice(0, -3) + '.tsx'];

    // Resolve each candidate relative to the importing file's
    // directory. `path.dirname(importer)` is the correct base
    // because the specifier is relative to the importer, not to
    // the config file or the project root.
    for (const candidate of candidates) {
      const resolved = path.resolve(path.dirname(importer), candidate);
      if (existsSync(resolved)) {
        return resolved;
      }
    }

    // No matching `.ts`/`.tsx` file. Return null so Vite's
    // default resolver runs — it will produce a clear
    // "module not found" error naming the missing file, which is
    // the correct diagnostic for this case.
    return null;
  },
});

// ============================================================
//  Export
// ============================================================

export default defineConfig({
  // Relative base — critical for the packaged Electron app. See
  // the file header for the full reasoning.
  base: './',

  // React plugin for JSX/TSX transform and Fast Refresh, plus
  // the local resolver for `.js`-suffixed imports of `.ts`
  // sources. Plugin order does not matter here — the resolver
  // uses `enforce: 'pre'` to run before Vite's defaults
  // regardless of where it sits in the array — but keeping
  // `react()` first reads naturally as "the main plugin, then
  // the helper".
  plugins: [react(), tsFromJsResolver()],

  build: {
    // Renderer output goes into its own subdirectory so it does
    // not collide with the main-process output that `tsc` writes
    // to `dist/main/`. Both subdirectories live under `dist/`,
    // which the electron-builder `files` glob in `package.json`
    // picks up in one pass.
    outDir: 'dist/renderer',

    // Clear this directory before each build. Only `dist/renderer`
    // is cleared — the sibling `dist/main/` is left alone, so a
    // `vite build` run does not wipe the main-process output that
    // was written by a previous `tsc` run.
    emptyOutDir: true,

    // Sourcemaps are emitted in dev builds and, by default, in
    // production builds too. The build script does not currently
    // pass `--mode production`, so Vite's default `mode` is
    // `production`, and this setting opts in to sourcemaps for
    // that mode. They are small enough at this codebase's size
    // to keep, and they are the difference between a readable
    // stack trace and a wall of minified identifiers when a
    // renderer bug surfaces in the packaged app.
    sourcemap: true,
  },

  server: {
    // Pin the dev server to 5173. The Electron main process loads
    // the renderer from `http://localhost:5173` in dev mode, so a
    // silent port shift would leave the main process pointed at a
    // dead URL and the window blank with no obvious error.
    port: 5173,

    // Fail loudly on a port collision rather than shifting to
    // 5174. See the comment above.
    strictPort: true,
  },

  // Do not clear the terminal between rebuilds. When Electron and
  // Vite are running together under a single terminal — the
  // common dev loop, orchestrated by the `dev` script — Vite's
  // default clear-screen would erase Electron's startup logs
  // every time Vite restarts. The logs are what a developer
  // needs most during a restart, so they are preserved.
  clearScreen: false,
});
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/admin/controllers/adminController.ts">
/**
 * HTTP handlers for the WriteSpeare admin feature.
 *
 * Admin-only management of system-wide presets. Every handler is
 * expected to be mounted behind BOTH `authenticate` and
 * `requireAdmin` at the route layer, so by the time a request
 * reaches here the caller is an authenticated administrator. The
 * controller does NOT re-check the role — that check has already
 * been performed by the middleware, and duplicating it here would
 * split the authorization contract across two files.
 *
 * What "admin config" means in this codebase:
 *
 *   The plan annotates the admin controller as "Config update
 *   endpoints". That phrase is the entire specification the plan
 *   gives, and it is ambiguous on its face — the plan declares
 *   no `AdminConfig`, `SystemConfig`, or `GlobalSettings` model,
 *   and none of the shared types describes a distinct
 *   admin-managed entity.
 *
 *   The service (`adminService.ts`) resolves the ambiguity by
 *   picking the ONE form of cross-user configuration the
 *   existing schema supports: the system-wide Preset. A preset
 *   with `userId: null` is the semantic marker for "system
 *   preset, visible to every user", and the user-scoped
 *   `settingsService.createPreset` deliberately refuses to
 *   manufacture one — it always stamps the caller's own userId.
 *   The admin feature is the one path that can create, edit, and
 *   delete presets in the system scope.
 *
 *   This controller exposes that capability through four
 *   endpoints, all under the `/api/admin/presets` sub-path. The
 *   service header documents the scope decision in full; this
 *   header only restates the shape so a reader of the controller
 *   does not have to jump files to understand why "admin config"
 *   maps onto the Preset collection.
 *
 * The inverted ownership model:
 *
 *   Every OTHER controller in this codebase either passes the
 *   CALLER's identity to its service (the ownership-scoped ones)
 *   or passes the TARGET's identity (the users feature). This
 *   controller passes NEITHER, because the entity it manages is
 *   owned by no one. A system preset is a shared resource: every
 *   administrator of the same installation manages the same
 *   system presets, and every user of the same installation
 *   reads the same system presets. There is no per-caller scope
 *   to filter on.
 *
 *   The consequence is that the defensive authentication guard
 *   this file applies — reading `req.user?.userId` and rejecting
 *   with a 401 if it is absent — is the ONLY thing the controller
 *   does with the caller's identity. The value is never passed to
 *   the service. Its sole purpose is to catch a route being
 *   misconfigured in a future refactor, where an admin-only
 *   handler is accidentally exposed without its middleware chain.
 *   That class of mistake is rare but has real consequences; the
 *   belt-and-braces guard is the cheap insurance.
 *
 * Response typing — the assignability bridge:
 *
 *   Every handler declares its `Response<T>` type as
 *   `ApiResponse<Preset>` or `ApiResponse<Preset[]>`. The service
 *   returns `PresetDocument` (Mongoose's in-process shape) which
 *   is structurally assignable to the shared `Preset` domain
 *   type — the only difference is that `PresetDocument._id` is a
 *   concrete `ObjectId` while `Preset._id` is `string | ObjectId`.
 *   Since `ObjectId` is a member of the union, the assignment is
 *   safe. At runtime, `res.json()` serialises the ObjectId to its
 *   hex string form.
 *
 * Validation is shallow:
 *
 *   The controller verifies the primitive type of each field that
 *   it reads from the request body or route params. It does NOT
 *   verify numeric ranges, slug formats, or anything else the
 *   Preset schema already enforces. Those checks are the schema's
 *   job; a Mongoose ValidationError is translated to a 400 by the
 *   terminal middleware with the schema's own message, which is
 *   exactly what a client should see. Duplicating the schema's
 *   rules here would create a second source of truth that could
 *   drift from the first.
 *
 * The upsert route's URL-vs-body precedence:
 *
 *   The upsert handler reads the preset's `name` from the route
 *   parameter (`/api/admin/presets/:name`) and the rest of the
 *   payload from the request body. The URL parameter is the
 *   authoritative source for the name — a `name` field in the
 *   body is IGNORED. This is the conventional REST behaviour for
 *   a resource whose identity is part of its URL, and it prevents
 *   a client from sending mismatched values (`PUT /presets/quick`
 *   with a body claiming `"name": "balanced"`) that would
 *   otherwise be ambiguous about which one wins.
 *
 *   The route is a PUT rather than a POST because the operation is
 *   idempotent: sending the same request twice produces the same
 *   final state (a single system preset with that name and the
 *   given configuration). PUT is the correct verb for that
 *   semantic, and it matches the service function's name
 *   (`upsertSystemPreset`).
 *
 * No try/catch appears anywhere in this file. Each route handler
 * is wrapped in `asyncHandler` at the route registration site,
 * which forwards any rejection to the terminal error middleware.
 * The middleware recognises the shared `AppError` class thrown by
 * the service — a 404 for a preset that does not exist, a 409 for
 * a name that collides within the system scope — and formats the
 * response with the same envelope this file uses on success.
 */

import type { Response } from 'express';

import {
  listSystemPresets as listSystemPresetsService,
  getSystemPresetByName as getSystemPresetByNameService,
  upsertSystemPreset as upsertSystemPresetService,
  deleteSystemPreset as deleteSystemPresetService,
} from '../services/adminService.js';

import type { AuthRequest } from '../../auth/middleware/authGuard.js';
import type {
  ApiResponse,
  Preset,
  PresetCreatePayload,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Primitive type predicates
// ============================================================
//
// The same predicates used by the settings controller for its
// create-preset and update-preset handlers. They are declared
// locally (rather than imported from a shared location) because
// the codebase's established convention is that each controller
// carries its own validation helpers — the settings controller
// does the same thing for the same fields, and no shared
// validators module exists in the plan's file tree.
//
// A future refactor could promote these predicates to a shared
// module (for example, `features/shared/utils/validators.ts`);
// that decision is out of scope for this file.

/**
 * A non-empty string. Rejects the empty string, which is the
 * common "client sent a field but left it blank" case.
 * Whitespace-only strings pass here and are rejected by the
 * schema's `trim: true` + `minlength` validators on the fields
 * that care.
 */
const isNonEmptyString = (value: unknown): value is string =>
  typeof value === 'string' && value.length > 0;

/**
 * A finite number. Rejects NaN, Infinity, and -Infinity — none of
 * which are meaningful for any numeric field on the preset
 * payload.
 */
const isNumber = (value: unknown): value is number =>
  typeof value === 'number' && Number.isFinite(value);

const isBoolean = (value: unknown): value is boolean =>
  typeof value === 'boolean';

/**
 * A `string[]`. Checks that the value is an array AND that every
 * element is a string — `Array.isArray` alone would accept
 * `[1, 2, 3]`.
 */
const isStringArray = (value: unknown): value is string[] =>
  Array.isArray(value) &&
  value.every((item) => typeof item === 'string');

/**
 * A two-element array of finite numbers. Used for the
 * `targetReadingGrade` tuple field on the preset payload.
 */
const isNumberTuple2 = (value: unknown): value is [number, number] => {
  if (!Array.isArray(value)) {
    return false;
  }
  if (value.length !== 2) {
    return false;
  }
  return value.every(
    (item) => typeof item === 'number' && Number.isFinite(item)
  );
};

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/admin/presets
// ============================================================

/**
 * List every system preset.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *      (See the file header for the belt-and-braces rationale —
 *      `requireAdmin` on the route already guarantees an
 *      authenticated admin reaches here.)
 *   2. Delegate to the service.
 *   3. Respond with 200 and the array. An empty array is a
 *      valid response for a fresh installation that has not yet
 *      run its preset seeder.
 *
 * No body, query, or route parameters are read. The endpoint's
 * only input is the fact that the caller is an administrator.
 */
export const listSystemPresets = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Preset[]>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Defensive authentication guard ----
  const callerId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!callerId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Delegate to the service ----
  const presets = await listSystemPresetsService();

  // ---- 3. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: presets,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/admin/presets/:name
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return a single system preset by its slug name.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:name` route parameter is missing
 *      or empty.
 *   3. Delegate to the service. The service normalizes the name
 *      (trim + lowercase) before querying, so a caller that
 *      supplies `"Balanced"` matches the same document as a
 *      caller that supplies `"balanced"`.
 *   4. A null result means "no such system preset"; this handler
 *      returns 404. Note that a user-owned preset with the same
 *      name is invisible here — the service's `{ userId: null }`
 *      filter excludes it — and correctly so, because it is not
 *      the system preset with that name.
 *   5. Respond with 200 and the preset, or 404.
 */
export const getSystemPresetByName = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Preset>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Defensive authentication guard ----
  const callerId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!callerId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const name = req.params['name'];
  if (!isNonEmptyString(name)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Preset name is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const preset = await getSystemPresetByNameService(name);
  if (!preset) {
    res.status(404).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'System preset not found.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: preset,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  PUT /api/admin/presets/:name
// ============================================================

/**
 * Create a new system preset, or update the existing one with
 * the same name. The operation is a true upsert — idempotent, so
 * sending the same request twice produces the same final state.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:name` route parameter is missing
 *      or empty.
 *   3. Reject with 400 if the request body is not a plain object.
 *   4. Validate every required field of the preset payload. The
 *      `name` field comes from the URL, not the body — see the
 *      file header for the URL-vs-body precedence rule. The
 *      remaining 21 fields are validated for their primitive
 *      types only; the schema is authoritative on ranges and
 *      formats.
 *   5. Delegate to the service. The service issues a single
 *      `findOneAndUpdate` with `upsert: true` and returns the
 *      resulting document.
 *   6. Respond with 200 and the resulting preset.
 *
 * Response status is 200 rather than 201. The operation is an
 * upsert, and the server does not distinguish "created" from
 * "updated" in the response body — both cases produce the same
 * document shape, and the client has no use for the distinction.
 * A separate 201-on-create / 200-on-update split would require
 * the service to report which branch ran, adding surface for no
 * benefit. Clients that want the distinction can compare the
 * returned document's `createdAt` against the current time; the
 * returned payload carries enough information.
 */
export const upsertSystemPreset = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Preset>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Defensive authentication guard ----
  const callerId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!callerId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const name = req.params['name'];
  if (!isNonEmptyString(name)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Preset name is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Body shape guard ----
  const rawBody: unknown = req.body;
  if (
    typeof rawBody !== 'object' ||
    rawBody === null ||
    Array.isArray(rawBody)
  ) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Request body must be a JSON object.',
    });
    return;
  }
  const body = rawBody as Record<string, unknown>;

  // ---- 4. Field-by-field validation ----
  // Every field is validated for its primitive type. Fields not
  // present in the body are rejected with a 400 — the payload
  // type requires all 21 non-name fields to be present, so a
  // missing field is a client error, not a "use the default"
  // case. (The schema has defaults for some of these fields, but
  // they apply when the SERVICE omits them, not when a client
  // does. A client building a system preset is expected to
  // specify the full configuration; the admin UI's form
  // pre-populates the fields from the schema's defaults.)

  const displayName = body['displayName'];
  if (!isNonEmptyString(displayName)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'displayName is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const sourceCount = body['sourceCount'];
  if (!isNumber(sourceCount)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'sourceCount must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const wordCount = body['wordCount'];
  if (!isNumber(wordCount)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'wordCount must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const searchEngines = body['searchEngines'];
  if (!isStringArray(searchEngines)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'searchEngines must be an array of strings.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const resultsPerPage = body['resultsPerPage'];
  if (!isNumber(resultsPerPage)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'resultsPerPage must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const maxResults = body['maxResults'];
  if (!isNumber(maxResults)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'maxResults must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const pageLoadTimeout = body['pageLoadTimeout'];
  if (!isNumber(pageLoadTimeout)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'pageLoadTimeout must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const maxRetries = body['maxRetries'];
  if (!isNumber(maxRetries)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'maxRetries must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const targetReadingGrade = body['targetReadingGrade'];
  if (!isNumberTuple2(targetReadingGrade)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'targetReadingGrade must be a 2-element array of numbers.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const minKeywordDensity = body['minKeywordDensity'];
  if (!isNumber(minKeywordDensity)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'minKeywordDensity must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const maxKeywordDensity = body['maxKeywordDensity'];
  if (!isNumber(maxKeywordDensity)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'maxKeywordDensity must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const maxTfidfSimilarity = body['maxTfidfSimilarity'];
  if (!isNumber(maxTfidfSimilarity)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'maxTfidfSimilarity must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const maxSemanticSimilarity = body['maxSemanticSimilarity'];
  if (!isNumber(maxSemanticSimilarity)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'maxSemanticSimilarity must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const maxAiMarkers = body['maxAiMarkers'];
  if (!isNumber(maxAiMarkers)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'maxAiMarkers must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const runReadabilityCheck = body['runReadabilityCheck'];
  if (!isBoolean(runReadabilityCheck)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'runReadabilityCheck must be a boolean.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const runSeoCheck = body['runSeoCheck'];
  if (!isBoolean(runSeoCheck)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'runSeoCheck must be a boolean.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const runOriginalityCheck = body['runOriginalityCheck'];
  if (!isBoolean(runOriginalityCheck)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'runOriginalityCheck must be a boolean.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const runAiMarkerCheck = body['runAiMarkerCheck'];
  if (!isBoolean(runAiMarkerCheck)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'runAiMarkerCheck must be a boolean.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const runGrammarCheck = body['runGrammarCheck'];
  if (!isBoolean(runGrammarCheck)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'runGrammarCheck must be a boolean.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const autoRegenerate = body['autoRegenerate'];
  if (!isBoolean(autoRegenerate)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'autoRegenerate must be a boolean.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const maxRegenerationAttempts = body['maxRegenerationAttempts'];
  if (!isNumber(maxRegenerationAttempts)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'maxRegenerationAttempts must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 5. Build the payload and delegate ----
  // The URL parameter is the authoritative `name` — a `name` field
  // in the body is deliberately ignored (the field is not read
  // from the body above). The payload's remaining fields come
  // from the validated body values. The object literal is
  // assignable to `PresetCreatePayload` because every required
  // field is present and correctly typed.
  const payload: PresetCreatePayload = {
    name,
    displayName,
    sourceCount,
    wordCount,
    searchEngines,
    resultsPerPage,
    maxResults,
    pageLoadTimeout,
    maxRetries,
    targetReadingGrade,
    minKeywordDensity,
    maxKeywordDensity,
    maxTfidfSimilarity,
    maxSemanticSimilarity,
    maxAiMarkers,
    runReadabilityCheck,
    runSeoCheck,
    runOriginalityCheck,
    runAiMarkerCheck,
    runGrammarCheck,
    autoRegenerate,
    maxRegenerationAttempts,
  };

  const preset = await upsertSystemPresetService(payload);

  // ---- 6. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: preset,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/admin/presets/:name
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete a system preset by its slug name.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:name` route parameter is missing
 *      or empty.
 *   3. Delegate to the service. The service issues a
 *      `findOneAndDelete` scoped to `{ userId: null, name }`, so
 *      a user-owned preset with the same name is not touched.
 *   4. A null result means "no system preset with that name";
 *      this handler returns 404. The 404 covers two cases the
 *      caller does not need to distinguish — the name names no
 *      preset at all, or it names a user-owned preset that the
 *      admin service does not manage.
 *   5. Respond with 200 and the deleted preset. Returning the
 *      deleted document gives the client a last-chance look at
 *      what was removed, which the admin UI uses for an undo
 *      affordance.
 *
 * No cascade: the deleted preset is a template, not a live
 * reference. Topics that were previously configured with it
 * store their own copy of the pipeline configuration and are
 * unaffected.
 */
export const deleteSystemPreset = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Preset>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Defensive authentication guard ----
  const callerId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!callerId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const name = req.params['name'];
  if (!isNonEmptyString(name)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Preset name is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const preset = await deleteSystemPresetService(name);

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: preset,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  listSystemPresets,
  getSystemPresetByName,
  upsertSystemPreset,
  deleteSystemPreset,
};
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/admin/routes/adminRoutes.ts">
/**
 * Route table for the WriteSpeare admin feature.
 *
 * Declares the four admin-only system-preset management endpoints
 * and the middleware chain that runs in front of each. The router
 * is mounted at `/api/admin` by the app factory (`src/app.ts`),
 * so the paths declared below are relative to that prefix:
 *
 *   GET    /presets                → list every system preset
 *   GET    /presets/:name          → read one system preset by name
 *   PUT    /presets/:name          → create or replace a system preset
 *   DELETE /presets/:name          → delete a system preset
 *
 * Every route is protected by BOTH `authenticate` AND
 * `requireAdmin`. This is the same dual-middleware arrangement
 * that `userRoutes.ts` uses (File 44), and the two route tables
 * are the only ones in the codebase that layer `requireAdmin` on
 * top of `authenticate` — every other feature's routes are
 * user-scoped and rely on `authenticate` alone.
 *
 * Why these paths are grouped under `/api/admin/presets` rather
 * than under `/api/presets`:
 *
 *   Presets already have a user-facing endpoint surface at
 *   `/api/settings/presets` (see `settingsRoutes.ts`, File 38).
 *   That surface exposes the user's OWN presets plus the system
 *   presets in a merged list, and it allows create/update/delete
 *   operations only on the caller's own presets — the
 *   user-scoped `settingsService` deliberately excludes the
 *   system scope from every write path.
 *
 *   The system-preset management operations that this file
 *   exposes are a DIFFERENT capability on a DIFFERENT scope: an
 *   administrator managing the shared, system-wide presets that
 *   every user reads. Keeping them under `/api/admin/presets`
 *   makes the distinction structural, not merely semantic — the
 *   URL alone tells a reader (and a middleware) that these
 *   operations are admin-scoped, and the `requireAdmin` guard
 *   that all four routes carry enforces it.
 *
 * Which middleware to use for the admin role check:
 *
 *   The plan's file tree declares an `admin/middleware/adminGuard.ts`
 *   with the annotation "Ensures admin role". That file exists on
 *   disk as an empty placeholder, and its annotated responsibility
 *   is the SAME responsibility that the auth feature's
 *   `requireAdmin` middleware already fulfills — the one that was
 *   written in Session 1 and is already in use by `userRoutes.ts`
 *   (File 44). There is only one admin-role check to perform, and
 *   it has one implementation.
 *
 *   This file therefore imports `requireAdmin` from
 *   `auth/middleware/authGuard.js` — the working, proven
 *   implementation — and leaves `admin/middleware/adminGuard.ts`
 *   as an unused placeholder. If the plan intended that file to
 *   contain a genuinely DIFFERENT check (a stricter policy, a
 *   second factor, anything beyond "the caller's role is
 *   admin"), that intent is not documented anywhere and cannot
 *   be guessed; the correct disposition is to leave the file
 *   alone and note the redundancy in the PLAN DELTA section of
 *   the execution response.
 *
 * Middleware order:
 *
 *   `authenticate` runs first and is applied via `asyncHandler`
 *   because it is an async function (it awaits a user lookup to
 *   confirm the account still exists and is active). The wrapper
 *   is required — without it, a rejection inside the middleware
 *   would reach the terminal error handler as an unhandled
 *   promise rejection on runtimes that do not forward the
 *   rejection automatically. This matches the wrapping pattern
 *   used in every previous route file.
 *
 *   `requireAdmin` runs second and is ALSO applied via
 *   `asyncHandler`, even though its current implementation is
 *   synchronous. The rationale is the same as in `userRoutes.ts`:
 *   uniformity across the three-middleware chain, and future-
 *   proofing in case `requireAdmin` is ever made async. The
 *   cost is one extra promise allocation per request, which is
 *   negligible.
 *
 *   The controller runs third, also wrapped in `asyncHandler`
 *   for the same reason as every other controller: the service
 *   behind it can throw an `AppError` (404 for a preset that
 *   does not exist, 409 for a name collision within the system
 *   scope), and the wrapper is what converts that throw into a
 *   well-formed response via the terminal error middleware.
 *
 * Route ordering — collection route before parameterized ones:
 *
 *   Express matches routes by segment count, so `GET /presets`
 *   (one segment after the mount point) can never collide with
 *   `GET /presets/:name` (two segments). The collection route is
 *   declared first as a defensive habit, consistent with every
 *   other route file in the codebase: declare more specific
 *   paths before more general ones. Today no collision exists;
 *   tomorrow, if a literal sub-path like `/presets/system` is
 *   added, the ordering will already be correct.
 *
 *   Within the parameterized group, all three routes live on the
 *   SAME path (`/presets/:name`) and are distinguished only by
 *   HTTP method — GET, PUT, and DELETE. Express's router keys on
 *   method + path, so the three cannot collide regardless of
 *   their declaration order. They are declared in the order
 *   GET → PUT → DELETE, which matches the natural reading order
 *   of "read, then write, then remove".
 *
 * The routes are declared as a flat sequence of `router.METHOD`
 * calls rather than as a route table or a declarative
 * configuration. This matches the convention established in
 * every previous route file — `authRoutes.ts`,
 * `topicRoutes.ts`, `documentRoutes.ts`, `articleRoutes.ts`,
 * `reportRoutes.ts`, `settingsRoutes.ts`, `versionRoutes.ts`,
 * and `userRoutes.ts`.
 *
 * No try/catch appears anywhere in this file. That is deliberate
 * — the asyncHandler wrappers, combined with the terminal error
 * middleware registered in `app.ts`, form the single error-
 * handling contract for every route in the application.
 */

import { Router } from 'express';

import {
  listSystemPresets,
  getSystemPresetByName,
  upsertSystemPreset,
  deleteSystemPreset,
} from '../controllers/adminController.js';

import {
  authenticate,
  requireAdmin,
} from '../../auth/middleware/authGuard.js';
import { asyncHandler } from '../../shared/middleware/errorHandler.js';

// ============================================================
//  Router instance
// ============================================================

const adminRoutes = Router();

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/admin/presets
// ============================================================
//
//  List every system preset. Admin-only. Returns the presets
//  sorted by name so the admin UI shows them in a stable,
//  predictable order.

adminRoutes.get(
  '/presets',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(requireAdmin),
  asyncHandler(listSystemPresets)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/admin/presets/:name
// ============================================================
//
//  Read a single system preset by its slug name. Admin-only. A
//  name that does not match any system preset returns 404; a
//  user-owned preset with the same name is invisible to this
//  endpoint (the service's `{ userId: null }` filter excludes
//  it), which is correct — this endpoint manages the system
//  scope, not the user scope.

adminRoutes.get(
  '/presets/:name',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(requireAdmin),
  asyncHandler(getSystemPresetByName)
);

// ============================================================
//  PUT /api/admin/presets/:name
// ============================================================
//
//  Create a new system preset, or update the existing one with
//  the same name. Admin-only. The operation is idempotent —
//  sending the same request twice produces the same final state
//  — which is why it is a PUT rather than a POST or PATCH. The
//  preset's `name` is taken from the URL, not the body; see the
//  controller header for the URL-vs-body precedence rule.

adminRoutes.put(
  '/presets/:name',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(requireAdmin),
  asyncHandler(upsertSystemPreset)
);

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/admin/presets/:name
// ============================================================
//
//  Delete a system preset by its slug name. Admin-only. A name
//  that matches a user-owned preset but no system preset
//  returns 404 — the user's preset is not touched. No cascade:
//  the deleted preset is a template, and topics that were
//  configured with it store their own copy of the pipeline
//  settings.

adminRoutes.delete(
  '/presets/:name',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(requireAdmin),
  asyncHandler(deleteSystemPreset)
);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default adminRoutes;

<file path="apps/server/src/features/admin/services/adminService.ts">
/**
 * Business logic for the WriteSpeare admin feature.
 *
 * SCOPE DECISION — what "Config upsert logic" means here:
 *
 *   The plan's file-tree annotation for this file reads simply
 *   "Config upsert logic". That phrase is the entire specification
 *   the plan gives, and it is ambiguous on its face — "config"
 *   could mean many things, and no model named `AdminConfig`,
 *   `SystemConfig`, or `GlobalSettings` exists anywhere in the
 *   codebase or in the plan's shared types.
 *
 *   This file resolves the ambiguity by picking the ONE form of
 *   cross-user configuration that the existing models actually
 *   support: the system-wide Preset. The Preset model already
 *   carries a nullable `userId` field whose `null` value is the
 *   semantic marker for "system preset, visible to every user" —
 *   see the Preset model header. The user-scoped
 *   `settingsService.createPreset` deliberately stamps every
 *   preset it creates with the CALLER's userId, so it cannot
 *   manufacture a system preset through any clean path. That is
 *   the genuine gap this service fills.
 *
 *   The choice has the following consequences, all of which are
 *   correct for the existing schema:
 *
 *     - No new model is introduced. The service operates on the
 *       Preset collection that already exists.
 *     - No new type is introduced. The service uses the existing
 *       `PresetCreatePayload` from `shared/types/index.ts`.
 *     - No new field is added to any existing document. A system
 *       preset is a preset with `userId: null` — a value the
 *       model already supports and the compound unique index on
 *       `{ userId, name }` already enforces uniqueness for.
 *
 *   If a future session decides the admin feature needs to
 *   manage a genuinely different "config" — a singleton
 *   application-settings document, a blocked-domain list, a
 *   usage-statistics collection — that decision requires new
 *   models and new types in `shared/types/index.ts` first, and
 *   those are out of scope for this file. The current file
 *   implements the interpretation the existing schema supports.
 *
 * The relationship to settingsService:
 *
 *   The settings feature already has a service
 *   (`settingsService.ts`) that exposes preset CRUD to ordinary
 *   users. Every operation in that service is ownership-scoped
 *   to the caller's `userId`:
 *
 *     - Read paths accept system presets (`userId: null`) AND the
 *       caller's own presets. A user can always see the built-in
 *       presets and their own customisations.
 *     - Write paths accept ONLY the caller's own presets. The
 *       system scope is excluded by the `{ _id, userId }` filter,
 *       which is what prevents a user from editing or deleting a
 *       system preset through the user-facing API.
 *
 *   That arrangement is correct for ordinary users — it is the
 *   entire point of the two-scope design — but it leaves no path
 *   for an administrator to manage system presets. The admin
 *   needs the ability to create a new system preset (perhaps for
 *   a new pipeline feature), edit an existing one (perhaps to
 *   tune the Balanced preset's word count), and delete one
 *   (perhaps to retire a preset no longer supported).
 *
 *   This service provides exactly those operations, and only
 *   those operations. It does NOT duplicate the ordinary user's
 *   preset CRUD — a system administrator who wants to create a
 *   personal preset uses `settingsService.createPreset` through
 *   the ordinary settings endpoint, and the resulting preset has
 *   their own userId as owner, not `null`.
 *
 * Why no `userId` argument on any function:
 *
 *   Every other service in this codebase takes a `userId` as its
 *   first argument — either the caller's (for ownership-scoped
 *   services) or the target's (for the users feature). This
 *   service takes NEITHER, because the entity it manages is
 *   owned by no one. A system preset is a shared resource: every
 *   administrator of the same installation manages the same
 *   system presets, and every user of the same installation
 *   reads the same system presets. There is no per-caller scope
 *   to filter on.
 *
 *   The authorization contract is therefore entirely at the
 *   controller and route layers: this service's functions are
 *   only reachable through admin-only endpoints, and the service
 *   trusts that guarantee. It does not re-verify the caller's
 *   role — it has no way of knowing the caller's identity, by
 *   design.
 *
 * Upsert semantics:
 *
 *   `upsertSystemPreset` accepts a full `PresetCreatePayload`
 *   whose `name` field is the identity of the preset being
 *   created or replaced. The service:
 *
 *     1. Normalizes the name (trim + lowercase) — the schema
 *        does this on write, but the query that matches the
 *        existing document must also use the normalized form,
 *        so the normalization happens explicitly here.
 *
 *     2. Issues a single `findOneAndUpdate` with
 *        `{ userId: null, name }` as the filter, `{ $set: {...} }`
 *        as the update, and `{ upsert: true, new: true,
 *        setDefaultsOnInsert: true, runValidators: true }` as the
 *        options.
 *
 *     3. Returns the resulting document — either the newly
 *        created one or the updated existing one.
 *
 *   The `$set` operator (rather than a full document replace)
 *   means the operation is a true upsert on both branches:
 *   on an existing document it overwrites only the fields the
 *   payload carries, leaving everything else untouched; on a new
 *   document it creates a fresh record with the payload's fields
 *   plus the schema's defaults for anything not supplied.
 *
 *   The `setDefaultsOnInsert: true` option is what makes the
 *   create branch apply the schema's `default: null` to the
 *   `userId` field, so the newly created document correctly
 *   lives in the system scope. Without that option, Mongoose
 *   would leave `userId` unset on insert, and the compound
 *   unique index would treat the resulting document as belonging
 *   to whichever null-equivalent the driver produces — which is
 *   usually `null` but is not guaranteed across driver versions.
 *
 *   The `runValidators: true` option ensures the schema's
 *   per-field validators run on both branches, so an invalid
 *   payload is rejected even on the update path where Mongoose's
 *   defaults-to-off behaviour would otherwise skip them.
 *
 * The compound unique index and what it enforces for this
 * service:
 *
 *   The Preset schema declares `{ userId: 1, name: 1 }` as a
 *   unique index. For this service, every query and every write
 *   targets `userId: null`, so the index behaves as a unique
 *   index on `name` alone within the system scope. Two system
 *   presets cannot share a name — the invariant is enforced at
 *   the database level, and this service relies on it rather
 *   than pre-checking. A concurrent pair of upsert calls for
 *   the same name will race, and the loser will receive a
 *   duplicate-key error (code 11000), which the terminal error
 *   middleware maps to a 409. That is the correct behaviour for
 *   an admin attempting to create the same system preset twice
 *   through two parallel requests.
 *
 * No cascade:
 *
 *   `deleteSystemPreset` does NOT cascade to any user's topics,
 *   articles, or other records. Presets are templates, not live
 *   references — a user's topic stores its pipeline configuration
 *   on itself at creation time, so removing the system preset
 *   it was based on does not affect the topic's ability to
 *   continue running its pipeline. This is the same reasoning
 *   the `settingsService.deletePreset` header gives for the
 *   user-scoped case; it applies identically here.
 *
 * Out of scope — the system-preset seeder:
 *
 *   The plan describes three system presets — Quick, Balanced,
 *   Deep — as shipped with the application. Nothing in this
 *   service creates them automatically: a seeder utility must
 *   call `upsertSystemPreset` for each of the three (or a
 *   similar operation) at some point during installation. That
 *   seeder is NOT declared anywhere in the plan's file tree and
 *   is therefore out of scope for this file. See the PLAN DELTA
 *   note in the execution response for the details. This service
 *   provides the primitive the seeder will consume; it does not
 *   run the seeder itself.
 */

import {
  PresetModel,
  type PresetDocument,
} from '../../settings/models/Preset.js';
import type { PresetCreatePayload } from '../../shared/types/index.js';
import { AppError } from '../../shared/middleware/errorHandler.js';

// ============================================================
//  listSystemPresets
// ============================================================

/**
 * List every system preset — every Preset document whose
 * `userId` is `null`. Sorted by `name` ascending so the picker
 * that consumes this endpoint shows the built-ins in a stable,
 * predictable order (Balanced, Deep, Quick, alphabetically)
 * rather than in the order the seeder happened to install them.
 *
 * The query is served by the compound index `{ userId: 1, name: 1 }`
 * on the Preset schema — MongoDB matches on the leftmost prefix
 * `userId: null` and reads the entries in `name` order without
 * a separate sort step.
 *
 * Returns an empty array when no system presets have been
 * seeded. That is a valid, non-error state — a fresh installation
 * that has not yet run its preset seeder has zero system presets,
 * and the correct client behaviour is to show an empty list, not
 * to surface a 404.
 */
export const listSystemPresets = async (): Promise<PresetDocument[]> => {
  return await PresetModel.find({ userId: null }).sort({ name: 1 });
};

// ============================================================
//  getSystemPresetByName
// ============================================================

/**
 * Read one system preset by its slug name. Returns `null` when
 * no system preset with that name exists.
 *
 * The name is normalized before the query — trimmed and
 * lowercased — so that a caller who supplies `"Balanced"` or
 * `"  balanced  "` matches the same document as a caller who
 * supplies `"balanced"`. The schema applies the same normalization
 * on write, so the query's normalized value always matches the
 * stored value.
 *
 * The query is served by the compound unique index
 * `{ userId: 1, name: 1 }` — a single index-covered lookup.
 *
 * Returns `null` rather than throwing on a missing preset. The
 * caller (the controller) converts the null into a 404, which is
 * the correct response for a well-formed request that happens to
 * name a preset that does not exist.
 *
 * @param name - The slug name of the system preset to read.
 */
export const getSystemPresetByName = async (
  name: string
): Promise<PresetDocument | null> => {
  const normalizedName = name.trim().toLowerCase();
  return await PresetModel.findOne({
    userId: null,
    name: normalizedName,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  upsertSystemPreset
// ============================================================

/**
 * Create a new system preset, or update the existing one with
 * the same name. The operation is a true upsert: on the create
 * branch the schema's defaults fill any field the payload omits;
 * on the update branch only the fields the payload carries are
 * overwritten, and every other field on the existing document
 * is left untouched.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Normalize the payload's `name` — trim + lowercase — so
 *      that both the query (which matches the existing document
 *      to update) and the eventual write use the same canonical
 *      form. The schema also lowercases on write, so the write
 *      side is belt-and-braces; the query side is the one that
 *      genuinely needs the explicit normalization, because the
 *      stored value was already lowercased by a previous write.
 *
 *   2. Issue a single `findOneAndUpdate` with:
 *
 *        filter:  { userId: null, name: normalizedName }
 *        update:  { $set: { ...payload, name: normalizedName,
 *                           userId: null } }
 *        options: { upsert: true, new: true,
 *                   setDefaultsOnInsert: true,
 *                   runValidators: true }
 *
 *      The `userId: null` inside the `$set` is redundant on the
 *      update branch (the field is already null on the matched
 *      document) but is required on the create branch to
 *      guarantee the new document belongs to the system scope.
 *      `setDefaultsOnInsert: true` would also apply the schema's
 *      `default: null` on insert, so the `$set` entry and the
 *      default are belt-and-braces against each other. Both are
 *      kept: the explicit `$set` documents the intent at the
 *      call site, and the default covers any future schema-level
 *      change to the field's initial value.
 *
 *   3. Return the resulting document.
 *
 * The `$set` operator (rather than a full document replace) is
 * deliberate: it means a caller who supplies a full payload
 * overwrites every field they name while leaving any field they
 * did NOT name (or any field the payload type does not carry)
 * at its existing value on the update branch. For the current
 * `PresetCreatePayload` type, which requires every field, the
 * practical effect is the same as a replace — but the semantics
 * are strictly more conservative, and they remain correct if the
 * payload type ever grows optional fields.
 *
 * The function does NOT pre-check for a name collision. The
 * compound unique index on `{ userId, name }` is the
 * authoritative guard, and a pre-check would introduce a race
 * between the check and the write. Two concurrent upserts for
 * the same name are resolved by the index: one succeeds, the
 * other receives a duplicate-key error, which the terminal
 * error middleware maps to a 409.
 *
 * @param payload - The full configuration of the system preset.
 *                  The `name` field is the identity key; every
 *                  other field is a value the preset carries.
 */
export const upsertSystemPreset = async (
  payload: PresetCreatePayload
): Promise<PresetDocument> => {
  const normalizedName = payload.name.trim().toLowerCase();

  const doc = await PresetModel.findOneAndUpdate(
    { userId: null, name: normalizedName },
    {
      $set: {
        ...payload,
        name: normalizedName,
        userId: null,
      },
    },
    {
      upsert: true,
      new: true,
      setDefaultsOnInsert: true,
      runValidators: true,
    }
  );

  // `findOneAndUpdate` with `upsert: true` and `new: true` is
  // documented to always return a document, but its TypeScript
  // signature still returns `T | null` — the compiler cannot
  // know that the upsert option guarantees non-null. The guard
  // is defensive: if it ever fires, the database is in a state
  // this service cannot recover from, and a 500 is the correct
  // response.
  if (!doc) {
    throw new AppError('Failed to upsert system preset.', 500);
  }

  return doc;
};

// ============================================================
//  deleteSystemPreset
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete a system preset by its slug name.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Normalize the name — trim + lowercase — for the same
 *      reason `getSystemPresetByName` and `upsertSystemPreset`
 *      normalize: the stored value is always in the canonical
 *      form, so the query must be too.
 *
 *   2. Issue a `findOneAndDelete` with `{ userId: null, name }`
 *      as the filter. The `userId: null` clause is what scopes
 *      the operation to the system presets only; a user-owned
 *      preset with the same name (which is legal, because the
 *      unique index is scoped by userId) is not touched.
 *
 *   3. Return the deleted document so the caller can log or
 *      display what was removed.
 *
 * Throws `AppError(404)` when no system preset with that name
 * exists. The 404 is correct in two distinct cases that the
 * caller does not need to distinguish:
 *
 *   - The name names no preset at all.
 *   - The name names a user-owned preset, which the admin service
 *     does not manage (it belongs to the user whose userId it
 *     carries).
 *
 * The two cases collapse to the same 404 because from the admin
 * service's perspective they are the same: "there is no system
 * preset with that name". A user's personal preset called
 * `balanced` is invisible here, and correct so — it is not the
 * system `balanced`, and modifying it is not the admin's job.
 *
 * No cascade: the deleted preset is a template, not a live
 * reference. Topics that were previously configured with it
 * store their own copy of the pipeline configuration and are
 * unaffected.
 *
 * @param name - The slug name of the system preset to delete.
 */
export const deleteSystemPreset = async (
  name: string
): Promise<PresetDocument> => {
  const normalizedName = name.trim().toLowerCase();

  const deleted = await PresetModel.findOneAndDelete({
    userId: null,
    name: normalizedName,
  });

  if (!deleted) {
    throw new AppError('System preset not found.', 404);
  }

  return deleted;
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  listSystemPresets,
  getSystemPresetByName,
  upsertSystemPreset,
  deleteSystemPreset,
};
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/admin/index.ts">
/**
 * Public export surface for the WriteSpeare admin feature.
 *
 * The plan declares this file with a single responsibility:
 * "Public exports." That is the entire specification, and this
 * file fills it in with the minimal surface that the rest of the
 * codebase can meaningfully consume — following the shape
 * established by the seven previous feature indexes:
 * `features/topics/index.ts`, `features/documents/index.ts`,
 * `features/articles/index.ts`, `features/reports/index.ts`,
 * `features/settings/index.ts`, `features/version/index.ts`,
 * and `features/users/index.ts`.
 *
 * This is the SECOND of the feature indexes with NO model
 * section (the first was the users feature, File 54):
 *
 *   The admin feature owns no collection of its own. Its
 *   service (`adminService.ts`) operates on the `Preset` model
 *   that lives under the settings feature at
 *   `features/settings/models/Preset.js`, managing the
 *   system-wide preset scope — the Preset documents with
 *   `userId: null` that every user of the installation reads.
 *   The user-facing preset management lives in the settings
 *   feature's own service; the admin feature is the one path
 *   that can create, edit, or delete presets in the SYSTEM
 *   scope, which the settings service deliberately excludes
 *   from its own write paths.
 *
 *   Because there is no model owned by this feature, there is
 *   no model to re-export. Re-exporting `PresetModel` from
 *   `features/settings/models/Preset.js` via this index would
 *   be misleading: it would tell a reader that the admin
 *   feature owns the Preset collection, when in fact the
 *   settings feature does. A consumer that needs the Preset
 *   model should import it from where it lives —
 *   `features/settings/models/Preset.js` — or, once the
 *   settings index is populated, from
 *   `features/settings/index.ts`.
 *
 * What belongs here — and what does not:
 *
 *   The admin feature contains five kinds of source files:
 *
 *     services/adminService.ts         — system-preset logic
 *     controllers/adminController.ts   — HTTP handlers
 *     routes/adminRoutes.ts            — the Express router
 *     middleware/adminGuard.ts         — an empty placeholder
 *                                        (see the note below)
 *     index.ts                         — this file
 *
 *   Of those five, only ONE is useful to a consumer OUTSIDE the
 *   feature:
 *
 *     The router. `app.ts` mounts it under `/api/admin`. That is
 *     the one import the feature's external boundary actually
 *     needs — the controller and service are internal
 *     implementation details between the router and the Preset
 *     collection, and nothing outside the feature should reach
 *     past the router for request-handling behavior.
 *
 *   The service and controller are NOT re-exported. Both are
 *   internal: the service is only ever consumed by the
 *   controller within the same feature, and the controller is
 *   only ever consumed by the router within the same feature.
 *   Additionally, their function names collide — both export
 *   `listSystemPresets`, `upsertSystemPreset`, etc. — and
 *   re-exporting both with bare names would produce a
 *   duplicate-export error.
 *
 *   The `admin/middleware/adminGuard.ts` file — the plan's
 *   empty placeholder for a role-check middleware — is NOT
 *   re-exported. That file is not imported by anything, and the
 *   admin routes use the working `requireAdmin` middleware from
 *   `auth/middleware/authGuard.js` instead. Re-exporting the
 *   empty file's (nonexistent) exports would be a compile error;
 *   leaving it out is the correct behavior. See the file header
 *   of `adminRoutes.ts` for the full reasoning on the redundant
 *   middleware declaration.
 *
 * Why the router is exported both as a named symbol AND as the
 * default:
 *
 *   The router file itself (`routes/adminRoutes.ts`) exports
 *   its router as the default. This index file preserves that
 *   shape for callers that prefer the default form — `import
 *   adminRoutes from '...features/admin'` — while also giving
 *   the named form — `import { adminRoutes } from
 *   '...features/admin'` — to callers that prefer named imports
 *   for uniformity with the rest of this file's exports.
 *
 *   The two forms resolve to the same router instance. There is
 *   no double-construction, no second Express `Router()`, and
 *   no chance of the router being registered twice by mistake.
 *
 * Note for readers who have been following the session:
 *
 *   The current `app.ts` imports the admin router from its deep
 *   path (`./features/admin/routes/adminRoutes.js`), not from
 *   this index. That import needs no change — this index is a
 *   forward-looking surface that a future refactor can adopt.
 *   Until that refactor, this file's exports are dormant —
 *   nothing in the codebase currently imports from it.
 *
 *   That is fine, and it is what the plan's "Public exports"
 *   annotation calls for. The surface exists so that when a
 *   consumer DOES need it, there is a declared, documented place
 *   for that import to come from — rather than a deep path that
 *   was chosen ad hoc.
 *
 *   With this file in place, only the auth feature's index
 *   (`features/auth/index.ts`) remains empty among the eight
 *   feature folders in the codebase. That one will be populated
 *   separately — the auth feature owns the `User` model, so it
 *   is the last index with a full router-and-model shape.
 */

// ============================================================
//  Router
// ============================================================
//
//  The router is the feature's only public API surface — the
//  one import that the app factory needs in order to mount the
//  admin system-preset endpoints. Both the default-export form
//  and the named-export form resolve to the same router
//  instance (see the file header for the reasoning).
//
//  There is no model section in this file. See the file header
//  for why: the admin feature owns no collection, and re-
//  exporting the settings feature's `PresetModel` from here
//  would misrepresent the ownership relationship.

export { default as adminRoutes } from './routes/adminRoutes.js';
export { default } from './routes/adminRoutes.js';

<file path="apps/server/src/features/articles/controllers/articleController.ts">
/**
 * HTTP handlers for the WriteSpeare Article entity.
 *
 * Thin request/response layer over `articleService`. Each handler
 * performs exactly four jobs and nothing else:
 *
 *   1. Read the authenticated user's ID from `req.user.userId`
 *      and reject the request with a 401 if it is absent. Every
 *      ownership-scoped operation in WriteSpeare keys off this
 *      value; a handler that is reached without an authenticated
 *      session would either crash on a null dereference or — far
 *      worse — silently operate on the wrong user's data.
 *
 *   2. Validate the shape of the request body / query / params
 *      just enough to reject requests that are so malformed the
 *      service would produce a confusing error. The schema (in
 *      `articles/models/Article.ts`) remains the authoritative
 *      validator for everything subtler — non-empty content,
 *      integer word counts, the closed status set — and a Mongoose
 *      ValidationError is translated to a 400 by the terminal
 *      error middleware. Doing anything more in the controller
 *      would duplicate the schema's rules and eventually drift
 *      from them.
 *
 *   3. Delegate to the service. The controller never touches the
 *      database directly — it does not import the Article model,
 *      does not build queries, and does not know what collection
 *      the data lives in. That is the service's job.
 *
 *   4. Format the success response using the shared `ApiResponse`
 *      envelope. Every response — success or failure — uses the
 *      same shape, so a client can unwrap it uniformly.
 *
 * No try/catch appears anywhere in this file. Each route handler
 * is wrapped in `asyncHandler` at the route registration site,
 * which forwards any rejection to the terminal error middleware.
 * The middleware recognises the shared `AppError` class thrown by
 * the service — a 404 for an article or topic that does not exist
 * or is not owned by the caller — and formats the response with
 * the same envelope this file uses on success.
 *
 * Response typing — the assignability bridge:
 *
 *   Every handler declares its `Response<T>` type explicitly. On
 *   success the service returns an `ArticleDocument` (Mongoose's
 *   in-process shape) which is structurally assignable to the
 *   shared `Article` domain type — the only difference is that
 *   `ArticleDocument._id` is a concrete `ObjectId` while
 *   `Article._id` is `string | ObjectId`. Since `ObjectId` is a
 *   member of the union, the assignment is safe. At runtime,
 *   `res.json()` serialises the ObjectId to its hex string form.
 *
 * The dual-purpose `getLatestArticle` route:
 *
 *   This handler exists to serve one specific query — "give me
 *   the current (highest-version) article for this topic" — that
 *   the topic-detail view issues on every render. It returns 404
 *   when the topic has no articles, when the topic does not exist,
 *   or when the topic belongs to a different user. The three
 *   cases collapse to the same 404, matching the enumeration-
 *   attack rationale used elsewhere in this file (see
 *   `getArticleById` and `deleteArticle`).
 *
 * Status transition route — why it is a sub-path, not a
 * full-resource PATCH:
 *
 *   Only one field of an article is mutable in place: `status`.
 *   Content is immutable by design — a change of content
 *   produces a new version, not a mutation. Rather than expose a
 *   generic `PATCH /api/articles/:id` that accepts arbitrary
 *   fields (which would then have to reject everything except
 *   `status`), the API exposes a narrower, more honest route:
 *   `PATCH /api/articles/:id/status`, whose body is `{ status }`
 *   and nothing else. This is the same style used by many REST
 *   APIs to model a state-machine transition as a distinct
 *   operation rather than as a field write.
 *
 * Ownership scoping:
 *
 *   The `userId` passed to the service is ALWAYS derived from the
 *   authenticated session — `req.user.userId` — and NEVER read
 *   from the request body or query. This is what makes it
 *   impossible for a client to create an article on behalf of
 *   another user: the ownership field is set from the token, not
 *   from anything the client controls.
 */

import type { Response } from 'express';

import {
  createArticle as createArticleService,
  listArticles as listArticlesService,
  getArticleById as getArticleByIdService,
  getLatestArticle as getLatestArticleService,
  updateArticleStatus as updateArticleStatusService,
  deleteArticle as deleteArticleService,
  deleteArticlesByTopic as deleteArticlesByTopicService,
} from '../services/articleService.js';

import type { AuthRequest } from '../../auth/middleware/authGuard.js';
import type {
  ApiResponse,
  Article,
  ArticleCreatePayload,
  ArticleStatus,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Runtime legal-value table and type guard
// ============================================================
//
// The `ArticleStatus` union is a compile-time type — it does not
// exist at runtime, so the value arriving from an untrusted
// client body cannot be checked against it directly. This array
// is the runtime counterpart, and the type annotation
// (`readonly ArticleStatus[]`) guarantees at compile time that
// every string in the array is a legal member of the union.

const ARTICLE_STATUS_VALUES: readonly ArticleStatus[] = [
  'draft',
  'validated',
  'exported',
];

/**
 * Narrow `unknown` to one of the three legal article statuses.
 *
 * The cast to `readonly string[]` before `.includes` is required
 * because `Array.prototype.includes` on a `readonly ArticleStatus[]`
 * expects an `ArticleStatus` argument, and the point of this
 * guard is to check an arbitrary unknown value against the array.
 */
const isArticleStatus = (value: unknown): value is ArticleStatus =>
  typeof value === 'string' &&
  (ARTICLE_STATUS_VALUES as readonly string[]).includes(value);

// ============================================================
//  POST /api/articles
// ============================================================

/**
 * Persist a generated article attached to a topic owned by the
 * authenticated user. The service computes the next version
 * number for the topic and writes it to the record.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the request body is not a plain object.
 *   3. Validate the three required fields on the request body:
 *      `topicId` (non-empty string), `content` (non-empty
 *      string), and `wordCount` (number). Length and content
 *      rules beyond "non-empty" are the schema's job — see the
 *      file header.
 *   4. Delegate to the service. The service validates that the
 *      parent topic exists and is owned by the caller; a 404
 *      thrown by that check propagates to the terminal
 *      middleware.
 *   5. Respond with 201 Created and the persisted article. The
 *      response includes the `version` value the service
 *      assigned.
 *
 * The `userId` argument to the service is derived from the
 * authenticated session. Any client-supplied `userId` field on
 * the request body is ignored — the body's `Record<string,
 * unknown>` type simply does not read that field.
 */
export const createArticle = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Article>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Body shape guard ----
  const rawBody: unknown = req.body;
  if (
    typeof rawBody !== 'object' ||
    rawBody === null ||
    Array.isArray(rawBody)
  ) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Request body must be a JSON object.',
    });
    return;
  }
  const body = rawBody as Record<string, unknown>;

  // ---- 3. Required fields ----

  const topicId = body['topicId'];
  if (typeof topicId !== 'string' || topicId.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'topicId is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const content = body['content'];
  if (typeof content !== 'string' || content.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'content is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const wordCount = body['wordCount'];
  if (typeof wordCount !== 'number') {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'wordCount must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 4. Build the payload and delegate ----
  // The `version` field is NOT part of `ArticleCreatePayload` by
  // design — the service computes it. Attempting to pass one
  // would be a compile error.
  const payload: ArticleCreatePayload = {
    topicId,
    content,
    wordCount,
  };

  const article = await createArticleService(userId, payload);

  // ---- 5. Respond ----
  res.status(201).json({
    success: true,
    data: article,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/articles
// ============================================================

/**
 * List the authenticated user's articles. An optional
 * `?topicId=` query parameter narrows the result to the articles
 * attached to a single topic.
 *
 * Sort order is chosen by the service based on whether the query
 * is topic-scoped:
 *
 *   - Topic-scoped: sorted by `version` descending (newest
 *     version first).
 *   - Cross-topic: sorted by `createdAt` descending (most
 *     recently written first).
 *
 * See the service header for the reasoning behind the two sort
 * orders.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. If a `?topicId=` query parameter is present, validate
 *      that it is a non-empty string. The service does not
 *      confirm ownership of the topic — a topicId that does not
 *      belong to the caller produces an empty list, not a 404.
 *      See the service header for the enumeration rationale.
 *   3. Delegate to the service.
 *   4. Respond with 200 and the array. An empty array is a valid,
 *      non-error response.
 */
export const listArticles = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Article[]>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Optional topicId filter ----
  const rawTopicId = req.query['topicId'];
  let topicId: string | undefined;
  if (rawTopicId !== undefined) {
    if (typeof rawTopicId !== 'string' || rawTopicId.length === 0) {
      res.status(400).json({
        success: false,
        error: 'Invalid topicId filter.',
      });
      return;
    }
    topicId = rawTopicId;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const articles = await listArticlesService(userId, topicId);

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: articles,
  });
};
