//  GET /api/articles/:id
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return a single article by its ID, scoped to the authenticated
 * user.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:id` route parameter is missing
 *      or empty. A malformed ID that is present but not a valid
 *      ObjectId is not rejected here — the service's `findOne`
 *      throws a CastError, which the terminal middleware maps to
 *      a 400.
 *   3. Delegate to the service. A null result means either "no
 *      such article" or "article belongs to a different user";
 *      this handler returns 404 for both.
 *   4. Respond with 200 and the article, or 404 if it was not
 *      found / not owned.
 */
export const getArticleById = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Article>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const articleId = req.params['id'];
  if (typeof articleId !== 'string' || articleId.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Article ID is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const article = await getArticleByIdService(userId, articleId);
  if (!article) {
    res.status(404).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Article not found.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: article,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  PATCH /api/articles/:id/status
// ============================================================

/**
 * Transition an article's lifecycle status, scoped to the
 * authenticated user.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:id` route parameter is missing
 *      or empty.
 *   3. Reject with 400 if the request body is not a plain object,
 *      or if the `status` field is missing / not a member of the
 *      closed set. The closed-set check is done against the
 *      runtime array declared at the top of this file — the
 *      union type alone cannot validate an untrusted value.
 *   4. Delegate to the service. The service writes the status
 *      with `runValidators: true`, so the schema's enum check
 *      runs a second time at the database boundary as a safety
 *      net — see the service header for the rationale.
 *   5. Respond with 200 and the updated article.
 *
 * The `status` field is the ONLY mutable field on an existing
 * article. Content changes produce a new version (a new article)
 * rather than an in-place edit — see the service header.
 */
export const updateArticleStatus = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Article>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const articleId = req.params['id'];
  if (typeof articleId !== 'string' || articleId.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Article ID is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Body shape guard ----
  const rawBody: unknown = req.body;
  if (
    typeof rawBody !== 'object' ||
    rawBody === null ||
    Array.isArray(rawBody)
  ) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Request body must be a JSON object.',
    });
    return;
  }
  const body = rawBody as Record<string, unknown>;

  // ---- 4. Status field validation ----
  const status = body['status'];
  if (!isArticleStatus(status)) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: `status must be one of: ${ARTICLE_STATUS_VALUES.join(', ')}.`,
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 5. Delegate to the service ----
  const article = await updateArticleStatusService(
    userId,
    articleId,
    status
  );

  // ---- 6. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: article,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/articles/:id

/**
 * Delete a single article, scoped to the authenticated user.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:id` route parameter is missing
 *      or empty.
 *   3. Delegate to the service. The service throws `AppError(404)`
 *      when the article does not exist or belongs to a different
 *      user.

 *      deleted document gives the client a last-chance look at
 *      what was removed, which the UI uses for an undo

 *

 * a Report that referenced the article is the reports feature's
 * responsibility — see the service header.
 */
export const deleteArticle = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Article>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const articleId = req.params['id'];
  if (typeof articleId !== 'string' || articleId.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Article ID is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const article = await deleteArticleService(userId, articleId);

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: article,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/articles/topic/:topicId
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete every article attached to the given topic, scoped to the
 * authenticated user.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:topicId` route parameter is
 *      missing or empty.
 *   3. Delegate to the service. The service returns the number of
 *      articles removed. Zero is a valid result — see the
 *      service header. The filter is scoped to
 *      `{ userId, topicId }`, so a caller cannot clear another
 *      user's topic by guessing its ID.
 *   4. Respond with 200 and `{ deletedCount }`.
 *
 * Route-path note — `/topic/:topicId` vs `/:id`:
 *
 *   Express matches routes segment-by-segment. A request to
 *   `DELETE /api/articles/topic/abc123` has two segments after
 *   the mount point (`topic` and `abc123`); a request to
 *   `DELETE /api/articles/xyz` has one (`xyz`). The two routes
 *   cannot collide. The nested form is used rather than a
 *   query-parameter form so that the URL alone communicates
 *   whether one article is being deleted or all of a topic's
 *   articles.
 */
export const deleteArticlesByTopic = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<{ deletedCount: number }>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const topicId = req.params['topicId'];
  if (typeof topicId !== 'string' || topicId.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Topic ID is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const deletedCount = await deleteArticlesByTopicService(
    userId,
    topicId
  );

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: { deletedCount },
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  createArticle,
  listArticles,
  getArticleById,
  getLatestArticle,
  updateArticleStatus,
  deleteArticle,
  deleteArticlesByTopic,
};
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/articles/models/Article.ts">
/**
 * Mongoose model for the WriteSpeare Article entity.
 *
 * An Article is one generated article attached to a Topic. One
 * Topic owns one or more Articles — the initial draft returned by
 * the writer step, plus any subsequent versions produced by the
 * corrective regeneration loop (see the shared `Article` interface
 * and its `version` field). Each Article is a numbered snapshot
 * of the writer step's output, and the version with the highest
 * number is the "current" article for its topic.
 *
 * Responsibilities:
 *
 *   1. Enforce the schema-level invariants of an article record:
 *      a non-empty body, a non-negative integer word count, a
 *      positive integer version number, and a status drawn from
 *      the closed `ArticleStatus` union (`draft`, `validated`,
 *      `exported`).
 *
 *   2. Own the two compound indexes that the articles feature's
 *      read paths exercise:
 *
 *        - "list every version of this topic's article, newest
 *           version first" — served by { userId, topicId, version: -1 }.
 *           The leftmost prefix { userId, topicId } also serves
 *           the "get the latest article for this topic" query
 *           that the desktop's topic-detail view issues on every
 *           render.
 *
 *        - "list every article owned by the current user, newest
 *           first across all topics" — served by
 *           { userId, createdAt: -1 }.
 *
 *      Both indexes are prefixed by `userId` for the same reason
 *      the Topic and Document models' indexes are: every query
 *      on this collection is scoped to a single authenticated
 *      user, and an index without the userId prefix would never
 *      be selected by the query planner.
 *
 *   3. Provide a single `toJSON` transform that strips Mongoose's
 *      `__v` version field, so a serialised Article matches the
 *      shared `Article` interface exactly.
 *
 * The `version` field and why it is schema-validated but not
 * schema-assigned:
 *
 *   The version number starts at 1 and increments each time the
 *   user requests a regeneration of the same topic. Assigning the
 *   next version is a cross-record decision — it requires reading
 *   the current maximum version for this topic and adding one —
 *   and cross-record decisions are the service's job, not the
 *   schema's. The schema only enforces that whatever version
 *   number the service writes is a positive integer. A schema-
 *   level default of 1 is provided as a convenience for the
 *   common "this is the first article for the topic" case, but a
 *   service that always writes the computed next version will
 *   override it every time.
 *
 *   Making the version unique per topic at the schema level (a
 *   compound unique index on { userId, topicId, version }) was
 *   considered and rejected: it would turn a service-level
 *   mistake (two concurrent regenerations racing to write the
 *   same version) into a duplicate-key error that the caller
 *   would have to catch and translate, when the correct response
 *   is to serialize regenerations in the service layer. The
 *   current design keeps the schema simple and the concurrency
 *   contract in one place.
 *
 * The status field and the corrective loop:
 *
 *   `draft`     — the article as first returned by the writer.
 *   `validated` — a Report has been produced against it.
 *   `exported`  — the user has exported it to a file.
 *
 *   The transitions are one-directional under normal operation:
 *   draft → validated → exported. A `validated` article that the
 *   user then edits returns to `draft` (the edit is not covered
 *   by the existing report), and that transition is the
 *   service's concern — the schema only enforces that the value
 *   is a member of the closed set.
 *
 * What this model does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not mark `content` as `select: false`. The field
 *     is the article body — the largest field on the record — and
 *     a "list articles for this topic" query does not need it
 *     (the list view shows word counts, versions, and status
 *     badges). That projection is the service layer's job: a list
 *     query issues `.select('-content')`, a read-for-display or
 *     read-for-validation query loads the full document. This
 *     mirrors the choice made for the Document model's `content`
 *     field.
 *
 *   - It does not enforce that `topicId` references an existing
 *     Topic, or that `userId` matches the Topic's owner. Cross-
 *     collection referential integrity is the service layer's
 *     concern — the article service validates the parent topic's
 *     ownership before persisting, exactly as the document
 *     service does for Document.
 *
 *   - It does not store the validation report. A Report is a
 *     separate entity (see `features/reports/models/Report.ts`)
 *     that references its owning Article by `articleId`. Keeping
 *     the two separate means a Report can be regenerated without
 *     touching the Article, and an Article can be edited without
 *     silently invalidating a stored Report.
 */

import mongoose, { Schema, Document as MongooseDocument } from 'mongoose';
import { Article, ArticleStatus } from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Document interface
// ============================================================

/**
 * The runtime shape of an Article document as returned by
 * Mongoose.
 *
 * Extends `Omit<Article, '_id'>` (the shared domain interface
 * minus its loosely-typed `_id`) and `MongooseDocument` (the
 * Mongoose base class), then re-declares `_id` with the concrete
 * ObjectId type Mongoose actually produces in-process. This is
 * the same pattern as `UserDocument`, `TopicDocument`, and
 * `DocumentDocument` — the shared domain type stays transport-
 * agnostic, while the document interface pins `_id` to what the
 * ODM gives you.
 *
 * No instance methods are declared. An Article has no per-record
 * behaviour beyond what Mongoose provides out of the box (save,
 * validate, toJSON). Business logic — computing the next version
 * number, transitioning status, deciding whether to re-validate
 * — lives in the service.
 */
export interface ArticleDocument
  extends Omit<Article, '_id'>,
    MongooseDocument {
  _id: mongoose.Types.ObjectId;
}

// ============================================================
//  Legal values (runtime counterpart of the union type)
// ============================================================

/**
 * The closed set of legal values for the `status` field.
 *
 * `ArticleStatus` in `shared/types/index.ts` is a string-literal
 * union type — it does not exist at runtime, so Mongoose cannot
 * use it directly as an `enum` option. This array is the runtime
 * source of truth, and its type annotation (`readonly ArticleStatus[]`)
 * guarantees at compile time that every string in the array is a
 * legal member of the union. A typo such as `'valiated'` would be
 * a type error, not a silent runtime surprise.
 *
 * What the annotation does NOT catch: a union member that is
 * missing from the array (a new status added to `ArticleStatus`
 * in `shared/types` without a corresponding array update). That
 * class of drift has to be caught by a reviewer or by an
 * integration test that exercises every legal value — which is
 * exactly what the `Article.ts` model file's counterpart in the
 * Topic model does for `TopicStatus`.
 */
const ARTICLE_STATUS_VALUES: readonly ArticleStatus[] = [
  'draft',
  'validated',
  'exported',
];

// ============================================================
//  Schema
// ============================================================

const ArticleSchema = new Schema<ArticleDocument>(
  {
    // ---- Ownership ----
    // Every article belongs to exactly one user via the topic it
    // is attached to. Denormalising `userId` onto the article
    // record — rather than deriving ownership by joining through
    // the parent Topic — follows the same pattern as the Document
    // model: it lets the indexes key on `userId` directly, and it
    // means every authorization check queries one collection
    // instead of two.
    userId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      required: [true, 'userId is required'],
    },

    // ---- Parent topic ----
    // The Topic this article belongs to. Together with `userId`
    // this forms the composite identity the compound indexes
    // below key on, and it is the field the "list articles for
    // topic X" query filters on.
    topicId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      required: [true, 'topicId is required'],
    },

    // ---- Body ----
    // The generated Markdown body of the article, with the H1
    // title preserved. Sized at a few kilobytes in the common
    // case (a 1200-word article is roughly 8–10 KB of Markdown)
    // and capped at one megabyte by the schema. The cap is a
    // safety rail, not a design target — the writer step's own
    // word-count guard keeps articles well under it in practice,
    // and an article hitting 1 MB would indicate the DeepSeek
    // automation has gone off the rails, not that a legitimate
    // user requested an exceptionally long piece.
    content: {
      type: String,
      required: [true, 'Content is required'],
      minlength: [1, 'Content must not be empty.'],
      maxlength: [1000000, 'Content must be at most 1,000,000 characters.'],
    },

    wordCount: {
      type: Number,
      required: [true, 'wordCount is required'],
      min: [0, 'wordCount must be non-negative.'],
      max: [100000, 'wordCount must be at most 100000.'],
      validate: {
        // The built-in Number type in Mongoose is a double. Word
        // counts are conceptually integers — a count of "1247.5
        // words" is meaningless and would only appear if the
        // writer pipeline passed a float by mistake. This
        // validator catches that at the schema boundary so no
        // downstream consumer has to think about rounding.
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'wordCount must be an integer.',
      },
    },

    // ---- Versioning ----
    // Starts at 1 for the first article produced for a topic and
    // increments by 1 for each regeneration. The schema enforces
    // that the number is a positive integer; the assignment of
    // the specific next value is the service's job (see the file
    // header). The default of 1 exists as a convenience for the
    // common case where the service does not override it.
    version: {
      type: Number,
      required: [true, 'version is required'],
      default: 1,
      min: [1, 'version must be at least 1.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'version must be an integer.',
      },
    },

    // ---- Lifecycle status ----
    // The closed set of article lifecycle states. The schema
    // validates that the value is one of them; it does not
    // enforce which transitions between them are legal. That is
    // the service's concern — the writer step creates a `draft`,
    // the validation step transitions it to `validated`, and the
    // export step transitions it to `exported`. An edit after
    // validation is expected to return the article to `draft`,
    // and enforcing that rule belongs in the service where the
    // surrounding context (whether the edit actually changed
    // anything) is available.
    status: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: ARTICLE_STATUS_VALUES,
        message:
          'Status must be one of: draft, validated, exported.',
      },
      default: 'draft',
      required: true,
    },
  },
  {
    timestamps: true,
    toJSON: {
      transform: (_doc, ret) => {
        // `__v` is Mongoose's internal version field. It is
        // added to every saved document automatically and is
        // not part of the shared `Article` interface, so it must
        // not appear in the JSON response.
        //
        // The cast to `Record<string, unknown>` is required
        // because TypeScript's `delete` operator refuses to
        // operate on non-optional properties (TS2790). The
        // transform callback's `ret` parameter is typed as the
        // schema's document type, which inherits `__v` as a
        // required property from Mongoose's base `Document`
        // interface. Casting to a record loosens the type enough
        // for the delete to be legal without changing any runtime
        // behaviour — the property is removed from the same
        // object either way. The same fix is applied in
        // `Topic.ts` and `Document.ts`.
        delete (ret as Record<string, unknown>)['__v'];
        return ret;
      },
    },
  }
);

// ============================================================
//  Indexes
// ============================================================
//
//  Two compound indexes cover the read paths the articles
//  feature exercises. Both are prefixed by `userId` because every
//  query on this collection is scoped to a single authenticated
//  user.
//
//    { userId: 1, topicId: 1, version: -1 }
//      Serves two related queries:
//        - "list all versions of this topic's article, newest
//           version first" — the version history view.
//        - "get the latest article for this topic" — the same
//           query with a `.limit(1)`, which is what the topic
//           detail view issues on every render.
//      The compound shape means MongoDB can satisfy both the
//      equality filter (userId + topicId) and the sort (version
//      descending) from the index alone.
//
//    { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 }
//      Serves the cross-topic list — "all my articles, newest
//      first" — which the desktop's dashboard view can offer as
//      an alternate landing page, and which the article service
//      uses to sort by most-recent-activity when it is not
//      filtering by topic.
//
//  A third index on { topicId: 1, version: -1 } was considered
//  and rejected for the same reason the analogous index on the
//  Document model was rejected: every query already carries a
//  userId, so an index without the userId prefix would never be
//  selected. If a future cascade-delete path ever needs to
//  remove articles by topicId alone, the correct move is to
//  carry the userId through that path and reuse the existing
//  compound index.

ArticleSchema.index({ userId: 1, topicId: 1, version: -1 });
ArticleSchema.index({ userId: 1, createdAt: -1 });

// ============================================================
//  Model
// ============================================================

export const ArticleModel = mongoose.model<ArticleDocument>(
  'Article',
  ArticleSchema
);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default ArticleModel;
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/articles/routes/articleRoutes.ts">
/**
 * Route table for the WriteSpeare Article entity.
 *
 * Declares the seven article endpoints and the middleware chain
 * that runs in front of each. The router is mounted at
 * `/api/articles` by the app factory (`src/app.ts`), so the paths
 * declared below are relative to that prefix:
 *
 *   POST   /api/articles                                → create a generated article
 *   GET    /api/articles                                → list the user's articles
 *   GET    /api/articles/:id                            → read a single article
 *   GET    /api/articles/topic/:topicId/latest          → read the current version
 *   PATCH  /api/articles/:id/status                     → transition lifecycle status
 *   DELETE /api/articles/:id                            → delete a single article
 *   DELETE /api/articles/topic/:topicId                 → bulk-delete by topic
 *
 * Every route is protected by `authenticate`. Articles are
 * user-scoped by design — the model's two compound indexes both
 * carry `userId` as their prefix, every service operation filters
 * on `userId`, and every controller handler derives the ownership
 * value from `req.user.userId` rather than from the request. A
 * public article surface does not exist.
 *
 * Middleware order:
 *
 *   `authenticate` runs first and is applied via `asyncHandler`
 *   because the function is async (it awaits a user lookup to
 *   confirm the account still exists and is active). The wrapper
 *   is required — without it, a rejection inside the middleware
 *   would reach the terminal error handler as an unhandled
 *   promise rejection on runtimes that do not forward the
 *   rejection automatically. The existing `authRoutes.ts`,
 *   `topicRoutes.ts`, and `documentRoutes.ts` files use the same
 *   wrapping pattern for the same reason, and all four must stay
 *   in step.
 *
 *   The controller runs second, also wrapped in `asyncHandler`,
 *   for the same reason: the service behind it can throw an
 *   `AppError` (404 for an article or parent topic that does not
 *   exist or belongs to another user; 400 for a schema-level
 *   validation failure such as empty content or a non-integer
 *   word count), and the wrapper is what converts that throw
 *   into a well-formed response via the terminal error
 *   middleware.
 *
 * Route ordering — the multi-segment paths vs the single-`:id`
 * paths:
 *
 *   Three of the routes in this file have more than one segment
 *   after the mount point:
 *
 *     GET    /topic/:topicId/latest       (three segments)
 *     DELETE /topic/:topicId              (two segments)
 *     PATCH  /:id/status                  (two segments)
 *
 *   The remaining four are single-segment or single-parameter:
 *
 *     POST   /
 *     GET    /
 *     GET    /:id                         (one segment)
 *     DELETE /:id                         (one segment)
 *
 *   Express matches routes segment-by-segment, so a request can
 *   never match two routes with different segment counts. That
 *   means the multi-segment routes CANNOT collide with the
 *   single-`:id` routes regardless of declaration order.
 *
 *   The multi-segment routes are nevertheless declared BEFORE the
 *   single-`:id` routes as defensive habit. The rule of thumb
 *   across all route files in this codebase: declare more specific
 *   paths before more general ones. Today no collision exists;
 *   tomorrow, if a literal sub-path like `/featured` is ever
 *   added, the ordering will already be correct.
 *
 *   Within the multi-segment group, `GET /topic/:topicId/latest`
 *   is declared before `DELETE /topic/:topicId` and before
 *   `PATCH /:id/status` — the three do not collide with each
 *   other either (different methods, or different segment names),
 *   but grouping the `/topic/...` routes together and the
 *   `/:id/status` route separately keeps the file readable.
 *
 * The routes are declared as a flat sequence of `router.METHOD`
 * calls rather than as a route table or a declarative
 * configuration. This matches the convention established in
 * `authRoutes.ts`, `topicRoutes.ts`, and `documentRoutes.ts` and
 * in every route file the plan will produce. A reader can scan
 * the file top to bottom and see exactly which middleware runs on
 * which route without holding any additional context.
 *
 * No try/catch appears anywhere in this file. That is deliberate
 * — the asyncHandler wrappers, combined with the terminal error
 * middleware registered in `app.ts`, form the single error-
 * handling contract for every route in the application.
 */

import { Router } from 'express';

import {
  createArticle,
  listArticles,
  getArticleById,
  getLatestArticle,
  updateArticleStatus,
  deleteArticle,
  deleteArticlesByTopic,
} from '../controllers/articleController.js';

import { authenticate } from '../../auth/middleware/authGuard.js';
import { asyncHandler } from '../../shared/middleware/errorHandler.js';

// ============================================================
//  Router instance
// ============================================================

const articleRoutes = Router();

// ============================================================
//  POST /api/articles
// ============================================================
//
//  Persist a generated article attached to a topic owned by the
//  authenticated user. The service computes the next version
//  number for the topic and writes it to the record — the client
//  never supplies a version. The service verifies that the parent
//  topic exists and is owned by the same caller before the
//  article is written.

articleRoutes.post(
  '/',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(createArticle)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/articles
// ============================================================
//
//  List the authenticated user's articles. An optional
//  `?topicId=` query parameter narrows the result to the
//  articles attached to a single topic. The sort order is chosen
//  by the service based on whether the query is topic-scoped —
//  see the service header for the dual-sort rationale.

articleRoutes.get(
  '/',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(listArticles)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/articles/topic/:topicId/latest
// ============================================================
//
//  Return the current (highest-version) article for a topic.
//  This is a dedicated query rather than a filter on the list
//  endpoint — the topic-detail view issues it on every render,
//  and the dedicated route lets the service answer it with a
//  single indexed findOne. A 404 is returned when the topic has
//  no articles, when the topic does not exist, or when the topic
//  belongs to a different user — all three collapse to the same
//  response for enumeration-safety reasons documented in the
//  controller.

articleRoutes.get(
  '/topic/:topicId/latest',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(getLatestArticle)
);

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/articles/topic/:topicId
// ============================================================
//
//  Bulk-delete every article attached to a topic, scoped to the
//  authenticated user. The filter is scoped to
//  `{ userId, topicId }` in the service, so a caller who does not
//  own the topic matches zero records and cannot clear another
//  user's articles by guessing the topic id.

articleRoutes.delete(
  '/topic/:topicId',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(deleteArticlesByTopic)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/articles/:id
// ============================================================
//
//  Return a single article by ID, scoped to the authenticated
//  user. The service merges the "not found" and "not owned"
//  cases and returns null for both; the controller converts that
//  null into a 404 without distinguishing the two — see the
//  controller header for the information-leak rationale.

articleRoutes.get(
  '/:id',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(getArticleById)
);

// ============================================================
//  PATCH /api/articles/:id/status
// ============================================================
//
//  Transition an article's lifecycle status. The `status` field
//  is the only mutable field on an existing article — content is
//  immutable by design, and a content change produces a new
//  version rather than an in-place edit. The narrow sub-path
//  (`/status` rather than a generic PATCH on `/:id`) makes the
//  single-field nature of the operation explicit in the URL.

articleRoutes.patch(
  '/:id/status',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(updateArticleStatus)
);

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/articles/:id
// ============================================================
//
//  Delete a single article, scoped to the authenticated user.
//  The service returns the deleted document so the client can
//  render an undo affordance without a second round trip. The
//  service does NOT cascade to the article's Reports — removing
//  a Report that referenced the article is the reports feature's
//  responsibility, not the articles feature's.

articleRoutes.delete(
  '/:id',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(deleteArticle)
);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default articleRoutes;
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/articles/services/articleService.ts">
/**
 * Business logic for the WriteSpeare Article entity.
 *
 * An Article is one generated article attached to a Topic. A
 * Topic can own multiple Article versions — the initial draft
 * returned by the writer step, plus any subsequent versions
 * produced by the corrective regeneration loop. Each Article is
 * a numbered snapshot; the article with the highest `version`
 * number is the "current" one for its topic.
 *
 * The service exposes seven ownership-scoped operations:
 *
 *   createArticle           — persist a generated article, with
 *                             the next version number computed
 *                             from the existing versions
 *   listArticles            — read the user's articles,
 *                             optionally filtered by topic
 *   getArticleById          — read a single article
 *   getLatestArticle        — read the current version for a topic
 *   updateArticleStatus     — transition the lifecycle status
 *   deleteArticle           — remove a single article
 *   deleteArticlesByTopic   — bulk-remove every article under a topic
 *
 * Every function takes a `userId` argument that the caller (the
 * controller) derives from `req.user.userId`. That value is never
 * read from the request body, query, or route params — the client
 * cannot choose whose articles they are reading or writing. This
 * is the same ownership contract used by `topicService.ts` and
 * `documentService.ts`.
 *
 * Cross-feature import — TopicModel:
 *
 *   This service imports `TopicModel` from the topics feature to
 *   verify, on the create path, that the parent topic exists and
 *   is owned by the caller before persisting the article. Without
 *   the check, a client could POST an article with any `topicId`
 *   — including one belonging to another user — and the article
 *   would be persisted with an inconsistent ownership pair. The
 *   import direction (child → parent) mirrors the same decision
 *   made in `documentService.ts`, and the same caveat applies:
 *   future cross-feature imports in the wrong direction would be
 *   rejected, but this one is fundamental to the hierarchy.
 *
 * Version computation:
 *
 *   Each call to `createArticle` computes the next version number
 *   by finding the current maximum for the `(userId, topicId)`
 *   pair and adding one. The first article for a topic is version
 *   1; every subsequent creation is version N+1. The computation
 *   is a single indexed query (the compound index
 *   `{ userId, topicId, version: -1 }` on the Article schema
 *   covers it), and the schema's `version` field only enforces
 *   that the result is a positive integer — the assignment of the
 *   specific next value is the service's job.
 *
 *   Two concurrent regenerations for the same topic could, in
 *   principle, both read the same current maximum and both write
 *   version N+1. The schema does NOT declare `(userId, topicId,
 *   version)` unique, so the second write would succeed and the
 *   topic would end up with two articles at the same version
 *   number. That outcome is acceptable for the current product —
 *   the desktop client serializes regenerations (one at a time,
 *   via the writer store's `isGenerating` flag), so the race
 *   cannot occur through the supported UI. If a future backend
 *   exposes concurrent regeneration, the correct fix is a unique
 *   compound index plus a retry loop in this function, not a
 *   change to the schema in isolation.
 *
 * Immutability of content:
 *
 *   There is no `updateArticleContent` function. An Article
 *   represents a specific snapshot of the writer step's output.
 *   If the user edits an article or regenerates it, the correct
 *   operation is to create a new version — this is what the
 *   "Regenerate" and "Edit" actions in the desktop client do, by
 *   calling `createArticle` with the new content. The only field
 *   that can be mutated in place is `status`, via the narrow
 *   `updateArticleStatus` function.
 *
 *   This design keeps the version history a clean log of every
 *   article state the topic has ever held. If article content
 *   were mutable, a Report produced against version 3 would
 *   become stale the moment the content changed, and there would
 *   be no way to reconstruct which version the report was
 *   actually validating. Immutable content plus a separate status
 *   field avoids that class of ambiguity entirely.
 *
 * The status transition and the corrective loop:
 *
 *   `draft`     — the article as first returned by the writer.
 *   `validated` — a Report has been produced against it.
 *   `exported`  — the user has exported it to a file.
 *
 *   The service does not enforce which transitions are legal from
 *   which state — it accepts any `ArticleStatus` value and writes
 *   it. Enforcing transition rules at the service level would
 *   require a lookup of the current status on every update and
 *   would add a second source of truth alongside the schema's
 *   enum. In practice the callers (the validation runner and the
 *   export handler) only ever advance the status forward, and the
 *   schema's enum restricts the values to the closed set. If a
 *   future requirement needs enforced transitions, the correct
 *   place to add them is here, guarded by a current-status read.
 *
 * Cascade semantics:
 *
 *   `deleteArticlesByTopic` exists so that a future cascade from
 *   topic deletion has a well-defined entry point, mirroring the
 *   same function on the Document service. The current topic
 *   service does NOT call it — see the header comment in
 *   `topicService.ts`, which explicitly notes that cascading is
 *   "a decision for each owning feature". The cascade is scoped
 *   to the caller's `userId`, so a caller who does not own the
 *   topic matches zero records and cannot clear another user's
 *   articles by guessing the topic id.
 */

import { ArticleModel, type ArticleDocument } from '../models/Article.js';
import { TopicModel } from '../../topics/models/Topic.js';
import type {
  MongoId,
  ArticleCreatePayload,
  ArticleStatus,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';
import { AppError } from '../../shared/middleware/errorHandler.js';

// ============================================================
//  createArticle
// ============================================================

/**
 * Persist a generated article attached to a topic owned by the
 * caller. The next version number for the topic is computed here
 * and written to the record; the caller does not supply a version.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Look up the parent topic by `(topicId, userId)`. The
 *      ownership check is part of the same query — a topic that
 *      exists but belongs to a different user is treated as "not
 *      found", which keeps the service from leaking other users'
 *      topic IDs through a 403.
 *
 *   2. If the topic does not exist or is not owned by the caller,
 *      throw `AppError(404)` with a message that refers to the
 *      topic, not the article. The caller is trying to attach an
 *      article to a topic they cannot see; the correct diagnostic
 *      is "that topic does not exist (from your point of view)".
 *
 *   3. Read the current maximum version number for this
 *      `(userId, topicId)` pair. A topic with no articles yet has
 *      no max, and the next version is 1.
 *
 *   4. Persist the article with the caller's `userId`, the
 *      supplied `topicId` and body fields, and the computed
 *      version. Status defaults to `draft` via the schema.
 *
 *   5. Return the saved document.
 *
 * The function does NOT catch validation errors from the schema.
 * A Mongoose ValidationError thrown here — empty content, a
 * negative word count, a non-integer word count — propagates to
 * the terminal error middleware, which maps it to a 400 with the
 * schema's own message.
 *
 * @param userId  - Ownership value, derived from the authenticated
 *                  session by the controller.
 * @param payload - The generated article's body and word count.
 *                  `version` and `userId` are NOT part of this
 *                  payload by design.
 */
export const createArticle = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  payload: ArticleCreatePayload
): Promise<ArticleDocument> => {
  // ---- 1. Verify the parent topic exists and is owned by the caller ----
  const parentTopic = await TopicModel.findOne({
    _id: payload.topicId,
    userId,
  });

  if (!parentTopic) {
    throw new AppError('Topic not found.', 404);
  }

  // ---- 2. Compute the next version number ----
  // The compound index { userId, topicId, version: -1 } on the
  // Article schema makes this query an index-only scan — no
  // collection fetch, no in-memory sort. The projection narrows
  // the returned document to the single field we need.
  const latest = await ArticleModel.findOne({
    userId,
    topicId: payload.topicId,
  })
    .sort({ version: -1 })
    .select('version');

  // `latest` is `ArticleDocument | null`. When it is null, the
  // topic has no articles yet and this is the first one — version
  // 1. When it is not null, the next version is one past the
  // current maximum.
  const nextVersion = latest ? latest.version + 1 : 1;

  // ---- 3. Persist the article ----
  // The spread of `payload` is safe: it contains exactly the
  // fields the schema expects for the caller-supplied portion
  // (topicId, content, wordCount), and no `userId` or `version`
  // field is present on the payload type. Both are added
  // explicitly here, from values this function controls.
  const doc = new ArticleModel({
    ...payload,
    userId,
    version: nextVersion,
  });

  return await doc.save();
};

// ============================================================
//  listArticles
// ============================================================

/**
 * List every article owned by the given user. If `topicId` is
 * provided, the result is narrowed to the articles attached to
 * that topic.
 *
 * Sort order depends on whether the query is topic-scoped:
 *
 *   - Topic-scoped (topicId provided): sorted by `version`
 *     descending, so the newest version appears first. This is
 *     the version-history view — a list of every regeneration a
 *     topic has produced, newest at the top. The compound index
 *     `{ userId, topicId, version: -1 }` covers both the filter
 *     and the sort without an in-memory stage.
 *
 *   - Cross-topic (topicId omitted): sorted by `createdAt`
 *     descending, so the most recently written article appears
 *     first across the user's entire collection. This is the
 *     dashboard view. The compound index
 *     `{ userId, createdAt: -1 }` covers it.
 *
 *   The two sort orders are not a design inconsistency — they
 *   reflect two different questions the client asks. Within a
 *   topic, "which is the latest version?" is naturally answered
 *   by version number; across topics, "what did I write most
 *   recently?" is naturally answered by timestamp. Both answers
 *   are what the corresponding UI views need.
 *
 * A `topicId` that does not belong to the caller returns an empty
 * list rather than a 404. See `documentService.ts` for the same
 * rationale — the list endpoint is a read-only projection, and
 * distinguishing "no articles under someone else's topic" from
 * "no articles under your own empty topic" would reopen the
 * enumeration channel the rest of the service closes.
 *
 * @param userId  - Ownership value.
 * @param topicId - Optional parent-topic filter.
 */
export const listArticles = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  topicId?: MongoId
): Promise<ArticleDocument[]> => {
  const filter: { userId: MongoId; topicId?: MongoId } = { userId };
  if (topicId !== undefined) {
    filter.topicId = topicId;
    // Topic-scoped: newest version first.
    return await ArticleModel.find(filter).sort({ version: -1 });
  }

  // Cross-topic: most recently written first.
  return await ArticleModel.find(filter).sort({ createdAt: -1 });
};

// ============================================================
//  getArticleById
// ============================================================

/**
 * Read a single article by id, scoped to the caller.
 *
 * Returns `null` when the article does not exist, OR when it
 * exists but belongs to a different user. The two cases are
 * intentionally indistinguishable — see the file header in
 * `documentService.ts` for the same enumeration-attack rationale
 * (which applies identically here).
 *
 * A malformed id string — one that is not a valid ObjectId — does
 * NOT return null; it causes Mongoose to throw a CastError, which
 * the terminal middleware maps to a 400.
 *
 * @param userId    - Ownership value.
 * @param articleId - The article's id, as a string from the route
 *                    parameter.
 */
export const getArticleById = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  articleId: string
): Promise<ArticleDocument | null> => {
  return await ArticleModel.findOne({ _id: articleId, userId });
};

// ============================================================
//  getLatestArticle
// ============================================================

/**
 * Read the current (highest-version) article for a topic, scoped
 * to the caller.
 *
 * Returns `null` when the topic has no articles yet, OR when the
 * topic does not exist, OR when the topic belongs to a different
 * user. The three cases collapse to the same null — the caller
 * (the topic-detail view, the validation runner) either has an
 * article to work with or it does not, and it has no use for the
 * distinction.
 *
 * This is a dedicated function rather than a `.slice(0)` on the
 * result of `listArticles(userId, topicId)` because:
 *
 *   1. The query is a single indexed findOne with an explicit
 *      sort — it terminates at the first matching document
 *      rather than fetching the entire version history and
 *      discarding all but one.
 *
 *   2. The name communicates intent. A future reader who sees
 *      `getLatestArticle(userId, topicId)` in a service method
 *      knows exactly what is being fetched; a reader who sees
 *      `listArticles(userId, topicId)[0]` has to reconstruct
 *      the intent from the surrounding context.
 *
 * The query is covered by the compound index
 * `{ userId, topicId, version: -1 }` — the filter matches on the
 * leftmost two fields, and the sort key is the trailing field.
 *
 * @param userId  - Ownership value.
 * @param topicId - The parent topic whose latest article is being
 *                  fetched.
 */
export const getLatestArticle = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  topicId: MongoId
): Promise<ArticleDocument | null> => {
  return await ArticleModel.findOne({ userId, topicId }).sort({
    version: -1,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  updateArticleStatus
// ============================================================

/**
 * Transition an article's lifecycle status, scoped to the caller.
 *
 * This is the ONLY field that can be mutated in place on an
 * existing article — see the file header for why content is
 * immutable and why version history is appended, not edited.
 *
 * The function accepts any `ArticleStatus` value. It does NOT
 * enforce that the new status represents a legal transition from
 * the current one; the schema's enum restricts the value to the
 * closed set, and the callers (the validation runner and the
 * export handler) only advance forward in practice. See the file
 * header for why transition enforcement belongs at the service
 * level only if a future requirement demands it.
 *
 * Returns the updated document, so the caller can immediately
 * reflect the new status in its response without a second read.
 *
 * Throws `AppError(404)` when the article does not exist or is
 * not owned by the caller.
 *
 * @param userId    - Ownership value.
 * @param articleId - The article's id.
 * @param status    - The new lifecycle status.
 */
export const updateArticleStatus = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  articleId: string,
  status: ArticleStatus
): Promise<ArticleDocument> => {
  const updated = await ArticleModel.findOneAndUpdate(
    { _id: articleId, userId },
    { $set: { status } },
    { new: true, runValidators: true }
  );

  if (!updated) {
    throw new AppError('Article not found.', 404);
  }

  return updated;
};

// ============================================================
//  deleteArticle
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete a single article by id, scoped to the caller.
 *
 * Returns the deleted document so the caller can cascade whatever
 * cleanup is appropriate (removing any Report that referenced the
 * article, for example — though the cascade itself is the
 * reports feature's responsibility, not this service's).
 *
 * Throws `AppError(404)` when the article does not exist or is
 * not owned by the caller. Same merged case as the read paths.
 *
 * @param userId    - Ownership value.
 * @param articleId - The article's id.
 */
export const deleteArticle = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  articleId: string
): Promise<ArticleDocument> => {
  const deleted = await ArticleModel.findOneAndDelete({
    _id: articleId,
    userId,
  });

  if (!deleted) {
    throw new AppError('Article not found.', 404);
  }

  return deleted;
};

// ============================================================
//  deleteArticlesByTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Bulk-delete every article attached to the given topic, scoped
 * to the caller.
 *
 * Returns the number of articles removed. A count of zero is a
 * legitimate, non-error result: it means either the topic has no
 * articles, or the topic does not exist, or the topic belongs to
 * a different user — the caller does not need to distinguish
 * those cases.
 *
 * The filter is scoped to `{ userId, topicId }`, not just
 * `topicId`. A caller who does not own the topic matches zero
 * records on the `userId` clause and therefore cannot clear
 * another user's topic by guessing its id.
 *
 * @param userId  - Ownership value.
 * @param topicId - The parent topic whose articles are being
 *                  removed.
 */
export const deleteArticlesByTopic = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  topicId: MongoId
): Promise<number> => {
  const result = await ArticleModel.deleteMany({ userId, topicId });
  return result.deletedCount;
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  createArticle,
  listArticles,
  getArticleById,
  getLatestArticle,
  updateArticleStatus,
  deleteArticle,
  deleteArticlesByTopic,
};

/**
 * Public export surface for the WriteSpeare articles feature.
 *
 * The plan declares this file with a single responsibility:
 * "Public exports." That is the entire specification, and this
 * file fills it in with the minimal, non-redundant surface that
 * the rest of the codebase can meaningfully consume — following
 * the exact shape established by the topics feature's index at
 * `features/topics/index.ts` and the documents feature's index
 * at `features/documents/index.ts`.
 *
 * What belongs here — and what does not:
 *
 *   The articles feature contains five kinds of source files:
 *
 *     models/Article.ts          — the Mongoose schema and its
 *                                  document interface
 *     services/articleService.ts
 *                                — the business-logic layer
 *     controllers/articleController.ts
 *                                — the HTTP handlers
 *     routes/articleRoutes.ts    — the Express router
 *     index.ts                   — this file
 *
 *   Of those five, only TWO are useful to a consumer OUTSIDE the
 *   feature:
 *
 *     (a) The router. `app.ts` mounts it under `/api/articles`.
 *         That is the one import the feature's external boundary
 *         actually needs — the controller and service are
 *         internal implementation details between the router and
 *         the model, and nothing outside the feature should
 *         reach past the router for request-handling behavior.
 *
 *     (b) The model. The reports feature owns records with an
 *         `articleId` field — a Report validates one Article —
 *         and its service (`reportService.ts`) already imports
 *         `ArticleModel` directly from `articles/models/Article.js`
 *         to validate that a parent article exists and is owned
 *         by the caller. Exporting the model from the feature
 *         index gives that consumer (and any future one) a
 *         single named entry point without requiring a code
 *         change in the consumer.
 *
 *   The service and controller are NOT re-exported. Both are
 *   internal: the service is only ever consumed by the
 *   controller within the same feature, and the controller is
 *   only ever consumed by the router within the same feature.
 *   Additionally, their function names collide — both export
 *   `createArticle`, `listArticles`, etc. — and re-exporting
 *   both with bare names would produce a duplicate-export error.
 *   The rule this file follows, matching the two previous
 *   features' indexes: export what is consumed, not everything
 *   that exists.
 *
 * Why the router is exported both as a named symbol AND as the
 * default:
 *
 *   The router file itself (`routes/articleRoutes.ts`) exports
 *   its router as the default. This index file preserves that
 *   shape for callers that prefer the default form — `import
 *   articleRoutes from '...features/articles'` — while also
 *   giving the named form — `import { articleRoutes } from
 *   '...features/articles'` — to callers that prefer named
 *   imports for uniformity with the rest of this file's exports.
 *
 *   The two forms resolve to the same router instance. There is
 *   no double-construction, no second Express `Router()`, and
 *   no chance of the router being registered twice by mistake.
 *
 * Note for readers who have been following the session:
 *
 *   The current `app.ts` imports its feature routers from their
 *   deep paths (`./features/articles/routes/articleRoutes.js`),
 *   not from the feature indexes. This index file does NOT
 *   change that pattern retroactively; it is a forward-looking
 *   surface that a future app-factory refactor can adopt. Until
 *   that refactor, this file's exports are dormant — nothing in
 *   the codebase currently imports from it.
 *
 *   That is fine, and it is what the plan's "Public exports"
 *   annotation calls for. The surface exists so that when a
 *   consumer DOES need it, there is a declared, documented place
 *   for that import to come from — rather than a deep path that
 *   was chosen ad hoc.
 */

<file path="apps/server/src/features/documents/controllers/documentController.ts">
/**
 * HTTP handlers for the WriteSpeare Document entity.
 *
 * Thin request/response layer over `documentService`. Each handler
 * performs exactly four jobs and nothing else:
 *
 *   1. Read the authenticated user's ID from `req.user.userId`
 *      and reject the request with a 401 if it is absent. Every
 *      ownership-scoped operation in WriteSpeare keys off this
 *      value; a handler that is reached without an authenticated
 *      session would either crash on a null dereference or — far
 *      worse — silently operate on the wrong user's data.
 *      `authenticate` on the route layer is the primary gate; this
 *      check is the belt-and-braces guard against a route that is
 *      misconfigured in a future refactor.
 *
 *   2. Validate the shape of the request body / query / params
 *      just enough to reject requests that are so malformed the
 *      service would produce a confusing error. The schema (in
 *      `documents/models/Document.ts`) remains the authoritative
 *      validator for everything subtler — URL parsing, platform
 *      slug format, string length bounds, integer constraints on
 *      the word count are all checked there, and a Mongoose
 *      ValidationError is translated to a 400 by the terminal
 *      error middleware. Doing anything more in the controller
 *      would duplicate the schema's rules and eventually drift
 *      from them.
 *
 *   3. Delegate to the service. The controller never touches the
 *      database directly — it does not import the Document model,
 *      does not build queries, and does not know what collection
 *      the data lives in. That is the service's job.
 *
 *   4. Format the success response using the shared `ApiResponse`
 *      envelope. Every response — success or failure — uses the
 *      same shape, so a client can unwrap it uniformly.
 *
 * No try/catch appears anywhere in this file. Each route handler
 * is wrapped in `asyncHandler` at the route registration site,
 * which forwards any rejection to the terminal error middleware.
 * The middleware recognises the shared `AppError` class thrown by
 * the service — a 404 for a document or topic that does not exist
 * or is not owned by the caller — and formats the response with
 * the same envelope this file uses on success. Putting a try/catch
 * here would duplicate the middleware's classification logic and
 * split the error-handling contract across two files.
 *
 * Response typing — the assignability bridge:
 *
 *   Every handler declares its `Response<T>` type explicitly. On
 *   success the service returns a `DocumentDocument` (Mongoose's
 *   in-process shape) which is structurally assignable to the
 *   shared `Document` domain type — the only difference is that
 *   `DocumentDocument._id` is a concrete `ObjectId` while
 *   `Document._id` is `string | ObjectId`. Since `ObjectId` is a
 *   member of the union, the assignment is safe and the response
 *   type can be declared as the domain type. At runtime,
 *   `res.json()` serialises the ObjectId to its hex string form,
 *   which is exactly what the client's `Document` interface
 *   expects.
 *
 * The `fetchedAt` conversion — why this file does it:
 *
 *   The `DocumentCreatePayload` type declares `fetchedAt: Date`,
 *   because that is the type the schema stores and the service
 *   receives. But an HTTP request body arrives as JSON, and JSON
 *   has no Date type — a `Date` serialised through `JSON.stringify`
 *   becomes an ISO-8601 string. The controller is therefore the
 *   one place where the wire format (string) meets the in-process
 *   type (Date), and the conversion — plus its associated
 *   validation that the string actually parses to a valid date —
 *   lives here. Every other layer of the stack receives a
 *   `Date` and never has to think about it.
 *
 *   The validation rejects two cases distinctly: a missing or
 *   non-string `fetchedAt` (400 "must be an ISO date string"),
 *   and a string that does not parse (400 "must be a valid ISO
 *   date string"). The two messages differ so a client developer
 *   can tell whether they omitted the field or sent the wrong
 *   kind of value.
 *
 * Route-ordering note for `deleteDocumentsByTopic`:
 *
 *   This file exposes a bulk-delete-by-topic route at
 *   `DELETE /api/documents/topic/:topicId`, alongside the
 *   single-document `DELETE /api/documents/:id`. Express matches
 *   routes by segment count, and the two paths differ in the
 *   number of segments they contain (`/topic/:topicId` has two,
 *   `/:id` has one), so no ambiguity exists regardless of which
 *   route is declared first in the route file. The route is
 *   exposed for the cascade-delete workflow described in the
 *   service's header comment — the current desktop IPC surface
 *   does not call it, but the backend's route table is the
 *   authoritative declaration of what the API can do, and this
 *   route is a legitimate operation the API supports.
 *
 * Ownership scoping:
 *
 *   The `userId` passed to the service is ALWAYS derived from the
 *   authenticated session — `req.user.userId` — and NEVER read
 *   from the request body or query. This is what makes it
 *   impossible for a client to create a document on behalf of
 *   another user: the ownership field is set from the token, not
 *   from anything the client controls.
 */

import type { Response } from 'express';

import {
  createDocument as createDocumentService,
  listDocuments as listDocumentsService,
  getDocumentById as getDocumentByIdService,
  deleteDocument as deleteDocumentService,
  deleteDocumentsByTopic as deleteDocumentsByTopicService,
} from '../services/documentService.js';

import type { AuthRequest } from '../../auth/middleware/authGuard.js';
import type {
  ApiResponse,
  Document,
  DocumentCreatePayload,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  POST /api/documents
// ============================================================

/**
 * Persist a scraped document attached to a topic owned by the
 * authenticated user.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the request body is not a plain object.
 *   3. Validate the eight required fields present on the request
 *      body. Each is checked for a primitive type — strings for
 *      the four text fields, a number for the word count, a
 *      string for the two identifiers. Length and content rules
 *      (URL parses, platform slug format, non-empty title,
 *      integer word count) are the schema's job and are not
 *      duplicated here.
 *   4. Convert `fetchedAt` from its wire-format ISO string into a
 *      `Date` and validate that the conversion succeeded. See the
 *      file header for why this conversion is the controller's
 *      responsibility.
 *   5. Delegate to the service. The service validates that the
 *      parent topic exists and is owned by the caller; a 404
 *      thrown by that check propagates to the terminal middleware.
 *   6. Respond with 201 Created and the persisted document.
 *
 * The `userId` argument to the service is derived from the
 * authenticated session. Any client-supplied `userId` field on
 * the request body is ignored — the body's `Record<string,
 * unknown>` type simply does not read that field.
 */
export const createDocument = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Document>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Body shape guard ----
  // The cast to `unknown` before the type check forces every
  // subsequent access to go through an explicit narrowing step,
  // which is what keeps a runtime-invalid value from silently
  // propagating into the payload below.
  const rawBody: unknown = req.body;
  if (
    typeof rawBody !== 'object' ||
    rawBody === null ||
    Array.isArray(rawBody)
  ) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Request body must be a JSON object.',
    });
    return;
  }
  const body = rawBody as Record<string, unknown>;

  // ---- 3. Required fields ----
  // Each field is checked for its primitive type only. Length
  // and content rules belong to the schema — see the file
  // header. The checks are ordered so that the error message a
  // client sees names the first missing field, which is more
  // useful than a generic "invalid body" for a client developer
  // iterating on their request shape.

  const topicId = body['topicId'];
  if (typeof topicId !== 'string' || topicId.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'topicId is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const url = body['url'];
  if (typeof url !== 'string' || url.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'url is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const platform = body['platform'];
  if (typeof platform !== 'string' || platform.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'platform is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const title = body['title'];
  if (typeof title !== 'string' || title.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'title is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const content = body['content'];
  if (typeof content !== 'string' || content.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'content is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  const wordCount = body['wordCount'];
  if (typeof wordCount !== 'number') {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'wordCount must be a number.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 4. fetchedAt conversion ----
  // The wire format is an ISO-8601 string; the in-process type
  // is a Date. The two failure modes are distinguished so a
  // client developer can tell whether the field was omitted,
  // sent as the wrong type, or sent as a string that does not
  // parse.
  const fetchedAtRaw = body['fetchedAt'];
  if (typeof fetchedAtRaw !== 'string') {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'fetchedAt must be an ISO date string.',
    });
    return;
  }
  const fetchedAt = new Date(fetchedAtRaw);
  if (Number.isNaN(fetchedAt.getTime())) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'fetchedAt must be a valid ISO date string.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 5. Build the payload and delegate ----
  const payload: DocumentCreatePayload = {
    topicId,
    url,
    platform,
    title,
    content,
    wordCount,
    fetchedAt,
  };

  const document = await createDocumentService(userId, payload);

  // ---- 6. Respond ----
  res.status(201).json({
    success: true,
    data: document,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/documents
// ============================================================

/**
 * List the authenticated user's documents, sorted newest first.
 * An optional `?topicId=` query parameter narrows the result to
 * the documents attached to a single topic.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. If a `?topicId=` query parameter is present, validate that
 *      it is a non-empty string. The service does not confirm
 *      ownership of the topic — a topicId that does not belong to
 *      the caller produces an empty list, not a 404. That is
 *      deliberate: the list endpoint is a read-only projection,
 *      and distinguishing "no documents under someone else's
 *      topic" from "no documents under your own empty topic"
 *      would reopen the enumeration channel the rest of the
 *      service closes. See the service header for the full
 *      rationale.
 *   3. Delegate to the service with the derived `userId` and the
 *      optional filter.
 *   4. Respond with 200 and the array. An empty array is a valid,
 *      non-error response.
 */
export const listDocuments = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Document[]>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Optional topicId filter ----
  // `req.query['topicId']` is typed `string | ParsedQs | (string
  // | ParsedQs)[] | undefined` under Express's default generics.
  // A repeated query parameter arrives as an array and is
  // rejected by the `typeof !== 'string'` check — the correct
  // behaviour, since the API accepts exactly one topicId filter
  // per request.
  const rawTopicId = req.query['topicId'];
  let topicId: string | undefined;
  if (rawTopicId !== undefined) {
    if (typeof rawTopicId !== 'string' || rawTopicId.length === 0) {
      res.status(400).json({
        success: false,
        error: 'Invalid topicId filter.',
      });
      return;
    }
    topicId = rawTopicId;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const documents = await listDocumentsService(userId, topicId);

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: documents,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/documents/:id
// ============================================================

/**
 * Return a single document by its ID, scoped to the authenticated
 * user.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:id` route parameter is missing
 *      or empty. A malformed ID that is present but not a valid
 *      ObjectId is not rejected here — the service's `findOne`
 *      throws a CastError, which the terminal middleware maps
 *      to a 400.
 *   3. Delegate to the service. A null result means either "no
 *      such document" or "document belongs to a different
 *      user"; this handler returns 404 for both. Returning 403
 *      for the "belongs to someone else" case would leak the
 *      existence of other users' document IDs to an authenticated
 *      attacker probing the endpoint.
 *   4. Respond with 200 and the document, or 404 if it was not
 *      found / not owned.
 */
export const getDocumentById = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Document>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const documentId = req.params['id'];
  if (typeof documentId !== 'string' || documentId.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Document ID is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const document = await getDocumentByIdService(userId, documentId);
  if (!document) {
    res.status(404).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Document not found.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: document,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/documents/:id
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete a single document, scoped to the authenticated user.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:id` route parameter is missing
 *      or empty.
 *   3. Delegate to the service. The service throws `AppError(404)`
 *      when the document does not exist or belongs to a different
 *      user — the same merged case as `getDocumentById`, and for
 *      the same reason.
 *   4. Respond with 200 and the deleted document. Returning the
 *      deleted document (rather than an empty body with 204)
 *      gives the client a last-chance look at what was removed,
 *      which the UI uses to render a "Deleted document X —
 *      Undo?" affordance without a second round trip.
 *
 * The service does NOT touch the filesystem. The `.md` file that
 * the extraction pipeline wrote lives on the desktop client's
 * disk; removing it is the desktop's job (via the IPC layer), not
 * the backend's. The backend owns only the metadata record.
 */
export const deleteDocument = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<Document>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const documentId = req.params['id'];
  if (typeof documentId !== 'string' || documentId.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Document ID is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const document = await deleteDocumentService(userId, documentId);

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: document,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/documents/topic/:topicId
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete every document attached to the given topic, scoped to
 * the authenticated user.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Reject with 401 if no authenticated user is attached.
 *   2. Reject with 400 if the `:topicId` route parameter is
 *      missing or empty.
 *   3. Delegate to the service. The service returns the number of
 *      documents removed. Zero is a valid result: it means either
 *      the topic has no documents, or the topic does not exist,
 *      or the topic belongs to a different user — the caller does
 *      not need to distinguish those cases. The filter is scoped
 *      to `{ userId, topicId }`, so a caller cannot clear another
 *      user's topic by guessing its ID.
 *   4. Respond with 200 and `{ deletedCount }`. The count is
 *      returned in the `data` field (rather than as a free-form
 *      message) so the client can read it programmatically — a
 *      toast saying "Cleared 8 documents" reads the number from
 *      this exact place.
 *
 * Route-path note — `/topic/:topicId` vs `/:id`:
 *
 *   Express matches routes segment-by-segment. A request to
 *   `DELETE /api/documents/topic/abc123` has two segments after
 *   the mount point (`topic` and `abc123`); a request to
 *   `DELETE /api/documents/xyz` has one (`xyz`). The route
 *   `/:id` matches exactly one segment and cannot collide with
 *   `/topic/:topicId`, which matches exactly two. Both routes can
 *   therefore be declared in the route file in either order
 *   without ambiguity. The nested form is used rather than a
 *   query parameter (`DELETE /api/documents?topicId=...`)
 *   because the query-parameter form collides semantically with
 *   the single-document delete — a caller cannot tell from the
 *   URL alone whether they are clearing one document or all of a
 *   topic's documents, and the nested path makes the intent
 *   explicit.
 */
export const deleteDocumentsByTopic = async (
  req: AuthRequest,
  res: Response<ApiResponse<{ deletedCount: number }>>
): Promise<void> => {
  // ---- 1. Authentication guard ----
  const userId = req.user?.userId;
  if (!userId) {
    res.status(401).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Authentication required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 2. Route parameter guard ----
  const topicId = req.params['topicId'];
  if (typeof topicId !== 'string' || topicId.length === 0) {
    res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: 'Topic ID is required.',
    });
    return;
  }

  // ---- 3. Delegate to the service ----
  const deletedCount = await deleteDocumentsByTopicService(
    userId,
    topicId
  );

  // ---- 4. Respond ----
  res.status(200).json({
    success: true,
    data: { deletedCount },
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  createDocument,
  listDocuments,
  getDocumentById,
  deleteDocument,
  deleteDocumentsByTopic,
};
