<file path="apps/server/src/features/reports/models/Report.ts">
/**
 * Mongoose model for the WriteSpeare Report entity.
 *
 * A Report is the validation output produced against one
 * Article. It carries six sections — readability, SEO, keywords,
 * originality, AI markers, grammar — that map one-for-one to the
 * six Python validators in `apps/desktop/src/resources/scripts/validation/`.
 * The backend stores what the desktop's validation runner
 * produces, exactly as produced; it does not reinterpret or
 * re-score the numbers.
 *
 * Responsibilities:
 *
 *   1. Enforce the schema-level invariants of a report record.
 *      Every leaf field has a type, a numeric range where
 *      meaningful, and — for the three closed-set unions
 *      (`ReportStatus`, keyword priority, and the section status
 *      that follows from `ReportStatus`) — a runtime enum array
 *      that mirrors the string-literal union declared in
 *      `shared/types`.
 *
 *   2. Own the two compound indexes that the reports feature's
 *      read paths exercise:
 *
 *        - "list every report for one article, newest first" —
 *           served by { userId, articleId, createdAt: -1 }. A
 *           single article can have multiple reports: one per
 *           validation run, produced against successive
 *           versions or against a single version re-checked
 *           after the user edits content. The most recent one
 *           is the "current" report.
 *
 *        - "list every report for one topic, newest first" —
 *           served by { userId, topicId, createdAt: -1 }. The
 *           topic-detail view uses this to build a per-topic
 *           validation history without needing the intermediate
 *           articleId.
 *
 *      Both indexes are prefixed by `userId` for the same reason
 *      every other model's indexes are: every query on this
 *      collection is scoped to a single authenticated user.
 *
 *   3. Provide a single `toJSON` transform that strips Mongoose's
 *      `__v` version field, so a serialised Report matches the
 *      shared `Report` interface exactly.
 *
 * Sub-schemas and why they are embedded:
 *
 *   Each of the six sections is declared as its own `Schema` with
 *   `{ _id: false }`, and the top-level schema embeds them as
 *   sub-documents. This is the correct choice for three reasons:
 *
 *   (a) A Report is always read as a whole. No code path needs
 *       the readability numbers without the SEO numbers, or the
 *       keywords without the originality scores. Splitting the
 *       sections into their own collections would force six
 *       joins per read for zero benefit.
 *
 *   (b) The sections are not independently addressable. There is
 *       no operation in the product that reads or writes one
 *       section in isolation — the validation runner produces
 *       all six in one pass, and the desktop renderer consumes
 *       all six in one view.
 *
 *   (c) The sections have no lifecycle of their own. They are
 *       created when the Report is created and deleted when the
 *       Report is deleted. Making them independent documents
 *       would require a cascade delete with no compensating
 *       benefit.
 *
 *   The `_id: false` option on each sub-schema is important: by
 *   default, Mongoose adds an auto-generated `_id` to every sub-
 *   document, which is wasteful here (nothing ever references a
 *   section by id) and adds an `_id` field to the JSON output
 *   that the shared `Report` interface does not declare.
 *
 * Why the whole report is stored, not a reference to a file:
 *
 *   The desktop's Python validators can also write a JSON file
 *   to disk (the `reports/` folder in the topic directory), but
 *   that file is a local cache — the authoritative copy of the
 *   report is this MongoDB record. Storing the numbers in the
 *   database means:
 *
 *   (a) The user can switch machines and still see their
 *       validation history, provided they log in to the same
 *       backend.
 *   (b) The Reports dashboard can list every report across every
 *       topic without touching the filesystem.
 *   (c) A future server-side feature (a fleet-wide dashboard, a
 *       usage analytics job) can query the numbers directly.
 *
 *   The file on disk is a convenience for the desktop's local
 *   history view; the database is the source of truth.
 *
 * What this model does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not enforce that `articleId` or `topicId` reference
 *     existing records. Cross-collection referential integrity is
 *     the service layer's concern — the report service verifies
 *     the parent Article's ownership before persisting, exactly
 *     as the article service verifies its parent Topic.
 *
 *   - It does not enforce that `overallStatus` is consistent with
 *     the six section statuses. The rule for computing
 *     `overallStatus` (the weakest of the six) is a service-level
 *     policy — it might change, and it depends on per-user
 *     configuration (a user who disables the AI-marker check
 *     should not have that check's status drag down their overall
 *     score). The schema only stores what it is given.
 *
 *   - It does not version reports the way Articles are versioned.
 *     A new report is simply a new document with a later
 *     `createdAt`; the "current" report for an article is the one
 *     with the highest `createdAt` for that article. This is the
 *     right model for validation output — unlike an article,
 *     which is a user-facing artifact that the user may want to
 *     diff across versions, a report is a point-in-time snapshot
 *     and the only comparison the user cares about is "did the
 *     score improve since the last run".
 */

import mongoose, { Schema, Document as MongooseDocument } from 'mongoose';
import { Report, ReportStatus } from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Document interface
// ============================================================

/**
 * The runtime shape of a Report document as returned by Mongoose.
 *
 * Extends `Omit<Report, '_id'>` (the shared domain interface
 * minus its loosely-typed `_id`) and `MongooseDocument` (the
 * Mongoose base class), then re-declares `_id` with the concrete
 * ObjectId type Mongoose actually produces in-process. Same
 * pattern as `UserDocument`, `TopicDocument`, `DocumentDocument`,
 * and `ArticleDocument`.
 *
 * No instance methods are declared. A Report has no per-record
 * behaviour beyond what Mongoose provides out of the box (save,
 * validate, toJSON). Business logic — computing `overallStatus`
 * from the section statuses, applying per-user thresholds —
 * lives in the service.
 */
export interface ReportDocument
  extends Omit<Report, '_id'>,
    MongooseDocument {
  _id: mongoose.Types.ObjectId;
}

// ============================================================
//  Legal values (runtime counterparts of the union types)
// ============================================================

/**
 * The closed set of legal values for any status field — the
 * section-level `status` on each of the six sections, and the
 * top-level `overallStatus`.
 *
 * `ReportStatus` in `shared/types/index.ts` is a string-literal
 * union type — it does not exist at runtime, so Mongoose cannot
 * use it directly as an `enum` option. This array is the runtime
 * source of truth, and its type annotation (`readonly ReportStatus[]`)
 * guarantees at compile time that every string in the array is a
 * legal member of the union.
 *
 * The same array is reused for every status field on every
 * sub-schema, so there is exactly one place to change if the set
 * of legal statuses ever expands.
 */
const REPORT_STATUS_VALUES: readonly ReportStatus[] = [
  'good',
  'warning',
  'fail',
];

/**
 * The closed set of legal values for a keyword's priority.
 *
 * `KeywordReportEntry.priority` in `shared/types` is the union
 * `'primary' | 'secondary' | 'supporting'`. That union is not
 * exported as a named type from `shared/types`; this array is
 * declared locally, annotated with the equivalent inline union so
 * the compiler can verify that every string is a legal member.
 *
 * The priorities are used by the UI to sort keyword rows and by
 * a future scoring adjustment that weights primary keywords more
 * heavily than supporting ones. For now the schema only enforces
 * that the value is one of the three.
 */
const KEYWORD_PRIORITY_VALUES: readonly [
  'primary',
  'secondary',
  'supporting',
] = ['primary', 'secondary', 'supporting'];

// ============================================================
//  Sub-schemas
// ============================================================
//
//  Each of the six sections is a separate Schema, declared with
//  `{ _id: false }` so Mongoose does not auto-generate an `_id`
//  on every embedded sub-document. The schemas are declared as
//  standalone constants and embedded by reference below — this
//  keeps the top-level schema readable (each section is one line
//  in the top-level definition) and lets each sub-schema carry
//  its own validation rules in one place.

// ---- Readability ----

const ReadabilityReportSchema = new Schema(
  {
    fleschReadingEase: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      // 0–100 in theory; textstat can report slightly above 100
      // for very short texts composed almost entirely of one-
      // syllable words, so the upper bound is generous rather
      // than exactly 100. A negative score is possible for very
      // dense academic prose.
      min: [-100, 'fleschReadingEase must be at least -100.'],
      max: [200, 'fleschReadingEase must be at most 200.'],
    },
    fleschKincaidGrade: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [-10, 'fleschKincaidGrade must be at least -10.'],
      max: [30, 'fleschKincaidGrade must be at most 30.'],
    },
    gunningFog: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'gunningFog must be non-negative.'],
      max: [30, 'gunningFog must be at most 30.'],
    },
    smogIndex: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'smogIndex must be non-negative.'],
      max: [30, 'smogIndex must be at most 30.'],
    },
    avgSentenceLength: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'avgSentenceLength must be non-negative.'],
      max: [200, 'avgSentenceLength must be at most 200.'],
    },
    readingTimeSeconds: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'readingTimeSeconds must be non-negative.'],
      validate: {
        // Reading time is a count of whole seconds. A float
        // would indicate the Python validator returned a raw
        // division without rounding, which is a pipeline bug
        // worth catching at the schema boundary.
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'readingTimeSeconds must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    status: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: REPORT_STATUS_VALUES,
        message: 'status must be one of: good, warning, fail.',
      },
      required: true,
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

// ---- SEO ----

const SeoReportSchema = new Schema(
  {
    wordCount: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'wordCount must be non-negative.'],
      max: [1000000, 'wordCount must be at most 1000000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'wordCount must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    h2Count: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'h2Count must be non-negative.'],
      max: [1000, 'h2Count must be at most 1000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'h2Count must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    h3Count: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'h3Count must be non-negative.'],
      max: [1000, 'h3Count must be at most 1000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'h3Count must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    avgParagraphWords: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'avgParagraphWords must be non-negative.'],
      max: [10000, 'avgParagraphWords must be at most 10000.'],
    },
    passiveVoicePercent: {
      // Stored as a fraction (0–1), matching the shared type's
      // documented units. The Python validator is responsible for
      // normalizing to this scale; the schema just checks the
      // bounds.
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'passiveVoicePercent must be between 0 and 1.'],
      max: [1, 'passiveVoicePercent must be between 0 and 1.'],
    },
    transitionWordsPercent: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'transitionWordsPercent must be between 0 and 1.'],
      max: [1, 'transitionWordsPercent must be between 0 and 1.'],
    },
    status: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: REPORT_STATUS_VALUES,
        message: 'status must be one of: good, warning, fail.',
      },
      required: true,
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

// ---- Keywords ----

const KeywordReportEntrySchema = new Schema(
  {
    keyword: {
      type: String,
      required: true,
      trim: true,
      minlength: [1, 'keyword must not be empty.'],
      maxlength: [200, 'keyword must be at most 200 characters.'],
    },
    priority: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: KEYWORD_PRIORITY_VALUES,
        message:
          'priority must be one of: primary, secondary, supporting.',
      },
      required: true,
    },
    count: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'count must be non-negative.'],
      max: [100000, 'count must be at most 100000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'count must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    density: {
      // Fraction of word count (0–1). A density of 0.02 means
      // the keyword accounts for 2% of the article's words.
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'density must be between 0 and 1.'],
      max: [1, 'density must be between 0 and 1.'],
    },
    inTitle: {
      type: Boolean,
      required: true,
    },
    inIntro: {
      type: Boolean,
      required: true,
    },
    inH2Count: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'inH2Count must be non-negative.'],
      max: [1000, 'inH2Count must be at most 1000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'inH2Count must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    status: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: REPORT_STATUS_VALUES,
        message: 'status must be one of: good, warning, fail.',
      },
      required: true,
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

const KeywordReportSchema = new Schema(
  {
    keywords: {
      type: [KeywordReportEntrySchema],
      default: [],
    },
    status: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: REPORT_STATUS_VALUES,
        message: 'status must be one of: good, warning, fail.',
      },
      required: true,
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

// ---- Originality ----

const FlaggedSentenceSchema = new Schema(
  {
    text: {
      type: String,
      required: true,
      trim: true,
      minlength: [1, 'text must not be empty.'],
      // 5000 characters is generous for a single sentence — the
      // longest legitimate sentence in normal prose is a few
      // hundred characters. The bound exists to reject a
      // malformed entry that accidentally contains a whole
      // paragraph.
      maxlength: [5000, 'text must be at most 5000 characters.'],
    },
    similarity: {
      // 0–1 cosine similarity. Values above the user's configured
      // threshold are what caused this sentence to be flagged.
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'similarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
      max: [1, 'similarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
    },
    sourceTitle: {
      type: String,
      required: true,
      trim: true,
      minlength: [1, 'sourceTitle must not be empty.'],
      maxlength: [500, 'sourceTitle must be at most 500 characters.'],
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

const OriginalityReportSchema = new Schema(
  {
    maxTfidfSimilarity: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'maxTfidfSimilarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
      max: [1, 'maxTfidfSimilarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
    },
    maxSemanticSimilarity: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'maxSemanticSimilarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
      max: [1, 'maxSemanticSimilarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
    },
    flaggedSentences: {
      type: [FlaggedSentenceSchema],
      default: [],
    },
    status: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: REPORT_STATUS_VALUES,
        message: 'status must be one of: good, warning, fail.',
      },
      required: true,
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

// ---- AI markers ----

const AiMarkerEntrySchema = new Schema(
  {
    phrase: {
      type: String,
      required: true,
      trim: true,
      minlength: [1, 'phrase must not be empty.'],
      maxlength: [200, 'phrase must be at most 200 characters.'],
    },
    count: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'count must be non-negative.'],
      max: [100000, 'count must be at most 100000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'count must be an integer.',
      },
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

const AiMarkersReportSchema = new Schema(
  {
    markerCount: {
      // The total number of AI-tell phrases found across the
      // whole article — not the number of distinct phrases.
      // A phrase that appears four times contributes 4 to this
      // count and appears once in the `markers` array with
      // `count: 4`.
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'markerCount must be non-negative.'],
      max: [100000, 'markerCount must be at most 100000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'markerCount must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    markers: {
      type: [AiMarkerEntrySchema],
      default: [],
    },
    status: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: REPORT_STATUS_VALUES,
        message: 'status must be one of: good, warning, fail.',
      },
      required: true,
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

// ---- Grammar ----

const GrammarIssueSchema = new Schema(
  {
    ruleId: {
      // LanguageTool's rule identifier, e.g. 'EN_QUOTES',
      // 'UPPERCASE_SENTENCE_START'. Opaque to the backend —
      // stored and returned verbatim.
      type: String,
      required: true,
      trim: true,
      minlength: [1, 'ruleId must not be empty.'],
      maxlength: [200, 'ruleId must be at most 200 characters.'],
    },
    message: {
      type: String,
      required: true,
      trim: true,
      minlength: [1, 'message must not be empty.'],
      maxlength: [2000, 'message must be at most 2000 characters.'],
    },
    offset: {
      // Character position in the article body where the issue
      // starts. Non-negative; the article can be up to a million
      // characters, so the upper bound matches.
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'offset must be non-negative.'],
      max: [1000000, 'offset must be at most 1000000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'offset must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    length: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'length must be non-negative.'],
      max: [1000000, 'length must be at most 1000000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'length must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    replacements: {
      type: [String],
      default: [],
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

const GrammarReportSchema = new Schema(
  {
    issueCount: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'issueCount must be non-negative.'],
      max: [100000, 'issueCount must be at most 100000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'issueCount must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    issues: {
      type: [GrammarIssueSchema],
      default: [],
    },
    status: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: REPORT_STATUS_VALUES,
        message: 'status must be one of: good, warning, fail.',
      },
      required: true,
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

// ============================================================
//  Top-level schema
// ============================================================

const ReportSchema = new Schema<ReportDocument>(
  {
    // ---- Ownership ----
    // Every report belongs to exactly one user via the article
    // and topic it is attached to. Denormalising `userId` onto
    // the report follows the same pattern as the Document and
    // Article models: it lets the indexes key on `userId`
    // directly and means every authorization check queries one
    // collection instead of three.
    userId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      required: [true, 'userId is required'],
    },

    // ---- Parent references ----
    // Both the immediate parent (articleId) and the grandparent
    // (topicId) are stored, denormalised, so that the two list
    // queries the reports feature exposes — "reports for this
    // article" and "reports for this topic" — are each a single
    // indexed query on this collection, with no join through
    // the Article collection for the topic-scoped case.
    articleId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      required: [true, 'articleId is required'],
    },
    topicId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      required: [true, 'topicId is required'],
    },

    // ---- Six sections ----
    // Each section is an embedded sub-document. The subschema
    // constants declared above carry the field-level validation;
    // the entries here only wire the sub-schemas in by reference.
    readability: {
      type: ReadabilityReportSchema,
      required: true,
    },
    seo: {
      type: SeoReportSchema,
      required: true,
    },
    keywords: {
      type: KeywordReportSchema,
      required: true,
    },
    originality: {
      type: OriginalityReportSchema,
      required: true,
    },
    aiMarkers: {
      type: AiMarkersReportSchema,
      required: true,
    },
    grammar: {
      type: GrammarReportSchema,
      required: true,
    },

    // ---- Aggregate status ----
    // The weakest of the six section statuses, computed by the
    // service. The schema enforces that the value is a member of
    // the closed set; it does NOT recompute or verify the value
    // against the section statuses — see the file header for why
    // that rule belongs in the service.
    overallStatus: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: REPORT_STATUS_VALUES,
        message:
          'overallStatus must be one of: good, warning, fail.',
      },
      required: true,
    },
  },
  {
    timestamps: true,
    toJSON: {
      transform: (_doc, ret) => {
        // `__v` is Mongoose's internal version field. It is
        // added to every saved document automatically and is
        // not part of the shared `Report` interface, so it must
        // not appear in the JSON response.
        //
        // The cast to `Record<string, unknown>` is required
        // because TypeScript's `delete` operator refuses to
        // operate on non-optional properties (TS2790). The same
        // fix is applied in `Topic.ts`, `Document.ts`, and
        // `Article.ts`.
        delete (ret as Record<string, unknown>)['__v'];
        return ret;
      },
    },
  }
);

// ============================================================
//  Indexes
// ============================================================
//
//  Two compound indexes cover the read paths the reports feature
//  exercises. Both are prefixed by `userId` for the same reason
//  as every other model's indexes.
//
//    { userId: 1, articleId: 1, createdAt: -1 }
//      Serves "list every report for this article, newest
//      first". An article can accumulate multiple reports — one
//      per validation run — and the newest is the "current"
//      report. The compound shape lets MongoDB satisfy the
//      filter (userId + articleId) and the sort (createdAt
//      descending) from the index alone.
//
//    { userId: 1, topicId: 1, createdAt: -1 }
//      Serves "list every report for this topic, newest first",
//      which the topic-detail view uses to build a validation
//      history without going through the intermediate Article
//      collection. Same reasoning: filter and sort covered by
//      the index in one pass.
//
//  A third index on `overallStatus` was considered and rejected:
//  no read path filters by status alone, and a status filter
//  would always be combined with one of the two ownership-scoped
//  filters above. If a future feature wants to query "all my
//  failed reports", the correct shape is a compound index
//  { userId, overallStatus, createdAt: -1 }, which can be added
//  without a migration.

ReportSchema.index({ userId: 1, articleId: 1, createdAt: -1 });
ReportSchema.index({ userId: 1, topicId: 1, createdAt: -1 });

// ============================================================
//  Model
// ============================================================

export const ReportModel = mongoose.model<ReportDocument>(
  'Report',
  ReportSchema
);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default ReportModel;
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/reports/routes/reportRoutes.ts">
/**
 * Route table for the WriteSpeare Report entity.
 *
 * Declares the eight report endpoints and the middleware chain
 * that runs in front of each. The router is mounted at
 * `/api/reports` by the app factory (`src/app.ts`), so the paths
 * declared below are relative to that prefix:
 *
 *   POST   /api/reports                            → create a validation report
 *   GET    /api/reports                            → list the user's reports
 *   GET    /api/reports/article/:articleId/latest  → latest report for an article
 *   GET    /api/reports/topic/:topicId/latest      → latest report for a topic
 *   DELETE /api/reports/article/:articleId         → bulk-delete by article
 *   DELETE /api/reports/topic/:topicId             → bulk-delete by topic
 *   GET    /api/reports/:id                        → read a single report
 *   DELETE /api/reports/:id                        → delete a single report
 *
 * Every route is protected by `authenticate`. Reports are user-
 * scoped by design — the model's two compound indexes both carry
 * `userId` as their prefix, every service operation filters on
 * `userId`, and every controller handler derives the ownership
 * value from `req.user.userId` rather than from the request. A
 * public report surface does not exist.
 *
 * Middleware order:
 *
 *   `authenticate` runs first and is applied via `asyncHandler`
 *   because the function is async (it awaits a user lookup to
 *   confirm the account still exists and is active). The wrapper
 *   is required — without it, a rejection inside the middleware
 *   would reach the terminal error handler as an unhandled
 *   promise rejection on runtimes that do not forward the
 *   rejection automatically. The existing `authRoutes.ts`,
 *   `topicRoutes.ts`, `documentRoutes.ts`, and `articleRoutes.ts`
 *   files use the same wrapping pattern for the same reason, and
 *   all five must stay in step.
 *
 *   The controller runs second, also wrapped in `asyncHandler`,
 *   for the same reason: the service behind it can throw an
 *   `AppError` (404 for a report or parent article that does not
 *   exist or belongs to another user; 400 for a schema-level
 *   validation failure such as a status value outside the closed
 *   set or a similarity score outside [0, 1]), and the wrapper is
 *   what converts that throw into a well-formed response via the
 *   terminal error middleware.
 *
 * Route ordering — multi-segment paths before single-`:id` paths:
 *
 *   Six of the eight routes in this file are multi-segment, or
 *   have a literal segment in addition to a parameter:
 *
 *     GET    /article/:articleId/latest   (three segments)
 *     GET    /topic/:topicId/latest       (three segments)
 *     DELETE /article/:articleId          (two segments)
 *     DELETE /topic/:topicId              (two segments)
 *
 *   The remaining four are the collection routes and the single-
 *   resource routes:
 *
 *     POST   /
 *     GET    /
 *     GET    /:id                          (one segment)
 *     DELETE /:id                          (one segment)
 *
 *   Express matches routes segment-by-segment, so a request can
 *   never match two routes with different segment counts. The
 *   four multi-segment routes CANNOT collide with the two single-
 *   `:id` routes regardless of declaration order.
 *
 *   The multi-segment routes are nevertheless declared BEFORE the
 *   single-`:id` routes as defensive habit. The rule of thumb
 *   across all route files in this codebase: declare more
 *   specific paths before more general ones. Today no collision
 *   exists; tomorrow, if a literal sub-path like `/recent` is
 *   ever added under the collection route, the ordering will
 *   already be correct.
 *
 *   Within the multi-segment group, the four routes are grouped
 *   by their segment name — `article/...` first, then
 *   `topic/...` — which mirrors the naming convention across
 *   the codebase (article-scoped before topic-scoped, because
 *   the article is the direct parent of a report and the topic
 *   is the grandparent). The grouping is for readability; the
 *   router does not care about the order within a group.
 *
 * The routes are declared as a flat sequence of `router.METHOD`
 * calls rather than as a route table or a declarative
 * configuration. This matches the convention established in
 * `authRoutes.ts`, `topicRoutes.ts`, `documentRoutes.ts`, and
 * `articleRoutes.ts` and in every route file the plan will
 * produce. A reader can scan the file top to bottom and see
 * exactly which middleware runs on which route without holding
 * any additional context.
 *
 * No try/catch appears anywhere in this file. That is deliberate
 * — the asyncHandler wrappers, combined with the terminal error
 * middleware registered in `app.ts`, form the single error-
 * handling contract for every route in the application.
 */

import { Router } from 'express';

import {
  createReport,
  listReports,
  getReportById,
  getLatestReportByArticle,
  getLatestReportByTopic,
  deleteReport,
  deleteReportsByArticle,
  deleteReportsByTopic,
} from '../controllers/reportController.js';

import { authenticate } from '../../auth/middleware/authGuard.js';
import { asyncHandler } from '../../shared/middleware/errorHandler.js';

// ============================================================
//  Router instance
// ============================================================

const reportRoutes = Router();

// ============================================================
//  POST /api/reports
// ============================================================
//
//  Persist a validation report attached to an article owned by
//  the authenticated user. The service derives the report's
//  `topicId` from the parent article and computes the
//  `overallStatus` from the six section statuses — neither is
//  accepted from the client. See the controller header for the
//  full rationale.

reportRoutes.post(
  '/',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(createReport)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/reports
// ============================================================
//
//  List the authenticated user's reports, sorted newest first.
//  Optional `?articleId=` and `?topicId=` query parameters
//  narrow the result. The controller validates each filter's
//  shape before delegating; the service returns an empty array
//  (not a 404) when a filter matches no records the caller
//  owns.

reportRoutes.get(
  '/',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(listReports)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/reports/article/:articleId/latest
// ============================================================
//
//  Return the newest report for a specific article. This is a
//  dedicated query rather than a filter on the list endpoint
//  because the article view issues it on every render, and the
//  dedicated route lets the service answer it with a single
//  indexed findOne. A 404 is returned when the article has no
//  reports, when the article does not exist, or when the
//  article belongs to a different user — all three collapse to
//  the same response for enumeration-safety reasons documented
//  in the controller.

reportRoutes.get(
  '/article/:articleId/latest',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(getLatestReportByArticle)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/reports/topic/:topicId/latest
// ============================================================
//
//  Return the newest report for a topic — the most recently
//  produced report across all the topic's articles. Same
//  reasoning as the article-scoped latest route above: a
//  dedicated indexed query, a single-object response, and a
//  404 that merges the three missing cases.

reportRoutes.get(
  '/topic/:topicId/latest',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(getLatestReportByTopic)
);

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/reports/article/:articleId
// ============================================================
//
//  Bulk-delete every report attached to an article, scoped to
//  the authenticated user. The filter is scoped to
//  `{ userId, articleId }` in the service, so a caller who does
//  not own the article matches zero records and cannot clear
//  another user's reports by guessing the article id. This
//  route is the entry point for a future cascade from article
//  deletion.

reportRoutes.delete(
  '/article/:articleId',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(deleteReportsByArticle)
);

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/reports/topic/:topicId
// ============================================================
//
//  Bulk-delete every report attached to a topic, scoped to the
//  authenticated user. Scoped to `{ userId, topicId }` in the
//  service, same reasoning as the article-scoped bulk delete
//  above. This route is the entry point for a future cascade
//  from topic deletion.

reportRoutes.delete(
  '/topic/:topicId',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(deleteReportsByTopic)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/reports/:id
// ============================================================
//
//  Return a single report by ID, scoped to the authenticated
//  user. The service merges the "not found" and "not owned"
//  cases and returns null for both; the controller converts
//  that null into a 404 without distinguishing the two — see
//  the controller header for the information-leak rationale.

reportRoutes.get(
  '/:id',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(getReportById)
);

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/reports/:id
// ============================================================
//
//  Delete a single report, scoped to the authenticated user.
//  The service returns the deleted document so the client can
//  render an undo affordance without a second round trip.
//  Reports have no children — removing a report is a leaf
//  operation with no cascade to consider.

reportRoutes.delete(
  '/:id',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(deleteReport)
);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default reportRoutes;
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/reports/services/reportService.ts">
/**
 * Business logic for the WriteSpeare Report entity.
 *
 * A Report is the six-section validation output produced against
 * one Article. Every section maps one-for-one to a Python
 * validator in `apps/desktop/src/resources/scripts/validation/`:
 * readability, seo, keywords, originality, aiMarkers, grammar.
 * An Article can accumulate multiple Reports — one per validation
 * run, produced against successive versions or against a single
 * version re-checked after the user edits content — and the
 * newest report is the "current" one.
 *
 * The service exposes eight ownership-scoped operations:
 *
 *   createReport             — persist a validation report, with
 *                              the parent article's ownership
 *                              verified and the topicId and
 *                              overallStatus derived
 *   listReports              — read the user's reports, filtered
 *                              by article and/or topic
 *   getReportById            — read a single report
 *   getLatestReportByArticle — read the newest report for an article
 *   getLatestReportByTopic   — read the newest report for a topic
 *   deleteReport             — remove a single report
 *   deleteReportsByArticle   — bulk-remove by parent article
 *   deleteReportsByTopic     — bulk-remove by parent topic
 *
 * Every function takes a `userId` argument that the caller (the
 * controller) derives from `req.user.userId`. That value is never
 * read from the request body, query, or route params — the client
 * cannot choose whose reports they are reading or writing. This
 * is the same ownership contract used by `topicService.ts`,
 * `documentService.ts`, and `articleService.ts`.
 *
 * Cross-feature import — ArticleModel:
 *
 *   This service imports `ArticleModel` from the articles feature
 *   to verify, on the create path, that the parent article exists
 *   and is owned by the caller before persisting the report. The
 *   import direction (child → parent) mirrors the same decision
 *   made in `documentService.ts` (child → topic) and
 *   `articleService.ts` (child → topic). Every ownership-scoped
 *   write in this backend validates its immediate parent's
 *   ownership in the same query that checks the parent's
 *   existence.
 *
 * Why the topicId is derived, not accepted from the client:
 *
 *   The Report schema stores both `articleId` (immediate parent)
 *   and `topicId` (grandparent) denormalized, so that the two
 *   list views — "reports for this article" and "reports for
 *   this topic" — are each a single indexed query with no join.
 *   Storing both is a performance choice; the invariant is that
 *   they must be consistent. If the client supplied a `topicId`
 *   directly, a malicious or buggy caller could post a report
 *   with an `articleId` that belongs to them and a `topicId`
 *   that belongs to someone else, and the denormalized pair
 *   would be internally inconsistent — every report-for-topic
 *   query would then be at risk of leaking article content
 *   across users.
 *
 *   The fix is to never trust a client-supplied `topicId`. The
 *   service looks up the parent article by `(articleId, userId)`,
 *   reads the article's own `topicId` field, and writes THAT
 *   value into the report. The report's `topicId` is therefore
 *   always equal to its parent article's `topicId` by
 *   construction, and the denormalization invariant cannot be
 *   violated from the client side.
 *
 * Why the overallStatus is computed, not accepted from the client:
 *
 *   The `overallStatus` is the weakest of the six section
 *   statuses — a `fail` in any section makes the whole report
 *   `fail`, otherwise a `warning` in any section makes it
 *   `warning`, otherwise it is `good`. This rule is a policy
 *   decision: it is currently fixed, but the plan's settings
 *   model anticipates per-user thresholds and per-user check
 *   enablement, so the rule could change (a user who disables
 *   the AI-marker check should not have that check's status
 *   drag down their overall score). Because it is a policy, it
 *   belongs in the service, and the client should never supply
 *   it — accepting it would create a second source of truth for
 *   a value that the server is supposed to be the authority on.
 *
 *   The schema only enforces that whatever the service writes is
 *   a member of the closed status set.
 *
 * Immutability:
 *
 *   There is no `updateReport` function. A Report represents the
 *   validation output produced by a specific run of the Python
 *   validators against a specific snapshot of an article. If the
 *   user edits the article or regenerates it, the correct
 *   operation is to run validation again — which produces a new
 *   report via `createReport`. The only in-place mutation of a
 *   report is deletion.
 *
 *   This mirrors the immutability rule on Article content: the
 *   version history of everything the pipeline produces is a
 *   clean append-only log, and no downstream consumer ever has
 *   to reason about whether a report has been edited since it
 *   was produced.
 *
 * Cascade semantics:
 *
 *   `deleteReportsByArticle` and `deleteReportsByTopic` exist so
 *   that future cascade paths from article deletion or topic
 *   deletion have well-defined entry points. The current article
 *   and topic services do NOT call them — cascade is a decision
 *   for each owning feature, and the reports feature is the one
 *   that owns the decision of whether to cascade from its
 *   parents. Both functions are scoped to `{ userId, ... }`, so
 *   a caller who does not own the parent matches zero records
 *   and cannot clear another user's reports by guessing an id.
 */

import { ReportModel, type ReportDocument } from '../models/Report.js';
import { ArticleModel } from '../../articles/models/Article.js';
import type {
  MongoId,
  Report,
  ReportStatus,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';
import { AppError } from '../../shared/middleware/errorHandler.js';

// ============================================================
//  Payload type
// ============================================================
//
// The shared types module does not yet declare a dedicated
// `ReportCreatePayload` interface (see the PLAN DELTA note in the
// execution response). Rather than import a symbol that does not
// exist, this file derives the payload type locally from the
// domain `Report` interface by omitting the fields the service
// owns:
//
//   _id           — assigned by MongoDB
//   userId        — derived from the authenticated session
//   topicId       — derived from the parent article (see the
//                   file header for why it is not trusted from
//                   the client)
//   createdAt     — assigned by Mongoose timestamps
//   overallStatus — computed by this service from the six
//                   section statuses (see the file header)
//
// The remaining fields — articleId and the six section objects —
// are exactly what the client is expected to submit. If a future
// session promotes this type into `shared/types/index.ts` as a
// first-class interface, the sole change required here is to
// swap the local alias for an import.
export type ReportCreatePayload = Omit<
  Report,
  '_id' | 'userId' | 'topicId' | 'createdAt' | 'overallStatus'
>;

// ============================================================
//  Internal helpers
// ============================================================

/**
 * Compute the overall status from the six section statuses.
 *
 * Rule: the weakest status wins. Any `fail` in any section makes
 * the report `fail`; otherwise any `warning` makes it `warning`;
 * otherwise the report is `good`.
 *
 * This function is deliberately private to the service — the
 * rule is a policy decision, not a schema-level invariant, and
 * hiding it behind this name (rather than inlining the ternary
 * chain at the call site) means a future change to the rule has
 * exactly one place to go.
 */
const computeOverallStatus = (
  sectionStatuses: readonly ReportStatus[]
): ReportStatus => {
  if (sectionStatuses.includes('fail')) {
    return 'fail';
  }
  if (sectionStatuses.includes('warning')) {
    return 'warning';
  }
  return 'good';
};

// ============================================================
//  createReport
// ============================================================

/**
 * Persist a validation report attached to an article owned by
 * the caller.
 *
 * Flow:
 *
 *   1. Look up the parent article by `(articleId, userId)`. The
 *      ownership check is part of the same query — an article
 *      that exists but belongs to a different user is treated
 *      as "not found", which keeps the service from leaking
 *      other users' article IDs through a 403.
 *
 *   2. If the article does not exist or is not owned by the
 *      caller, throw `AppError(404)`. The message refers to the
 *      article, not the report — the caller is trying to attach
 *      a report to an article they cannot see.
 *
 *   3. Derive the report's `topicId` from the article's own
 *      `topicId` field. This is what makes the denormalized
 *      ownership pair `(articleId, topicId)` internally
 *      consistent by construction — see the file header.
 *
 *   4. Compute `overallStatus` from the six section statuses on
 *      the payload. See the file header for why this is a
 *      service-level computation.
 *
 *   5. Persist the report with the caller's `userId`, the
 *      derived `topicId`, and the computed `overallStatus`. Every
 *      other field comes from the payload.
 *
 *   6. Return the saved document.
 *
 * The function does NOT catch validation errors from the schema.
 * A Mongoose ValidationError thrown here — a status value outside
 * the closed set, a similarity score outside [0, 1], a negative
 * word count — propagates to the terminal error middleware, which
 * maps it to a 400 with the schema's own message. The Python
 * validators are the source of truth for what the numbers mean;
 * the schema's job is only to check that the numbers are legal
 * values of their declared types, not to re-derive them.
 *
 * @param userId  - Ownership value, derived from the
 *                  authenticated session by the controller.
 * @param payload - The six validation sections plus the parent
 *                  articleId. `topicId`, `userId`, and
 *                  `overallStatus` are NOT part of this payload —
 *                  the first two are derived from the parent
 *                  article, and the third is computed here.
 */
export const createReport = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  payload: ReportCreatePayload
): Promise<ReportDocument> => {
  // ---- 1. Verify the parent article exists and is owned by the caller ----
  const parentArticle = await ArticleModel.findOne({
    _id: payload.articleId,
    userId,
  });

  if (!parentArticle) {
    throw new AppError('Article not found.', 404);
  }

  // ---- 2. Derive the topicId from the article ----
  // The article's topicId is the authoritative value. It is never
  // read from the client payload — see the file header for why.
  const topicId = parentArticle.topicId;

  // ---- 3. Compute the overall status ----
  const overallStatus = computeOverallStatus([
    payload.readability.status,
    payload.seo.status,
    payload.keywords.status,
    payload.originality.status,
    payload.aiMarkers.status,
    payload.grammar.status,
  ]);

  // ---- 4. Persist the report ----
  // The spread of `payload` is safe: it contains exactly the
  // seven fields the schema expects from the caller-supplied
  // portion (articleId and the six sections), and no `userId`,
  // `topicId`, or `overallStatus` field is present on the payload
  // type. All three are added explicitly here from values this
  // function controls.
  const doc = new ReportModel({
    ...payload,
    userId,
    topicId,
    overallStatus,
  });

  return await doc.save();
};

// ============================================================
//  listReports
// ============================================================

/**
 * List the authenticated user's reports, optionally filtered by
 * articleId and/or topicId. Sorted newest first.
 *
 * The filter object has two optional fields:
 *
 *   - `articleId` — narrows to the reports attached to one
 *     article. Covered by the compound index
 *     `{ userId, articleId, createdAt: -1 }`.
 *
 *   - `topicId` — narrows to the reports attached to one topic
 *     (across all the topic's articles). Covered by the compound
 *     index `{ userId, topicId, createdAt: -1 }`.
 *
 *   When both are provided, MongoDB intersects the two filters —
 *   reports for one article are a subset of reports for one
 *   topic, so the intersection is well-defined. When neither is
 *   provided, the query returns every report owned by the user.
 *   That last case is not covered by a purpose-built index (see
 *   the PLAN DELTA note in the execution response); it is a
 *   legitimate operation whose performance profile is acceptable
 *   at the current collection size.
 *
 * A filter whose value does not correspond to any records the
 * caller owns produces an empty array, not a 404. See
 * `documentService.ts` and `articleService.ts` for the same
 * enumeration rationale — the list endpoint is a read-only
 * projection and does not confirm the existence or ownership of
 * the filter's target.
 *
 * @param userId - Ownership value.
 * @param filter - Optional `articleId` and/or `topicId` filter.
 */
export const listReports = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  filter: { articleId?: MongoId; topicId?: MongoId } = {}
): Promise<ReportDocument[]> => {
  const query: {
    userId: MongoId;
    articleId?: MongoId;
    topicId?: MongoId;
  } = { userId };

  if (filter.articleId !== undefined) {
    query.articleId = filter.articleId;
  }
  if (filter.topicId !== undefined) {
    query.topicId = filter.topicId;
  }

  return await ReportModel.find(query).sort({ createdAt: -1 });
};

// ============================================================
//  getReportById
// ============================================================

/**
 * Read a single report by id, scoped to the caller.
 *
 * Returns `null` when the report does not exist, OR when it
 * exists but belongs to a different user. The two cases are
 * intentionally indistinguishable — see `documentService.ts` for
 * the same enumeration rationale (which applies identically
 * here).
 *
 * A malformed id string — one that is not a valid ObjectId —
 * does NOT return null; it causes Mongoose to throw a CastError,
 * which the terminal middleware maps to a 400.
 *
 * @param userId   - Ownership value.
 * @param reportId - The report's id, as a string from the route
 *                   parameter.
 */
export const getReportById = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  reportId: string
): Promise<ReportDocument | null> => {
  return await ReportModel.findOne({ _id: reportId, userId });
};

// ============================================================
//  getLatestReportByArticle
// ============================================================

/**
 * Read the newest report for an article, scoped to the caller.
 *
 * Returns `null` when the article has no reports yet, OR when
 * the article does not exist, OR when the article belongs to a
 * different user. The three cases collapse to the same null —
 * the caller (the article view, the corrective regeneration
 * loop) either has a report to work with or it does not.
 *
 * The query is covered by the compound index
 * `{ userId, articleId, createdAt: -1 }` — the filter matches on
 * the leftmost two fields, and the sort key is the trailing
 * field. The `.limit(1)` form is not used because Mongoose's
 * `findOne` already implies a limit of one; a further `.limit(1)`
 * would be redundant.
 *
 * @param userId    - Ownership value.
 * @param articleId - The parent article whose newest report is
 *                    being fetched.
 */
export const getLatestReportByArticle = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  articleId: MongoId
): Promise<ReportDocument | null> => {
  return await ReportModel.findOne({ userId, articleId }).sort({
    createdAt: -1,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  getLatestReportByTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Read the newest report for a topic, scoped to the caller.
 *
 * "Newest for the topic" means the most recently produced report
 * across all the topic's articles — the topic-detail view uses
 * this to show the current validation state without needing to
 * know which article is current.
 *
 * Returns `null` under the same three collapsing conditions as
 * `getLatestReportByArticle`: no reports yet, no such topic, or
 * the topic is not owned by the caller.
 *
 * Covered by the compound index `{ userId, topicId, createdAt: -1 }`.
 *
 * @param userId  - Ownership value.
 * @param topicId - The parent topic whose newest report is being
 *                  fetched.
 */
export const getLatestReportByTopic = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  topicId: MongoId
): Promise<ReportDocument | null> => {
  return await ReportModel.findOne({ userId, topicId }).sort({
    createdAt: -1,
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  deleteReport
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete a single report by id, scoped to the caller.
 *
 * Returns the deleted document so the caller can log or display
 * what was removed. Reports have no children, so there is no
 * cascade to consider.
 *
 * Throws `AppError(404)` when the report does not exist or is
 * not owned by the caller. Same merged case as the read paths.
 *
 * @param userId   - Ownership value.
 * @param reportId - The report's id.
 */
export const deleteReport = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  reportId: string
): Promise<ReportDocument> => {
  const deleted = await ReportModel.findOneAndDelete({
    _id: reportId,
    userId,
  });

  if (!deleted) {
    throw new AppError('Report not found.', 404);
  }

  return deleted;
};

// ============================================================
//  deleteReportsByArticle
// ============================================================

/**
 * Bulk-delete every report attached to the given article, scoped
 * to the caller.
 *
 * Returns the number of reports removed. A count of zero is a
 * legitimate, non-error result: it means either the article has
 * no reports, or the article does not exist, or the article
 * belongs to a different user — the caller does not need to
 * distinguish those cases.
 *
 * The filter is scoped to `{ userId, articleId }`, not just
 * `articleId`. A caller who does not own the article matches
 * zero records on the `userId` clause and therefore cannot clear
 * another user's reports by guessing an article id.
 *
 * @param userId    - Ownership value.
 * @param articleId - The parent article whose reports are being
 *                    removed.
 */
export const deleteReportsByArticle = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  articleId: MongoId
): Promise<number> => {
  const result = await ReportModel.deleteMany({ userId, articleId });
  return result.deletedCount;
};

// ============================================================
//  deleteReportsByTopic
// ============================================================

/**
 * Bulk-delete every report attached to the given topic, scoped
 * to the caller.
 *
 * "Attached to the topic" means every report whose denormalized
 * `topicId` field matches — including reports for articles that
 * are themselves about to be deleted, or that have already been
 * deleted. This is intentional: the denormalized `topicId` makes
 * the topic-scoped delete a single indexed operation with no
 * join through the article collection.
 *
 * Returns the number of reports removed. A count of zero is a
 * legitimate result, same collapsing cases as
 * `deleteReportsByArticle`.
 *
 * The filter is scoped to `{ userId, topicId }`. A caller who
 * does not own the topic matches zero records on the `userId`
 * clause.
 *
 * @param userId  - Ownership value.
 * @param topicId - The parent topic whose reports are being
 *                  removed.
 */
export const deleteReportsByTopic = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  topicId: MongoId
): Promise<number> => {
  const result = await ReportModel.deleteMany({ userId, topicId });
  return result.deletedCount;
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  createReport,
  listReports,
  getReportById,
  getLatestReportByArticle,
  getLatestReportByTopic,
  deleteReport,
  deleteReportsByArticle,
  deleteReportsByTopic,
};

<file path="apps/server/src/features/reports/index.ts">
/**
 * Public export surface for the WriteSpeare reports feature.
 *
 * The plan declares this file with a single responsibility:
 * "Public exports." That is the entire specification, and this
 * file fills it in with the minimal, non-redundant surface that
 * the rest of the codebase can meaningfully consume — following
 * the exact shape established by the topics feature's index at
 * `features/topics/index.ts`, the documents feature's index at
 * `features/documents/index.ts`, and the articles feature's
 * index at `features/articles/index.ts`.
 *
 * What belongs here — and what does not:
 *
 *   The reports feature contains five kinds of source files:
 *
 *     models/Report.ts            — the Mongoose schema and its
 *                                   document interface
 *     services/reportService.ts
 *                                 — the business-logic layer
 *     controllers/reportController.ts
 *                                 — the HTTP handlers
 *     routes/reportRoutes.ts      — the Express router
 *     index.ts                    — this file
 *
 *   Of those five, only TWO are useful to a consumer OUTSIDE the
 *   feature:
 *
 *     (a) The router. `app.ts` mounts it under `/api/reports`.
 *         That is the one import the feature's external boundary
 *         actually needs — the controller and service are
 *         internal implementation details between the router and
 *         the model, and nothing outside the feature should
 *         reach past the router for request-handling behavior.
 *
 *     (b) The model. A Report references its parent Article by
 *         `articleId`, and no feature BELOW reports references
 *         a report — reports are currently the leaf of the
 *         Topic → Document → Article → Report chain. So no
 *         consumer in the codebase imports `ReportModel` today.
 *         The export exists for symmetry with the other feature
 *         indexes and for any future feature (a report-
 *         aggregation view, a cross-article comparison, an
 *         analytics roll-up) that would need to read reports
 *         from outside this feature's HTTP surface.
 *
 *   The service and controller are NOT re-exported. Both are
 *   internal: the service is only ever consumed by the
 *   controller within the same feature, and the controller is
 *   only ever consumed by the router within the same feature.
 *   Additionally, their function names collide — both export
 *   `createReport`, `listReports`, etc. — and re-exporting both
 *   with bare names would produce a duplicate-export error.
 *   The rule this file follows, matching the three previous
 *   features' indexes: export what is consumed, not everything
 *   that exists.
 *
 * Why the router is exported both as a named symbol AND as the
 * default:
 *
 *   The router file itself (`routes/reportRoutes.ts`) exports
 *   its router as the default. This index file preserves that
 *   shape for callers that prefer the default form — `import
 *   reportRoutes from '...features/reports'` — while also
 *   giving the named form — `import { reportRoutes } from
 *   '...features/reports'` — to callers that prefer named
 *   imports for uniformity with the rest of this file's exports.
 *
 *   The two forms resolve to the same router instance. There is
 *   no double-construction, no second Express `Router()`, and
 *   no chance of the router being registered twice by mistake.
 *
 * Note for readers who have been following the session:
 *
 *   The current `app.ts` imports its feature routers from their
 *   deep paths (`./features/reports/routes/reportRoutes.js`),
 *   not from the feature indexes. This index file does NOT
 *   change that pattern retroactively; it is a forward-looking
 *   surface that a future app-factory refactor can adopt. Until
 *   that refactor, this file's exports are dormant — nothing in
 *   the codebase currently imports from it.
 *
 *   That is fine, and it is what the plan's "Public exports"
 *   annotation calls for. The surface exists so that when a
 *   consumer DOES need it, there is a declared, documented place
 *   for that import to come from — rather than a deep path that
 *   was chosen ad hoc.
 */

// ============================================================
//  Router
// ============================================================
//
//  The router is the feature's public API surface — the one
//  import that the app factory needs in order to mount the
//  report endpoints. Both the default-export form and the
//  named-export form resolve to the same router instance (see
//  the file header for the reasoning).

export { default as reportRoutes } from './routes/reportRoutes.js';
export { default } from './routes/reportRoutes.js';

// ============================================================
//  Model
// ============================================================
//
//  The Mongoose model and its hydrated document interface.
//  Exported so that any future feature which ever needs to read
//  reports from outside the feature's HTTP surface has a
//  single, documented import path.
//
//  The `ReportDocument` type is re-exported with the `type`
//  modifier so the compiler can erase it at emit time; it has
//  no runtime representation.

export { ReportModel, type ReportDocument } from './models/Report.js';
