<file path="apps/server/src/features/settings/models/Preset.ts">
/**
 * Mongoose model for the WriteSpeare Preset entity.
 *
 * A Preset is a named bundle of pipeline settings that fully
 * describes how a topic's pipeline should run. The three system
 * presets — Quick, Balanced, Deep — ship with the app and are
 * identifiable by their `userId: null` field. A user who tunes
 * the settings for their own workflow can save the resulting
 * configuration as a preset with a custom name; that preset
 * carries the owning user's ObjectId.
 *
 * A preset is deliberately self-contained. Every field the
 * pipeline reads at run time is present on the preset document,
 * so loading a preset replaces the entire effective configuration
 * rather than merging with a global default. That guarantees the
 * same preset produces the same pipeline behaviour regardless of
 * what else the user has configured — a property that would be
 * lost if presets were sparse overrides on a shared base.
 *
 * Responsibilities:
 *
 *   1. Enforce the schema-level invariants of a preset record:
 *      a slug-form `name`, a non-empty `displayName`, sensible
 *      numeric ranges on every count and timeout field, and
 *      either an ObjectId or `null` for `userId` (nothing else).
 *
 *   2. Own the two indexes the preset feature's read paths
 *      exercise:
 *
 *        - A compound UNIQUE index on { userId, name } — which
 *          enforces two separate uniqueness rules with one index:
 *
 *          (a) No two system presets share a name. Since all
 *              system presets have `userId: null`, the tuple
 *              `(null, 'quick')` can exist at most once.
 *
 *          (b) No two presets belonging to the same user share a
 *              name. The tuple `(someObjectId, 'quick')` can
 *              exist at most once for that specific
 *              `someObjectId`.
 *
 *          A user preset named 'quick' is NOT in conflict with
 *          the system 'quick' preset, because their userIds
 *          differ. That is the intended behaviour: a user who
 *          wants to shadow a system preset with their own
 *          variant simply names it the same.
 *
 *        - A compound index on { userId, createdAt: -1 } — serves
 *          the "list my presets, newest first" query that the
 *          preset picker issues. The leftmost prefix { userId }
 *          also serves "list every system preset" (queried with
 *          `{ userId: null }`).
 *
 *   3. Provide a single `toJSON` transform that strips Mongoose's
 *      `__v` version field, so a serialised Preset matches the
 *      shared `Preset` interface exactly.
 *
 * The userId field is nullable:
 *
 *   Unlike every other model in this codebase, the `userId` field
 *   on a Preset is nullable. The nullable case is the semantic
 *   marker for "this preset is a system preset, visible to every
 *   user", while a non-null value means "this preset belongs to
 *   one user and is only visible to them". This is the same
 *   pattern the plan's shared `Preset.userId: MongoId | null`
 *   declares, and the schema mirrors it exactly. The `default:
 *   null` on the field means a preset created without an explicit
 *   `userId` is automatically treated as a system preset — that
 *   is not a mistake, it is the semantic default the plan wants
 *   for the seeder that ships the three built-in presets.
 *
 * The `targetReadingGrade` tuple:
 *
 *   The shared `Preset` interface declares this field as a
 *   two-element tuple `[number, number]` — `[min, max]` of an
 *   acceptable grade band. MongoDB does not have a tuple type,
 *   so the schema stores it as an array of numbers and enforces
 *   the "exactly two elements, both finite numbers" invariant
 *   with a validator. A well-formed record can be trusted by
 *   every reader to have the tuple shape the interface declares.
 *
 * What this model does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not seed the three system presets. That is the
 *     job of a future seeder script (`seedPresets` or its
 *     equivalent) that will run alongside the admin seeder in
 *     `features/shared/utils/`. The model is only responsible
 *     for the shape of a preset document, not for populating
 *     the collection with the built-in three.
 *
 *   - It does not enforce cross-field constraints between the
 *     numeric fields. For example, `maxKeywordDensity` should
 *     logically be greater than or equal to `minKeywordDensity`,
 *     and `maxResults` should logically be greater than or equal
 *     to `resultsPerPage`. Neither is checked here — Mongoose's
 *     cross-field validation is awkward to write, and a violation
 *     is a bug in the caller's configuration, not a bad value on
 *     a single field. The service layer is the right place for
 *     those checks, where the full preset is available as a unit
 *     and the error can name both fields.
 *
 *   - It does not distinguish "user-created preset" from "system
 *     preset copied and edited by a user" beyond the `userId`
 *     value. If a user saves an edited copy of Balanced under the
 *     name 'my-balanced', it is simply a user preset named
 *     'my-balanced'. There is no linkage back to the system
 *     preset it was derived from, and no flag marking it as
 *     "customised". That simplification is deliberate: the plan's
 *     product model does not need to track derivation, and adding
 *     it would invite a whole class of stale-reference bugs
 *     without solving any current problem.
 */

import mongoose, { Schema, Document as MongooseDocument } from 'mongoose';
import { Preset } from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Document interface
// ============================================================

/**
 * The runtime shape of a Preset document as returned by Mongoose.
 *
 * Extends `Omit<Preset, '_id'>` (the shared domain interface
 * minus its loosely-typed `_id`) and `MongooseDocument` (the
 * Mongoose base class), then re-declares `_id` with the concrete
 * ObjectId type Mongoose actually produces in-process. Same
 * pattern as every other model in this codebase.
 *
 * No instance methods are declared. A Preset has no per-record
 * behaviour beyond what Mongoose provides out of the box (save,
 * validate, toJSON). Business logic — applying a preset to a
 * topic, deriving a custom preset from a system one — lives in
 * the service.
 */
export interface PresetDocument
  extends Omit<Preset, '_id'>,
    MongooseDocument {
  _id: mongoose.Types.ObjectId;
}

// ============================================================
//  Schema
// ============================================================

const PresetSchema = new Schema<PresetDocument>(
  {
    // ---- Ownership ----
    // `null` marks a system preset (visible to every user); a
    // non-null ObjectId marks a user-owned preset. See the file
    // header for why the field is nullable. The `default: null`
    // makes the system-preset case the implicit one, matching
    // the seeder's intent: a preset created without an owner is
    // a system preset.
    userId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      default: null,
    },

    // ---- Identity ----
    // The slug-form identifier the pipeline uses to reference
    // the preset. Format matches the platform slug convention
    // used elsewhere in the codebase (lowercase letters, digits,
    // hyphens) so a future "find by name" query has one
    // canonical form to match against.
    name: {
      type: String,
      required: [true, 'Name is required'],
      trim: true,
      lowercase: true,
      match: [/^[a-z0-9-]+$/, 'name must be a lowercase slug.'],
      minlength: [1, 'name must be at least 1 character.'],
      maxlength: [50, 'name must be at most 50 characters.'],
    },
    displayName: {
      type: String,
      required: [true, 'displayName is required'],
      trim: true,
      minlength: [1, 'displayName must be at least 1 character.'],
      maxlength: [100, 'displayName must be at most 100 characters.'],
    },

    // ---- Pipeline configuration ----
    // The two headline numbers that drive the pipeline. Bounds
    // mirror the Topic model's bounds for the same fields, so a
    // preset's targets are always within the range a topic can
    // legitimately request.
    sourceCount: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [1, 'sourceCount must be at least 1.'],
      max: [50, 'sourceCount must be at most 50.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'sourceCount must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    wordCount: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [100, 'wordCount must be at least 100.'],
      max: [10000, 'wordCount must be at most 10000.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'wordCount must be an integer.',
      },
    },

    // ---- Search behaviour ----
    // The ordered list of search engines the search step will
    // try, most-preferred first. Example: ['google',
    // 'duckduckgo']. The list is NOT a closed enum at the
    // schema level — new engines are added on the Python side
    // over time, and a schema change would be required every
    // time one was added. The dispatcher on the Python side is
    // the authoritative validator for what engines it can
    // actually run.
    searchEngines: {
      type: [String],
      default: ['google', 'duckduckgo'],
    },
    resultsPerPage: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [1, 'resultsPerPage must be at least 1.'],
      max: [100, 'resultsPerPage must be at most 100.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'resultsPerPage must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    maxResults: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [1, 'maxResults must be at least 1.'],
      max: [200, 'maxResults must be at most 200.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'maxResults must be an integer.',
      },
    },

    // ---- Extraction behaviour ----
    // Per-page navigation timeout in milliseconds. Minimum one
    // second, maximum two minutes. The bounds reject obviously
    // bad configurations (a timeout of 0 would fail every page
    // load instantly; a timeout of an hour would hang the
    // pipeline on a dead page).
    pageLoadTimeout: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [1000, 'pageLoadTimeout must be at least 1000 ms.'],
      max: [120000, 'pageLoadTimeout must be at most 120000 ms.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'pageLoadTimeout must be an integer.',
      },
    },
    maxRetries: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'maxRetries must be non-negative.'],
      max: [10, 'maxRetries must be at most 10.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'maxRetries must be an integer.',
      },
    },

    // ---- Validation thresholds ----
    // The target reading grade band, as [min, max]. Stored as a
    // two-element numeric array; the validators enforce the
    // tuple shape the shared interface declares.
    targetReadingGrade: {
      type: [Number],
      required: true,
      validate: [
        {
          validator: (value: number[]): boolean => value.length === 2,
          message: 'targetReadingGrade must have exactly 2 elements.',
        },
        {
          validator: (value: number[]): boolean =>
            value.every(
              (n) => typeof n === 'number' && Number.isFinite(n)
            ),
          message: 'targetReadingGrade elements must be finite numbers.',
        },
      ],
    },

    // Keyword densities are fractions of word count (0–1). A
    // min of 0 means "no minimum"; a max of 1 means "up to
    // every word being the keyword", which is nonsensical in
    // practice but structurally valid.
    minKeywordDensity: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'minKeywordDensity must be at least 0.'],
      max: [1, 'minKeywordDensity must be at most 1.'],
    },
    maxKeywordDensity: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'maxKeywordDensity must be at least 0.'],
      max: [1, 'maxKeywordDensity must be at most 1.'],
    },

    // Similarity ceilings for the two originality checks (TF-IDF
    // and semantic embedding). Both are fractions of similarity
    // (0–1); a value of 0.30 means "flag anything that resembles
    // any source by more than 30%".
    maxTfidfSimilarity: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'maxTfidfSimilarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
      max: [1, 'maxTfidfSimilarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
    },
    maxSemanticSimilarity: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'maxSemanticSimilarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
      max: [1, 'maxSemanticSimilarity must be between 0 and 1.'],
    },

    // Maximum number of AI-tell phrases permitted before the
    // report flags the AI-marker section.
    maxAiMarkers: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'maxAiMarkers must be non-negative.'],
      max: [100, 'maxAiMarkers must be at most 100.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'maxAiMarkers must be an integer.',
      },
    },

    // ---- Per-check toggles ----
    // Which of the six validators run when this preset is in
    // effect. A user who is confident in their grammar, for
    // example, can disable the grammar check to shave seconds
    // off every validation run.
    runReadabilityCheck: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: true,
      required: true,
    },
    runSeoCheck: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: true,
      required: true,
    },
    runOriginalityCheck: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: true,
      required: true,
    },
    runAiMarkerCheck: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: true,
      required: true,
    },
    runGrammarCheck: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: true,
      required: true,
    },

    // ---- Corrective loop ----
    // Whether the pipeline should re-run the writer with a
    // corrective prompt when validation fails, and how many
    // attempts to try before giving up. A max of 0 with
    // autoRegenerate true would be a contradiction — the service
    // is expected to reject that configuration — but the schema
    // does not enforce the cross-field constraint (see the file
    // header for why).
    autoRegenerate: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: false,
      required: true,
    },
    maxRegenerationAttempts: {
      type: Number,
      required: true,
      min: [0, 'maxRegenerationAttempts must be non-negative.'],
      max: [10, 'maxRegenerationAttempts must be at most 10.'],
      validate: {
        validator: (value: number): boolean => Number.isInteger(value),
        message: 'maxRegenerationAttempts must be an integer.',
      },
    },
  },
  {
    timestamps: true,
    toJSON: {
      transform: (_doc, ret) => {
        // `__v` is Mongoose's internal version field. It is added
        // to every saved document automatically and is not part
        // of the shared `Preset` interface, so it must not appear
        // in the JSON response.
        //
        // The cast to `Record<string, unknown>` is required
        // because TypeScript's `delete` operator refuses to
        // operate on non-optional properties (TS2790). The same
        // fix is applied in every other model in this codebase.
        delete (ret as Record<string, unknown>)['__v'];
        return ret;
      },
    },
  }
);

// ============================================================
//  Indexes
// ============================================================
//
//  Two compound indexes cover the read paths the preset feature
//  exercises. Both include `userId` as their leftmost field
//  because every query on this collection is scoped either to a
//  specific user or to the system-wide `null` scope.
//
//    { userId: 1, name: 1 } — UNIQUE
//      Enforces the "no two presets share a name within the same
//      scope" invariant. See the file header for the two
//      uniqueness rules this single index provides. Also serves
//      the primary read path: `findOne({ userId, name })` is
//      an index-covered lookup with no collection scan.
//
//      The unique constraint is declared here (rather than via
//      `unique: true` on either field alone) because Mongoose
//      only creates a compound unique index from an explicit
//      `.index(...)` call — putting `unique: true` on `userId`
//      and `name` independently would create two single-field
//      unique indexes, which is the wrong thing: a single-field
//      unique index on `userId` alone would allow at most one
//      preset per user (wrong — users can have many), and a
//      single-field unique index on `name` alone would forbid
//      two users from both having a preset called 'draft'.
//
//    { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 }
//      Serves "list my presets, newest first" (the preset
//      picker's default view) and "list all system presets"
//      (queried with `{ userId: null }`, which the leftmost
//      prefix serves). The compound shape means MongoDB can
//      satisfy both the equality filter on userId and the sort
//      on createdAt from the index alone, without an in-memory
//      sort stage.
//
//  A third index on `name` alone was considered and rejected:
//  the read paths that look up a preset by name always know the
//  userId first (either a specific user's, or `null` for a
//  system preset), so a name-only index would never be chosen
//  by the query planner. If a future feature needs to look up a
//  preset by name without knowing its scope, the correct change
//  is to extend the compound unique index's prefix, not to add
//  a redundant one.

PresetSchema.index({ userId: 1, name: 1 }, { unique: true });
PresetSchema.index({ userId: 1, createdAt: -1 });

// ============================================================
//  Model
// ============================================================

export const PresetModel = mongoose.model<PresetDocument>(
  'Preset',
  PresetSchema
);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default PresetModel;
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/settings/models/UserSetting.ts">
/**
 * Mongoose model for the WriteSpeare UserSetting entity.
 *
 * A UserSetting document holds the per-user preferences that
 * apply across every topic a user works on: which preset a new
 * topic should start with, which profile, which prompt template,
 * whether the pipeline auto-saves after each stage, whether the
 * user wants a notification when a topic finishes, and which
 * theme the desktop UI should render.
 *
 * The per-topic values (the keyword list, the word count, the
 * source count, the preset, the profile, the prompt file) live on
 * the `Topic` document itself — the UserSetting document holds
 * only the defaults a new topic is seeded with, plus the two
 * cross-cutting toggles (auto-save and notifications) and the
 * theme preference.
 *
 * Responsibilities:
 *
 *   1. Enforce the schema-level invariants of a settings record:
 *      a required `userId`, the six fields of the embedded
 *      `settings` sub-document, and closed-set validation on the
 *      three fields whose values come from a string-literal
 *      union (`defaultPreset`, `defaultProfile`, `theme`).
 *
 *   2. Enforce the one-document-per-user invariant via a unique
 *      index on `userId`. The service is expected to perform an
 *      upsert — find the user's settings, create if absent,
 *      update if present — and the unique index is the safety
 *      net that prevents a race between two concurrent reads
 *      from producing two settings documents for the same user.
 *      Without the index, a concurrent double-create would leave
 *      the second document as an orphan that the service would
 *      never read (its findOne would return the first), and the
 *      user's settings would diverge invisibly.
 *
 *   3. Provide a single `toJSON` transform that strips Mongoose's
 *      `__v` version field, so a serialised UserSetting matches
 *      the shared `UserSetting` interface exactly.
 *
 * Why the settings sub-document is embedded, not a top-level
 * object:
 *
 *   The shared `UserSetting` interface declares `settings` as a
 *   nested object of type `UserSettingsMap`. That nesting is not
 *   cosmetic — it exists so that a future addition (say, a new
 *   default field, or a new preference that spans multiple
 *   features) can be added to the settings map without changing
 *   the outer schema's shape. Mongoose's support for embedded
 *   sub-documents with `{ _id: false }` is exactly the mechanism
 *   that preserves the nesting without introducing an auto-
 *   generated ObjectId on the sub-document.
 *
 *   An alternative design — flattening the six fields to the top
 *   level of the schema — was rejected because it would break the
 *   shared type's shape and would make the eventual promotion of
 *   a new settings field a breaking change to the outer schema.
 *
 * Why the settings map is declared as a sub-schema constant:
 *
 *   The pattern matches the one established in `Report.ts` for
 *   the six validation sections: declare a standalone `Schema`
 *   constant, then embed it by reference in the top-level schema.
 *   The alternative — inlining the entire sub-schema as an object
 *   literal in the top-level definition — would make the top-
 *   level schema harder to read and would scatter the field-level
 *   validation rules across two locations.
 *
 * Defaults on every field:
 *
 *   Every field in the settings map has a default. This is
 *   deliberate: a freshly-created user should have working
 *   settings the moment their first request is served, without
 *   the service having to seed them explicitly or the controller
 *   having to handle the "settings not yet configured" case.
 *   The defaults are chosen to match the plan's documented
 *   product behaviour — 'balanced' preset, 'blog-post' profile,
 *   'default.md' prompt, auto-save on, notify on, light theme.
 *   A user who never opens the Settings page gets a fully
 *   functional app with sensible behaviour.
 *
 * What this model does NOT do:
 *
 *   - It does not enforce that the `defaultPromptFile` names a
 *     file that exists on disk. The desktop's Python scripts own
 *     the prompt file directory, and the backend has no way to
 *     read the local filesystem. The prompt picker in the
 *     desktop UI is responsible for validating that a user's
 *     chosen prompt file is one that exists; the model only
 *     stores the string.
 *
 *   - It does not link back to a `User` document by foreign key.
 *     Cross-collection referential integrity is the service
 *     layer's concern — the settings service validates the
 *     caller's identity from the authenticated session before
 *     reading or writing, exactly as the other feature services
 *     do. A model-level foreign key would require a pre-save
 *     hook that queries the users collection, which is
 *     unnecessary at this collection size.
 *
 *   - It does not track which fields the user has explicitly set
 *     versus which are defaults. That distinction is not needed
 *     by the current product — the settings document always
 *     holds the full effective settings for the user, and the
 *     UI shows the effective values as editable fields. If a
 *     future feature needs to distinguish "explicitly set" from
 *     "still default", the correct change is to add a parallel
 *     `overrides` map, not to change this document's shape.
 */

import mongoose, { Schema, Document as MongooseDocument } from 'mongoose';
import {
  UserSetting,
  PresetName,
  ProfileName,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';

// ============================================================
//  Document interface
// ============================================================

/**
 * The runtime shape of a UserSetting document as returned by
 * Mongoose.
 *
 * Extends `Omit<UserSetting, '_id'>` (the shared domain
 * interface minus its loosely-typed `_id`) and `MongooseDocument`
 * (the Mongoose base class), then re-declares `_id` with the
 * concrete ObjectId type Mongoose actually produces in-process.
 * Same pattern as `UserDocument`, `TopicDocument`,
 * `DocumentDocument`, `ArticleDocument`, and `ReportDocument`.
 *
 * No instance methods are declared. A UserSetting has no per-
 * record behaviour beyond what Mongoose provides out of the box
 * (save, validate, toJSON). Business logic — applying defaults on
 * first read, merging a partial update from the settings page —
 * lives in the service.
 */
export interface UserSettingDocument
  extends Omit<UserSetting, '_id'>,
    MongooseDocument {
  _id: mongoose.Types.ObjectId;
}

// ============================================================
//  Legal values (runtime counterparts of the union types)
// ============================================================
//
// Each array is annotated with its union type, which gives a
// compile-time guarantee that every string is a legal member. A
// typo would be a type error, not a silent runtime surprise.
//
// The `theme` union is declared inline as a readonly tuple
// because the shared types module does not export a named type
// for it — the `UserSettingsMap.theme` field uses the inline
// union `'light' | 'dark'` directly. The tuple is structurally
// equivalent to the union and satisfies the same check.

const PRESET_VALUES: readonly PresetName[] = [
  'quick',
  'balanced',
  'deep',
  'custom',
];

const PROFILE_VALUES: readonly ProfileName[] = [
  'blog-post',
  'news-article',
  'product-review',
  'academic',
];

const THEME_VALUES: readonly ['light', 'dark'] = ['light', 'dark'];

// ============================================================
//  Settings sub-schema
// ============================================================
//
//  Declared as a standalone `Schema` constant with `{ _id: false }`
//  so Mongoose does not auto-generate an `_id` on the embedded
//  sub-document. The sub-schema is embedded by reference in the
//  top-level schema below.

const UserSettingsMapSchema = new Schema(
  {
    defaultPreset: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: PRESET_VALUES,
        message:
          'defaultPreset must be one of: quick, balanced, deep, custom.',
      },
      default: 'balanced',
      required: true,
    },
    defaultProfile: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: PROFILE_VALUES,
        message:
          'defaultProfile must be one of: blog-post, news-article, ' +
          'product-review, academic.',
      },
      default: 'blog-post',
      required: true,
    },
    defaultPromptFile: {
      type: String,
      default: 'default.md',
      trim: true,
      minlength: [1, 'defaultPromptFile must not be empty.'],
      maxlength: [200, 'defaultPromptFile must be at most 200 characters.'],
    },
    autoSaveAfterEachStage: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: true,
      required: true,
    },
    notifyOnCompletion: {
      type: Boolean,
      default: true,
      required: true,
    },
    theme: {
      type: String,
      enum: {
        values: THEME_VALUES,
        message: 'theme must be one of: light, dark.',
      },
      default: 'light',
      required: true,
    },
  },
  { _id: false }
);

// ============================================================
//  Top-level schema
// ============================================================

const UserSettingSchema = new Schema<UserSettingDocument>(
  {
    // ---- Ownership ----
    // Every settings document belongs to exactly one user. The
    // unique index declared below enforces the one-to-one
    // relationship — a user cannot have two settings documents.
    userId: {
      type: Schema.Types.ObjectId,
      required: [true, 'userId is required'],
      unique: true,
    },

    // ---- Preferences ----
    // The embedded settings sub-document. The sub-schema declared
    // above carries the field-level validation and defaults; the
    // entry here only wires the sub-schema in by reference.
    settings: {
      type: UserSettingsMapSchema,
      required: true,
      // Provide an empty-object default so that a document created
      // with only a `userId` (the common case on first read) is
      // valid: Mongoose applies the sub-schema's field-level
      // defaults to the empty object, producing a settings map
      // populated with the plan's documented product defaults.
      default: () => ({}),
    },
  },
  {
    timestamps: true,
    toJSON: {
      transform: (_doc, ret) => {
        // `__v` is Mongoose's internal version field. It is added
        // to every saved document automatically and is not part of
        // the shared `UserSetting` interface, so it must not
        // appear in the JSON response.
        //
        // The cast to `Record<string, unknown>` is required
        // because TypeScript's `delete` operator refuses to
        // operate on non-optional properties (TS2790). The same
        // fix is applied in every other model in this codebase.
        delete (ret as Record<string, unknown>)['__v'];
        return ret;
      },
    },
  }
);

// ============================================================
//  Indexes
// ============================================================
//
//  The unique index on `userId` is created implicitly by the
//  `unique: true` option on the field itself, so it is not
//  re-declared here. Its purpose is twofold:
//
//    (a) Guarantee the one-to-one relationship at the database
//        level. Even if two concurrent requests both find "no
//        settings for this user" and both attempt to create a
//        document, the second insert fails with a duplicate-key
//        error rather than producing an orphan record.
//
//    (b) Serve the primary read path — `findOne({ userId })` —
//        as a single index-covered lookup with no collection
//        scan.
//
//  No additional indexes are needed. Every query on this
//  collection is scoped to exactly one user, and the unique
//  index on `userId` is the only access path the service
//  exercises.

// ============================================================
//  Model
// ============================================================

export const UserSettingModel = mongoose.model<UserSettingDocument>(
  'UserSetting',
  UserSettingSchema
);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default UserSettingModel;
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/settings/routes/settingsRoutes.ts">
/**
 * Route table for the WriteSpeare settings feature.
 *
 * Declares the seven settings and preset endpoints and the
 * middleware chain that runs in front of each. The router is
 * mounted at `/api/settings` by the app factory (`src/app.ts`),
 * so the paths declared below are relative to that prefix:
 *
 *   GET    /                        → read the user's settings
 *   PATCH  /                        → partial update of settings
 *   GET    /presets                 → list visible presets
 *   POST   /presets                 → create a user-owned preset
 *   GET    /presets/:id             → read one preset
 *   PATCH  /presets/:id             → update one user-owned preset
 *   DELETE /presets/:id             → delete one user-owned preset
 *
 * Every route is protected by `authenticate`. Settings and presets
 * are user-scoped by design:
 *
 *   - Settings: exactly one settings document per user, with
 *     ownership enforced by the unique index on `userId`.
 *
 *   - Presets: system presets are visible to every user but are
 *     not writable through any route here; a user's own presets
 *     are visible and writable only to that user. The visibility
 *     and write-authorization rules live in the service (see
 *     `settingsService.ts`), and every route below simply
 *     delegates with the authenticated `userId`.
 *
 * Middleware order:
 *
 *   `authenticate` runs first and is applied via `asyncHandler`
 *   because the function is async (it awaits a user lookup to
 *   confirm the account still exists and is active). The wrapper
 *   is required — without it, a rejection inside the middleware
 *   would reach the terminal error handler as an unhandled
 *   promise rejection on runtimes that do not forward the
 *   rejection automatically. The existing `authRoutes.ts`,
 *   `topicRoutes.ts`, `documentRoutes.ts`, `articleRoutes.ts`,
 *   and `reportRoutes.ts` files use the same wrapping pattern for
 *   the same reason, and all six must stay in step.
 *
 *   The controller runs second, also wrapped in `asyncHandler`,
 *   for the same reason: the service behind it can throw an
 *   `AppError` (404 for a settings document or preset that does
 *   not exist or belongs to a different user; 409 for a preset
 *   name collision within the caller's scope), and the wrapper
 *   is what converts that throw into a well-formed response via
 *   the terminal error middleware.
 *
 * Route ordering — the `/presets/:id` routes vs the `/presets`
 * collection routes:
 *
 *   Express matches routes segment-by-segment, so a request for
 *   `GET /presets` cannot match `GET /presets/:id` (different
 *   segment counts) and vice versa. There is no collision to
 *   avoid at the ordering level, and either declaration order
 *   would produce identical behaviour.
 *
 *   The collection routes are nevertheless declared before the
 *   parameterised ones, as a defensive habit. The rule of thumb
 *   across all route files in this codebase: declare more
 *   specific paths before more general ones. If a future
 *   addition ever introduces a literal sub-path under `/presets`
 *   — say, `GET /presets/system` — the ordering will already be
 *   correct.
 *
 * The two top-level routes (`GET /` and `PATCH /`) have no
 * siblings at the root level, so there is no ordering question
 * for them. They are declared first, before the `/presets`
 * group, to keep the file readable: the settings-only routes
 * come first, then the presets group in a visually separate
 * section.
 *
 * The routes are declared as a flat sequence of `router.METHOD`
 * calls rather than as a route table or a declarative
 * configuration. This matches the convention established in
 * every previous route file and in every route file the plan
 * will produce. A reader can scan the file top to bottom and see
 * exactly which middleware runs on which route without holding
 * any additional context.
 *
 * No try/catch appears anywhere in this file. That is deliberate
 * — the asyncHandler wrappers, combined with the terminal error
 * middleware registered in `app.ts`, form the single error-
 * handling contract for every route in the application.
 */

import { Router } from 'express';

import {
  getUserSettings,
  updateUserSettings,
  listPresets,
  createPreset,
  getPresetById,
  updatePreset,
  deletePreset,
} from '../controllers/settingsController.js';

import { authenticate } from '../../auth/middleware/authGuard.js';
import { asyncHandler } from '../../shared/middleware/errorHandler.js';

// ============================================================
//  Router instance
// ============================================================

const settingsRoutes = Router();

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/settings
// ============================================================
//
//  Read the authenticated user's settings. The service upserts
//  on read, so a user who has never opened the Settings page
//  receives a document with schema defaults applied — never a
//  404 for "settings not configured".

settingsRoutes.get(
  '/',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(getUserSettings)
);

// ============================================================
//  PATCH /api/settings
// ============================================================
//
//  Partial update of the authenticated user's settings. Every
//  field on the settings map is optional in the body; fields
//  that are absent are left unchanged. A body with no
//  recognised fields is a valid no-op.

settingsRoutes.patch(
  '/',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(updateUserSettings)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/settings/presets
// ============================================================
//
//  List every preset visible to the authenticated user — the
//  system presets (userId: null) plus the caller's own. Presets
//  owned by other users are excluded by the service's read
//  filter.

settingsRoutes.get(
  '/presets',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(listPresets)
);

// ============================================================
//  POST /api/settings/presets
// ============================================================
//
//  Create a preset owned by the authenticated user. The service
//  sets the owner from the session, never from the body, so a
//  client cannot create a system preset or a preset on behalf
//  of another user. A duplicate name within the caller's own
//  preset set produces a 409 via the compound unique index on
//  (userId, name).

settingsRoutes.post(
  '/presets',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(createPreset)
);

// ============================================================
//  GET /api/settings/presets/:id
// ============================================================
//
//  Read a single preset by ID. The service's read filter accepts
//  both system presets and the caller's own presets; a preset
//  owned by a different user produces a null, which the
//  controller converts to a 404 without distinguishing the
//  "missing" case from the "not yours" case.

settingsRoutes.get(
  '/presets/:id',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(getPresetById)
);

// ============================================================
//  PATCH /api/settings/presets/:id
// ============================================================
//
//  Partial update of a preset the authenticated user owns.
//  System presets are not updatable through this route — the
//  service's write filter excludes the system scope, and the
//  resulting service error surfaces as a 404. The preset's
//  `name` field is deliberately not read from the body; see the
//  controller header for the rationale.

settingsRoutes.patch(
  '/presets/:id',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(updatePreset)
);

// ============================================================
//  DELETE /api/settings/presets/:id
// ============================================================
//
//  Delete a preset the authenticated user owns. System presets
//  are not deletable through this route for the same reason
//  they are not updatable — the service's write filter excludes
//  the system scope. Presets have no children, so there is no
//  cascade to consider.

settingsRoutes.delete(
  '/presets/:id',
  asyncHandler(authenticate),
  asyncHandler(deletePreset)
);

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default settingsRoutes;
</file>

<file path="apps/server/src/features/settings/services/settingsService.ts">
/**
 * Business logic for the WriteSpeare settings feature.
 *
 * Two related entities live under this one feature folder because
 * they share a controller and a route table in the plan's file
 * tree, and because they are always consumed together:
 *
 *   UserSetting — the per-user preferences that apply across
 *                 every topic a user works on. Exactly one
 *                 settings document per user, enforced by a
 *                 unique index on `userId`.
 *
 *   Preset      — a named bundle of pipeline settings. Three
 *                 system presets ship with the app (Quick,
 *                 Balanced, Deep) and are visible to every user;
 *                 a user can also save their own presets, which
 *                 are visible only to them.
 *
 * The service exposes seven ownership-scoped operations:
 *
 *   getUserSettings       — read the caller's settings, creating
 *                           them with defaults on first read
 *   updateUserSettings    — partial update of the caller's
 *                           settings
 *   listPresets           — list every preset visible to the
 *                           caller (system presets plus the
 *                           caller's own)
 *   getPresetById         — read one preset (system or owned)
 *   createPreset          — create a preset owned by the caller
 *   updatePreset          — update a preset the caller owns
 *   deletePreset          — delete a preset the caller owns
 *
 * The upsert-on-read behaviour of getUserSettings:
 *
 *   A user who has never opened the Settings page has no
 *   UserSetting document in the database. Rather than requiring
 *   every caller to handle the "settings not yet configured"
 *   case, `getUserSettings` performs a `findOneAndUpdate` with
 *   `upsert: true` — if the document exists, it is returned
 *   unchanged; if not, a new one is created with the schema's
 *   defaults applied and returned. The operation is idempotent,
 *   so calling it concurrently from two requests produces the
 *   same result — the unique index on `userId` guarantees that
 *   only one of the two racing inserts can succeed, and the
 *   losing caller receives the document the winner created.
 *
 *   The `$setOnInsert: { userId }` clause ensures the filter's
 *   userId field is written into the new document; without it,
 *   MongoDB would apply the schema defaults but leave the userId
 *   unset, which the schema would then reject.
 *
 * The preset visibility and authorization rules:
 *
 *   Read visibility — `listPresets` and `getPresetById` accept
 *   presets whose `userId` is `null` (system presets) OR equal
 *   to the caller's own userId. A preset owned by a different
 *   user is invisible — it is filtered out of list results by
 *   the list query, and `getPresetById` returns null for it
 *   (which the controller converts to a 404, not a 403, to
 *   avoid leaking the existence of other users' presets).
 *
 *   Write authorization — `updatePreset` and `deletePreset`
 *   filter on `{ _id, userId }` WITHOUT the `$or` branch that
 *   the read paths use. This is what forbids a caller from
 *   modifying or deleting a system preset: a system preset has
 *   `userId: null`, which never matches the caller's ObjectId,
 *   so the write filter matches zero documents and the service
 *   throws a 404. A user CAN shadow a system preset by creating
 *   their own preset with the same name; the two coexist
 *   because they have different userIds.
 *
 * Why `createPreset` cannot create a system preset:
 *
 *   The plan's product model is that system presets are seeded
 *   by the app — a seeder creates the three built-in presets
 *   once, and they are never created through the API. The
 *   service enforces this by always setting `userId` to the
 *   caller's ObjectId, never accepting it from the payload. A
 *   client that wanted to create a system preset would need a
 *   separate admin-only endpoint, which the plan does not
 *   describe, and which would be the wrong place to put this
 *   logic anyway.
 *
 * Cross-field validation:
 *
 *   Two cross-field constraints are deliberately NOT enforced by
 *   the Preset schema and are also NOT enforced here, in
 *   keeping with the plan's product decision to keep the service
 *   as thin as the schema permits:
 *
 *   - `maxKeywordDensity >= minKeywordDensity`. A preset that
 *     violated this would be internally inconsistent but not
 *     dangerous — the Python validator would simply flag every
 *     keyword against the same threshold. The user-facing
 *     consequence is a validation report that always reads
 *     "below minimum" and never "above maximum". The preset
 *     editor in the desktop UI prevents the configuration from
 *     being saved in this state; the backend is not the load-
 *     bearing guard.
 *
 *   - `autoRegenerate === true` implies `maxRegenerationAttempts
 *     >= 1`. Same reasoning — the desktop UI prevents the
 *     contradictory state, and a preset that reached the backend
 *     with it would simply produce zero regeneration attempts
 *     and a report the user could still export.
 *
 *   If a future requirement needs the backend to be the
 *   authoritative guard on either constraint, the correct place
 *   to add it is here, in a pre-save check inside `createPreset`
 *   and `updatePreset`. The file header records the decision so
 *   it is not mistaken for an oversight.
 */

import {
  UserSettingModel,
  type UserSettingDocument,
} from '../models/UserSetting.js';
import { PresetModel, type PresetDocument } from '../models/Preset.js';
import type {
  MongoId,
  UserSettingsMap,
  PresetCreatePayload,
} from '../../shared/types/index.js';
import { AppError } from '../../shared/middleware/errorHandler.js';

// ============================================================
//  Local payload types
// ============================================================
//
// The shared types module declares `UserSettingsMap` (all fields
// required) but does not declare a dedicated update-payload
// interface for it. The update-payload shape is trivially
// `Partial<UserSettingsMap>` — every field optional, so a caller
// can send a patch containing any subset. The alias is exported
// so the controller can import it from this service without
// re-deriving it.
//
// The Preset update payload is likewise not declared in
// shared/types. Its shape is `Partial<PresetCreatePayload>` for
// the same reason. That one is NOT exported as a named alias
// because it appears in exactly one place — the `updatePreset`
// signature — and a one-off alias for a single use adds surface
// without benefit.

export type UserSettingsUpdatePayload = Partial<UserSettingsMap>;

// ============================================================
//  getUserSettings
// ============================================================

/**
 * Read the authenticated user's settings, creating them with
 * schema defaults if they do not yet exist.
 *
 * The upsert is performed via a single `findOneAndUpdate` with
 * `upsert: true`. This is atomic at the database level — two
 * concurrent calls from the same user both resolve to the same
 * settings document, and the unique index on `userId` guarantees
 * that the second insert cannot produce a duplicate.
 *
 * The `$setOnInsert: { userId }` clause is required: without it,
 * MongoDB would apply the schema's field defaults to the new
 * document but would not populate the filter's `userId` field,
 * and the resulting document would fail the schema's `required`
 * validation on save.
 *
 * The `setDefaultsOnInsert: true` option is what makes the
 * schema's defaults fire on the upsert path. Without it, the
 * `settings` sub-document would be created empty and the
 * field-level defaults inside it would not run.
 *
 * Returns the settings document. The function is idempotent —
 * calling it twice in a row produces the same result and does
 * not modify the document on the second call.
 *
 * @param userId - Ownership value, derived from the authenticated
 *                  session by the controller.
 */
export const getUserSettings = async (
  userId: MongoId
): Promise<UserSettingDocument> => {
  const settings = await UserSettingModel.findOneAndUpdate(
    { userId },
    { $setOnInsert: { userId } },
    {
      upsert: true,
      new: true,
      setDefaultsOnInsert: true,
    }
  );

  // `findOneAndUpdate` with `upsert: true` and `new: true` is
  // documented to always return a document, but its TypeScript
  // signature still returns `T | null` — the compiler cannot
  // know that the upsert option guarantees non-null. The guard
  // is defensive: if it ever fires, the database is in a state
  // this service cannot recover from (the upsert was silently
  // rejected), and a 500 is the correct response.
  if (!settings) {
    throw new AppError('Failed to load settings.', 500);
  }

  return settings;
};

// ============================================================
//  updateUserSettings
// ============================================================

/**
 * Apply a partial update to the authenticated user's settings,
 * creating the document with defaults if it does not yet exist.
 *
 * Every field in the patch is optional. Fields omitted from the
 * patch are left unchanged. A patch with no fields is a valid
 * no-op — the function returns the current settings without
 * modifying anything.
 *
 * The update is expressed as a `$set` on dotted paths
 * (`settings.<field>`), rather than a full replacement of the
 * `settings` sub-document. This is what makes the operation
 * partial: MongoDB merges the `$set` fields into the existing
 * sub-document, leaving every other field untouched. A full
 * replacement would require reading the current settings first
 * and would introduce a race between the read and the write.
 *
 * The `runValidators: true` option is set so the schema's
 * per-field validation runs on the update, even though the
 * controller has already narrowed each field's type. Belt-and-
 * braces: the schema is the authoritative validator, and any
 * future caller of this service benefits from the check.
 *
 * The `upsert: true` and `setDefaultsOnInsert: true` options
 * mirror `getUserSettings` — a user who has never opened the
 * Settings page but sends an update directly (via the API, not
 * the UI) gets their settings document created with defaults,
 * and the patch is applied on top. The desktop UI does not do
 * this, but the API should not require the UI's cooperation to
 * produce a valid state.
 *
 * @param userId - Ownership value.
 * @param patch  - A partial settings map. Only the fields present
 *                  in the patch are modified.
 */
export const updateUserSettings = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  patch: UserSettingsUpdatePayload
): Promise<UserSettingDocument> => {
  // ---- Build the $set object from the patch ----
  // Each field is checked for presence explicitly rather than via
  // iteration, because `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` treats each
  // optional field as a distinct type (`PresetName | undefined`,
  // `string | undefined`, etc.) and an iteration would need a
  // per-field cast to recover the correct type. The explicit
  // form is more verbose but keeps every field's type intact
  // from the caller's perspective.
  //
  // The dotted-path form (`settings.<field>`) is what allows
  // MongoDB to merge the patch into the existing sub-document
  // rather than replace it.
  const setObj: Record<string, unknown> = {};

  if (patch.defaultPreset !== undefined) {
    setObj['settings.defaultPreset'] = patch.defaultPreset;
  }
  if (patch.defaultProfile !== undefined) {
    setObj['settings.defaultProfile'] = patch.defaultProfile;
  }
  if (patch.defaultPromptFile !== undefined) {
    setObj['settings.defaultPromptFile'] = patch.defaultPromptFile;
  }
  if (patch.autoSaveAfterEachStage !== undefined) {
    setObj['settings.autoSaveAfterEachStage'] =
      patch.autoSaveAfterEachStage;
  }
  if (patch.notifyOnCompletion !== undefined) {
    setObj['settings.notifyOnCompletion'] = patch.notifyOnCompletion;
  }
  if (patch.theme !== undefined) {
    setObj['settings.theme'] = patch.theme;
  }

  // ---- Empty-patch short circuit ----
  // A patch with no recognized fields is a no-op. Calling the
  // database with an empty `$set` is legal (MongoDB treats it as
  // "nothing to do") but the response would still be correct,
  // so skipping the round trip is a pure optimization. It also
  // makes the function's behaviour more predictable for a caller
  // that inspects the return value: the same settings object is
  // returned whether the patch was empty or full.
  if (Object.keys(setObj).length === 0) {
    return await getUserSettings(userId);
  }

  // ---- Perform the update ----
  const settings = await UserSettingModel.findOneAndUpdate(
    { userId },
    { $set: setObj },
    {
      upsert: true,
      new: true,
      setDefaultsOnInsert: true,
      runValidators: true,
    }
  );

  if (!settings) {
    // Same defensive guard as `getUserSettings` — an upsert that
    // returns null indicates a database-level failure the service
    // cannot recover from.
    throw new AppError('Failed to update settings.', 500);
  }

  return settings;
};

// ============================================================
//  listPresets
// ============================================================

/**
 * List every preset visible to the caller: all system presets
 * (`userId: null`) plus the caller's own presets. Presets owned
 * by other users are excluded.
 *
 * Sort order is `createdAt` ascending — the three system presets
 * appear in the order they were seeded, and the user's own
 * presets appear in the order they were created. This matches
 * the preset picker's expectation: the built-in three at the
 * top, the user's customisations below them in chronological
 * order.
 *
 * Sort is served by the compound index `{ userId, createdAt: -1 }`
 * — the sort direction does not have to match the index direction
 * for the index to be used; MongoDB can scan the index in reverse.
 *
 * Returns an array. A user with no custom presets and no system
 * presets seeded yet (a fresh install) receives an empty array.
 *
 * @param userId - Ownership value.
 */
export const listPresets = async (
  userId: MongoId
): Promise<PresetDocument[]> => {
  return await PresetModel.find({
    $or: [{ userId: null }, { userId }],
  }).sort({ createdAt: 1 });
};

// ============================================================
//  getPresetById
// ============================================================

/**
 * Read a single preset by id, scoped to the caller's visibility
 * rules.
 *
 * Returns `null` when the preset does not exist, OR when it
 * exists but is owned by a different user. A system preset
 * (`userId: null`) is always readable. The two "not visible"
 * cases collapse to the same null — the caller (the controller)
 * converts it to a 404, never a 403, so an authenticated user
 * cannot enumerate other users' preset IDs by probing the
 * endpoint and watching for a status-code change.
 *
 * A malformed id string — one that is not a valid ObjectId —
 * causes Mongoose to throw a CastError, which the terminal
 * middleware maps to a 400.
 *
 * @param userId   - Ownership value.
 * @param presetId - The preset's id, as a string from the route
 *                   parameter.
 */
export const getPresetById = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  presetId: string
): Promise<PresetDocument | null> => {
  return await PresetModel.findOne({
    _id: presetId,
    $or: [{ userId: null }, { userId }],
  });
};

// ============================================================
//  createPreset
// ============================================================

/**
 * Create a preset owned by the caller. The payload is expected
 * to conform to `PresetCreatePayload` — every field except
 * `userId` (which is derived from the authenticated session)
 * and the timestamps (which Mongoose assigns).
 *
 * A user can create a preset whose `name` shadows a system
 * preset's name — the compound unique index on `{ userId, name }`
 * allows `(null, 'quick')` and `(someObjectId, 'quick')` to
 * coexist. This is the intended behaviour: a user who wants
 * their own tuned variant of "quick" can simply name it that,
 * and their variant is the one the picker shows them for topics
 * they create.
 *
 * A duplicate name within the caller's own preset set produces
 * a Mongo duplicate-key error (code 11000), which the terminal
 * middleware maps to a 409 with a "Duplicate value for field
 * ..." message. The service does not pre-check for a collision —
 * doing so would introduce a race between the check and the
 * insert, and the unique index is the authoritative guard.
 *
 * @param userId  - Ownership value.
 * @param payload - The preset's configuration. Every field
 *                  required by `PresetCreatePayload` is expected;
 *                  `userId` is derived here, not read from the
 *                  payload.
 */
export const createPreset = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  payload: PresetCreatePayload
): Promise<PresetDocument> => {
  // The payload's fields are copied into the document, and
  // `userId` is set from the authenticated session. The payload
  // type does not include a `userId` field, so there is no risk
  // of the caller's value overriding the session value — the
  // compiler enforces that.
  const doc = new PresetModel({
    ...payload,
    userId,
  });

  return await doc.save();
};

// ============================================================
//  updatePreset
// ============================================================

/**
 * Apply a partial update to a preset the caller owns. System
 * presets (`userId: null`) are NOT updatable through this
 * function — the write filter is `{ _id, userId }`, which
 * matches only the caller's own presets.
 *
 * Every field in the patch is optional. Fields omitted from the
 * patch are left unchanged. A patch with no actionable fields
 * returns the current document unchanged, without a database
 * write.
 *
 * The `name` field is deliberately not included in the
 * updatable set. A preset's name is its identity within the
 * user's scope and is the key the compound unique index uses;
 * renaming would require a second uniqueness check and would
 * change the preset's URL identity from the client's
 * perspective. A user who wants a differently-named preset can
 * delete this one and create a new one — the operation is
 * cheap and unambiguous.
 *
 * Returns the updated document, so the caller can reflect the
 * new state without a second read.
 *
 * Throws `AppError(404)` when the preset does not exist, when
 * it is owned by a different user, OR when it is a system preset
 * (because the write filter excludes the system scope). All
 * three cases collapse to the same 404 for the same enumeration-
 * safety reason.
 *
 * @param userId   - Ownership value.
 * @param presetId - The preset's id.
 * @param patch    - A partial set of the preset's configuration
 *                    fields. `name` and `userId` are not
 *                    updatable and are not accepted.
 */
export const updatePreset = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  presetId: string,
  patch: Partial<PresetCreatePayload>
): Promise<PresetDocument> => {
  // ---- Build the $set object from the patch ----
  // Only the fields that are present in the patch and are in the
  // updatable set are copied. `name` and `displayName` are
  // intentionally excluded — see the docstring above for the
  // rationale on `name`. `displayName` is included below: the
  // user can rename the human-readable label without changing
  // the underlying slug.
  const setObj: Record<string, unknown> = {};

  if (patch.displayName !== undefined) {
    setObj['displayName'] = patch.displayName;
  }
  if (patch.sourceCount !== undefined) {
    setObj['sourceCount'] = patch.sourceCount;
  }
  if (patch.wordCount !== undefined) {
    setObj['wordCount'] = patch.wordCount;
  }
  if (patch.searchEngines !== undefined) {
    setObj['searchEngines'] = patch.searchEngines;
  }
  if (patch.resultsPerPage !== undefined) {
    setObj['resultsPerPage'] = patch.resultsPerPage;
  }
  if (patch.maxResults !== undefined) {
    setObj['maxResults'] = patch.maxResults;
  }
  if (patch.pageLoadTimeout !== undefined) {
    setObj['pageLoadTimeout'] = patch.pageLoadTimeout;
  }
  if (patch.maxRetries !== undefined) {
    setObj['maxRetries'] = patch.maxRetries;
  }
  if (patch.targetReadingGrade !== undefined) {
    setObj['targetReadingGrade'] = patch.targetReadingGrade;
  }
  if (patch.minKeywordDensity !== undefined) {
    setObj['minKeywordDensity'] = patch.minKeywordDensity;
  }
  if (patch.maxKeywordDensity !== undefined) {
    setObj['maxKeywordDensity'] = patch.maxKeywordDensity;
  }
  if (patch.maxTfidfSimilarity !== undefined) {
    setObj['maxTfidfSimilarity'] = patch.maxTfidfSimilarity;
  }
  if (patch.maxSemanticSimilarity !== undefined) {
    setObj['maxSemanticSimilarity'] = patch.maxSemanticSimilarity;
  }
  if (patch.maxAiMarkers !== undefined) {
    setObj['maxAiMarkers'] = patch.maxAiMarkers;
  }
  if (patch.runReadabilityCheck !== undefined) {
    setObj['runReadabilityCheck'] = patch.runReadabilityCheck;
  }
  if (patch.runSeoCheck !== undefined) {
    setObj['runSeoCheck'] = patch.runSeoCheck;
  }
  if (patch.runOriginalityCheck !== undefined) {
    setObj['runOriginalityCheck'] = patch.runOriginalityCheck;
  }
  if (patch.runAiMarkerCheck !== undefined) {
    setObj['runAiMarkerCheck'] = patch.runAiMarkerCheck;
  }
  if (patch.runGrammarCheck !== undefined) {
    setObj['runGrammarCheck'] = patch.runGrammarCheck;
  }
  if (patch.autoRegenerate !== undefined) {
    setObj['autoRegenerate'] = patch.autoRegenerate;
  }
  if (patch.maxRegenerationAttempts !== undefined) {
    setObj['maxRegenerationAttempts'] = patch.maxRegenerationAttempts;
  }

  // ---- Empty-patch short circuit ----
  // A patch with no actionable fields is a no-op: read the
  // existing document and return it, without a database write.
  // The read is still ownership-scoped — a caller who provides
  // no fields but targets someone else's preset still gets a 404,
  // matching the behaviour of the write path.
  if (Object.keys(setObj).length === 0) {
    const existing = await PresetModel.findOne({
      _id: presetId,
      userId,
    });
    if (!existing) {
      throw new AppError('Preset not found.', 404);
    }
    return existing;
  }

  // ---- Perform the update ----
  // The filter `{ _id, userId }` deliberately does NOT include
  // the `$or: [{ userId: null }, ...]` branch that the read
  // paths use. This is what forbids a caller from updating a
  // system preset — the system preset's `userId: null` never
  // matches the caller's ObjectId.
  const updated = await PresetModel.findOneAndUpdate(
    { _id: presetId, userId },
    { $set: setObj },
    { new: true, runValidators: true }
  );

  if (!updated) {
    throw new AppError('Preset not found.', 404);
  }

  return updated;
};

// ============================================================
//  deletePreset
// ============================================================

/**
 * Delete a preset the caller owns. System presets
 * (`userId: null`) are NOT deletable through this function —
 * the delete filter is `{ _id, userId }`, which matches only
 * the caller's own presets.
 *
 * Returns the deleted document so the caller can log or display
 * what was removed. Presets have no children — deleting a preset
 * does not affect any topic or article that was previously
 * configured with it, because the pipeline copies the preset's
 * values onto the Topic document at creation time (see the
 * Topic model's `preset`, `profile`, `promptFile`, `wordCount`,
 * and `sourceCount` fields). A user who deletes a preset and
 * later wants its behaviour back can recreate it from the
 * values on any topic that used it.
 *
 * Throws `AppError(404)` when the preset does not exist, when
 * it is owned by a different user, OR when it is a system
 * preset. Same collapsing rule as `updatePreset`.
 *
 * @param userId   - Ownership value.
 * @param presetId - The preset's id.
 */
export const deletePreset = async (
  userId: MongoId,
  presetId: string
): Promise<PresetDocument> => {
  const deleted = await PresetModel.findOneAndDelete({
    _id: presetId,
    userId,
  });

  if (!deleted) {
    throw new AppError('Preset not found.', 404);
  }

  return deleted;
};

// ============================================================
//  Default export
// ============================================================

export default {
  getUserSettings,
  updateUserSettings,
  listPresets,
  getPresetById,
  createPreset,
  updatePreset,
  deletePreset,
};

<file path="apps/server/src/features/settings/index.ts">
/**
 * Public export surface for the WriteSpeare settings feature.
 *
 * The plan declares this file with a single responsibility:
 * "Public exports." That is the entire specification, and this
 * file fills it in with the minimal, non-redundant surface that
 * the rest of the codebase can meaningfully consume — following
 * the exact shape established by the topics feature's index at
 * `features/topics/index.ts`, the documents feature's index at
 * `features/documents/index.ts`, the articles feature's index at
 * `features/articles/index.ts`, and the reports feature's index
 * at `features/reports/index.ts`.
 *
 * This is the first of the feature indexes to export TWO models,
 * because the settings feature owns two collections — UserSetting
 * (per-user preferences, one document per user) and Preset
 * (named pipeline configuration bundles, which may be system-wide
 * or user-owned). Both models live under `features/settings/models/`
 * per the plan's file tree.
 *
 * What belongs here — and what does not:
 *
 *   The settings feature contains seven kinds of source files:
 *
 *     models/UserSetting.ts             — per-user preferences
 *     models/Preset.ts                  — pipeline configuration
 *     services/settingsService.ts       — business logic for both
 *     controllers/settingsController.ts — HTTP handlers
 *     routes/settingsRoutes.ts          — the Express router
 *     index.ts                          — this file
 *
 *   Of those six, three are useful to a consumer OUTSIDE the
 *   feature:
 *
 *     (a) The router. `app.ts` mounts it under `/api/settings`.
 *         That is the one import the feature's external boundary
 *         actually needs — the controller and service are
 *         internal implementation details between the router and
 *         the models, and nothing outside the feature should
 *         reach past the router for request-handling behavior.
 *
 *     (b) `PresetModel`. The admin feature's service
 *         (`adminService.ts`) manages system-wide presets — the
 *         `userId: null` scope — and imports `PresetModel`
 *         directly from `settings/models/Preset.js` to do so.
 *         That is a real, active cross-feature dependency, and
 *         exporting the model here gives it (and any future
 *         consumer) a single named entry point.
 *
 *     (c) `UserSettingModel`. No consumer exists today — the
 *         model is only used by the settings feature's own
 *         service. The export exists for symmetry with the
 *         other feature indexes and for any future feature
 *         (an admin-facing "view all user settings" view, a
 *         user-preferences audit log) that would need to read
 *         from outside the feature's HTTP surface.
 *
 *   The service and controller are NOT re-exported. Both are
 *   internal: the service is only ever consumed by the
 *   controller within the same feature, and the controller is
 *   only ever consumed by the router within the same feature.
 *   Additionally, their function names collide — both export
 *   `getUserSettings`, `updateUserSettings`, etc. — and
 *   re-exporting both with bare names would produce a
 *   duplicate-export error. The rule this file follows,
 *   matching the four previous features' indexes: export what
 *   is consumed, not everything that exists.
 *
 *   The `UserSettingsUpdatePayload` type that the service
 *   declares and exports is also NOT re-exported here. It is a
 *   service-level type — a `Partial<UserSettingsMap>` alias
 *   used by the settings controller — not a feature-boundary
 *   type. The controller imports it directly from the service,
 *   and no consumer outside the feature has any use for it.
 *
 * Why the router is exported both as a named symbol AND as the
 * default:
 *
 *   The router file itself (`routes/settingsRoutes.ts`) exports
 *   its router as the default. This index file preserves that
 *   shape for callers that prefer the default form — `import
 *   settingsRoutes from '...features/settings'` — while also
 *   giving the named form — `import { settingsRoutes } from
 *   '...features/settings'` — to callers that prefer named
 *   imports for uniformity with the rest of this file's exports.
 *
 *   The two forms resolve to the same router instance. There is
 *   no double-construction, no second Express `Router()`, and
 *   no chance of the router being registered twice by mistake.
 *
 * Note for readers who have been following the session:
 *
 *   The current `app.ts` imports the settings router from its
 *   deep path (`./features/settings/routes/settingsRoutes.js`),
 *   not from this index. The current `adminService.ts` imports
 *   `PresetModel` from `./features/settings/models/Preset.js`,
 *   not from this index either. Neither import needs to change
 *   — this index is a forward-looking surface that a future
 *   refactor can adopt. Until that refactor, this file's
 *   exports are dormant — nothing in the codebase currently
 *   imports from it.
 *
 *   That is fine, and it is what the plan's "Public exports"
 *   annotation calls for. The surface exists so that when a
 *   consumer DOES need it, there is a declared, documented place
 *   for that import to come from — rather than a deep path that
 *   was chosen ad hoc.
 */

//  and the named-export form resolve to the same router

export { default as settingsRoutes } from './routes/settingsRoutes.js';
export { default } from './routes/settingsRoutes.js';
